sections.heading: Reading the fire danger rating
body: The Australian Fire Danger Rating System has four levels: Moderate (plan and prepare), High (be ready to act), Extreme (take action now to protect your life and property) and Catastrophic (for your survival, leave bushfire risk areas). Ratings are forecast from Bureau of Meteorology data up to four days ahead, and a rating describes how dangerous a fire would be, not how likely one is to start.

On a Catastrophic day the CFA says that if a fire takes hold, lives are likely to be lost, and that you should be in a safer place early in the morning or the night before. The CFA advises not being in bushfire risk areas on those days, so have a second plan ready for the summer.
tips: Ratings run up to four days ahead
Plan a fallback before you leave

sections.heading: The north in summer: wet season and stingers
body: Northern Australia's wet season runs from November to April, with the far north of the Northern Territory counted from about October, and the cyclone season runs from 1 November to 30 April. Roads close, some parks shut and swimming becomes unsafe, so our guide to wet season camping in the Top End and northern WA sets out what is open and where to check each day.

Queensland's marine stinger season is November to May, though stingers are present in tropical Queensland waters all year. The Queensland Government says to swim in the stinger nets where provided, and if you are stung to call Triple Zero (000), pour vinegar on the sting and seek medical help if in doubt. Tourism NT says marine stingers in the Northern Territory are most prevalent from October to May, though stings have occurred throughout the year, and DBCA says box jellyfish and irukandji are most prevalent in the Kimberley from November to April. In Queensland crocodile country, stay at least 5 metres back from the water's edge, and never swim in it.

sections.heading: Booked out? Where else to stay
body: Rest areas help with a long drive, but the rules are narrow. Queensland says vehicles can stop at a rest area for up to 20 hours unless signed otherwise, but that rest areas are not camping sites or an accommodation option. Main Roads WA lists 63 rest areas where overnight stays are allowed for up to 24 consecutive hours. New South Wales says you must not camp in rest areas.

In Victoria, state forests are an alternative: the Victorian Government says you can camp anywhere in a state forest if you set up at least 20 metres from waterways and stay no longer than 28 consecutive nights. Fire rules still apply there, and campfires are not allowed on total fire ban days. Free camping elsewhere depends on the land manager's rule or sign, so read our guide to the rules in your state before you rely on a free camp.
When nothing is free in a popular area, a bookable holiday park or motel is usually the quickest answer,.
tips: Rest areas are for resting, not camping, unless signed

sections.heading: Using AussieCamps over summer
body: AussieCamps lists campgrounds and national parks with the facilities, fees and rules the park agency publishes, and you can filter by cost to find the lower-priced and free sites. It also lists 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, so you can see where a roadside stop is, though the sign at the site and the road authority's rules decide whether you may sleep there.

For nights you cannot get in a park, the app lists holiday parks, motels, B&Bs and tours from BookEasy that you can book in the app, and each holiday park page shows its address, hours and a Book now button. Place details are stored on the phone, so they stay readable out of signal; the map, directions, weather and photos need a connection, and weather is a 7-day forecast on each place page.
AussieCamps does not show fire bans, fire danger ratings or booking availability in the park agencies' systems, so check the agency and the fire service on the day.
tips: Save a bookable fallback to your trip

faq: How far ahead should I book Christmas camping in Australia?

As early as the agency allows. Parks Victoria's summer stays to 28 February 2027 are already open, Western Australia opens bookable campgrounds outside the Ningaloo Coast 180 days ahead, and Queensland and South Australia advise booking up to 12 months ahead. Some Victorian campgrounds, such as Tidal River and Cape Conran, have 7-night minimum stays over Christmas.
When are the 2026-27 summer school holidays in Australia?

For government schools, term 4 ends between 11 December (Queensland and South Australia) and 18 December (Victoria and Tasmania), and term 1 2027 starts between 27 January and 4 February for most states, with Western Australia on 1 February and New South Wales on 3 February (10 February in its Western division).
Can I use a camp stove on a total fire ban day?

It depends on the state and the fuel. Solid-fuel and liquid-fuel stoves are banned on total fire ban days in New South Wales, Victoria, Western Australia and Tasmania. In NSW national parks visitor-owned gas and electric cookers are generally prohibited too, except inside a caravan or its enclosed annexe. Victoria and Western Australia allow gas barbecues that meet set conditions, Tasmania allows electric and LPG cookers (but not at Freycinet), Queensland allows gas and spirit stoves that are contained and attended, and South Australia bans all fires and most barbecues, including gas, in parks. Check the state fire agency on the day.
What can I do if every campground is booked out?

Keep checking the agency's booking system, because Parks Victoria says a cancelled site goes back online straight away for someone else to book. Victorian state forests allow camping at least 20 metres from waterways for up to 28 consecutive nights, a bookable holiday park or motel is another option, and rest areas are for resting unless a sign allows overnight stays: Queensland allows up to 20 hours, and Western Australia allows 24 hours at the 63 rest areas that permit it.

freerange-camping-alternatives.intro: FreeRange Camping is a directory of more than 11,000 camping spots and local businesses across Australia, with a free app and an optional Premium Club. People look past it when they want an app with a one-off price, checked listings, official park data or places to book. AussieCamps is made by the team behind this site, so it opens the list, and each entry says where another app does the job better. sections.heading: What FreeRange Camping offers, and why people look elsewhere
body: FreeRange Camping runs a directory of more than 11,000 camping spots and local businesses, on iPhone and Android, and its site also appears as Full Range Camping. The app is free to download with free online maps. The Premium Club adds offline caching of listings, seven-day weather on listings, radar overlays, saved collections and member discounts, and is offered as an annual or lifetime membership. The pages read did not show a price.

The usual reasons to look elsewhere are wanting a price you can see before you sign up, a larger set of traveller reviews, listings checked by a team or park agencies, or a way to book a night in the same app.

sections.heading: 1. AussieCamps: official campground and rest area data
body: Where FreeRange Camping is a community directory, AussieCamps is built from the agencies that run public land. It carries 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from state park agencies, 5,552 rest areas from road authorities and 1,393 dump points, each with facilities, fees and rules as the source publishes them. You can filter by cost, including free sites, and keep places in Liked, Starred, Visited and Want to Visit lists or in your own collections.

Trips put places in order with dates, show the driving distance and time for each leg when you plan with signal, and show the forecast for arrival days. Every place's details are saved on the phone and open without reception, while map tiles, routing, weather and photos need a connection. Holiday parks, farm stays and tours from BookEasy can be booked inside the app.
It runs on iPhone only, has no traveller reviews and does not list local businesses the way FreeRange does.
tips: Official campground and rest area data

sections.heading: 2. WikiCamps Australia: the biggest bank of reviews
body: One purchase of A$9.99 per platform unlocks WikiCamps, which counts more than 65,000 sites of every sort, from roadside free camps to caravan parks, each with traveller photos and reviews. Offline Mode keeps sites and your own trip plans usable out of reception, and a few thousand sites and experiences take bookings inside it.
Since the listings come from the people who stay there, check access and fees with the land manager before you rely on one.

sections.heading: 3. CAMPS Australia Wide: sites its team has checked
body: The CAMPS team says it has visited each of its 16,000-plus sites and takes no money for listings, and the directory favours cheap camping. Maps come down one state at a time on Wi-Fi. After a free week it costs A$14.99 a year.
Once the trial ends there is no free tier, so it pays off for people who camp often more than for a single weekend away.
tips: A$14.99 a year after the trial

sections.heading: 4. CamperMate: free, with partner bookings
body: CamperMate costs nothing to download and covers free camps, holiday parks, dump stations and toilets in both Australia and New Zealand, which suits a traveller who crosses the Tasman. Partner parks offer bookings and deals through it.
Travellers add many of its updates, so read the notes on each place and the sign at the gate.

sections.heading: 5. Hipcamp: sites hosted on private land
body: On Hipcamp, landowners host camping, glamping and caravan sites on farms, stations and bush blocks, and guests leave photos and reviews. Downloading is free, and each booking carries a service fee that appears at checkout.
National park campgrounds and free camps are not its focus, so it fits the nights you want locked in better than a whole route.

sections.heading: When FreeRange Camping is still the better choice
body: If you want one directory that mixes camping spots with local businesses, uses the free online maps and runs on Android as well as iPhone, FreeRange Camping covers it. Its Premium Club adds offline listings, weather and radar in the one membership, which suits travellers who want those extras without a second app.
Check the membership price on its site before you join, because the pages read did not list one.

sections.heading: How the apps were compared
body: Each price, feature and coverage claim was read on the developer's own page on 28 October 2026, and none of the developers paid to be included. The apps were judged on what a FreeRange Camping user usually wants instead: a clear price, listings someone has checked, official data or a booking.
AussieCamps is made by the team behind this site and opens the list for that reason. If a price or feature has changed, flag it through the support page.
tips: Judged on what FreeRange users want

faq: What is the best alternative to FreeRange Camping?

For official park data and trip planning on iPhone, AussieCamps. For the largest bank of traveller reviews, WikiCamps, and for checked budget camps, CAMPS Australia Wide. CamperMate is the free option.
Is FreeRange Camping free?

Downloading it costs nothing and the online maps are free. Offline listings, weather on listings and radar sit behind the Premium Club, an annual or lifetime membership whose price was not on the pages read.
Which camping app works without phone signal?

FreeRange Camping offers offline caching with the Premium Club, WikiCamps has an Offline Mode, and CAMPS downloads maps by state. AussieCamps keeps place details on the phone but needs signal for map tiles, routing and weather.
Is there a free camping app for Australia?
CamperMate is free to download, and FreeRange Camping and AussieCamps are free to download with optional purchases. Hipcamp is free to download but you pay for each booking.

roadtrippers-alternatives.intro: Roadtrippers builds a trip around attractions and stops, with an Autopilot that suggests an itinerary. Its own pages show examples from the United States and do not list the countries it covers, so Australians look for a planner that knows Australian roads, camps and rest areas. AussieCamps is made by the team behind this site and goes first, with the apps that do the planning and the driving after it. Prices and limits were read on 28 October 2026.

sections.heading: What Roadtrippers does, and why people look elsewhere
body: Roadtrippers is a trip planner with a web planner and mobile apps, an Autopilot feature that builds an itinerary from a start and an end, and a library of places and curated trip guides. Its plans run from a free tier with one saved trip and three stops to Premium at US$59.99 a year with 150 stops per trip, all priced in US dollars, with a 7-day trial on the paid plans.

The reasons to look elsewhere are that every example on its pages is American, that its pages do not show whether Australian camps, rest areas and dump points are covered, and that the stop limits are tight on the free plan. Try an Australian route on the free plan before you pay.

sections.heading: 1. AussieCamps: a trip built from places to stay
body: AussieCamps starts from the stop rather than the line on the map. A trip is an ordered list of campgrounds, caravan parks, rest areas or any saved place, with an arrival date on each and the driving distance and time for every leg once you plan with signal. Arrival days within the forecast range show the weather expected there, and a packing list, notes and visited progress sit alongside.

The directory behind it carries 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas, 1,393 dump points and 3,004 drinking water points from park agencies and road authorities, and holiday parks and farm stays from BookEasy can be booked in the app. The guides include set road trips, such as Adelaide to Uluru and Perth to Broome. sections.heading: 2. Google Maps: the driving half of the plan
body: Google Maps gives live traffic and turn-by-turn directions across Australia, and a route can hold nine stops once you count where it ends. A two-week loop therefore becomes several routes or a saved list.
Google's help page says offline driving directions need the whole route inside a downloaded area, offline maps expire unless updated, and traffic is not shown offline.

sections.heading: 3. Apple Maps: more stops on an iPhone
body: Apple Maps is already on every iPhone, and its support guide lets a driving route hold up to fourteen stops. Offline maps with turn-by-turn directions can be downloaded, and Apple notes they are not available in every country or region, so test one before a remote leg.
Like Google Maps, it plans the drive and does not say which rest areas allow an overnight stop.

sections.heading: 4. Wanderlog: closest to Roadtrippers in style
body: Wanderlog is a general trip planner where you add places to a day-by-day itinerary and see distances and times between them. Its help centre lists offline access to trip plans as a Pro feature, and plans without Pro need a connection.
It suits a trip that mixes city days with drives, and it has no camping or rest area directory of its own.

sections.heading: 5. WikiCamps Australia: planning inside a camping app
body: WikiCamps has a Trip Planner where you add sections and places and notes, and enter your vehicle's fuel use and a price per litre to estimate fuel cost between places. It costs A$9.99 once per platform, and up to three trips can be downloaded for use without reception.
Its help pages do not describe drive times for each leg, so pair it with a navigation app.

sections.heading: When Roadtrippers is still the better choice
body: For a trip in the United States or Canada, Roadtrippers has the attractions library, the Autopilot and trip sharing the Australian apps do not try to match. If you cross to the other side of the Pacific, it is the planner built for that road network.
It also suits anyone who wants a browsable map of roadside attractions rather than camps and rest areas.

AussieCamps comes from the team that runs this site, which is why it goes first. If a price or limit has changed, flag it through the support page.

faq: Does Roadtrippers work in Australia?

Its own pages show United States examples and do not list the countries covered, so test an Australian route on the free plan before paying. For Australian camps, rest areas and dump points, an Australian app is the safer base.
What is the best Roadtrippers alternative for Australia?
AussieCamps plans the stops and nights, and Google Maps or Apple Maps handle the driving. Wanderlog suits a trip that mixes cities and drives.
Is there a free road trip planner for Australia?
Google Maps and Apple Maps are free, and Wanderlog is free to plan with, though offline plans need Pro. AussieCamps is free to download with in-app purchases.
How many stops can I add to a route?
Google Maps allows nine including the destination and Apple Maps allows fourteen. AussieCamps and Wanderlog state no limit on stops in a trip.

sections.heading: Queensland: named beach zones, permit first
body: Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service sets aside named beach camping zones on K'gari, and you need the zone's name when you book. Permits cannot be bought from rangers on the island. At Teewah Beach in Cooloola there are no marked sites: you camp behind the vegetated foredunes on the existing tracks, stay in the zone you booked, and carry a portable toilet.

On Cape York, camping at Captain Billy Landing needs a camping permit, booked online as an e-permit, with the tag displayed at your site. Access is 4WD and off-road camper trailers only, generators are not permitted, and the maximum stay is 21 consecutive nights. The camping area has closed at times for cultural activities, so check the park alerts before you go.

sections.heading: New South Wales and Victoria: campgrounds beside the beach
body: Diamond Head in Crowdy Bay National Park has 75 beachside sites booked through NSW National Parks, where park entry fees can be paid at booking and fires are allowed in off-the-ground braziers only. On Stockton Bight, camping in the Worimi Conservation Lands is allowed only at the Ganyamalbaa camping area, which is booked in advance. Camping anywhere else there, including sleeping in a vehicle on the beach, is not permitted, and the beach vehicle permit is a separate cost.

At Cape Conran Coastal Park in Victoria, Binn Beach, Gunnai Beach and Pearl Point are non-bookable and first come, first served, with fires only in designated fireplaces. Banksia Bluff, in the same park, is the bookable campground, but Parks Victoria says it is temporarily closed, with reopening expected before summer 2026/27.

sections.heading: South Australia and Western Australia
body: South Australian national parks charge camping fees that must be paid before you arrive. Coffin Bay National Park has designated campgrounds, most reachable only by 4WD, and Black Springs has eight sites within 50 metres of the beach. Some beaches ban camping altogether: on Yorke Peninsula, overnight camping and large camping vehicles are not permitted on Wauraltee Beach, and a $315 fine plus a $102 victims of crime levy may apply.

In Western Australia, Explore Parks WA says camping on the Nyinggulu (Ningaloo) Coastal Reserves is permitted in designated campgrounds only, and points to Park Stay WA for bookings. Tropical Cyclone Narelle damaged campgrounds along the Ningaloo coast in 2026, so check the DBCA alerts for closures before you book.

sections.heading: Tasmania and the Northern Territory
body: Camping in the Bay of Fires Conservation Area is permitted only in designated campgrounds such as Swimcart and Seatons Cove. Parks and Wildlife Service Tasmania says these campgrounds are free, need no booking, and have a maximum stay of four weeks.

In the Northern Territory, the NT Parks Booking System says non-residents need a Visitor Pass to reserve a campsite, and residents must still book and pay for camping. Crocodiles shape where you pitch: the NT Government says to camp at least 50 metres from the water's edge and to swim only in signposted designated swimming areas, not at Top End beaches.
tips: Bay of Fires: free, no booking

sections.heading: What to do instead
body: If the beach you want bans camping, camp behind it. On Yorke Peninsula, the council's Wauraltee Bush Campground sits behind the beach, with unpowered sites from $20 a night and a permit bought on the council's website. In NSW, Ganyamalbaa is the camping option on Stockton Bight.

For a first-come night with no booking, Cape Conran in Victoria and the Bay of Fires in Tasmania are the sites checked here. Arrive in daylight and have a booked site as a second choice, because non-bookable campgrounds can fill.

sections.heading: Check this rule at the place in AussieCamps
body: Each coastal campground has a place page in AussieCamps with the facilities, fees and rules the park agency publishes, so the agency's own notes on a beach site stay in your pocket. The app lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks; a collection keeps the beaches you are weighing and a trip lines them up along the coast. Stored details open with no coverage, but the map, routing, weather and photos need a connection. It is an iPhone app.
It does not replace the official rule. Confirm with the land manager whether a beach zone is open and what permit it needs, and check the park alerts before you travel.

faq: Can I sleep on the beach in a swag or tent in Australia?

Only at a campground or camping zone the land manager has set aside. On Stockton Bight in NSW, camping is allowed only at the booked Ganyamalbaa camping area, and on Wauraltee Beach in South Australia overnight camping, including swags and tents, is not permitted.
Can I camp on a beach in a national park without booking?

Sometimes. The Bay of Fires campgrounds in Tasmania and Binn Beach, Gunnai Beach and Pearl Point at Cape Conran in Victoria take no bookings. In Queensland you need a camping permit bought before you set up camp, and Ningaloo Coast campsites in WA are booked through Park Stay WA.
Is beach camping free in Australia?

Rarely. The Bay of Fires campgrounds in Tasmania are free and need no booking, but the Queensland, NSW and South Australian beach campgrounds above need a paid permit or booking. Check the camping fees guide for the state you are visiting.
Is it safe to camp on a beach in northern Australia?

Not near the water's edge in crocodile country. The Northern Territory Government says to camp at least 50 metres from the water's edge, and to swim only in signposted designated swimming areas, not at Top End beaches.

can-i-drive-on-the-beach-in-australia.title: Can I Drive on the Beach in Australia? Rules by State 2026
can-i-drive-on-the-beach-in-australia.description: Only where the land manager allows it, often with a vehicle access permit and a 4WD. Beach driving rules for Qld, NSW, Vic, SA, WA, Tas and NT, 2026.
can-i-drive-on-the-beach-in-australia.imageAlt: Four-wheel drives parked on the sand beside tyre tracks on the beach at K'gari (Fraser Island), Queensland
can-i-drive-on-the-beach-in-australia.intro: It depends on the beach: you can drive on some beaches in Queensland, NSW, South Australia, Western Australia and Tasmania, but only where the land manager allows it, often with a vehicle access permit and a 4WD. Victoria prohibits private vehicles on beaches except where an exemption applies, and where driving is allowed you keep to the permitted beach, tracks and areas.

sections.heading: The short answer by state
body: Beach driving is a permit and 4WD question in most states, and a no in Victoria. Queensland and South Australia both say normal road rules apply on beaches, so the vehicle must be registered and the driver licensed. Camping on the beach has separate rules, covered in the beach camping guide.

sections.heading: Queensland: permit, high-clearance 4WD and the tide
body: Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service says every vehicle entering K'gari needs a vehicle access permit, and you must show a copy, printed or digital, to an authorised officer on request. K'gari's beaches and sandy inland roads suit high-clearance 4WD vehicles with low-range gearing, and QPWS says SUVs and all-wheel-drive vehicles are not suitable in its sand parks. All Queensland road rules apply on the beach.

On K'gari the limit is 80 km/h at most on the eastern beach and 30 km/h on inland roads, and QPWS says a safe speed can be lower than the signed limit. QPWS advises planning beach driving around low tide and avoiding the two hours either side of high tide.

sections.heading: New South Wales and Victoria
body: On Stockton Bight, the Worimi Conservation Lands need a 4WD and a Worimi beach vehicle permit for every vehicle, and annual NSW National Parks passes do not apply. Drive only on the waterfront, and do not drive or park on the frontal dune, grass or vegetation. Do not drive over shell accumulations either, as this may damage Aboriginal cultural sites. Entry is free for walkers, cyclists and horse riders. MidCoast Council runs its own beach permit, displayed on the windscreen, with a 40 km/h limit, 15 km/h within 100 metres of other vehicles and people, and driving only between the tide marks.

Victoria is the exception. Parks Victoria says off-road access to marine and coastal Crown land and beaches by private vehicles is prohibited, except where specified exemptions apply. Six commercial fishers were prosecuted over driving on the beach at Discovery Bay, and one was fined $3,000 plus $6,450 in costs after being found guilty of 22 charges, including operating a motor vehicle in an area of public land.

sections.heading: South Australia and Western Australia
body: South Australia's Coastal Driving Code of Practice says some beaches do not allow vehicles, some ban camping or camping vehicles, and others allow boat launching only or need a permit. The default beach speed limit is 40 km/h, and 25 km/h when passing pedestrians. On Yorke Peninsula, large camping vehicles are not permitted on Wauraltee Beach, though daytime access for other vehicles remains, and Thidna Beach is limited to a small area near Gleeson's Landing.

At Cable Beach in Broome, the Shire of Broome sets a 15 km/h limit, and asks drivers to stay off soft sand and avoid driving on the beach at night. Turtle season brings limits: from 1 to 30 November the ramp is closed to all but essential and approved vehicles from 8pm to 6am and on days when high tides exceed nine metres, and from 1 December to 28 February it is closed to all but essential and approved vehicles. The Shire's page said the ramp was closed for foreshore works until mid to late 2026, so check it has reopened. Explore Parks WA says vehicles must stay on designated roads and tracks, off-road vehicles must be registered with the Department of Transport, and special considerations apply on beaches and in coastal national parks.

sections.heading: Tasmania and the Northern Territory
body: In the Arthur-Pieman Conservation Area, Parks and Wildlife Service Tasmania says drivers taking a 4WD off-road need an Arthur-Pieman Recreational Driver Pass. Vehicles must be registered and drivers licensed, and driving is limited to the tracks, beaches and areas shown in the recreational driving guide.

We did not find a statewide beach driving rule for the Northern Territory, so ask the park or council for the beach you plan to use. We also could not confirm the beach driving rules at Eighty Mile Beach in Western Australia.
tips: NT: ask the park or council

sections.heading: Tides, tyres and recovery
body: Tides decide whether a beach is drivable. South Australia's code says that when tides are very high there may be no hard sand to drive on, and that it is best not to be on the beach in those conditions. MidCoast Council puts it plainly: high tides leave no room for error.

QPWS says you can lower tyre pressure on soft sand and South Australia's code says to drop it to suit the surface. Stay within your manufacturer's limits and re-inflate before you reach harder surfaces or sealed roads. South Australia's code says to carry a tyre pressure gauge, a compressor and recovery gear, to tell someone where you are going, and warns that emergency rescue may be far away and costly.

sections.heading: Hire vehicles: check the agreement
body: Sixt's Australian rental insurance guide says driving across beaches, and through streams, rivers and floods, can exclude you from protection. QPWS says SUVs and all-wheel-drive vehicles are not suitable in its sand parks, so a standard hire car or SUV is not the right vehicle for K'gari's beaches.
Check the rental agreement for any beach, sand or off-road clause before you book, and ask the hire company in writing if you are unsure.
tips: Ask before you drive on sand

sections.heading: What to do instead
body: If you do not have a permitted 4WD, walk. Entry to the Worimi Conservation Lands is free for walkers. The Worimi Conservation Lands site also lists guided tours. A guided trip is an option where you have no suitable 4WD.
Where driving is banned, park at the access point and walk to the sand, as the rule requires on Victorian beaches, where private vehicles are prohibited except under an exemption.

sections.heading: Check this rule at the place in AussieCamps
body: Place pages in AussieCamps give the facilities, fees, rules and access notes the park agency publishes, and a filter for vehicle access narrows the list to sites that suit your vehicle. There are 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks in the app. Stored details open without coverage, while map tiles, routing, weather and photos need a connection. It is for iPhone only.
It does not replace the official rule or the tide table. Confirm the permit, the closures and the conditions with the land manager before you drive onto a beach.
tips: Access notes from the park agency

faq: Do I need a permit to drive on Stockton Beach?

Yes. Every vehicle entering the Worimi Conservation Lands needs a Worimi beach vehicle permit, and NSW National Parks annual passes are not valid there. A 4WD is required, and fines apply to vehicles without a valid permit.
Can I drive on any beach in Victoria?

No. Parks Victoria says off-road access to marine and coastal Crown land and beaches by private vehicles is prohibited under the Land Conservation (Vehicle Control) Act 1972 and its 2013 Regulations, unless a specific exemption applies.
Is it safe to drive on the beach at high tide?

Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service advises avoiding beach driving for two hours either side of high tide, and South Australia's Coastal Driving Code says there may be no hard sand to drive on when tides are very high. Plan the drive around low tide.
Can I take a hire car on the beach?

Not without checking the rental agreement first. Sixt's Australian rental guide says driving across beaches can exclude you from insurance protection, and a hire vehicle that is not a 4WD is not suitable on sand parks such as K'gari.

can-i-camp-in-a-national-park-without-bo.title: Can I Camp in a National Park Without Booking? 2026 Rules
can-i-camp-in-a-national-park-without-bo.description: Sometimes, but not in Queensland, South Australia or the NT, where you book before you arrive. Which national park campgrounds need no booking, by state, 2026.
can-i-camp-in-a-national-park-without-bo.imageAlt: A white tent pitched among ferns and eucalypts at the Sealers Cove campsite in Wilsons Promontory National Park, Victoria
can-i-camp-in-a-national-park-without-bo.intro: Sometimes, but not everywhere: in Queensland, South Australia and the Northern Territory you must book and pay before you arrive, while New South Wales, Victoria, Western Australia and Tasmania each have campgrounds that take no bookings. The deciding rule is the campground's own page, which says whether it is bookable, first come, first served or a self-registration site.

sections.heading: The short answer by state
body: Booking rules differ by state and by campground, so check the campground's own page on the agency's website instead of relying on a general rule. Fees are covered in the camping fees guide, so this page sticks to booking.
tips: Book first in Qld, SA and NT

sections.heading: Queensland, South Australia, the Northern Territory and the ACT: book first
body: Queensland says you must book and pay for a camping permit before you arrive at a camping area, usually online, with the permit emailed to you. The tag must be displayed at your site.

South Australia's national parks run on online booking: its guide says signage in the parks emphasises that online bookings are required for camping, and the vehicle entry fee is waived with most campground bookings. A park pass skips the vehicle entry booking but does not cover your campsite, and the Desert Parks Pass is the exception in some parks. If you are collecting a hire car, enter HIRECAR in the registration field and update it after pickup.

In the Northern Territory, you must have a pass to reserve a campsite (NT residents do not need the Visitor Pass), and residents must still book and pay for camping. In the ACT, Parks ACT says bookings are essential at the Namadgi campgrounds Honeysuckle, Orroral and Mount Clear.
tips: SA: park pass does not cover camping

sections.heading: New South Wales: most campgrounds are booked, a few are not
body: NSW National Parks has more than 350 campgrounds, and you book many of them online. Some campgrounds with no camping fee still need one: Brou Lake charges no camping fee but a $6 booking fee applies, and the booking limit is eight people or two sites online.

A few basic campgrounds take no bookings, such as Tuross River in Wadbilliga National Park. NPWS also says you do not need a booking for remote camping, meaning campgrounds not listed on its website, but it highly recommends filling in a trip intention form before you arrive.
tips: Free sites can still carry a $6 fee

sections.heading: Victoria: some campgrounds are first come
body: Parks Victoria says you need to book popular bookable campsites in advance, especially in busy holiday periods, and to check each park page to see which campsites need booking.

Plenty of Victorian campgrounds take no bookings. At Cape Conran Coastal Park, Binn Beach, Gunnai Beach and Pearl Point are first come, first served, and Banksia Bluff is the bookable campground there, though the park page says it is closed for essential works, with reopening expected before summer 2026/27. Camping is permitted only at your designated site, and a site may be occupied only by the party that made the booking.
tips: Use only the site you booked

sections.heading: Western Australia and Tasmania: mixed systems
body: Explore Parks WA says online bookings are available for some of the most popular campgrounds, with card payment at booking. At other campgrounds the payment instructions are displayed at the park entry or campground, and you pay park staff or a campground host, or use a self-registration envelope. Mitchell Falls Campground is non-bookable and uses envelopes.

In Tasmania, a valid parks pass is required to enter national parks. The Bay of Fires campgrounds are free, need no booking and have a four-week maximum stay, and camping is allowed only in the designated campgrounds. The conservation area's northern end lies within Mount William National Park, which needs a parks pass. At Freycinet, Parks and Wildlife Service Tasmania has paused new bookings for stays from 3 November 2026 while the Parks Online Booking System starts, and for stays from that date cancellations less than five days from arrival are not refunded.

sections.heading: What to do instead if you cannot book
body: Pick a non-bookable campground as your first choice and a bookable one as your backup. In Victoria that means Cape Conran's beach camps, in NSW Tuross River, and in Tasmania the Bay of Fires (camp only in the designated campgrounds). Arrive in daylight, because first-come campgrounds can fill and some have a stay limit.

If a bookable campground is full, check the same park's page for a non-bookable camp nearby. For a fully remote trip in NSW, unlisted campgrounds need no booking, but fill in the NPWS trip intention form.

sections.heading: Check this rule at the place in AussieCamps
body: The place page for a national park campground in AussieCamps shows the facilities, fees and rules drawn from the state park agencies, a quick way to see what the agency says before you open its booking site. The app lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks, and a collection or a trip keeps your shortlist together. Stored details open with no coverage; maps, routing, weather and photos need a connection. It runs on iPhone only.
It does not replace the official rule. Confirm with the park agency whether a campground needs booking, and keep your booking confirmation on your phone.
tips: Facilities, fees and rules on place pages

faq: Can I just turn up at a national park campground in Australia?

Only at campgrounds that take no bookings, such as Binn Beach, Gunnai Beach and Pearl Point at Cape Conran in Victoria, or Tuross River in NSW. In Queensland, South Australia and the Northern Territory you book and pay first, and many other campgrounds in NSW, Victoria and WA are bookable.
Do I need to book camping in a Queensland national park?
Yes. Queensland says you must book and pay for a camping permit before you arrive at a camping area, and the permit is emailed to you. Display the tag at your site.
Is there free camping in a national park with no booking?

Sometimes. The Bay of Fires campgrounds in Tasmania are free and need no booking, though the northern end of the area lies within Mount William National Park, which needs a parks pass. Some NSW campgrounds with no camping fee, such as Brou Lake, still charge a $6 booking fee and need a booking.
Do I need a parks pass as well as a camping booking?

Often. Tasmania needs a valid parks pass to enter its national parks, non-residents need an NT Visitor Pass to reserve a campsite, and in NSW park entry fees are separate from camping fees where they apply. In South Australia a park pass does not cover camping, except the Desert Parks Pass in some parks.

can-i-collect-firewood-while-camping-in-.title: Can I Collect Firewood Camping in Australia? 2026 Rules
can-i-collect-firewood-while-camping-in-.description: Mostly no. Parks in Victoria, Queensland, SA, WA and Tasmania ban collecting firewood, and NSW allows it only in some backcountry. Some state forests allow it.
can-i-collect-firewood-while-camping-in-.imageAlt: A stack of split firewood logs in a woodpile in Hobart, Tasmania
can-i-collect-firewood-while-camping-in-.intro: No, not in a national park: the park agencies in Victoria, Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia and Tasmania ban collecting firewood there, and NSW allows it only in some remote backcountry areas, so you bring your own wood or cook on gas. Collecting is only allowed in designated areas of some state forests, usually with a permit, set seasons or volume limits.

sections.heading: The short answer by state
body: Fallen timber is habitat, so park agencies treat wood on the ground as part of the park. The rules below cover firewood collection only. Campfire rules and fire bans are covered in the campfire guide.

sections.heading: National parks and reserves: assume you cannot collect
body: Parks Victoria says collection is not permitted in national parks, conservation parks, and nature and bushland reserves, and the Victorian Government says the ban covers national, state, regional and metropolitan parks. Queensland Parks and Wildlife says firewood must not be collected and that campfires are only for existing fireplaces, fire rings or fire locations. Tasmania's Parks and Wildlife Service says cutting and collecting firewood is not permitted in its national parks and reserves, and South Australia's national parks tell campers to bring their own.

In NSW, the National Parks and Wildlife Service prohibits taking firewood out of a park for use elsewhere, and asks campers to bring their own wood or use wood provided, not fallen timber. Its policy allows on-site collection in backcountry areas, except where a sign, notice or plan of management prohibits it, so do not collect unless the park's own page says you can.

Parks Victoria lists six regional parks where designated parts allow free firewood collection until 1 July 2029: Bendigo, Barkstead, Blackwood, Fingerpost and Spargo Creek, plus the southern addition to Hepburn. That is a narrow exception, and Pyrenees Regional Park is excluded.
tips: Regional parks differ from national parks

sections.heading: State forests: where collecting is allowed
body: Victoria runs domestic firewood collection areas in State forest, managed by Forest Fire Management Victoria. The seasons are 1 March to 30 June and 1 September to 30 November, and areas can close at short notice. You may take only wood already on the ground, up to 2 cubic metres per person per day and 16 cubic metres per household per financial year, and you cannot sell it.

In NSW, Forestry Corporation says you need authorisation to collect firewood from State forests, you take fallen timber only, and some forests are not offered at all. Western Australia allows collection from designated State forest areas in the Perth Hills, where a permit valid for one visit is needed, and in the South West, where it is not. Both WA areas allow up to one tonne at a time, and from 1 June to 30 September one tonne every 60 days.

Tasmania's Sustainable Timber Tasmania sells permits for designated areas of production forest, for wood already on the ground only, with a yearly maximum of 30 cubic metres per customer. In Queensland, the Government sells forest products including firewood by short-term permit or one-off sale under the Forestry Act 1959. These are domestic firewood schemes, so a weekend camper is usually better off buying a bundle.
tips: Permit first in NSW, Qld and Tas

sections.heading: Bringing firewood, and what to bring
body: Where a fire is allowed, bring or buy your wood. Parks Victoria says to bring your own unless collection is permitted at that site, and South Australia asks for wood free from dirt and weeds so pests do not enter the park. ACT Parks tells visitors to bring firewood or buy it from the Namadgi Visitor Centre.

NSW policy notes that wood carried into a park can spread pests and pathogens, which is why parks control it. Buy from a campground shop or a reputable supplier near the park, because not all firewood on sale in Victoria is legally sourced.

sections.heading: Moving firewood between states
body: Biosecurity Tasmania lists firewood among the items checked by inspectors at the Devonport terminal, says items may be seized at the border, and says to leave them at home if in doubt. Penalties may apply for non-compliance.

In Western Australia, firewood cannot be removed from the Polyphagous shot hole borer Quarantine Area, and DBCA says to buy firewood close to where you will burn it. The interstate biosecurity guide covers the other items to leave at home.
tips: Buy it where you burn it

sections.heading: Fire bans override everything
body: A Total Fire Ban stops all campfires, and parks add seasonal campfire bans. The campfire guide has the state-by-state fire rules, so check it before you buy wood.

sections.heading: What to do instead
body: A gas stove avoids the firewood question entirely. Tasmania's Parks and Wildlife Service allows LPG cookers on a Total Fire Ban day but not liquid fuel stoves, and other states differ, so check the campfire guide first. If a campfire is allowed where you are staying, buy a bundle from the campground or a shop in town and burn it all, rather than carrying leftovers on.

Tasmania's fuel stove only areas ban campfires all year, so a stove is the only choice there. If you want to collect wood for a home fire, use a designated State forest area with the right authorisation.

sections.heading: Check this rule at the place in AussieCamps
body: A place page in AussieCamps lists the campground's facilities and rules as the park agency publishes them, so you can read the rules it publishes for the site before the drive. The app holds 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks. Place details are saved on the phone and open without coverage, while live maps, directions and forecasts need a connection. It works on iPhone only.
It does not replace the official rule. Confirm with the land manager whether a fire is allowed and whether firewood is sold at the site.

faq: Can I pick up fallen sticks for a campfire in a national park?

No, not in most parks. Parks Victoria, Queensland Parks and Wildlife, Tasmania's Parks and Wildlife Service, South Australia and WA all prohibit collecting firewood in their parks, and NSW National Parks asks campers to bring their own wood and not use fallen timber. Bring your own wood where a campfire is allowed, or cook on a gas stove.
Is it legal to collect firewood from a state forest?

Sometimes, in designated areas only. Victoria has domestic firewood collection areas open from 1 March to 30 June and 1 September to 30 November, NSW needs an authorisation from Forestry Corporation, WA has designated areas in the Perth Hills and South West, and Tasmania needs a Sustainable Timber Tasmania permit.
Can I take firewood across the border or onto the Spirit of Tasmania?

Leave it at home if in doubt. Biosecurity Tasmania lists firewood among the items checked at Devonport and says it may be seized, and WA bans removing firewood from its borer quarantine area. Buying wood close to where you will burn it is the safe habit.
Can I collect firewood during a fire ban?
No campfire can be lit on a Total Fire Ban day, so there is nothing to collect it for. Some parks also ban campfires for a whole season, so check the fire rules before you buy or gather any wood.

can-i-fly-a-drone-while-camping-in-austr.title: Can I Fly a Drone in a National Park or Campsite? 2026
can-i-fly-a-drone-while-camping-in-austr.description: Usually not. CASA allows flying for fun, but most park agencies ban drones or need approval, and Queensland bans them in camping areas. Rules by state, 2026.
can-i-fly-a-drone-while-camping-in-austr.imageAlt: A camera drone hovering against a clear sky at Lamberts Beach Lookout, Slade Point, Queensland
can-i-fly-a-drone-while-camping-in-austr.intro: It depends, but in a national park or park campground the answer is usually no. CASA lets you fly a drone for fun, and then the land manager decides: Victoria, Tasmania, the ACT, Kakadu and Uluru-Kata Tjuta do not allow recreational flying, NSW needs approval, and Queensland bans drones in all its camping areas.

sections.heading: The short answer by state
body: CASA sets the national rules for flying a drone for fun. The park agency or land manager then adds its own, and those are usually stricter, so check the one for the park you are camping in.

sections.heading: CASA's rules for flying for fun
body: CASA says you do not need a licence or accreditation to fly for fun, and that registration of recreational drones over 250 g is on hold. The rules that apply are these: fly no higher than 120 m above ground level, keep the drone in sight with your own eyes, fly only in daylight, and fly only one drone at a time.

Keep the drone at least 30 m from other people and never fly over anyone. Do not fly in a populous area, which CASA defines as anywhere people are living or gathered for a purpose, and says includes parks, beaches, roads and festivals. A drone over 250 g must stay out of 5.5 km of a controlled airport, and you must not fly over or near emergency operations such as firefighting. CASA recommends checking a CASA-verified drone safety app before each flight.

sections.heading: Parks where the answer is no
body: Parks Victoria says members of the public cannot fly drones for recreation on land it manages, and visitors who do may be fined. Tasmania's Parks and Wildlife Service says the operation and use of drones by visitors on reserved land, including national parks, is not permitted, with exceptions only for commercial and event filming and scientific research. In the ACT, flying a drone is prohibited in nature conservation reserves, which include Namadgi.

In South Australia it is an offence to fly a drone over national parks, conservation parks, game reserves, recreation parks or regional reserves without a permit, and permits are considered only for scientific research and commercial filming or photography. Two Commonwealth parks go further. Kakadu prohibits drones except under a management plan or a park permit, and says permits are not issued for recreational use. Uluru-Kata Tjuta is a no-drone park where use is approved only in exceptional circumstances after consultation with the Central Land Council.
tips: SA: permit, research and filming only
Kakadu and Uluru: no recreational permits

sections.heading: Where you can ask for permission, or fly with conditions
body: In NSW, NPWS requires approval to launch, land or operate a drone from within a park for recreation. You apply with the NPWS form, first checking that the park is not a drone exclusion area, and NPWS may refuse or add conditions. Park alerts override any approval, and the Kosciuszko plan of management prohibits recreational drones across the whole park.

In Western Australia, DBCA says recreational drone use in parks needs no department approval, provided you follow CASA's rules, do not disturb wildlife or other visitors, avoid emergency operations, and contact the district office before each flight. The Swan Canning Riverpark needs a separate permit. In the Northern Territory, some parks need an operation of aircraft permit, some sites have their own flying limits, and a Territory permit is not valid in Kakadu or Uluru-Kata Tjuta.

sections.heading: At the campsite itself
body: In Queensland, drones are prohibited in all camping areas in protected areas, recreation areas and forests, and QPWS says to keep any drone you have stored in a container in your vehicle or vessel. It is also an offence to fly one into a drone restriction area from outside it.

Elsewhere, the park rules above apply to the campground as well, and a campground is a place where people gather, which makes CASA's 30 m and populous-area rules hard to meet. On other land, such as a holiday park or a private campground, ask the manager before you fly.

sections.heading: What to do instead
body: Leave the drone in the vehicle and take photos from the ground, from lookouts and from walking tracks. If you want footage of a park where approval is possible, apply early: NSW requires approval before you launch, and any NT permit has to be in hand before you fly.

Parks Victoria and Tasmania's Parks and Wildlife Service both give disturbance to wildlife as a reason for their rules, and WA asks flyers not to disturb wildlife. If the answer is a clear no, the lawful option is to not fly.

sections.heading: Check this rule at the place in AussieCamps
body: Open a campground in AussieCamps and its place page shows the facilities, fees, rules and access notes drawn from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets. That is a prompt to look up the park agency's drone rule, not an answer to it. The app lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks; stored details open without coverage, and the map, weather and photos need a connection. It is for iPhone only.
The app does not replace the official rule. Confirm with the park agency or land manager before you fly.

faq: Do I need a licence or to register a drone to fly it for fun in Australia?

No. CASA says flying for fun needs no licence or accreditation, and registration of recreational drones over 250 g has been paused. You still have to follow CASA's safety rules, and the land manager's rules where you fly.
Can I fly a drone in a national park in Australia?

Usually not. Parks Victoria, Tasmania's Parks and Wildlife Service, the ACT, Kakadu and Uluru-Kata Tjuta do not allow recreational flying, NSW needs approval, and South Australia only considers permits for research and commercial filming. Western Australia is the exception: DBCA says visitors need no approval but must follow set conditions.
Can I fly a drone at a campsite in Queensland?
No. Drones are prohibited in all camping areas in Queensland's national parks, recreation areas and forests. If you have one with you, keep it securely stored in a container in your vehicle.
How close can I fly a drone to people while camping?
CASA says keep it at least 30 m from other people and never fly over anyone. A campground is a place where people gather, so even where a drone is allowed, there is rarely a spot to fly it.

can-i-fish-without-a-licence-while-campi.title: Do I Need a Fishing Licence While Camping in Australia? 2026
can-i-fish-without-a-licence-while-campi.description: It depends on the state. NSW, Victoria, Tasmania (inland) and WA (boat, freshwater) need a licence; Queensland, SA, NT and the ACT do not. Fees checked 2026.
can-i-fish-without-a-licence-while-campi.imageAlt: Fishing rods in holders on the Palm Cove fishing jetty near Cairns, Queensland, with a tackle box and bucket beside the rail
can-i-fish-without-a-licence-while-campi.intro: It depends on the state: NSW and Victoria require a licence or fee for recreational fishing, Tasmania for inland angling, and WA for specific activities, while Queensland, South Australia, the Northern Territory and the ACT have no general licence. Everywhere, bag and size limits apply, and fishing is banned in marine park sanctuary zones.

sections.heading: The short answer by state
body: There is no national fishing licence. Each state and territory sets its own, and some licences are for one activity only, such as fishing from a boat or taking rock lobster.

table.caption: Recreational fishing licences by state and territory, checked 21 October 2026. Fees are as published by each government.

sections.heading: Where you need a licence
body: In NSW, one fee covers saltwater and freshwater. It covers line fishing, spearfishing, bait collecting and collecting invertebrates by hand, and under-18s are exempt. Victoria says you need a licence for recreational fishing in its waters, and under-18s and people aged 70 and over can apply for a free fisher card instead.

Tasmania requires an angling licence for inland waters, and children under 14 do not need one. In the sea, Tasmania's rod and line fishing needs no licence, but rock lobster, abalone, scallop, nets and set lines do. WA also requires a licence for fishing from a powered boat, whether you fish with a line, catch crabs or use a spear.

sections.heading: Where you do not need a licence
body: Queensland has no general licence, but anyone aged 18 or over needs a Stocked Impoundment Permit to line fish in a stocked dam or weir, and one permit covers every impoundment in the scheme. Under-18s do not need one. South Australia does not require a licence for recreational fishing, but fishing in a reservoir needs a permit, and PIRSA suggests contacting SA Water for the detail.

The Northern Territory does not require a licence, and fishing permits are not required in NT parks and reserves, although some parks need access or camping permits. Much of the NT's intertidal water lies over Aboriginal land, where you may need a permit or registration. The ACT does not require a licence in public waters, but Googong Reservoir follows NSW rules and needs a NSW licence.

sections.heading: Western Australia: licences by activity
body: WA licenses the activity, not the angler. DPIRD lists a recreational fishing from a boat licence at $40, and licences at $50 each for south-west freshwater angling, rock lobster, abalone, marron and net fishing. Licences last 12 months from the day payment is received, and you must not fish until you receive the receipt.

Fees are halved for people under 16, Seniors Card holders and some pensioners, and a 10 per cent discount applies when you apply for more than one activity at once. Rowing or paddling without a motor does not trigger the boat licence.

sections.heading: Bag and size limits apply everywhere
body: No licence does not mean no rules. PIRSA says South Australia's fishery is not licensed but has size, bag, boat and possession limits, and the ACT says anglers must follow the Fisheries Act 2000 even without a licence. In the NT, barramundi have a possession limit and a minimum size, with tighter rules in Kakadu and the Mary and Daly River zones.

Limits vary by species, by zone and sometimes by season, so check the official limits for the water you are on. A free app from the state fisheries agency is the easiest way to do it, and the NSW, Victorian and South Australian apps also show marine park zones.

sections.heading: Marine parks: sanctuary zones ban fishing
body: Fishing is banned in marine park sanctuary zones and no-take areas, even if you hold a licence. NSW sanctuary zones ban fishing by any method, Victoria's marine national parks and marine sanctuaries are no-take areas, and South Australia's sanctuary zones are no-take areas where you cannot use fishing gear. South Australia's penalties run from a formal warning for a first offence to a maximum of $100,000 or two years in prison for serious or repeat offenders.

Check the official zoning maps before you cast: the NSW Department of Primary Industries publishes marine park zoning maps and the FishSmart NSW app, the Victorian Fisheries Authority has a Can I fish here? feature in its app, and South Australia's Marine Parks site has maps and GPS coordinates. NSW has changed some zones over the years, so use the current map for the park, not an old one.

sections.heading: Fishing near water in croc country
body: In the Top End, assume crocodiles are present in any waterway. NT Government Be Crocwise guidance says to stand at least 5 metres back from the water's edge when fishing, and NT Parks says not to clean fish within 50 metres of the water unless you use a designated fish cleaning facility.
The Northern Territory and Queensland camping rules guides cover where to pitch and croc warnings in more detail.

sections.heading: What to do instead
body: If the licence cost is the problem, buy a short one: NSW offers 3 days and 1 month, Victoria offers 3 days and 28 days, Queensland sells a stocked dam permit by the week, and Tasmania sells inland licences for 48 hours, 7 days and 28 days. Victoria sells its licence online and at participating angling shops or authorised agents.

If you would rather skip a licence entirely, plan the trip around Queensland, South Australia, the Northern Territory or the ACT, and check for reservoir permits and Aboriginal land permits first. In every state, choose a spot outside a sanctuary zone.

sections.heading: Check this rule at the place in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps place pages carry facilities, fees and rules as the park agency publishes them for 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks, so you can see a campground's own notes before you pack the rods. The app does not list fishing licences or zones. Place details open without coverage, while the map, weather and photos need a connection. It is an iPhone app.
It does not replace the official rule. Confirm the licence and the zone with the fisheries agency or park manager before you fish.

faq: Do I need a fishing licence in Queensland?

Not for most fishing. Queensland has no general recreational fishing licence, but anyone aged 18 or over needs a Stocked Impoundment Permit to line fish in a stocked dam or weir, and size and possession limits apply everywhere.
Can I fish from the beach in Australia without a licence?

In the sea, it depends on the state. NSW needs a fishing fee for saltwater, Queensland, South Australia, the Northern Territory and the ACT do not need a licence, and Tasmania and WA do not list rod and line fishing from the shore among their licensed activities. Beaches inside a sanctuary zone ban fishing altogether.
Do kids need a fishing licence in Australia?

Often not. NSW exempts under-18s from its fee, Victoria and Queensland do not require under-18s to hold a licence or a stocked dam permit, Tasmania does not require an inland licence under 14, and WA does not require a south-west freshwater licence under 16.
Is there a fishing licence for the whole of Australia?
No. Each state and territory sets its own recreational fishing rules and fees, as the table above shows. If you cross a border on a camping trip, check the rules for each state you will fish in.

can-i-use-a-generator-at-a-campsite-in-a.title: Can I Use a Generator Camping in Australia? Rules by State
can-i-use-a-generator-at-a-campsite-in-a.description: It depends, and often no. Most Queensland and NSW parks ban generators unless a sign allows them, with set hours in WA and Tasmania. Rules by state, 2026.
can-i-use-a-generator-at-a-campsite-in-a.imageAlt: Caravans and tents under trees and palms at the Eighty Mile Beach caravan park on the north-west coast of Western Australia
can-i-use-a-generator-at-a-campsite-in-a.intro: It depends, and in most parks the answer is no: Queensland says generators are not permitted in most parks and forests, and NSW generally does not permit them unless a sign or the park manager allows it. Where they are allowed it is campground by campground, within set hours, so read the sign or the park's own page before you bring one.

sections.heading: The short answer by state
body: There is no national rule. Each park agency decides, and most decide campground by campground. The table covers what each one says on its own pages, so treat it as a guide to the question you should ask the land manager.

table.caption: Generators at campsites by state and territory, checked 21 October 2026.
head: State or territory
What the land manager says
Source
rows: Generally not permitted in parks. Allowed where a sign says so or the park manager consents. One generator per group, placed closer to your camp than to neighbours, and any noise curfew in the campground applies.
NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service

No single park-wide rule found. Wilsons Promontory and Jimmy Creek campground (Grampians) list no generators. Warby-Ovens National Park allows them with fire-safety conditions. State forests allow them if used safely.
Not permitted in most parks and forests. Where allowed, low-noise generators up to 2.0 kVA and 65 dB at 7 m, with hours set on each park's page.
Check with the local parks office. Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre allows generators in daylight hours only, and Onkaparinga River says none except where permitted.
National Parks and Wildlife Service SA, Department for Environment and Water
Allowed at some campgrounds only, usually between 8am and 9pm but it varies. Banned at others. None on total fire ban days.
Set per reserve. Lime Bay off by 9pm, Peggs Beach and Black River 10am to 8pm. Not permitted in Narawntapu National Park or over the bridge at Cockle Creek.
Not permitted unless authorised or signed as permitted. Keep River allows them at one campground, 7.30am to 8.30pm. Litchfield and Nitmiluk do not allow them.
Motorised generator use is prohibited at Namadgi's Mount Clear campground.
Set per campground in Kakadu: Mardugal One lists generators permitted, Maguk lists none.

sections.heading: Where generators are allowed: the sign decides
body: NSW says generators are generally not permitted in parks, but some have signposted areas where they are. If there is no sign, you cannot use one without consent from the park manager. The NSW policy also counts a vehicle engine left running to charge batteries or power equipment as a generator.

Queensland's rule is the same in spirit: most parks and forests do not allow generators, and each park's page says whether yours does. In WA, the Northern Territory and Tasmania, the answer sits on the individual campground page, and a few larger WA campgrounds have separate generator and quiet areas.

A rule can also change on the day. NSW says use can be stopped for a period in a campground where it was previously allowed, for example for roosting birds or a local fire ban, and it must put up signs when it does.
tips: Rules can change on the day

sections.heading: Hours and noise
body: Where generators are allowed, hours are short and set per site. Explore Parks WA says permitted hours are posted at the campground, usually 8am to 9pm. Peggs Beach and Black River in Tasmania allow them from 10am to 8pm, Lime Bay requires them off by 9pm along with all other noise, and Keep River's Goorrandalng campground runs 7.30am to 8.30pm. At Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre in South Australia, generators are for daylight hours only.

Queensland sets a noise limit as well as park-by-park hours: low-decibel generators up to 2.0 kVA, with a maximum of 65 dB at 7 m, unless the park says otherwise. NSW asks you to take reasonable measures to minimise noise and to obey any noise curfew in the campground.

sections.heading: Fire bans and safe set-up
body: NSW, Queensland and Western Australia all say never to use a generator on a day of local fire ban or total fire ban. Parks Victoria's Warby-Ovens page is different: a generator may be used on a Total Fire Ban day only if a 3-metre area around it is cleared of anything flammable. That is one park, so do not assume it applies elsewhere.

The set-up rules are consistent. NSW and Queensland ask you to keep the generator clear of fuels and dry grass, run extension cords that are rated for outdoor use and do not cross access tracks, follow the manufacturer's guidelines and never leave it running unattended. Explore Parks WA asks for at least 3 m of clear space around it. Victoria's state forest page says to fit a spark arrestor to the exhaust, keep 1.5 m of cleared space around it, and have water or a stored-pressure extinguisher to hand. We did not find an official rule on fuel storage, so check the park's page.
tips: No generator on fire ban days

sections.heading: Rest areas and the roadside
body: At a Queensland general vehicle rest area, you must not operate a generator or engine-driven equipment between 7pm and 7am. A person who camps on a state-controlled road to manage fatigue must not operate a generator while camping, and the maximum penalty for breaching that rule is 20 penalty units.
We found no equivalent generator rule for rest areas in the other states, so the sign at the site is the guide. Queensland also says its rest areas are not camping sites.

sections.heading: Medical and disability exemptions
body: NSW, Queensland and Western Australia all make a path for people who need a generator for a medical device or disability aid. NSW asks you to contact the local NPWS office before you enter the park or book, with evidence such as a medical certificate. Queensland allows a small low-decibel generator of up to 2.0 kVA to charge auxiliary batteries for a medical device where generators are otherwise not allowed, with a current medical certificate. WA invites an application for exemption through its contact page.
tips: Contact the park before you go

sections.heading: What to do instead
body: Queensland's own advice is to consider solar panels, inverters or charging while driving. A battery and inverter or a portable power station runs a fridge and charges devices without a generator's noise, and Victoria's forest page also encourages solar or battery power.

For power on tap, book a powered site at a holiday park or caravan park, which is where air conditioning and appliances belong. None of the WA park campgrounds have powered campsites, according to Explore Parks WA, so power there means bringing your own source or choosing a private park.

sections.heading: Check this rule at the place in AussieCamps
body: A place page in AussieCamps shows the land manager's facilities and rules as the park agency publishes them, and a power filter narrows 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks to sites that list power. The stored place details need no coverage; live maps, routing, weather and photos do. AussieCamps is made for iPhone.
It does not replace the official rule. Confirm with the land manager whether generators are allowed and when.

faq: Can I use a generator in a national park in Australia?

Only where the park allows it. Queensland says generators are not permitted in most parks and forests, NSW generally does not permit them without a sign or the park manager's consent, and Western Australia and Tasmania allow them at named campgrounds within set hours. Check the campground's own page or sign before you pack one.
What time do I have to turn my generator off at a campsite?

It depends on the campground. Explore Parks WA says permitted hours are usually between 8am and 9pm, Lime Bay in Tasmania requires generators off by 9pm, and Keep River National Park in the Northern Territory allows them from 7.30am to 8.30pm at one campground. In NSW parks that have noise curfews, generators fall under them.
Can I run a generator at a roadside rest area?

Not overnight in Queensland. The state's rules bar operating a generator or engine-driven equipment at a general vehicle rest area between 7pm and 7am, and a person camping on a state-controlled road must not operate one at all. Other states do not publish a rest-area generator rule we could confirm, so follow the sign.
Can I use a generator on a total fire ban day?

Usually not. NSW, Queensland and Western Australia all say not to use a generator on a day of local fire ban or total fire ban. Victoria's Warby-Ovens National Park is the exception we found, where a generator may be used on a Total Fire Ban day only if a 3-metre area around it is cleared of anything flammable.

can-i-stay-overnight-at-a-rest-area-in-a.title: Can I Stay Overnight at a Rest Area in Australia? 2026
can-i-stay-overnight-at-a-rest-area-in-a.description: It depends on the sign and the state. Queensland allows 20 hours unless signed, WA 24 hours only where signed. Rest area time limits by road authority, 2026.
can-i-stay-overnight-at-a-rest-area-in-a.imageAlt: A roadside rest area on the New England Highway at Bolivia, New South Wales, with toilet blocks, bins and a rock outcrop behind the gum trees
can-i-stay-overnight-at-a-rest-area-in-a.intro: It depends on the road authority and the sign: Queensland allows up to 20 hours at a rest area unless a sign says otherwise, and Western Australia allows up to 24 consecutive hours only at rest areas signed for overnight stops. Elsewhere the sign and the local council decide, and Queensland, Western Australia and NSW all say rest areas are not for camping.

sections.heading: The short answer by state
body: Only Queensland, Western Australia and the Northern Territory publish a time limit we could confirm. In the other states the sign at the site decides, and councils can add their own rules. The sleeping in a car guide and the free camping guide cover the wider picture. This page is about the rest area itself.
tips: Limits are in hours, not nights

table.caption: Overnight stays at roadside rest areas by state and territory, checked 21 October 2026.
head: State or territory
Overnight stay at a rest area
Source
rows: Advice conflicts. Service NSW says rest areas are not for camping and Transport for NSW says you cannot stay overnight. The July 2026 planning practice note says camping may be permitted unless a no camping or no overnight stays sign is up.
Service NSW, Transport for NSW, NSW Department of Planning
No statewide time limit found in the official sources we could open. Councils can ban overnight stays under local laws, so read the sign.
Victorian road authority and council pages
Up to 20 hours in the 24 hours from when you entered, unless signed otherwise. Not camping sites. Heavy vehicle rest areas are for heavy vehicles only.
No statewide overnight limit found. Some councils ban camping or overnight stays at rest areas, for example the Barossa Council.
Up to 24 consecutive hours, only at rest areas signed to permit it. No overnight stop without that sign.
No statewide rest-area stay limit found. Some councils run permit areas for self-contained vehicles, for example 48 hours free in Northern Midlands.
Territory policy says no more than 24 hours at any one rest area. The Territory lists which highway stops allow 24-hour overnight camping, and some are marked camping not permitted.

sections.heading: What the signs mean
body: A blue guide sign with a white tree and picnic table marks a rest area in Queensland, and a rest area ahead sign gives the distance. It tells you the rest area is there. It does not say you may sleep there.

In Western Australia the sign that matters is the 24-hour information sign. Main Roads' policy says rest areas where 24-hour or overnight stays are permitted have a sign in a prominent position where every motorist entering can see it, and no overnight stops are allowed if there is no such signage. Signs showing a limit or a ban on overnight stays override the general rule in Queensland too, because the road authority can set a different period or restrict use.
tips: Blue tree and table sign: rest area only
WA: no 24-hour sign, no overnight stop

sections.heading: Time limits by road authority
body: Queensland's regulation says that where a rest area sign states no period, the maximum stay is 20 hours within the 24-hour period starting when the person first entered. The maximum penalty for breaching a sign or that limit is 20 penalty units. Queensland says there are just over 450 rest areas, and the three types are motorist, heavy vehicle and combined.

Main Roads WA says there are some 24-hour rest areas across the state, that they are not intended for camping, and that stopping at them should not exceed 24 consecutive hours. Its policy says most of its rest areas are not meant to be a camping place or for stays beyond 24 hours. The Northern Territory's rest area policy likewise says road users may not stay at any one rest area longer than 24 hours, while allowing limited overnight stays so tired drivers can rest. The Territory's rest stop list marks which highway stops allow 24-hour overnight camping and which do not.
tips: NT: 24 hours at one rest area

sections.heading: What a rest area is for
body: Rest areas exist to manage fatigue. Main Roads WA explains the effect of overnight use: a rest area heavily occupied by people on free overnight stays becomes unavailable to motorists with genuine fatigue, and its policy says 24-hour rest areas are in general not built close to civic sites that serve towns or where they would compete with local businesses. About 200 of its rest areas are heavy vehicle rest areas for truck drivers.

Queensland says truck drivers need to rest in the heavy vehicle rest areas, which are not for other motorists, and that fines may apply if you are not driving a commercial or heavy vehicle and are found using one. In Queensland, using a heavy vehicle rest area without a reasonable excuse can bring a maximum penalty of 20 penalty units.

sections.heading: When the site says No Camping
body: Do not stay. A no camping or no overnight stays sign, put up by a council or a road authority, is the line the NSW practice note draws, and Queensland requires road users to comply with the sign or marking at a designated rest area. A council can also ban camping outright: the Barossa Council in South Australia says camping or overnight stays are prohibited in any public reserve, car park, road or rest area in its region, and people found camping can face an on-the-spot fine.

Queensland's roadside rule is narrower than most people expect. A person may camp on a state-controlled road, other than a motorway or toll road, only to manage fatigue, between 4pm and 8am, outside a built-up area, at least 200 m from any kerb, 100 m from a rest area entry or exit and 9 m from the nearest traffic lane, and where no sign or marking prohibits it. A fire, fire pit or generator is not allowed while camping there.
tips: Sign beats any app or guide

sections.heading: Staying respectful
body: Queensland's regulation sets the baseline for a general vehicle rest area: put litter in the bins provided, do not light a fire or use a fire pit, do not operate a generator or engine-driven equipment between 7pm and 7am, and do not use machinery or appliances that unreasonably interfere with others. The road authority can direct you to leave if you breach these.

Practical habits follow from that. Keep your set-up inside the vehicle, leave bays free for other drivers, take your rubbish with you if the bins are full and leave early. Main Roads WA asks visitors to leave heavy vehicle rest areas free for trucks where they can, or leave enough room for trucks to pull up safely.
tips: No fire, no generator at night

sections.heading: What to do instead
body: If a rest area does not allow an overnight stop, a caravan park or a booked campground removes the doubt. Some councils run their own overnight areas, and Northern Midlands Council in Tasmania issues free permits for up to 48 hours for self-contained vehicles at designated, signposted areas, with no waste discharge allowed.

State forests in NSW and Victoria are the usual free option for camping, and the free camping guide covers where it is legal. The sleeping in a car guide covers the safety side of a night in the vehicle.

sections.heading: Check this rule at the place in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 5,552 rest areas from road authorities and public datasets next to 1,838 campgrounds, and a rest area's place page carries the facilities, such as toilets, that the authority publishes. Stored details open with no coverage, while the map, routing, weather and photos need a connection. It runs on iPhone only.
The app does not replace the sign. A listing can be out of date, so confirm the time limit on site or with the road authority or council.

faq: How long can I stay at a rest area in Queensland?

Up to 20 hours within the 24-hour period starting when you first entered, unless a sign gives a different limit. Queensland says general and recreational vehicles can stop at a rest area for that long, but rest areas are not camping sites or an accommodation option. Heavy vehicle rest areas are for heavy vehicles only.
Can I sleep overnight at a rest area in Western Australia?

Only where a sign permits it, and for no more than 24 consecutive hours. Main Roads WA says its 24-hour rest areas are not intended for camping, and its policy says no overnight stops are allowed if there is no signage permitting them.
Can I stay overnight at a rest area in NSW?

The official advice conflicts. Service NSW says rest areas are not for camping, and Transport for NSW says you cannot stay overnight. A July 2026 planning practice note says camping in a roadside rest area may be permitted unless a no camping or no overnight stays sign has been placed there, so read the sign and check the council.
What does a No Camping sign at a rest area mean?

It means do not set up camp or stay overnight there, and the sign beats any app listing or guide. In Queensland, a person must comply with the sign or marking for a rest area, and the maximum penalty for failing to is 20 penalty units. Move on to a caravan park, campground or a rest area that allows an overnight stop.
