can-i-camp-on-aboriginal-land-without-a-.title: Do I Need a Permit to Camp on Aboriginal Land in Australia?
can-i-camp-on-aboriginal-land-without-a-.description: Yes, on Aboriginal land off public roads. Permits cover roads like the Great Central Road, and camping is allowed only at named sites. Rules by state, 2026.
can-i-camp-on-aboriginal-land-without-a-.imageAlt: A red dirt road running through desert scrub towards Kata Tjuta on Tjukaruru Road in the Northern Territory
can-i-camp-on-aboriginal-land-without-a-.intro: Yes, for Aboriginal land off public roads: it is private land, and you need a permit from the land council or Aboriginal body to enter it, travel its roads such as the Great Central Road, or stay overnight. Passing through a community on a public road needs no permit to reach its public areas such as the store, and where camping is allowed on Aboriginal land it is at designated sites that the permit or park names.

sections.heading: The short answer by state
body: There is no single Australian permit. Each land council, state agency or Aboriginal corporation issues its own, and the same trip can need two or three. Apply before you leave, because the land council or agency consults Traditional Owners before it decides.
tips: Permits are not shared across borders

table.caption: Permits for Aboriginal land by state and territory, checked 21 October 2026.
head: State or territory
Permit and who issues it
Camping
Source
rows: Central Land Council transit permits for Tjukaruru Road, Gary Junction Road, Sandy Blight Road and Glen Helen to Papunya Road. Mereenie Tour Pass for the Mereenie Loop. Entry permit for other non-public roads and the Simpson Desert tracks.
Tjukaruru Road: only at the Kaltukatjara (Docker River) campground. Mereenie Loop: no camping.
Northern Land Council permit to enter Aboriginal land, use its private roads, or visit a community. Allow up to 10 days, and more for recreation permits.
Only if camping is written into the permit, at recreation sites the Traditional Owners have identified.

Transit permit through the Aboriginal Lands Trust reserves from the Department of Planning, Lands and Heritage, plus a 3-day Ngaanyatjarra Council permit for the Great Central Road and other roads on its list.
The Council's transit permit gives three days and two nights. Great Central Road visitors cannot enter communities.
Uunguu Visitor Pass for Mitchell River National Park, bought online before you arrive.
DBCA camping fees apply at the park's campgrounds.
APY Lands: no transit permits for tourists. Maralinga Tjarutja Lands and Mamungari Conservation Park: permit from Maralinga Tjarutja, allow 4 to 6 weeks.
Mamungari Conservation Park: entry is free and camping fees apply.
No single permit. Contact the Land Trust or local council for permission to camp on Aboriginal land.
Pre-book national park campsites in advance.
Park pass for Kakadu and for Uluru-Kata Tjuta. These are entry fees, not Aboriginal land permits.
No camping inside Uluru-Kata Tjuta. Kakadu: designated campgrounds, with a permit to camp elsewhere.

sections.heading: Why a permit is needed
body: The Central Land Council says Aboriginal people own more than half the land in its region as inalienable freehold under the Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act 1976, and that it is private land. The Northern Land Council says the same: Aboriginal land is not Crown land or public land, and Commonwealth and Northern Territory law require a written permit to enter it.

Travellers who stay on public roads in the CLC region do not need one. The CLC says anyone passing through a community on a public road can visit its public areas, such as the store, art centre or local government office, without a permit. A transit permit is needed if the community is reached by a non-public road. In Western Australia, the Aboriginal Lands Trust estate covers over 8 per cent of the state, and entry onto its reserved lands needs an Entry Permit.

sections.heading: Which routes need a permit
body: In Central Australia the CLC lists Tjukaruru Road between Uluru-Kata Tjuta and the WA border, Gary Junction Road, the Sandy Blight Road and the Glen Helen to Papunya Road. The last allows day access for individuals only, for the Ikuntji Arts Centre, with no photography or driving around the community. The Mereenie Loop uses a Mereenie Tour Pass, free from CLC reception in Alice Springs, and available for a small fee from outlets including Tourism Central Australia and Kings Canyon Resort. The CLC also says visitors to the Simpson Desert's Madigan Line, Hay River Track and Colson Track need an entry permit. The Tanami Road is not on the CLC's transit list, but ask the CLC before camping beside it.

In Western Australia, Ngaanyatjarra Council permits cover the Great Central Road, Gunbarrel Highway, Connie Sue Highway, Heather Highway, Ngaanyatjarra Southern Road, Sandy Blight Junction Road and Giles Mulga Park Road, and the abandoned section of the Gunbarrel is not open to the public. Permits for the Anne Beadell Highway and Gary Junction Road come from the state department, not the Council. In South Australia, the Anne Beadell also needs a Woomera Prohibited Area Tourist Access Permit and, in the Maralinga Tjarutja Lands and Mamungari Conservation Park, a Maralinga Tjarutja permit.

sections.heading: How to get one, cost and timing
body: The CLC issues transit permits free and self-issued online (the Mereenie Tour Pass is the exception), and entry permits take at least a week. The NLC says to allow up to 10 days, although its recreation FAQ says at least 10 days may be needed, and says in most cases there is no charge, although Traditional Owners have set access and camping fees for some locations. Western Australian transit permits are free, are issued on weekdays in business hours, are required for each vehicle, and should be applied for several weeks ahead but not more than 30 days before you travel. Some communities and native title holders also charge for entry or camping, or require a Visitor's Pass.

For the Great Central Road, the Shire of Ngaanyatjarraku says to allow two to three weeks for the two applications. The APY asks for 30 days and says processing takes 10 to 14 days. Maralinga Tjarutja asks for 4 to 6 weeks. Group members can share one application with the CLC. In WA, each vehicle in a convoy needs its own.
tips: One application per vehicle in WA

sections.heading: Where you can camp
body: A permit to enter is not a permit to camp. The NLC says permits generally only provide for entry and access unless camping, fishing or filming is written into them, and its recreation permits cover sites the Traditional Owners have identified, each with rules on visitor numbers and length of stay. Along transit routes it says stopping is permitted only in certain locations. The one exception it lists is the Cox Peninsula, where its Kenbi Open Area Declaration Map shows areas that allow restricted access and camping without a permit.

In Cape York, the tourism guide says you must contact the Land Trust or local council for permission before camping on Aboriginal land. At Kakadu, camping is at the park's campgrounds, and you need a permit to camp outside designated sites. Camping is not permitted inside Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park, which has campgrounds at Ayers Rock Resort and Curtin Springs outside it.

sections.heading: What not to do
body: Stay on the permitted road and do not turn into a community unless your permit covers it. The Shire of Ngaanyatjarraku says visitors on the Great Central Road may not enter any community, and only people providing essential services may. The CLC says the possession, consumption and sale of alcohol on Aboriginal land in its region is prohibited, although transit visitors may carry it provided they do not drink it, so check the rules for each community on your route.

Do not photograph people without their permission, and ask first. The CLC says non-commercial private photography needs no media permit, but filming or photographing for commercial or publishing purposes does. Closures for ceremonies and funerals can happen at short notice, and the NLC asks visitors to respect them. Without a permit, the NLC says unauthorised entry can bring a fine of 50 penalty units under Commonwealth law, or 8 penalty units under Northern Territory law, and insurance claims may depend on a valid permit.
tips: Do not enter communities on transit
Carry alcohol, do not drink it

sections.heading: What to do instead
body: If you do not want to arrange permits, use public roads and parks that welcome campers. Kakadu has campgrounds in all seven regions and a 7-day park pass, and the Northern Territory's park campgrounds are bookable. The Red Centre Way guide covers the Mereenie Loop and the West MacDonnell Ranges, and the Northern Territory and Western Australia guides cover the rest of the permit picture.
A guided tour is another option. The NLC says tour operators on Aboriginal land need a work permit, so ask an operator which permits it holds for your route.

sections.heading: Check this rule at the place in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps carries 745 national parks and 1,838 campgrounds with the land manager's facilities and rules as the park agency publishes them, plus guides and trips for planning a route. Stored place details open without coverage, while the map, routing, weather and photos need a connection. It is for iPhone only.
It does not show whether you need a permit. Confirm with the land council or park agency before you go.

faq: Do I need a permit to drive the Great Central Road?

Yes. Western Australia says a transit permit is required between the Northern Territory border and Laverton, and the Ngaanyatjarra Council issues a 3-day transit permit for its section. The Northern Territory part from Yulara needs a Central Land Council transit permit for Tjukaruru Road. Apply before you travel, and allow two to three weeks for the WA applications.
Can I get a transit permit to cross the APY Lands in South Australia?

No. The APY says transit permits are not issued to tourists, travellers or 4WD enthusiasts who want to pass through any part of the lands. Entry permits are for people with a purpose such as visiting family or friends or working there, and APY asks you to apply 30 days before your visit.
Do I need a permit for the Tanami Road?

It is not on the Central Land Council's list of roads that need a transit permit. The CLC does say visitors to Aboriginal land outside larger communities need a permit, so do not assume the land beside the road is open for camping. Ask the CLC before you leave the road.
Is a permit free, and how long does it take?

Often free, but the time varies. The CLC issues transit and simple permits free and entry permits take at least a week, the NLC says most permits have no charge and to allow up to 10 days (its recreation FAQ says at least 10 days may be needed), and Western Australian transit permits are free. Traditional Owners can set access or camping fees at some places, and permits can be refused.

can-i-take-a-campervan-or-caravan-on-the.title: Can I Take a Caravan or Campervan on the Spirit of Tasmania?
can-i-take-a-campervan-or-caravan-on-the.description: Yes. The Spirit of Tasmania takes caravans and campervans if you book the exact length and height, switch off gas and clear biosecurity. Rules checked 2026.
can-i-take-a-campervan-or-caravan-on-the.imageAlt: A Spirit of Tasmania ferry passing a breakwater footbridge as it enters Port Frederick at Devonport, Tasmania
can-i-take-a-campervan-or-caravan-on-the.intro: Yes. The Spirit of Tasmania carries campervans, motorhomes and caravans between Geelong and Devonport, provided you book the exact length and height, keep your gas turned off and tagged, and clear Tasmania's biosecurity rules. You are charged by total length, towed unit and attachments included, and TT-Line can deny passage if the size you declared turns out to be wrong.

sections.heading: The short answer by vehicle and item
body: Most of the rules come from two TT-Line documents, the booking pages and the carriage of dangerous goods policy, plus Biosecurity Tasmania. The table gives the rule for each part of a rig, checked on 21 October 2026.

table.caption: Taking a caravan or campervan on the Spirit of Tasmania, checked 21 October 2026.
head: Vehicle or item
What the rule says
Source
rows: Book it as a vehicle and choose the motorhome or campervan option. It has its own category, with or without a towed unit.
Book under the towing a caravan or trailer option. Registration details for every towed unit are needed at booking.
Measure end to end, including the towed unit, drawbar, bike racks and gas cylinders. Towed rigs are priced from a 0.01 to 7.00 metre band plus a rate for each extra metre.
Include roof racks, kayaks, bikes and any towed unit. There is no extra charge for height, but a wrong height can mean passage is denied at check-in.
One additional cylinder up to 25 kg (50 litres water capacity) in a caravan or motorhome, turned off, upright and secure. Gas systems must never be active on board.
Your caravan is off limits during the crossing. Book a cabin or recliner.
Fresh fruit and vegetables are not permitted. Honey is restricted. If in doubt, leave it at home.

sections.heading: How size and fares work
body: TT-Line charges by total length, so measure the whole rig as it will sail. That means the caravan and drawbar, any rear bike rack, and the gas cylinder on the front, not just the tow vehicle. Sizes are confirmed at check-in, and if the figures you gave were short you may pay extra for the added length.

Height does not change the price, but it still matters. The total includes roof racks and anything on the roof, and TT-Line warns that failing to give the correct height may mean passage is denied. Book your outward and return sailings together, because TT-Line says that gives access to its best fares and deck space.

Space for towed vehicles runs out. For school holidays, Christmas and Easter with fixed dates, TT-Line suggests booking 10 to 11 months ahead. Its 2026 release says bookings can be made up to 12 months ahead.

sections.heading: Gas cylinders and the fridge
body: Gas cylinders are Category 1 dangerous goods. A caravan, motorhome or camper may carry one additional cylinder of up to 25 kg (50 litres water capacity), and it must be secure, upright, turned off and in date. Cylinders must meet AS2468, AS2469 or AS2470, stamped on the cylinder, with an inspection within the last 10 years.

TT-Line staff check the LPG system on caravans and campervans, isolate it and put a HAZARD tag on it. It stays off for the whole voyage and until the vehicle has cleared the port precinct. A propane cylinder connected to an appliance is not permitted, so disconnect it first. Cylinders that fail the conditions are confiscated, or collected by staff and returned at the other port if they are only badly secured.

The policy does not mention fridges. Because gas systems must never be active on board, a fridge that runs on gas will be off for the crossing, so ask TT-Line how it handles battery or mains-powered fridges and pack food for the delay. Jerry cans may carry diesel only, up to 50 litres each.

sections.heading: Where you sleep and what about pets
body: You cannot live in the vehicle during the crossing. TT-Line says a caravan is off limits on the ship, and passengers are not permitted on the vehicle decks while the ship is at sea. Cabins include bedding, linen and towels, and budget recliners are offered in a private lounge.

Pets can travel, and TT-Line strongly recommends booking a kennel. Kennels are in a ventilated area, the price is shown when you book, and you cannot visit your pet on the vehicle decks while the ship is at sea. Dogs entering Tasmania need hydatid tapeworm treatment within 14 days before entry, a tick check and a signed declaration. Pet-friendly cabins for up to two pets are being added on the new ships.

sections.heading: Biosecurity at Geelong and Devonport
body: Biosecurity Tasmania says to clean vehicles, caravans and trailers of visible soil and mud before boarding, and to clean and dry camping gear, bikes, boats and fishing gear. Fresh fruit and vegetables, including potatoes, herbs, garlic, ginger and onion, are not permitted. Cooked, canned, preserved and commercially dried produce is allowed, and honey is restricted because of varroa mite on the mainland.

At Geelong, security staff ask biosecurity questions, and you may be asked to dispose of restricted items. A vehicle may get a Notice to Stop sticker, and if it does you make yourself known to the Biosecurity Inspectors at the Devonport terminal for a second inspection. Random vehicle checks also happen there. Leave firewood at home if you are unsure, because items can be inspected and seized.
Penalties may apply for non-compliance, and the officer has the final say on whether an item is allowed in. The interstate biosecurity guide covers planning the fridge around a crossing.

sections.heading: The new ships and the vehicle rules
body: TT-Line announced in September 2026 that Spirit of Tasmania IV would leave Geelong and Spirit of Tasmania V would leave Devonport on the first passenger sailings from 31 October 2026. Bookings for the expanded accommodation and capacity opened on 16 September, and the new ships carry more than three times the caravan capacity of the current vessels.

The release announcing this describes no change to the vehicle rules, and the ports stay Geelong and Devonport, with the new Spirit Quay terminal at Devonport, which TT-Line expected to be operational by late 2026. Check-in opens 1.5 to 2.5 hours before departure and closes 45 minutes before. All times are indicative, so read the live schedule and your e-ticket, and confirm which ship is on your sailing.

sections.heading: If your rig is longer or taller than the limit
body: TT-Line's pages we could open give no numeric maximum for a towed rig. The fare page gives 6.0 metres as the maximum total length for its standard vehicle and campervan or motorhome categories, and separately prices caravans, camper trailers and motorhomes with or without a towed unit in a 0.01 to 7.00 metre band plus a rate for each extra metre. TT-Line also says passage may be denied if your length or height cannot be accommodated. The cleanest fix is to ring the contact centre on 1800 634 906, Monday to Saturday, 10am to 6pm, or email contactus@spiritoftasmania.com.au, with the exact figures before you pay.
Do not shave the measurements to fit a booking. Check-in confirms them, and a wrong height can end the trip at the gate.

sections.heading: What to do instead
body: If the rig is too big, or the schedule too tight, consider leaving the van on the mainland and hiring a campervan in Tasmania, or travelling as a car passenger and staying in roofed accommodation or holiday parks once you arrive. Either way, book early, because TT-Line recommends booking 10 to 11 months ahead for fixed holiday dates and busy sailings fill.

Tasmania's park campgrounds and rules are set by the park agency, and the Tasmania camping rules guide covers the Parks Pass. The Tasmania loop guide shows how a ten-day trip fits around the crossing.

sections.heading: Plan the Tasmanian leg in AussieCamps
body: Once you land at Devonport, the island leg is where AussieCamps helps. A place page gathers what the park agency publishes for a site: facilities, fees, rules and access notes. The Tasmanian data includes 27 campgrounds and 80 dump points, filters narrow them by water, toilets, power and vehicle access, and a trip keeps ordered stops, arrival dates and route distance.

Core place details are stored on the phone and open without a connection, while live maps, directions, forecasts and photos need coverage. The app is for iPhone. It cannot check your rig against TT-Line limits or Tasmania's produce rules, so settle those with TT-Line and Biosecurity Tasmania.
tips: Build a trip for the loop

faq: How long can a caravan be on the Spirit of Tasmania?

TT-Line does not publish a numeric maximum for a towed rig on the pages we could open. It prices a towed rig from a 0.01 to 7.00 metre band plus a rate for each extra metre, and says passage can be denied if it cannot fit the length or height you booked. For a long or tall rig, phone the contact centre on 1800 634 906 before you book.
Can I sleep in my campervan or caravan on the Spirit of Tasmania?
No. TT-Line says your caravan is off limits during the crossing, and passengers may not go to the vehicle decks while the ship is at sea. Book a cabin or a recliner and pack an overnight bag.
Can I take gas bottles to Tasmania on the ferry?

Yes, within TT-Line's dangerous goods policy. A caravan or motorhome may carry one additional cylinder up to 25 kg (50 litres water capacity). It must be upright, secure, turned off, stamped to an Australian Standard and inspected within 10 years, and staff isolate and tag the gas system.
Can I bring fruit, vegetables or honey into Tasmania?

Fresh fruit and vegetables are not permitted. Honey is restricted, and Biosecurity Tasmania says to leave it at home if you are unsure. Security staff at Geelong ask biosecurity questions, you may be given a Notice to Stop to show inspectors at Devonport, and random checks happen there, so eat or bin produce before you board.

can-i-camp-on-private-land-or-a-farm-in-.title: Can I Camp on Private Land or a Farm in Australia? 2026 Rules
can-i-camp-on-private-land-or-a-farm-in-.description: Yes, with the owner's permission, or it is trespass. Hosts may also need council approval. NSW, WA and Victoria rules, fire bans and tips, checked 2026.
can-i-camp-on-private-land-or-a-farm-in-.imageAlt: Two dome tents pitched on grassy bush ground beside a creek near Mansfield, Victoria
can-i-camp-on-private-land-or-a-farm-in-.intro: Yes, but only with the owner's permission: camping on private land without consent is trespass. Whether the owner also needs council or planning approval to host you depends on the state and council, on how many people camp and for how long, and on whether anyone pays.

sections.heading: The short answer by state
body: Permission from the owner is the first rule everywhere. After that, approval rules for hosted camping are set by each state and, in many places, by each council. Hosts carry the approval duty, but a traveller who knows the basics can ask better questions.

table.caption: Camping on private land by state, checked 21 October 2026.
head: State or territory
What the rules say
Source
rows: Council approval is not needed for up to two caravans, campervans or tents on any land with the owner's permission, if each stay is no more than two days at a time and total use is no more than 60 days in 12 months. Farms of 15 hectares or more can host up to 20 people for 21 days a visit without planning or building approval, if requirements including tents 6 metres from buildings and vans are met.
NSW Planning practice note, 1 July 2026; NSW Planning agritourism page

You can camp up to 5 nights in any 28 consecutive days on land you own or have a legal right to occupy. More than 5 nights needs written approval from the local government (up to 24 months) or the Minister.
Caravan Parks and Camping Grounds Regulations 1997

Set by council local laws and the planning scheme. Mount Alexander Shire, for example, requires a permit to camp on land without a dwelling, outside an approved camping ground, though it says a Local Law 13 change lets people camp in caravans or tiny homes on wheels without one (conditions not listed). A park must be registered as a caravan park with the council.
Mount Alexander Shire; Consumer Affairs Victoria
Queensland, South Australia, Tasmania, NT and ACT
We could not confirm a single state rule for hosted farm camping. Councils decide through their planning schemes, so ask the host whether the council has approved the site.

sections.heading: Permission and trespass
body: Trespass is an offence, and each state has its own law. In NSW, the Inclosed Lands Protection Act 1901 makes it an offence to enter inclosed land without the consent of the owner, occupier or person in charge, or to stay after being asked to leave. Leaving a gate or slip-panel open is a separate offence under the same Act.

Queensland's Summary Offences Act makes it an offence to enter or remain in someone's house, yard or business premises without permission, with a maximum penalty of one year's imprisonment, and Legal Aid Queensland says police use discretion. Its page does not address paddocks or rural land, so ask a rural landholder before you rely on it. The practical rule is simple: no consent, no camp.
Get the owner's yes in a message or email, not only at the gate. It records the dates and number of people, and it helps if a neighbour or a ranger asks.

sections.heading: What the host has to get right
body: NSW treats a camping ground as a use needing development consent, plus a council approval under the Local Government Act unless an exemption applies. The 1 July 2026 practice note says a person who operates a camping ground without the required approval commits an offence, and councils can order the use to stop. Remote camping grounds can be approved as primitive camping grounds, which need a limited set of facilities including water, a toilet and refuse disposal, and allow an average of two sites per hectare.

Western Australia's rules turn on days. Up to 5 nights in 28 consecutive days needs the owner's approval only, according to the City of Kwinana, while longer stays need the owner and the local government. The City also says that if an owner regularly allows short-term camping, the property becomes a caravan park or camping ground and needs planning and building approvals. The WA Government says special approval is still required for more than one caravan on a single lot.
A host who charges campers can hit these limits quickly. That is their paperwork, but it explains why a farmer may say no, offer only two nights or point you to a registered site.

sections.heading: Fire bans and rural fire rules
body: Rural land carries the same fire rules as public land, with no ranger to remind you. In NSW, the Rural Fire Service says a Total Fire Ban means no fire in the open, and the exception for gas barbecues has conditions. Check the fire authority for the district on the morning you arrive, not just when you book.

Ask the owner where a fire is allowed, how close to dry grass or sheds, and where to find water. If a ban is on or a fire is not allowed on the property, plan a gas cooker meal or a cold one. The campfire guide covers the rules by state.
tips: Ask where a fire is allowed

sections.heading: Farm conditions to ask about
body: A campsite on a farm may have no mains water and no sewer. NSW expects approved temporary camping grounds to have an adequate water supply, toilets and rubbish facilities for the time they run, so a host who is approved should be able to tell you what exists. If they are not set up, bring your own water, a portable toilet and a way to carry out all rubbish.

Ask about stock and dogs. Livestock can move through a paddock overnight, and a farm may not take pets. Ask which tracks you may drive on, where to park to keep vehicles off wet ground, and who to ring if you need help.

sections.heading: Traveller tips for a farm stay
body: Ask first, and say how many people, what you are camping in and how long. Book through the farm or the platform it uses, and bring the confirmation. Arrive in daylight, because gates, creeks and cattle grids are harder to read after dark.

Leave gates as you found them: open if open, shut if shut. Stay on the tracks you were shown, keep noise down and take the whole camp out with you. Before you drive away, tell the owner you have left and thank them.

sections.heading: What to do instead
body: If the owner says no or the paperwork is unclear, there are plenty of legal options. Caravan parks and holiday parks have approvals and facilities. Park agency campgrounds and signed free camps are covered in the free camping legality guide, and the responsible camping guide covers leaving a place as you found it.

Private hosted sites are bookable through a few platforms, and the Hipcamp alternatives guide covers where to book. Whichever route you use, ask the host whether the site has any council approval it needs, and keep the booking confirmation with you.

sections.heading: Find the alternatives in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps is built around public campgrounds, roadside rest areas and accommodation, with 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks, not private paddocks. Open a nearby place page to see what the land manager publishes on facilities, fees, rules and access, then weigh it against the farm night you are considering. Saved collections hold a backup list, and a trip strings the stops together.

Without reception, the stored place details still open, while routing, forecasts and photos do not load. It is an iPhone app. It cannot tell you whether a property has council approval or allows fires, so put that question to the owner.

faq: Is it legal to camp on a farm in Australia?

Yes, if the owner or occupier says you can. Without that consent you are trespassing, and the owner can ask you to leave. Separately, the owner may need council approval to host campers, which is their responsibility, not yours.
Can I camp on my friend's land for a few nights?

Often yes, with the owner's permission, but the limit differs by state. In NSW the council approval exemption covers up to two caravans, campervans or tents for no more than two days at a time and 60 days a year. In Western Australia you can camp up to 5 nights in any 28 consecutive days on land you own or have a legal right to occupy.
Can I camp in a paddock if the gate is open?
Not on that basis. An open gate or a missing fence is not permission. Ask the owner or manager first, and leave any gate as you found it, because leaving one open can itself be an offence in NSW.
Does a farmer need approval to take paying campers?

Often yes. In NSW a camping ground generally needs development consent and a council approval, and operating one without approval is an offence. A farm stay exemption covers up to 20 people at a time, for up to 21 days a visit, on farms of at least 15 hectares, with other requirements to meet, and other states set their own rules, so ask the host whether they are covered.

can-i-take-alcohol-into-restricted-areas.title: Can I Take Alcohol Into Remote Communities in Australia?
can-i-take-alcohol-into-restricted-areas.description: Sometimes. Some remote communities allow none, others set a carriage limit, and breaches mean seizure and fines. Queensland, NT and WA rules, checked 2026.
can-i-take-alcohol-into-restricted-areas.imageAlt: A graded red dirt road running straight across dry grassland on the Savannah Way near Normanton in Queensland's Gulf Country
can-i-take-alcohol-into-restricted-areas.intro: It depends where you go: some remote communities allow no alcohol at all, some allow a fixed amount, and the rule is set for each community or region by its state or territory government. Check the sign and the government page before you cross the boundary, because breaching a limit can mean seized alcohol, a confiscated vehicle and fines of tens of thousands of dollars.

sections.heading: The short answer by state
body: There is no national rule, and the same trip can cross three systems. Queensland sets a carriage limit for 15 community areas, the Northern Territory declares dry protected areas, and Western Australia uses carriage limits in the Kimberley and a separate list of restricted communities. Each section below says which page to read.
tips: Check the sign and the page

table.caption: Alcohol rules for remote travel by state and territory, checked 21 October 2026.
head: State or territory
What applies to a traveller
Source
rows: Carriage limits in 15 community areas, zero in some. Penalties up to $64,762 for a first offence. Vehicles can be confiscated.

Interim alcohol protected areas ban bringing in, possessing, consuming, selling or supplying alcohol. Aboriginal land is dry unless a permit allows it. Penalty up to 200 penalty units or 12 months in jail.
Carriage limits in Broome, Derby, Fitzroy Crossing, Halls Creek, Kununurra, Wyndham and Carnarvon, and within 5 km of the shire boundaries. Fine of $40,000.
WA Department of Local Government, Sport and Cultural Industries

Bringing in and possessing liquor is prohibited in each listed community, with a $2,000 fine for most people ($5,000 for licensees and managers). Some list exemptions for transiting vehicles or tourists.
WA Department of Local Government, Sport and Cultural Industries
The APY says permit holders must comply with the laws on alcohol possession and sale on the lands. Transit permits are not issued to tourists.

sections.heading: Queensland: Cape York and Gulf communities
body: The Queensland Government lists 15 restricted community areas, and a restricted area is the whole shire unless the page says otherwise. A carriage limit is the most you can have, per person on foot or per vehicle, boat or aircraft however many people are in it. In some communities the limit is zero.

A bona fide traveller is someone, including a tourist, who can prove their destination is outside the restricted area, for example with an itinerary, camping permits, a licence with a home address elsewhere or a booking. On named roads only, such as the Savannah Way at Doomadgee, Frenchmen's Road and Portland Roads Road at Lockhart River and the Bloomfield Track at Wujal Wujal, extra alcohol may travel through if it is covered and secured, not taken out, not drunk, and you stop only at prescribed public facilities. That page was last updated in 2016, so confirm it by phone on 13 74 68.
tips: Zero in four Cape York communities

table.caption: Queensland carriage limits for Cape York and Gulf communities, from qld.gov.au, checked 21 October 2026.
head: Community
Carriage limit
Source
rows: Possession prohibited. The Peninsula Development Road through the shire is outside the restricted area.
2 litres unfortified wine and 4.5 litres (12 cans) of beer and pre-mix under 4%
4.5 litres (12 cans) of beer and pre-mix up to 4%
Up to 22.5 litres of beer under 4% (two cartons of 30 cans). Wine and spirits are zero.
11.25 litres (30 cans) of beer and pre-mix up to 4%
2 litres unfortified wine plus either 11.25 litres of beer or 9 litres of pre-mix up to 5.5%

sections.heading: Queensland fines and powers
body: Going into a restricted area with more than the limit is an offence. The maximum penalty is 375 penalty units for a first offence, 525 units or six months in jail for a second and 750 units or 18 months for a third, with the unit at $172.70 from 1 July 2026. Attempting to bring in alcohol above the limit carries up to 375 units.

Police can stop and search vehicles entering or in a restricted area, take alcohol, and take the vehicle used to bring it in. Mapoon, Hope Vale, Cherbourg, Palm Island, Woorabinda and Yarrabah also have restrictions, so read the community page before you go.

sections.heading: Northern Territory
body: Since 16 February 2023, communities previously under the Commonwealth's Stronger Futures law are dry again as interim alcohol protected areas. It is illegal to bring in, possess, consume, sell or supply alcohol in them. The Director of Liquor Licensing's notice says they repeal on 28 February 2027, but a Liquor Amendment Bill 2026 (introduced 23 July 2026) proposes moving them into the General Restricted Area framework, and a 17 October 2026 news report says it has passed. We could not open an official page confirming this, so check the current position with the NT Government before you travel. Boundaries are certified plans on the NTLIS site.

On Aboriginal land, alcohol is banned unless a permit allows it. The Central Land Council says transit visitors may carry alcohol provided they do not drink it on Aboriginal land, while the NT Government says bringing it into a protected area is an offence. Do not rely on the transit wording until you have checked that community. Police can stop and search vehicles and seize the vehicle used.

In towns, takeaway buyers anywhere in the NT need approved photo ID. Alice Springs has no takeaway on Mondays or Tuesdays, Tennant Creek none on Sundays, and hours are limited in Alice Springs, Tennant Creek and Katherine. Drinking in public is not permitted in those three towns or parts of Darwin, and across the NT you cannot drink within 2 km of licensed premises.
tips: NT dry areas: check current status

sections.heading: Western Australia: Kimberley and restricted communities
body: The Kimberley carriage limits cover Broome, Derby, Fitzroy Crossing, Halls Creek, Kununurra, Wyndham and Carnarvon, and the area within 5 km of the Broome, Carnarvon, Derby-West Kimberley, Halls Creek and Wyndham-East Kimberley shire boundaries. Per person, you may carry one carton (11.25 litres) of beer, cider or pre-mix at 2.7 to 7 per cent, 3 bottles (2.25 litres) of wine, or 1 litre of spirits or fortified wine, alone or with one other kind, and nothing with two or more other kinds. A vehicle's limit is based on its adult occupants, and the fine is $40,000.

The department lists exemptions for tourists, pastoralists, station owners and remote work site operators, but the page does not give their conditions, so confirm them before you rely on one. Takeaway rules also limit what you can buy: Kimberley-wide, no containers over 1 litre at 6 per cent or more (1.5 litre wine casks excepted) and no beer in glass bottles of 400 mL or more, and Fitzroy Crossing and Halls Creek restrict takeaway above 2.7 per cent to hotel lodgers, and liquor merchants at Halls Creek.

Separately, restricted communities, such as Looma, Strelley and Spinifex, prohibit bringing in and possessing liquor, with a $2,000 fine for most people ($5,000 for licensees and managers), and police can seize it. Some exempt transiting vehicles, meaning those that pass through on a public road without stopping, and some give tourists limited exceptions, such as 50 metres either side of the Anne Beadell Highway at Spinifex. These entries expire on set dates, so read the current list.

sections.heading: Aboriginal land and the APY Lands
body: A permit to enter Aboriginal land is not permission to bring alcohol. The Central Land Council says possession, consumption and sale of alcohol on Aboriginal land in its region is prohibited and severe penalties apply. The Aboriginal land permit guide covers the permits themselves.

In South Australia, the APY says permit holders must comply with the alcohol laws on the lands, and tourist transit permits are not issued. Confirm the current alcohol rules with the APY before you apply for any permit.

sections.heading: Drinking at camp and in town
body: Even where carrying is allowed, drinking may not be. In the Kimberley, drinking on public roads or in private vehicles is an offence unless a permit or licence applies, and so is drinking in parks or public places without the owner's or controlling authority's consent. Campgrounds and parks set their own rules on top, so read the notice at the entrance.

In the Northern Territory, a 2 km rule applies around licensed premises, so a roadside camp near a roadhouse can be inside it. Buy what you need in the last large town within the limits, and do not carry extra for a campfire night in a restricted area.

sections.heading: Plan your route in AussieCamps
body: On a remote leg, the app can show national park campgrounds and rest areas near your route, each with the facilities, fees and rules the land manager publishes. Trips hold ordered stops with dates and the distance between legs, and collections keep the stops you are comparing. Place details open from the phone's stored directory, while live maps, directions and weather need a connection. It runs on iPhone only.

AussieCamps does not map community boundaries or carry alcohol rules. Take those from the Queensland, Northern Territory and Western Australian pages in the sources, and trust the sign at the boundary.

faq: Can I drive through a dry community with alcohol in the car?

Sometimes. Queensland allows extra alcohol only on named roads for a bona fide traveller, kept covered and secured and not consumed. Some Western Australian communities exempt transiting vehicles. The Northern Territory Government says bringing alcohol into a protected area is an offence, while the Central Land Council says transit visitors may carry it if they do not drink it, so check the community first.
How much alcohol can I take to Cape York?

It depends on the community. Aurukun, Lockhart River, Napranum and Wujal Wujal prohibit possession altogether. Kowanyama and Pormpuraaw allow 4.5 litres of lower-strength beer or pre-mix, and the Northern Peninsula Area allows 2 litres of unfortified wine plus one carton of beer or pre-mix. Limits apply per person on foot or per vehicle.
What is the fine for taking alcohol into a restricted community?

In Queensland the first offence carries up to 375 penalty units, $64,762 at the $172.70 unit value from 1 July 2026, and a vehicle may be confiscated. In the Kimberley, going over the carriage limit carries a fine of $40,000, and Western Australian restricted communities carry $2,000 for most people ($5,000 for licensees). The Northern Territory lists up to 200 penalty units or 12 months in jail.
Can I drink at a campsite in a remote area?

Only where the land manager and local rules allow it. In the Kimberley, drinking in public roads, private vehicles and public places is an offence without a permit, licence or the owner's consent, and the Northern Territory bans drinking within 2 km of licensed premises. Read the campground's own rules as well.

can-i-camp-in-a-state-forest-in-australi.title: Can I Camp in a State Forest in Australia? Free and Paid by State 2026
can-i-camp-in-a-state-forest-in-australi.description: Yes, in most states. State forests are free in NSW, Victoria and Tasmania, paid in Queensland and booked in South Australia. Rules by state, 2026.
can-i-camp-in-a-state-forest-in-australi.imageAlt: A still dam surrounded by eucalypt forest at Firth Park Campground in Wombat State Forest, Victoria
can-i-camp-in-a-state-forest-in-australi.intro: Yes, in most states, and the price depends on where the forest is: New South Wales and Victoria let you camp in state forests for free without booking, Tasmania welcomes camping on forestry land unless a sign says no, Queensland charges for every camp, and South Australia books its forest campgrounds online. Western Australia limits park camping to designated campgrounds, so check its forest rules before you stop. The pages below were read on 28 October 2026.

sections.heading: State forests by state
body: A state forest is working forest land that also takes campers, and each state's forestry agency sets its own rules. They are not national parks, so the national park booking systems and entry passes mostly do not apply.
tips: Rules sit with the forestry agency
Free in some states, paid in others
Read the sign at the site

table.caption: Camping in state forests by state and territory, read 28 October 2026.
head: State
Camping in state forests
Cost and booking
rows: Almost anywhere in a state forest except Cumberland and Strickland, for up to four weeks unless a sign says less. Not in picnic areas, pine plantations or closed forest.
Anywhere at least 20 metres from a waterway for up to 28 consecutive nights, or in a campground. In forest reserves, use the campgrounds provided.
Free, no bookings. Murrindindi Scenic Reserve charges a small permit fee
Every camp in a state forest needs a permit, issued for a named camping area.
$7 a person a night from 1 July 2026, booked and paid before arrival
Sustainable Timber Tasmania welcomes camping on its land except where signs prohibit it.
ForestrySA runs bookable forest campgrounds in the Mount Lofty Ranges.
Booked online; camping closed for part of the year at some sites
Camping in WA's parks is allowed only in designated campgrounds. The page read did not set out a state forest rule.
Check the Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions

sections.heading: New South Wales and Victoria: free and first come
body: Forestry Corporation of NSW runs the state forests, and every one except Cumberland and Strickland allows free camping for up to four weeks. Sites cannot be booked, many forests have no bins, and solid fuel fire bans limit cooking to gas appliances on declared days, with a maximum penalty of $2,200.

In Victoria the rule is a distance, not a pitch: pick a spot at least 20 metres from a waterway and stay no more than 28 consecutive nights. More than 300 forest campgrounds are free, and sites cannot be booked. Closures in forest roads are mapped by Forest Fire Management Victoria, and driving a closed road can bring a fine.
tips: NSW: four weeks, not Cumberland or Strickland
Fire bans can limit you to gas

sections.heading: Queensland: a permit for every camp
body: Queensland treats camping in a state forest like camping in a national park: you book and pay for a permit before you arrive, through the Queensland National Parks Booking Service or by phone on 13 QGOV (13 74 68). The fee is $7 a person a night from 1 July 2026, and about 525 camping areas across the parks and forests use the system.

Camping without a permit, or with more people than the permit covers, carries a maximum penalty of 20 penalty units. Dogs are not allowed in Queensland national parks, though some state forests accept them.
tips: Same permit system as the parks

sections.heading: South Australia and Tasmania
body: ForestrySA offers campgrounds in the Mount Lofty Ranges, including Chookarloo in Kuitpo Forest and Chalk's and Rocky Paddock in Mount Crawford, booked online. Chalk's and Rocky Paddock list a camping ban from 1 December to 31 March, and fires are banned in ForestrySA forests from 1 November to 30 April.

Tasmania takes the opposite approach. Sustainable Timber Tasmania welcomes camping on the land it manages except where signs prohibit it, so look for signs at the gate and on the track before you pitch.
tips: SA: some sites closed 1 December to 31 March

sections.heading: What facilities to expect
body: Facilities are basic. Victorian forest campgrounds typically have a pit toilet, a picnic table and a fireplace, and some are only a cleared area. New South Wales forests often have no bins, and Queensland says none of its permit camping areas has electricity.
Carry your own water and take every bit of rubbish out. A forest campsite is not a holiday park, and the guide to powered and unpowered sites covers what a paid site adds.

sections.heading: Fire, closures and weather
body: Forest closures and fire bans change by the day. Check the forestry agency's alerts and the state fire service before you drive in, because tracks close after rain and in fire danger, and a road closure applies even when a campground looks open on a map.

Dogs are welcome in all New South Wales state forests if under control, and Forestry Corporation asks that they stay on a lead. Victorian state forests also allow dogs on a lead or under control around camps.

sections.heading: Find forest campgrounds in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps carries 1,838 campgrounds from state park agencies and forestry agencies, and you can filter by cost to show the free ones. A place page lists the facilities and rules the agency publishes, and you can keep the ones you like in Starred or Want to Visit.

The details of each place sit on the phone, so they open without reception, while the map, directions, weather and photos need a connection. It runs on iPhone only, and a listing never replaces the sign at the forest gate.

faq: Is camping in state forests free in Australia?
In New South Wales, Victoria and on most Tasmanian forestry land, yes. Queensland charges for every camp in a state forest, and South Australia's forest campgrounds are booked and paid online.
Do I need to book a state forest campsite?

Not in New South Wales or Victoria, where sites are first come, first served. In Queensland you must book and pay for a permit before you arrive, and ForestrySA campgrounds in South Australia are booked online.
Can I have a campfire in a state forest?

Only when no ban applies. New South Wales state forests declare solid fuel fire bans that allow gas appliances only, and ForestrySA bans fires in its forests from 1 November to 30 April. Check the agency's page for the day you camp.
Are dogs allowed in state forests?
Often, on a lead or under control. New South Wales and Victoria allow them in state forests, and Queensland accepts them in some state forests, though not in its national parks.

Forestry Corporation of NSW: solid fuel fire bans
Explore Outdoors Victoria: before you go
Queensland Parks: camping bookings and permits
Explore Parks WA: where and when to camp

can-i-sleep-in-a-campervan-in-the-city-i.title: Can I Sleep in a Campervan in the City in Australia? Capital City Rules 2026
can-i-sleep-in-a-campervan-in-the-city-i.description: Usually not on the street. Brisbane and Darwin ban it in public places, Perth needs approval, and councils elsewhere set the rule. Capital city rules, 2026.
can-i-sleep-in-a-campervan-in-the-city-i.imageAlt: Cars parked at the kerb on High Street in Fremantle, Western Australia, at dusk
can-i-sleep-in-a-campervan-in-the-city-i.intro: Usually not on the street. Brisbane makes it illegal to camp overnight in a vehicle on a road, Darwin regulates camping in a motor vehicle or campervan in public spaces, and Perth needs approval to camp in a caravan on land that is not a caravan park. Elsewhere the council sets the rule, so a legal bed in a city means a holiday park or a signed overnight area. The pages below were read on 28 October 2026.

sections.heading: What the main cities say
body: Australia has no single rule for sleeping in a campervan in a city. Councils write local laws and by-laws, and the answer changes at each council boundary. The table shows what each official source says.
tips: Holiday parks are the safe answer

table.caption: Sleeping in a vehicle in capital cities, from council and official pages read 28 October 2026.
head: City
What the source says
Source
rows: Illegal to camp overnight in a vehicle on a road, including footpaths, road shoulders and reserves. Exceptions for fatigue, personal safety, emergencies, signed areas and tourist accommodation.
Brisbane City Council, Health, Safety and Amenity Local Law 2021
Camping in public spaces is regulated under a by-law that covers sleeping in a motor vehicle, campervan, caravan or tent. Rangers can issue on-the-spot fines.
Approval may be needed to camp or occupy a caravan on land that is not a caravan park or camping ground.
South Australia has no state law against sleeping in a car, but most councils have by-laws that stop it in parks and car parks. Signs may or may not be posted.
Camping on public unleased land without a permit is an offence, with a maximum of 20 penalty units.
No single city-wide answer was found on the official pages read. The rule comes from each council's local law and parking signs.

sections.heading: Why cities say no
body: A kerbside bed in a suburb is camping in a public place for most council laws, and councils use those laws to keep streets, beaches and parks for residents. Rangers patrol the busy spots, and the penalty is usually an on-the-spot fine, and in Darwin unattended camping gear can be impounded.
The state road rules and the council's rules are separate. A space you can legally park in for the day may still be a place you may not camp in overnight.
tips: A legal park is not a legal bed

sections.heading: The exceptions that exist
body: Brisbane's page names the cases it allows: managing fatigue, personal safety, an emergency, a designated signed area, or tourist accommodation such as a caravan park. Fatigue is a real reason to stop, and the RAA recommends a designated rest stop or a caravan park for a nap.
A fatigue stop is short and in the right place. It is not a way to stay the night in a city street, and a ranger who finds you there will judge it on the signs and the time.

sections.heading: Legal places to sleep near a city
body: A holiday park or caravan park inside or near the city is the plain answer, with a legal site and showers for a nightly price you can compare before you book. The guide to holiday park prices shows what the published tariffs look like.

Councils and showgrounds sometimes run signed overnight areas for self-contained vehicles, and rest areas on the highways outside the city follow the road authority's rule. The rest area guide covers those, and the free camping guide covers where free camping is legal.
tips: Ask the council about overnight areas

sections.heading: If a ranger knocks
body: Be polite, move on when asked and keep the vehicle's papers to hand. Penalties are set by the council, and a hire company will pass a fine on to the hirer.

Photograph any sign at the spot, because a sign decides what the local law allows. If you slept somewhere that turned out to be banned, do not argue at 2am: drive to a legal site and sort out any fine afterwards.

sections.heading: Plan the legal nights in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 5,552 rest areas from park agencies and road authorities, and holiday parks from BookEasy that you can book in the app. Put each night's place into a trip and the app shows the driving distance and time between them.

Place details are kept on the phone and open without reception, and the map, routing and weather need signal. It is made for iPhone, and city street rules are not in its data, so read the sign and the council's page.

faq: Can I sleep in my campervan on a city street in Australia?

Usually not. Brisbane's local law makes it illegal to camp overnight in a vehicle on a road, and Darwin regulates camping in a motor vehicle or campervan in public spaces. Other cities set the rule council by council, so read the signs.
Is it legal to sleep in a car in Australia?
There is no national ban. The RAA says South Australia has no state law against it, but most councils there have by-laws that stop people sleeping overnight in parks and car parks.
When can I sleep in a vehicle in Brisbane?

Brisbane lists exceptions for managing fatigue, personal safety and emergencies, in signed areas, and in tourist accommodation such as caravan parks and camping grounds. Outside those, camping overnight in a vehicle on a road is illegal.
What is the cheapest legal place to park a campervan near a city?

A caravan park or holiday park gives you a legal site and facilities for a published nightly price. Some councils and showgrounds also run low-cost overnight areas for self-contained vehicles, so ask the local council.

can-i-drive-a-2wd-hire-campervan-on-4wd-.title: Can I Drive a 2WD Hire Campervan on 4WD Roads in Australia? 2026
can-i-drive-a-2wd-hire-campervan-on-4wd-.description: No. Hire contracts ban 2WD campers from unsealed roads beyond short campground access roads, and some roads are 4WD only. What is banned and what to hire instead.
can-i-drive-a-2wd-hire-campervan-on-4wd-.imageAlt: Road condition signs for the Gibb River Road and Kalumburu Road in the Kimberley, Western Australia, noting that four wheel drive is recommended
can-i-drive-a-2wd-hire-campervan-on-4wd-.intro: No. The hire contracts read ban 2WD campervans from unsealed roads, apart from a short access road to a recognised campground, and breaking the rule can void your damage cover. Some famous roads are 4WD only as well, so a 2WD camper stays on sealed highways such as the Stuart Highway and Eyre Highway. The pages below were read on 28 October 2026, and your own contract is the final word.

sections.heading: What hire companies say
body: Hire contracts are stricter than the law. A 2WD campervan can be driven on a gravel road by any licensed driver, but the hire company decides where its vehicle may go, and the contract decides who pays if something breaks.
tips: Read the clause before you book

table.caption: Unsealed road rules in three hire companies' help pages, read 28 October 2026.
head: Company
What its page says
rows: 2WD campers cannot be driven on unsealed roads, except well-maintained access roads under 12 kilometres long to recognised commercial campgrounds or major tourist attractions. Driving into restricted areas without permission may void the liability option.

Excess reduction cover does not apply if you drive on an unsealed road. Off-road conditions include fire trails, beaches, sand, tracks, fields and paddocks. Reasonable use of access roads to recognised commercial campgrounds is the carve-out.
Vehicles are used on sealed roads, and closed or restricted roads are out unless authorised in writing.

sections.heading: What counts as unsealed
body: An unsealed road is any road not sealed with a hard surface such as bitumen, tar or concrete. That includes graded gravel and dirt roads that a family sedan could drive, which is why a hire contract can ban a road that looks easy.
The short access road to a recognised commercial campground is the usual exception, and the limit differs by company, so ask before you rely on it for a free camp or a farm gate.
tips: Access roads have a length limit
Free camps and farm gates may not qualify

sections.heading: Roads that are 4WD only or close to it
body: Some roads fail a 2WD vehicle before any contract applies. On K'gari, Queensland Parks says the sand tracks are rough and suit only high clearance 4WD vehicles with low range, all-wheel drive is not recommended, and a vehicle access permit must be bought before you go.

The Gibb River Road in Western Australia is mostly unsealed, and the road condition signs at its junctions show closed sections and recommend four wheel drive on the Kalumburu Road. Outback roads such as the Oodnadatta Track and the Birdsville Track are also unsealed, so a 2WD hire campervan is out of bounds on them, and the guide to the Queensland Outback Way covers a long outback route in detail.
tips: K'gari: high clearance 4WD and a permit

sections.heading: Beaches and sand
body: Driving on a beach is a separate rule, and the hire contracts list beaches as off limits for 2WD campers. The beach driving guide covers where driving on sand is legal and which permits apply.
A 4WD hire vehicle has its own terms, so read the one for the vehicle you actually book rather than assuming the 2WD rules carry over.

sections.heading: What to do instead
body: Stay on sealed highways. The Stuart Highway, the Eyre Highway across the Nullarbor and the Great Ocean Road are sealed, and the drive guides on this site cover many sealed routes in detail.
If the trip needs an unsealed road, hire a vehicle that the company allows on it, or book a tour. Ask for the permission in writing, because a verbal yes at pick-up is hard to prove later.
tips: Hire a 4WD or take a tour

sections.heading: Check road type in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps carries 1,838 campgrounds and 5,552 rest areas from park agencies and road authorities, and a place page lists the access notes the agency publishes, such as 4WD-only tracks. Trips show the driving distance and time between stops.

Place details open without reception, while the map, routing and weather need signal. It runs on iPhone only and does not label every road as sealed or unsealed, so confirm the road with the hire company before you go.

faq: Can I drive a 2WD hire campervan on unsealed roads in Australia?
Generally not. Britz says its 2WD campers cannot be driven on unsealed roads, apart from well-maintained access roads under 12 kilometres to recognised commercial campgrounds or major attractions.
What happens if I take a hire campervan on a road it is banned from?

Britz says driving into a restricted area without permission may void the liability option, and Jucy says its excess reduction cover does not apply on an unsealed road. You would pay for any damage yourself.
Is the Gibb River Road a 4WD road?

It is mostly unsealed, and road condition signs at its junctions list closed sections and recommend four wheel drive on the Kalumburu Road. A 2WD hire campervan is not allowed on it under the contracts read.
Can a hire campervan drive on K'gari (Fraser Island)?
Not a 2WD one. Queensland Parks says K'gari's sand tracks suit only high clearance 4WD vehicles with low range, and a vehicle access permit is needed.

sydney-to-melbourne-drive.title: Sydney to Melbourne Drive 2026: Route Options, Stops and Campsites
sydney-to-melbourne-drive.description: Sydney to Melbourne is about 870 to 900 km and 11 hours on the Hume Highway, or about 1,040 km on the Princes Highway coast. Routes compared, with overnight stops, tolls, rest areas and dump points.
sydney-to-melbourne-drive.imageAlt: The Hume Freeway bypass at Albury, New South Wales, facing south
sydney-to-melbourne-drive.intro: Sydney to Melbourne is about 870 to 900 km and around 11 hours of driving on the Hume Highway, the fastest route. The Princes Highway along the coast is about 1,040 km and 14 to 15 hours without stops, so it is a three or four day drive rather than a transfer.

sections.heading: Sydney to Melbourne routes compared
body: There are two main roads. The Hume Highway (M31) runs inland through Goulburn, Gundagai, Wagga Wagga, Albury and Wangaratta. The Princes Highway follows the coast through Nowra, Batemans Bay, Eden and Lakes Entrance. A third option swings through Canberra and rejoins the Hume near Gundagai, adding about 74 km and an hour.

Distances are about, because roads and start points change the total. Wikipedia gives about 840 km for the Hume Highway itself and about 1,040 km for the Princes Highway. The times below come from OSRM routing on OpenStreetMap data, computed on 21 October 2026, for a car from city centre to city centre with no stops. A caravan or campervan is slower, and fuel and meal stops add more.
tips: Princes: slower, scenic, two lanes for much of it

sections.heading: Day 1: Sydney to Gundagai
body: Gundagai is about 375 km and four and a half hours from Sydney by OSRM routing: Sydney to Goulburn is about 194 km (2 h 22 min), then about 181 km (2 h 8 min) on to Gundagai. Goulburn is the usual coffee stop. If you would rather break the day, BIG4 Governors Hill Caravan Park and South Goulburn Caravan Park are both in town. Check availability with the park.

Gundagai Cabins and Tourist Park is at 1 Nangus Road, a short walk from the town centre. Wagga Wagga is another 80 km and about an hour further, and BIG4 Ingenia Holidays Wagga Wagga is the larger park there. The AussieCamps data lists Mundoonan Rest Area on both sides of the Hume near Goulburn, with toilets, shelter, picnic tables and barbecues, and Ampol Foodary Pheasants Nest Southbound at about 85 km, which lists toilets and showers.

sections.heading: Day 2: Gundagai to Melbourne
body: From Gundagai it is about 520 km and six hours to Melbourne by OSRM routing: Wagga Wagga about 80 km, Albury about 126 km further, Wangaratta about 74 km, then about 240 km to Melbourne. Albury has a bypass, opened on 6 March 2007, and the Hume has been dual carriageway end to end since the Holbrook bypass opened on 7 August 2013.

If you want a third night, Albury Gardens Tourist Park and Albury Holiday Park are both in Lavington, and Painters Island Holiday Park is on the Ovens River in Wangaratta, about 300 m from the centre by footbridge. Victoria's Hume rest areas, including Chiltern, Iron Bark, Wangaratta South, Glenrowan, Benalla and Avenel, list toilets, drinking water, picnic tables and barbecues in the AussieCamps data, and most list a heavy vehicle area.
tips: Rest areas are for a break, not a bed

sections.heading: The Princes Highway option, in four days
body: The coast road is about 1,042 km. Wikivoyage suggests it is possible in two days with one overnight stop, and recommends at least four days to enjoy it. OSRM legs are Sydney to Nowra about 162 km (2 h 25 min), Nowra to Batemans Bay about 117 km (1 h 42 min), Batemans Bay to Eden about 199 km (2 h 51 min), Eden to Lakes Entrance about 242 km (3 h 9 min), Lakes Entrance to Sale about 107 km (1 h 33 min) and Sale to Melbourne about 215 km (2 h 52 min).

The stretch from Eden to Orbost is the quiet one: Wikivoyage describes it as about 185 km with scattered services. Towns on the way are Genoa, Cann River and Orbost, and Cann River is the usual halfway stop. For the south coast of New South Wales, the Sydney south coast guide covers the campsites in detail, and the Great Ocean Road guide picks up where Victoria's other famous coast road starts.
tips: Eden to Orbost about 185 km of scattered services
Cann River is the usual halfway stop
Check VicEmergency and Live Traffic NSW on the day

sections.heading: Fuel and services
body: Wikivoyage describes petrol stations as plentiful on both routes, and says EV chargers are widely available on the Hume but still patchy on the Princes Highway. The longest stretch between big towns on the Hume is Goulburn to Gundagai at about 181 km, with service centres between, such as Pheasants Nest near Sydney and Avenel in Victoria. Fill up before the Princes Highway between Eden and Orbost, because fuel and opening hours at the small towns there could not be confirmed.

Both roads are busy from Christmas to the end of January and accommodation is often full, so book parks ahead in the holidays. For fuel budgeting, the road trip fuel planning guide shows how to work out the cost from the distance.
tips: Hume: services every hour or so
Princes: fill up before Eden to Orbost
Book ahead from Christmas to January

sections.heading: Road conditions, tolls and closures
body: Check Live Traffic NSW (livetraffic.com or 132 701) and VicTraffic and VicEmergency before you go. No current closure was listed in the sources checked on 21 October 2026. The Princes Highway has closed in past bushfire summers, notably between Bruthen or Orbost and the New South Wales border, so check the day before for Cann River to Genoa. Kangaroos are common at dusk and night, and both roads have fixed and mobile speed cameras. The wildlife and fatigue guide covers how to drive at dawn and dusk.

The Hume Highway itself is not tolled, but Sydney's M5 and M7 meet it at Prestons and are. NSW says that if you use a toll road without an account or pass you have 72 hours to pay, and Service NSW lists a casual pass for visitors. In Melbourne, Linkt's Visitor's Pass covers up to 30 days on any toll road in Melbourne and can cover CityLink trips made up to 5 days ago and EastLink trips made up to 3 days ago. There is no alpine pass on the Hume or the Princes Highway, so you do not need chains. The Australian Alps and Victoria high country guides cover roads that do.

sections.heading: Border rules between New South Wales and Victoria
body: No fruit fly checkpoint turned up on the Hume or Princes Highway crossings. Agriculture Victoria says the Greater Sunraysia Pest Free Area was in place from 2006 and regulation ended in July 2024, so there are no longer restrictions on carrying Queensland fruit fly host produce into or out of Sunraysia. The Hume and Princes crossings are not in Sunraysia. Victoria still regulates Mediterranean fruit fly, so check Agriculture Victoria (136 186) before bringing produce.

The Interstate Quarantine site also lists a NSW Phylloxera Infested Zone around Albury and Corowa and the Sydney basin, where you should not take soil, grapevine plants, mulch or garden organics out, and a NSW Rice Biosecurity Zone across most of the Murrumbidgee and Murray regions. None of that affects normal camping food, but the interstate biosecurity guide has the full list.
tips: No fruit fly checkpoint on these crossings found
Skip soil, plants and mulch in phylloxera zones

sections.heading: Dump points along the Hume
body: The AussieCamps data lists dump points at Ampol Foodary Pheasants Nest Southbound near Sydney (no washout tap listed), Uranquinty Rest Area near Wagga Wagga (no washout tap listed), Warreena Park in Wangaratta, Airport and RV Dump Point in Benalla and Memorial Park in Wandong (all three with a washout tap listed). That is what the data covers, not every dump point on the road, so check the dump points guide and the town council.
If a rest area has no sign allowing overnight stays, treat it as a place for a break. The rest area guide has the rules for New South Wales and Victoria.
tips: Wangaratta, Benalla and Wandong list a washout tap
Pheasants Nest and Uranquinty list none

sections.heading: Plan the Sydney to Melbourne drive in AussieCamps
body: Pick your route and save the overnight stops to a trip in AussieCamps: it keeps the stops in order, shows the leg distance and drive time between them, and shows the forecast for each stop on the day you plan to arrive. AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and a place page carries the facilities those sources publish.

Stored place details, saved places and guides work with no signal. Map tiles, routing, weather and photos need a connection, so load the trip before the Princes Highway stretch east of Eden. AussieCamps runs on iPhone only, and it is free to download, with in-app purchases.
tips: Save each overnight stop to a trip
Forecast shows for each arrival day

faq: How long does it take to drive from Sydney to Melbourne?

About 11 hours of driving on the Hume Highway, roughly 870 to 900 km, with no stops. Allow two days if you tow or want to enjoy the trip, and about 14 to 15 hours for the Princes Highway coast route, roughly 1,040 km, which most people split over three or four days.
Is the Hume Highway all dual carriageway?

Wikipedia says it has been dual carriageway for its full length since the Holbrook bypass opened on 7 August 2013, with a 110 km/h limit. Roadworks and speed zones can change that, so check Live Traffic NSW and VicTraffic before you leave.
Do I need to pay tolls between Sydney and Melbourne?

Not on the Hume itself, but Sydney's M5 and M7 and Melbourne's CityLink and EastLink are tolled. NSW says you have 72 hours after travelling to pay or open an account, and Linkt sells a Visitor's Pass for Melbourne roads that covers up to 30 days.
Can I take fruit between New South Wales and Victoria?

No fruit fly checkpoint turned up on the Hume or Princes Highway crossings, and Agriculture Victoria says Queensland fruit fly regulation ended in the Greater Sunraysia area in July 2024. Victoria still regulates Mediterranean fruit fly, so check Agriculture Victoria on 136 186 before you bring produce.

brisbane-to-sydney-drive.title: Brisbane to Sydney Drive 2026: Pacific Highway or New England, Stops and Campsites
brisbane-to-sydney-drive.description: Brisbane to Sydney is about 907 km and 11 hours on the Pacific Highway, or 970 km and 13 hours on the New England Highway. Routes compared, overnight stops, fire ant rules, tolls and dump points.
brisbane-to-sydney-drive.imageAlt: The dual carriageway Pacific Highway near Wootton on the New South Wales mid north coast, seen from a bridge
brisbane-to-sydney-drive.intro: Brisbane to Sydney is about 907 km and roughly 10 h 52 min on the Pacific Motorway and Pacific Highway along the coast, or about 970 km and roughly 13 h 8 min on the New England Highway inland, by OSRM routing without stops. The coast road is four lanes all the way, the inland road is quieter, and either is an easy two or three day drive.

sections.heading: Brisbane to Sydney routes compared
body: The coast route is the Pacific Motorway out of Brisbane, then the Pacific Highway through Tweed Heads, Ballina, Grafton, Coffs Harbour, Port Macquarie, Taree and Newcastle. An Australian Government infrastructure listing says the full 657 km of the Pacific Highway between Hexham and the Queensland border has been open as a four-lane divided road since 17 December 2020. The inland route follows the Cunningham Highway to Warwick, then the New England Highway through Tenterfield, Glen Innes, Armidale, Tamworth and Singleton.

The distances and times are from OSRM routing on OpenStreetMap data, checked on 3 November 2026, for a car from city centre to city centre with no stops. Towing, fuel and meal stops add more. A third option stays on the Pacific Highway but detours through Forster and Bulahdelah near the Myall Lakes, adding about 33 km and 45 minutes.
tips: Coast: four lanes, busier, more towns
Inland: mostly single carriageway with overtaking lanes
