petrol-diesel-prices-australia-2026.title: Petrol and Diesel Prices in Australia 2026: Price per Litre by City
petrol-diesel-prices-australia-2026.description: Petrol averaged $2.34 a litre and diesel $2.77 in the five largest cities on 28 October 2026. Prices for every capital, the outback gap and what a tank costs.
petrol-diesel-prices-australia-2026.imageAlt: A BP service station at Semaphore in Adelaide, South Australia, with a white four-wheel drive at the pumps, photographed during the 2026 fuel crisis
petrol-diesel-prices-australia-2026.intro: On 28 October 2026, regular unleaded petrol averaged $2.34 a litre and diesel $2.77 a litre across Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth, from the ACCC's weekly figures published by the Australian Government's Fuel Plan site. Canberra, Hobart and Darwin were dearer, at $2.43 to $2.46 for petrol, and country towns pay more again. Prices are well above where they were before the Middle East conflict began in February 2026, and diesel has risen the most.

sections.heading: Prices by capital city
body: The table gives the average retail price per litre in each capital on 28 October 2026. Adelaide was the cheapest city for petrol and Perth for diesel. Canberra was the dearest for both.
City averages are a guide, not a quote: the price at one station can sit well above or below its city's average, and an app or state price site shows the station you are driving past.

table.caption: Average retail fuel prices per litre on 28 October 2026, from the ACCC weekly report via the Australian Government's Fuel Plan site.
head: City
Unleaded petrol
Diesel

sections.heading: Why fuel costs more in 2026
body: Prices jumped after the Middle East conflict began in late February 2026. The Australian Government halved fuel excise in April, cut the discount to 16 cents a litre from 1 July to 2 August, and restored the full rate from 3 August, which pushed pump prices up again.

By late October prices had eased from their peak: on 28 October the five-city average was 23 cents a litre lower for petrol and 46 cents lower for diesel than on 31 March. They were still well above pre-conflict levels. On 21 October, petrol was 63 cents a litre and diesel 100 cents a litre higher than on 20 February.
tips: Excise back in full from 3 August
Diesel up a dollar on February

sections.heading: Country and outback prices
body: Fuel costs more the farther you are from a capital, because of freight and smaller sales. The Northern Territory Treasury's July 2026 brief put regular unleaded at 254.0 cents a litre in Alice Springs and 235.9 in Katherine, against 184.4 in Darwin: a gap of about 70 cents a litre between Darwin and Alice Springs.

Roadhouses on long remote stretches often charge more than the nearest town. Do not skip one to save a few dollars if the next fuel is out of range: plan fills in the larger towns and buy what you need to reach the next one.
tips: Alice Springs: 70 cents above Darwin in July
Never skip fuel to save money

sections.heading: When to fill up
body: The ACCC says petrol price cycles, in which prices climb sharply and then fall over days or weeks, have mostly not occurred in Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Adelaide since late February 2026, so there is no reliable cheap day this year. The ACCC publishes buying tips for the five largest cities, but not for Canberra, Hobart or Darwin.

Western Australia works differently. Under FuelWatch, each station sets its price for the next day and cannot change it for 24 hours, and FuelWatch publishes tomorrow's prices from 2.30 pm. In Perth and the WA towns it covers, check tonight and fill up wherever tomorrow is cheaper.
tips: WA prices are fixed a day ahead

sections.heading: What a tank costs
body: At the October averages, filling a 60-litre petrol tank from empty costs about $140, and an 80-litre diesel tank about $222. A campervan using 12 litres per 100 km on diesel costs about 33 cents a kilometre to fuel, so a 1,000 km week costs about $330.

To cost a whole trip, multiply the distance by the vehicle's consumption and the price per litre, then add a margin for remote fills. The road trip fuel cost guide and the fuel cost calculator do that from your route.
tips: Diesel van: about 33 cents a km

sections.heading: Fuel at the pump
body: Australian pumps label petrol as unleaded 91, premium 95 and premium 98, plus E10, a blend with 10% ethanol, and diesel. Use the fuel named on the filler cap or in the hire agreement; the wrong fuel can stop the engine and lead to an expensive repair.

Most stations are self-serve: fill first, note the pump number, then pay inside. In remote areas some pumps take a card before they start, and small roadhouses keep shorter hours, so fill up before dark.
tips: Some remote pumps close at night

sections.heading: Plan fuel stops in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps adds up the driving distance between the stops in your trip, so you can see the long legs and plan where to fill before you leave. Save the towns where you will refuel alongside your campsites.
Place details are saved on the phone for use without signal. The map, routing and weather need a connection, and AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: How much is petrol in Australia right now?

On 28 October 2026, regular unleaded averaged $2.34 a litre across Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth, from $2.28 in Adelaide to $2.46 in Canberra. Diesel averaged $2.77 a litre in the same five cities. Country towns usually pay more.
Why is diesel more expensive than petrol in Australia in 2026?

Diesel rose further after the Middle East conflict that began in late February 2026. On 21 October, the five-city average was 63 cents a litre above its 20 February level for petrol and 100 cents above it for diesel, so diesel now costs about 40 cents a litre more than petrol at the pump.
Is fuel cheaper in the city or the outback?

In the city. The Northern Territory Treasury's July 2026 brief put unleaded at 254.0 cents a litre in Alice Springs against 184.4 in Darwin. Remote roadhouses charge more again, so fill up in the larger towns and treat the price at a lone roadhouse as the cost of getting there.
Is there a cheapest day to buy petrol in Australia?

Not reliably in 2026. The ACCC says the usual price cycles have mostly not occurred in Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Adelaide since late February 2026. In Perth, FuelWatch fixes each station's price for the next day and publishes it from 2.30 pm, so you can see tomorrow's price before you fill up.

toll-roads-australia-hire-car-campervan.title: Toll Roads in Australia 2026: How Visitors Pay in a Hire Car or Campervan
toll-roads-australia-hire-car-campervan.description: Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane have toll roads. How to pay without an e-tag, the days you have after a trip, Linkt passes and what hire companies charge per toll.
toll-roads-australia-hire-car-campervan.imageAlt: The CityLink freeway in Melbourne looking north from the Toorak Road bridge at dusk, with traffic and street lights
toll-roads-australia-hire-car-campervan.intro: Only Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane have toll roads, and none of them has a toll booth: a camera or e-tag reader records each trip. Without an e-tag, buy a pass online before you drive or soon after, within 3 days in Queensland, 72 hours in New South Wales or 5 days for Melbourne's CityLink. In a hire car or campervan, the company pays the toll and charges your card, usually with a fee of about $3 per toll. We read each toll operator's and government page on 3 November 2026.

sections.heading: Where the toll roads are
body: Sydney has the most, including the Sydney Harbour Bridge and Tunnel and the motorways of the WestConnex network. Melbourne has CityLink and EastLink. Brisbane has the Gateway and Logan Motorways, the Clem7 and Legacy Way tunnels, the Go Between Bridge and AirportlinkM7.

Adelaide, Perth, Hobart, Darwin and Canberra have no toll roads, and neither do the highways between the capitals. A sat-nav or map app can avoid tolls if you set it to, at the cost of a slower drive through the city.
tips: Tolls only in Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane
No toll booths: cameras and tags
Set your map to avoid tolls if you prefer

sections.heading: How long you have to pay
body: Each state gives you a few days after the trip to buy a pass or open an account. After that, the vehicle's registered owner gets a notice with fees added, and in a hire car that owner is the rental company, which passes the cost on to you.

In Melbourne the window depends on the road: Linkt says a pass covers CityLink trips made up to 5 days before, but EastLink trips only up to 3 days before, and only on its Visitor's Pass. Weekend and 24-hour CityLink passes do not cover EastLink.

table.caption: How long you have to pay for a toll trip without an e-tag. From each state's payment provider or government, read 3 November 2026.
head: City
Roads
Pay within
Where to pay
rows: Linkt for most roads; E-Toll for the Harbour Bridge and Tunnel

sections.heading: Passes for visitors
body: In Sydney, Linkt's Sydney Pass costs $1.50 to start online, or $3.30 by phone, and charges the tolls to your card, plus a video matching fee of $0.75 per trip because there is no tag. Service NSW also lists the E-Toll eMU Casual Pass for visitors and anyone using NSW toll roads for up to 30 days.

In Melbourne, a Linkt pass covers CityLink, and the Visitor's Pass also covers EastLink. In Brisbane, Linkt sells passes for the Queensland toll roads. Register the pass to the number plate of the vehicle you are driving, and update it if you swap cars.

sections.heading: Tolls in a hire car or campervan
body: Most hire companies receive the tolls on their vehicles and charge them to the card on your booking, with their own fee for each toll. JUCY lists a service fee of $3.45 per toll, Enterprise $3 per toll and Redspot $3.36 per toll transaction, and other companies charge per toll or per day of the hire.

On a week in Sydney, those fees can cost more than the tolls. Ask at pick-up whether the vehicle carries a tag and how tolls are charged, and if a company allows it, buy your own pass for the vehicle's number plate before you drive on a toll road.
tips: Expect about $3 a toll in fees
Ask whether a tag is fitted
A pass can avoid the hire fee

sections.heading: If you miss the window
body: In New South Wales, the registered owner gets an unpaid toll reminder, with 48 hours to pay, then a Toll Payment Demand, which can include a video matching fee. In Victoria, Fines Victoria says you must have a valid account or pass to use a toll road, and Linkt says an unpaid trip brings a toll notice in the mail within 4 weeks.

In Queensland, the registered owner gets an unpaid toll notice from the road's payment provider if the toll is not paid within 3 days, and fees rise with each notice that goes unpaid. Pay on the day you drive and you avoid every one of these.
tips: Victoria: a pass is the law
Pay on the day you drive

sections.heading: Plan city legs in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps shows campgrounds, holiday parks and rest areas around Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane, so you can stop outside the city and drive in by public transport, or plan the day you cross town. A trip adds up the driving distance between stops.
Place details are saved on the phone for use without signal. The map, routing and weather need a connection, and AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: How do I pay tolls in Australia without an e-tag?

Buy a pass online, either before you drive or within the window after the trip: 3 days in Queensland, 72 hours in New South Wales, and 5 days for CityLink in Melbourne (3 days for EastLink). Linkt sells passes for all three cities. Miss the window and the vehicle's owner gets a toll notice with fees added.
Do I pay tolls in a hire car or campervan?

Yes. The hire company receives the toll and charges your card, usually with a fee per toll: JUCY lists $3.45, Enterprise $3 and Redspot $3.36. Read the toll section of your rental agreement before you drive, and ask whether a tag is fitted.
Which Australian cities have toll roads?
Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane. You can drive around the country on the highways between the capitals without paying a toll, but the fastest routes into and through those three cities often use one.
What happens if I forget to pay a toll in Sydney?

Service NSW says you can buy a pass or open an account up to 72 hours after the trip. After that, the registered owner may get an unpaid toll reminder by email or text, with 48 hours to pay, and then a Toll Payment Demand that can include a video matching fee. In a hire car, the company passes it on to you with its own fee.

australia-biosecurity-camping-gear.title: Australia Biosecurity 2026: Declaring Tents, Boots and Camping Gear
australia-biosecurity-camping-gear.description: Used tents, hiking boots, fishing gear and food must be declared when you land in Australia. What to clean before you fly, what officers check and what declaring costs.
australia-biosecurity-camping-gear.imageAlt: The international arrivals hall at Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport, with signs to trains, taxis and domestic transfers
australia-biosecurity-camping-gear.intro: Every traveller landing in Australia must declare food, plant and animal products, and anything with soil on it or used in freshwater, which takes in hiking boots, tents and fishing gear. Declaring costs nothing: Tourism Australia says you will not be penalised for declaring goods, even ones that are not allowed in. A false or missing declaration can bring a fine and the loss of the item, and the Department of Agriculture warns it can also cost you your visa. Clean and dry your gear at home and the check is usually quick. We checked the official guidance on 9 November 2026.

sections.heading: What you must declare
body: Tourism Australia lists the goods every arriving passenger must declare: meat, poultry, fish, seafood, eggs, dairy, fruit and vegetables; animals and animal products, including pet food, shells and bee products; and soil, items with soil attached, or items used in freshwater areas, such as sports and recreational equipment and shoes. Customs goods are on the same card, including purchases over A$900 per adult and A$10,000 or more in cash.

The Department of Agriculture names camping equipment, backpacks included, along with hiking and fishing gear, as things to declare if they carry soil or other contamination. It also asks travellers who have been in a rural area or near farm animals to say so on the card. If you are unsure whether something counts, declare it.

table.caption: Common camping items and what to expect when you declare them. From Tourism Australia and the Department of Agriculture, checked 9 November 2026.
head: Item
Declare it?
What usually happens
rows: Yes, if dirty or used near freshwater
Inspected; soil means cleaning or treatment at your cost
Yes, if soil or plant material is on them
Inspected and returned if clean and dry
Inspected for water, mud and plant material

sections.heading: Clean and dry your gear before you fly
body: The Department of Agriculture says equipment and clothing used overseas should be thoroughly cleaned and dried before you travel, and that you must still declare it for inspection. Its cleaning steps for footwear are to shake or scrape off loose soil and plant matter, then wash the soles, laces, velcro and outside surfaces with soap or detergent, water and a brush.

Do the same for a tent: shake it out, wash the pegs and the groundsheet, and let everything dry fully before you pack it, because damp fabric and mud are what officers look for. Camping and sporting equipment is allowed in, but the department says it must be clean and dry on arrival, or it is treated, exported or destroyed at your expense. Pack used gear near the top of a bag so it is easy to show.

sections.heading: At the airport: the card, the dogs and the X-ray
body: Cabin crew hand out the Incoming Passenger Card before landing, and Tourism Australia says cards are also available near the border area in several languages. The Department of Agriculture says a digital version, the Australia Travel Declaration, has been piloted with Qantas on some flights; if you are not offered it, fill in the paper card.

After passport control, a Border Force officer collects the card and may ask what you are carrying. Detector dogs work the arrivals halls, bags can be X-rayed and searched, and that applies even when you declare nothing. Bins before the customs line let you throw out food you would rather not declare.

sections.heading: What declaring costs, and what hiding costs
body: Declared goods go to a biosecurity officer, who decides the risk. Tourism Australia says that in most cases goods are low risk and are handed back after the inspection. If an item carries risk, you can pay for it to be treated, pay to send it out of the country, or give it up.

Not declaring is where it goes wrong. Tourism Australia says undeclared or falsely declared items can be seized and the traveller fined, or even jailed for a criminal offence. The Department of Agriculture adds that your visa may be cancelled, in which case you are refused entry and may not be able to return for up to three years.
tips: A cancelled visa can mean three years out

sections.heading: Inside Australia: the next borders
body: Clearing the airport is not the last check. Several states keep their own biosecurity rules, so fresh fruit, vegetables, honey, plants and soil can be stopped again at the Western Australian, South Australian and Tasmanian borders, with disposal bins at the checkpoints. Tourism Australia notes that plant and food items such as fruit, vegetables and honey are not allowed between some state borders.

Plan food shopping around those lines, and keep cleaning boots and tent pegs between regions: soil moves plant disease inside Australia as easily as it does from overseas. Western Australia's dieback areas have boot-cleaning stations at walk entrances.
tips: Run the fridge down before a border

sections.heading: Plan the first nights in AussieCamps
body: Once you are through, AussieCamps lists campgrounds, rest areas, drinking water points and dump points around each arrival city, with the facilities, fees and access notes the park agencies publish. It also lists holiday parks, motels and B&Bs you can book in the app for a first night with a shower.

Save your first stops to a trip and AussieCamps shows the driving distance and time for each leg. Place details stay readable with no signal; the map, directions and weather need a connection. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Do I need to declare my tent and hiking boots when I arrive in Australia?

Yes, if they have soil or plant material on them or have been used in freshwater areas. Tick yes on the arrival card, then show them to the officer. Clean, dry gear is usually inspected and handed back to you.
What happens if I declare food at Australian customs?

An officer inspects it. Tourism Australia says most declared goods are low risk and are returned after the inspection. Risky items can be treated or exported at your cost, or left for destruction, and you are not penalised for declaring them, even if they are not allowed in.

mosquitoes-march-flies-camping-australia.title: Mosquitoes, March Flies, Midges and Ticks: Camping in Australia 2026
mosquitoes-march-flies-camping-australia.description: Where and when biting insects are worst on an Australian camping trip, the diseases mosquitoes carry, the repellents health departments recommend and how to remove a tick.
mosquitoes-march-flies-camping-australia.imageAlt: A grey and black march fly with clear veined wings resting on a weathered timber board
mosquitoes-march-flies-camping-australia.intro: Mosquitoes are the biting insect that matters most on an Australian camping trip, because they spread Ross River and Barmah Forest viruses everywhere, and in some places Japanese encephalitis and dengue. March flies hurt more and biting midges itch for longer, but midges carry no known human disease here, and ticks matter mostly for allergic reactions. A repellent with DEET, picaridin or oil of lemon eucalyptus, long loose clothes at dawn and dusk, and a pitch away from still water and mangroves deal with most of it. We read each health department page on 9 November 2026.

sections.heading: What bites, where and when
body: Four groups do most of the biting. Mosquitoes are found across the country and are busiest in warm, wet weather. The Australian Museum says march flies live throughout Australia around freshwater creeks, estuaries and mangroves, and that only the females bite, because they need blood to breed.

Western Australia's health department says biting midges bite around dawn and dusk, can keep going through the night, and bite all day when it is overcast, mostly in tropical and subtropical areas near sandy estuaries and mangroves. Ticks used to live mainly on the east coast but now have populations inland too, and the risk is there all year.

table.caption: Biting insects on an Australian camping trip. From healthdirect, the Australian Museum, Healthy WA and the Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy, read 9 November 2026.

Where
When
Main risk
rows: Across Australia, most near wetlands, rivers and mangroves

sections.heading: The mosquito diseases to know
body: Healthdirect, the national health advice service, lists Ross River virus, Barmah Forest virus, dengue, Japanese encephalitis and Murray Valley encephalitis among the mosquito-borne diseases in Australia. Ross River and Barmah Forest are the common ones, with fever, rash and sore joints. There is no vaccine for either, so the only protection is not being bitten.

Japanese encephalitis has a vaccine. The Australian Immunisation Handbook recommends it for some people who live, work or spend time in risk areas, and states have offered it free to campers in high-risk areas in recent seasons, so ask a GP or pharmacist before a summer trip along inland rivers; protection can take up to two weeks. Dengue is a risk in north Queensland: Queensland Health says the mosquito that spreads it lives in north and central Queensland, and outbreaks start when a traveller brings the virus in.
tips: Ask about the Japanese encephalitis vaccine

sections.heading: Repellent and clothing that work
body: Healthdirect says the best repellents contain DEET, picaridin or oil of lemon eucalyptus, and that you should use products approved by the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority. Put repellent on after sunscreen, on exposed skin only. An adult should apply it to children under 5, and it is not advised for babies under 3 months, who are better protected by clothing and a net over the pram or cot.

For midges, Healthy WA says DEET or picaridin works best and that a higher concentration lasts longer, so match the strength to the time you will be outside. Cover up with long, loose and light-coloured clothing at dawn and dusk. Even if you have had a vaccine, healthdirect says you still need to avoid bites.

sections.heading: Pick the pitch and close the camp
body: Mosquitoes breed in still water and midges in estuary mud, so the same campground can be bearable on one side and miserable on the other. Choose a site with a breeze, away from mangroves, swamps and stagnant creeks, and arrive early enough to judge it in daylight.

Healthy WA says midges are small enough to get through standard fly screens, so screen caravans and tents with fine mesh, and notes that a fan or moving air discourages them. Close up before dusk, keep the screen door shut while you cook, and sleep under a net if your tent or van has gaps.

sections.heading: Ticks: freeze it, don't squeeze it
body: The Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy says the paralysis tick can cause allergic reactions when it is disturbed, because squeezing it makes it inject more saliva. Its advice is to freeze the tick with a product that rapidly freezes and kills it, usually an ether-containing spray, and let it drop off, or to leave it in place and get medical help.

Do not pull it out with tweezers, and do not dab it with methylated spirits or kerosene. The society also links tick bites to mammalian meat allergy, a reaction to beef, lamb, pork and kangaroo meat that can appear later. After a walk through long grass or scrub on the east coast, check your skin and your hairline.

sections.heading: When a bite is more than a bite
body: Most bites only itch. See a doctor if a fever, rash or joint pain follows a trip, and say where you camped, because that is what points to Ross River, Barmah Forest or dengue.

A severe allergic reaction to a tick or an insect bite is an emergency: trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or collapse. Call triple zero (000). Where there is no coverage, 112 will try any available network from a mobile phone.
tips: Fever after a trip: see a GP

sections.heading: Choose breezier camps in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps shows campgrounds and national parks across Australia with the facilities, access and fees the park agencies publish, and a 7-day forecast on each place page, so you can see whether a still, humid night is coming. Filters for water, toilets, showers and power help you find a site where you can close up early and still cook and wash.
Place details stay readable with no signal, which is useful in the mangrove and river country where reception drops. The map, directions and weather need a connection. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: When are mosquitoes worst when camping in Australia?

In the warmer months, after rain and flooding, and near wetlands, rivers, creeks and mangroves. Biting midges, which Australians often call sandflies, are worst at dawn and dusk and on still, overcast days near estuaries and mangroves.
How do you remove a tick in Australia?

Freeze it and let it drop off. The Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy says to use a freezing spray, usually ether-based, which kills the tick within about five minutes, and not to pull it out with tweezers or touch it, because disturbing it can inject more allergen. If you are allergic to ticks, have it removed at a hospital emergency department.

sources.label: healthdirect: mosquito bites and mosquito-borne diseases
ASCIA: tick allergy and tick removal

speed-limits-australia-visitors.title: Speed Limits in Australia 2026: Default Limits by State for Visitors
speed-limits-australia-visitors.description: Australian speed limits for visitors: 50 km/h in towns, 100 or 110 km/h on open roads, 130 km/h on parts of four NT highways, plus school zones, cameras and fines in a hire car.
speed-limits-australia-visitors.imageAlt: A 130 km/h speed limit sign beside a highway in the Northern Territory, with dry grass and scrub behind it
speed-limits-australia-visitors.intro: Where there is no sign, Australia's default speed limit is 50 km/h in a built-up area and 100 km/h outside one. Western Australia and the Northern Territory set the open-road default at 110 km/h, and the Northern Territory's built-up default is 60 km/h unless a town signs it lower. Signs override every default, school zones drop to 40 km/h or less at set times, and cameras are common, including average speed cameras that time you between two points. In a hire car the fine goes to the company, which passes it on to you. We read each state's road authority page on 9 November 2026.

sections.heading: Default limits by state
body: A default limit applies on a road with no speed sign, or after an end speed limit sign. In New South Wales, a built-up area is one with street lights and buildings beside the road less than 100 m apart; most states use the same idea. The table sets out each default, with the limits that apply to learner and provisional drivers where a state publishes them.
Visitors on a full overseas licence follow the same limits as local drivers. The lower learner and provisional limits apply to drivers on local L or P plates.
tips: 100 km/h outside, 110 in WA and the NT

Built-up area

sections.heading: Where 130 km/h is legal, and where it isn't
body: The Northern Territory is the only place in Australia with 130 km/h limits. The NT Government says some sections of the Barkly, Stuart, Victoria and Arnhem highways have a 130 km/h maximum, shown on signs, while heavy vehicles are held to 100 km/h. Everywhere else the highest posted limit is 110 km/h.

A 130 sign is a maximum for good conditions, not a target. In a hire campervan, at dusk, or with kangaroos and cattle beside the road, 130 km/h leaves no time to stop. Hire agreements can add their own rules for remote roads, so read yours before a long Territory leg.
tips: Not a target in a campervan

sections.heading: School zones and other low limits
body: Every state cuts speed around schools on school days, with the hours on the sign. New South Wales uses 40 km/h, marks zones with flashing lights and zigzag lines painted on the road, and fines speeding in a school zone more heavily. Victoria uses 30, 40 or 60 km/h depending on the road, with time-based zones from 8 to 9.30 am and 2.30 to 4 pm on weekdays in term time, but not on public holidays.

South Australia is the exception to remember: drivers must slow to 25 km/h in a school zone whenever children are present, and when passing a school bus that has stopped to pick up or set down children. The Northern Territory uses 40 km/h at the times shown. Shared zones are 10 km/h in New South Wales, and you give way to people walking in them.
tips: Read the times on the sign
SA: 25 km/h when children are there

sections.heading: Speed cameras, including average speed cameras
body: Expect fixed cameras, mobile cameras in parked cars and vans, and cameras at traffic lights that also check speed. Transport for NSW says every mainland state and the ACT except New South Wales uses average speed cameras for both cars and heavy vehicles, timing you between two points on a highway. New South Wales has used them on trucks since 2010, and after a trial on two regional highways it is keeping them switched on for cars at those sites.

A camera does not stop you, so the first you hear of it is the notice. New South Wales says learner and P1 drivers lose their licence for any speeding offence, and most states add demerit points as well as a fine. Several states, New South Wales among them, apply double demerit points over holiday periods.
tips: Average speed cameras in most states

sections.heading: Fines in a hire car or campervan
body: A camera fine goes to the registered owner of the vehicle. In a hire car or campervan that is the hire company, which nominates you as the driver. Tourism Australia says the fine is sent to your car hire company, and that if you do not pay it, it can come off your credit card or security bond.

Most companies add an administration fee for handling each notice, so one camera can cost more than the fine. Keep the hire agreement until the bond is back, and check the card statement for a few weeks after you return the vehicle.
tips: Watch your card after the trip

sections.heading: Driving below the limit
body: Queensland's rule of thumb holds everywhere: a posted limit is the maximum in good conditions, and rain, darkness or a hazard call for less. The same goes for gravel, which Tasmania limits to 80 km/h by default, and for a tall campervan in a crosswind.

If you are towing a caravan, lower vehicle limits can apply on top of the posted one, and they differ by state. Slow down for roadworks, emergency vehicles with flashing lights and stock on the road, and pull over to let traffic past when a queue builds behind you.
tips: Slower on gravel and in wind

sections.heading: Plan shorter legs in AussieCamps
body: Speed limits matter less when the day is short. Add your stops to a trip in AussieCamps and it shows the driving distance and time for each leg and the whole journey, so you can see where a day runs long and add a rest area or campground between.

AussieCamps lists 5,552 rest areas and 1,838 campgrounds from road authorities and park agencies. Place details stay readable with no signal; the map, directions and weather need a connection. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: What is the speed limit on Australian highways?

Whatever the sign says, usually 100 or 110 km/h. Where there is no sign, the default outside built-up areas is 100 km/h in most states and 110 km/h in Western Australia and the Northern Territory. Parts of the Stuart, Barkly, Victoria and Arnhem highways in the Northern Territory are signed 130 km/h.
Do speeding fines reach tourists in hire cars?

Yes. Camera fines go to the registered owner, which is the hire company. Tourism Australia says the company passes the fine on, and if you do not pay it the amount can come off your credit card or security bond, usually with the company's own fee added.

left-side-driving-australia.title: Driving on the Left in Australia: A First-Day Guide for Visitors
left-side-driving-australia.description: Australia drives on the left. Where right-side habits come back, how roundabouts, overtaking and Melbourne's hook turns work, and how to set up a hire car before you move.
left-side-driving-australia.imageAlt: A yellow and white Keep Left sign in English, German, French and Chinese beside Indian Ocean Drive in Western Australia
left-side-driving-australia.intro: Australia drives on the left, with the driver on the right of the car. Tourism Australia's rule of thumb is to keep the driver's side close to the centre of the road, stay in the left lane unless you are overtaking, and give way to the right at roundabouts. Most visitors manage the open road; the mistakes happen when turning out of a car park, after a fuel stop on an empty highway, or at the first roundabout. Hire an automatic if you can, set the car up before you move, and keep the first day short. We read each official page on 9 November 2026.

sections.heading: Set the car up before you move
body: Tourism Australia suggests hiring a car with automatic transmission if you are not used to driving on the left, so changing gear with your left hand is one thing you do not have to learn. It warns that the indicator and windscreen wiper stalks may be on the opposite side of the steering wheel to your car at home, while the brake and accelerator are always in the same place.

Before leaving the hire depot, adjust the seat and all three mirrors, pair your phone and start the navigation, because Australian law bans touching a phone while you drive, even when stopped at lights. Then drive a lap of the car park. Expect to switch on the wipers when you meant to indicate for the first day or two; it is harmless, and it fades.
tips: Set the phone before you move

sections.heading: Where right-side habits come back
body: On a busy road, other cars show you where to be. The risk comes when there are none: pulling out of a car park or driveway, rejoining an empty highway after a rest stop, or turning at a quiet T-intersection. In those moments the brain falls back on what it knows, and drivers end up on the right.

Say a short check out loud each time you start moving or turn: driver to the centre line. On a right turn you cross the oncoming lane and end up in the far lane; on a left turn you keep tight to the kerb. A passenger who reads the signs and says keep left at each turn helps more than any app.
tips: Left turns tight, right turns wide

sections.heading: Roundabouts
body: Roundabouts in Australia run clockwise. The NSW Government says you must slow down or stop to give way to all vehicles already in the roundabout, which means traffic on your right, and vehicles that entered from your left or from directly opposite you.

Indicate when turning at a roundabout and keep indicating as you turn; when you leave, indicate left if it is practical, and stop indicating once you are out. On roundabouts with more than one lane, follow the arrows on the road surface or the signs: to turn left, use the left lane unless the arrows allow another.
tips: Clockwise, give way to the right

sections.heading: Lanes and overtaking
body: Stay in the left lane unless you are overtaking, and always pass on the right. Tourism Australia explains the centre lines: a single broken white line means you can overtake when it is safe, and where there are two lines you may only overtake when the line closest to you is broken. Where a Keep Left Unless Overtaking sign is posted, sitting in the right lane is an offence.

On country highways, wait for a signed overtaking lane rather than pulling out on a short straight. Road trains can be over 50 m long and take far longer to pass than they look, so the safe move is often to stay behind until the road opens up.
tips: Two lines: overtake only on your broken side

sections.heading: City quirks: hook turns, trams and parking
body: Central Melbourne uses hook turns at signed intersections, so that cars turning right stay clear of the trams in the middle of the road. You turn right from the left lane: move to the far left of the intersection with your right indicator on, wait until the lights on the street you are turning into go green, then complete the turn. The sign reads Right Turn From Left Only.

In Melbourne and Adelaide, trams share the road, and you must stop behind a tram that has stopped for passengers unless there is a safety zone. Tourism Australia also reminds visitors to park on the left-hand side of the road, as parking facing oncoming traffic is illegal, and to read time limits such as 2P, meaning two hours.
tips: Hook turns: right from the left lane

sections.heading: Keep the first day short
body: A long flight, a new car and the other side of the road add up. Collect the vehicle in the morning, after a night's sleep, and make the first day's drive short, ideally to a campground or holiday park within two hours of the airport. Tourism Australia advises against driving at night in the outback and country areas, because kangaroos and other animals are hard to see in the dark.

Fatigue makes old habits stronger, so take a break at least every two hours and swap drivers if you can. After a few days on the left, most visitors find the habit sticks; the moments to stay alert are the quiet ones.
tips: Pick up after a night's sleep

sections.heading: Plan a short first leg in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists campgrounds, holiday parks and rest areas around every major airport, with the facilities and access notes the park agencies publish, so you can find a first night close to the depot. Add it to a trip and AussieCamps shows the driving distance and time before you set off.

When you are ready, AussieCamps hands directions to Apple Maps or Google Maps, so turn-by-turn guidance tells you which lane to be in. Place details stay readable with no signal; the map, directions and weather need a connection. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.
tips: A first night near the depot
Directions in Apple or Google Maps

faq: Which side of the road do you drive on in Australia?

The left. The driver sits on the right of the car and should stay close to the centre line. You overtake on the right, go clockwise around roundabouts and give way to traffic already in the roundabout.
What is a hook turn in Melbourne?

A right turn made from the left lane, used at signed intersections in central Melbourne so cars stay clear of the trams in the middle of the road. You move to the far left of the intersection with your right indicator on, wait until the lights for the street you are turning into go green, then turn.

drink-driving-limits-australia-visitors.title: Drink Driving Limit in Australia for Visitors 2026: 0.05, Zero and Breath Tests
drink-driving-limits-australia-visitors.description: Australia's drink driving limit is under 0.05 on a full licence and zero on a learner or provisional one, in every state. How random breath tests work and the morning after.
drink-driving-limits-australia-visitors.imageAlt: NSW Police highway patrol officers stopping cars at a random breath testing site on Travers Street in Wagga Wagga
drink-driving-limits-australia-visitors.intro: In every Australian state and territory, a driver on a full licence must keep their blood or breath alcohol concentration (BAC) under 0.05, and a learner or provisional driver must keep it at zero. Visitors on a full licence from home use the 0.05 limit; the NSW and Northern Territory governments say so in as many words. Police can stop and breath test any driver at any time, without a reason, and Tourism Australia notes that random breath and drug testing happens on roadsides across the country. The safe plan is to keep drinking and driving apart entirely, including the morning after. We read each state's road safety page on 9 November 2026.

sections.heading: The limits by licence and state
body: The general limit is the same everywhere: under 0.05, which means less than 50 mg of alcohol in every 100 ml of blood. Every state sets a zero limit for learner and provisional drivers, and most add zero or 0.02 limits for drivers of buses, taxis and heavy vehicles. Western Australia goes further, with a zero limit for every novice driver in their first two years on a licence.

If you are visiting on a full licence from your own country, the NSW Government lists you under the 0.05 limit, and the Northern Territory lists fully licensed drivers from interstate and overseas the same way. Queensland applies the zero limit to drivers whose overseas licence is the equivalent of a learner, provisional or probationary one.

table.caption: Legal alcohol limits for drivers by state, from each road safety authority, read 9 November 2026. BAC is grams of alcohol per 100 ml of blood.

Full licence, including visitors
Learner and provisional
Lower limits for others
rows: Bus, taxi, heavy vehicle and dangerous goods drivers: zero
Bus and taxi drivers carrying passengers: zero
Bus, taxi, heavy vehicle over 15 t: zero

sections.heading: Random breath testing and drug testing
body: Random breath testing, which Australians call RBT, means police can stop any driver at any time and test their breath, with no suspicion needed. The NSW Government says police can ask you to speak or blow into a breath-testing device and can test any driver involved in a crash. Victoria Police also run larger testing stations, often called booze buses, where you must stop when directed.

Police can also stop drivers at random to test saliva for illegal drugs, with a stick wiped down the tongue. Victoria says refusing a breath test is generally treated more seriously than being over the limit, so stop, wait and follow the officer's directions. A site can sit on a country road on a Sunday morning as easily as outside a city pub on a Friday night.

sections.heading: What a drink adds up to
body: There is no reliable way to count drinks to a BAC. Weight, food, sex, tiredness and the strength of the pour all change it, and Australian beers, wines and pub measures vary widely. Victoria says coin-operated and personal breath testers can be used as a guide but can be inaccurate and cannot be used as evidence.

Victoria's road safety advice puts the risk plainly: at a BAC of 0.05, your risk of a crash is about double the risk at zero. The only reliable plan is to choose who drives before anyone drinks, and for that person not to drink at all.
tips: Choose a driver who doesn't drink

sections.heading: The morning after
body: Alcohol leaves the body slowly, and sleep does not speed it up. Victoria warns that if you drank a lot the night before, you are still likely to be over the legal limit the next day, and that learner, probationary and professional drivers on a zero limit should rethink driving at all.

On a road trip, the morning after a campground barbecue is when this catches people, because the first leg starts early. Plan a late start or a short first leg after a big night, and let a driver who did not drink take the wheel.
tips: Sleep does not sober you up
Late start after a big night

sections.heading: Alcohol and fatigue together
body: Alcohol and tiredness each slow your reactions, and together they compound. Both are worst on the first day of a trip, after a long flight, and on a long day's drive to a campground where a cold drink is waiting at the end.

Fatigue is the larger everyday risk on Australian highways, so plan days of four hours or less behind the wheel and stop every two hours. Some outback and Aboriginal communities also restrict carrying alcohol at all, with signs on the roads into them, so check the rules for the area before you stock the fridge.
tips: Tired plus a drink is worse

sections.heading: Penalties, licences and hire cars
body: Penalties rise with the reading. In Western Australia, a first offence between 0.05 and 0.08 can be settled with an infringement notice, but a second offence goes to court, with a fine of up to $2,000, at least six months' disqualification and possibly an alcohol interlock. Higher readings bring immediate licence suspension in every state, and a high-range offence is a criminal matter.

A suspension stops you driving in that state whatever licence you hold, and a conviction can affect a visa. Hire agreements also set their own rules for a driver over the legal limit, so read yours before you collect the vehicle.
tips: Suspension on the spot for higher readings

sections.heading: Plan the drive around the night in AussieCamps
body: The easiest way to keep drinking and driving apart is to stay where you eat. AussieCamps lists campgrounds and holiday parks close to towns, wineries and pubs, with the facilities the park agencies publish, and bookable holiday parks and motels you can reserve in the app.

Add the next morning's leg to a trip and AussieCamps shows its distance and time, so you can see whether a late start still gets you there in daylight. Place details stay readable with no signal; the map, directions and weather need a connection. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: What is the drink driving limit in Australia for tourists?

A blood or breath alcohol concentration under 0.05 if you hold a full licence from home, in every state and territory. If your licence is a learner or provisional one, the limit is zero. Bus, taxi and some heavy vehicle drivers have a zero or 0.02 limit.
Can police breath test you without a reason in Australia?

Yes. Police in every state run random breath testing: they can stop any driver at any time and ask for a breath sample, and they can also test any driver involved in a crash. Random roadside drug testing works the same way. Refusing a test is an offence, usually with a heavier penalty than being over the limit.

best-travel-apps-australia.title: Best Apps for Travelling Australia in 2026: 10 to Install Before a Road Trip
best-travel-apps-australia.description: The apps worth installing for an Australian road trip in 2026: entry, navigation, weather, emergency calls, fuel, tolls, city transport and where to stay, with prices and ratings checked November 2026.
best-travel-apps-australia.imageAlt: A green distance sign on the Eyre Highway at Border Village showing Nullarbor 184, Ceduna 479 and Adelaide 1253 kilometres
best-travel-apps-australia.intro: An Australian road trip needs fewer apps than the App Store suggests, but the right ones save money and trouble: the official ETA app is the only place to apply for that visa, a fuel app pays for itself on a long drive, and the triple zero app reads out your coordinates when you do not know where you are. These are the ten we would install, grouped by the job they do. We make AussieCamps and list it honestly alongside the rest; every price, rating and update date comes from the Australian App Store on 9 November 2026.

sections.heading: The apps at a glance
body: Install the entry and emergency apps before you fly, then the road apps once you have a local SIM or eSIM. Every app below is free to download; the prices column shows what costs money.

sections.heading: 1. AussieCamps: where to stay, and the plan for the whole trip
body: We make AussieCamps, so read this entry with that in mind. It lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 745 national parks, plus 1,393 dump points, 3,004 drinking water points and 1,186 toilets, from state park agencies, road authorities and public facility datasets, with filters for water, toilets, showers, power, dogs, vehicle access and fees. It also lists holiday parks, motels, B&Bs and tours you can book in the app.

Trips let you add stops in order and show the driving distance and time for each leg, arrival dates with a forecast for each stop, a checklist and a packing list, with sharing and Calendar sync. Place details stay readable with no signal; the map, directions and weather need a connection. It runs on iPhone only, has no traveller reviews or fuel prices, and is new, so it has no Australian rating yet.
tips: Official camp and rest area data

sections.heading: 2. AustralianETA: the visa app for eligible passports
body: The Department of Home Affairs publishes AustralianETA, the app you use to apply for an Electronic Travel Authority if your passport is eligible, which includes the United States, Canada, Japan, Singapore and Malaysia. The app is free, but each application carries an A$20 service charge that is not refunded if the ETA is refused. It is rated 4.6 from 1,206 Australian ratings and was updated on 30 October 2026.

Passport holders from much of Europe apply for the free eVisitor online instead, and other travellers need a different visa. Check which one applies before you pay, and use only the official app: sites that sell an ETA form charge more for the same thing.

sections.heading: 3. Google Maps: navigation, downloaded before you need it
body: Google Maps is free, rated 4.6 from 503,750 Australian ratings, and lets you download an area to keep driving directions working without signal. Download the regions you will cross while you still have Wi-Fi, because reception drops quickly outside towns, and set the app to avoid tolls if you would rather not use Sydney, Melbourne or Brisbane's toll roads.
Apple Maps is the alternative already on an iPhone. Either one takes directions handed over from a camping app, so you can plan in one and drive with the other.

sections.heading: 4. BOM Weather: forecasts and warnings you can trust
body: The Bureau of Meteorology's own app is free, rated 4.6 from 473,513 Australian ratings, and shows forecasts, radar, rain alerts and official warnings for cyclones, floods, storms and fire weather. It is the app to check each morning on a road trip, especially in summer.

For fires and floods, add the warning app for the state you are in: Hazards Near Me in New South Wales and VicEmergency in Victoria are both free. Their ratings are low because people rate them in the middle of an emergency, but they carry the official warnings.

sections.heading: 5. Emergency Plus: triple zero with your location
body: Emergency Plus is the official triple zero app, published by the National Triple Zero Awareness Work Group. It calls 000 from a single tap and shows your GPS coordinates, the nearest street address and a what3words address, so you can read your location to the operator when you are on a highway or a track with no landmarks. It is free and rated 3.9 from 524 Australian ratings.
It still needs a mobile network to place the call. Where your own network has no coverage, a mobile phone can still reach emergency services through 112 on any network in range.
tips: Still needs a network to call

sections.heading: 6. Petrol Spy: fuel prices across the states
body: Petrol Spy compares fuel prices across Australia and is free with ads; it is rated 4.8 from 187,024 Australian ratings, though its last update was in July 2025. In New South Wales, the government's own NSW FuelCheck app shows prices from every station by law and is rated 4.8 from 123,128 ratings.
Fuel prices in Australia move in weekly cycles in the big cities, and country prices can be much higher, so a minute in the app before filling up can save a few dollars a tank on a long trip.

sections.heading: 7. Linkt: tolls in Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane
body: Only Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane have toll roads, and none has a toll booth. Transurban's Linkt app, rated 4.6 from 165,962 Australian ratings, lets you buy a visitor pass or open an account for the number plate you are driving, so tolls are charged to your card rather than turning into a notice with fees.
In a hire car, ask first: many hire companies pay the toll and charge you a fee for each one, and a pass may or may not be allowed. If you never drive in those three cities, you can skip this app.

sections.heading: 8. Opal Travel and the PTV app: city transport
body: In Sydney you can tap on to trains, buses, ferries and light rail with a contactless card or phone, and the Opal Travel app, rated 4.5 from 37,008 ratings, plans trips and shows live times. In Melbourne, the Public Transport Victoria app, rated 4.6 from 64,108 ratings, does the same for trains, trams and buses.

Leaving the campervan at a holiday park outside the city and going in by train is often cheaper and easier than city parking. Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide have their own apps, with more mixed ratings.
tips: Tap on with a card or phone

sections.heading: 9. Xe: exchange rates and money
body: Xe shows live exchange rates and converts prices in your own currency, and it can send money abroad; it is free and rated 4.8 from 49,718 Australian ratings. It is useful for checking what a campground, a hire bond or a fuel bill costs you at home.
Most Australian businesses take contactless cards, but some remote campgrounds and honesty boxes take cash only, so carry some notes for the outback.
tips: Carry some cash for remote camps

sections.heading: How we chose
body: We picked one app for each job a visitor's road trip needs, and checked each price, rating and update date on the Australian App Store on 9 November 2026. We left out booking and ride-share apps, which most travellers already have, and paid offline topographic map apps, which matter only for remote four-wheel-drive routes.
We make AussieCamps and put it first; no other developer here paid to be included. Spotted something that has changed since? Say so on the support page.

faq: What apps do I need for a trip to Australia?

For a road trip: the AustralianETA app if your passport is eligible, Google Maps or Apple Maps, BOM Weather, Emergency Plus for triple zero calls, a fuel price app such as Petrol Spy, Linkt for city tolls, and an app for finding places to stay, such as AussieCamps. Add Opal Travel for Sydney and the PTV app for Melbourne if you use public transport.
Is the Australian ETA app free?

The app is free to download, but there is an A$20 service charge for each ETA application made through it, and that charge is not refunded if the application is refused. European passport holders usually apply for the eVisitor instead, which is free and done online.

australia-three-week-campervan-route.title: 3 Week Campervan Itinerary Australia: Sydney to Adelaide by the Coast
australia-three-week-campervan-route.description: A 3-week Australian campervan route from Sydney to Adelaide along the south-east coast: 2,517 km, 15 driving days, Wilsons Promontory, the Great Ocean Road and the Grampians.
australia-three-week-campervan-route.imageAlt: Mallacoota Inlet in Croajingolong National Park, Victoria, with sand flats, a wooded island and blue hills behind
australia-three-week-campervan-route.intro: Three weeks is enough to drive from Sydney to Adelaide along the south-east coast without rushing, but not enough to add every detour. This route runs 2,517 km, about 34 hours at the wheel across 15 driving days, with seven nights spent in pairs so you get days without the campervan moving. It follows the New South Wales south coast, crosses into Victoria at Mallacoota, takes in Wilsons Promontory and the Great Ocean Road, turns inland to the Grampians and ends along the Coorong. Distances and times are from OSRM routing on OpenStreetMap data, worked out on 9 November 2026.

sections.heading: The route at a glance
body: The plan has 21 days, 20 nights and no leg over four hours. The longest day is Lakes Entrance to Wilsons Promontory, and the two nights at each of seven stops are what keep the trip from becoming a transfer.

A one-way hire from Sydney to Adelaide usually costs more than a return, and not every company has a depot in both cities, so check that before you plan. Driving it the other way, from Adelaide to Sydney, works just as well.

sections.heading: Week one: the New South Wales south coast
body: Leave Sydney early and drive the 186 km to Jervis Bay. Booderee National Park, run by Parks Australia, has campsites at Green Patch, Cave Beach and Bristol Point, and its own park pass, which a NSW national parks pass does not cover; Green Patch weekends are generally booked out up to a month ahead from October to May. Spend the second day on the white-sand beaches, then move south to Batemans Bay for two nights near Murramarang National Park, where kangaroos graze the beach campgrounds at Pebbly and Depot beaches.

Day 5 is the longest on this coast, 198 km to Eden on the Princes Highway. Beowa National Park, renamed from Ben Boyd National Park in 2022, has vehicle campgrounds at Saltwater Creek and Bittangabee Bay south of town. Day 6 is a short 85 km to Mallacoota, inside Croajingolong National Park on the Victorian side, for two nights on the inlet.

sections.heading: Week two: Gippsland, the Prom and Melbourne
body: Drive 203 km to Lakes Entrance on day 8, then the trip's longest leg, 286 km and almost four hours, to Tidal River in Wilsons Promontory National Park. Parks Victoria now takes instant bookings for Tidal River rather than running a ballot, but in summer the campground has a minimum stay: between 20 December 2026 and 24 January 2027 camping is booked by the week, arriving and leaving on a Sunday. Outside that window two nights is enough for the Mount Oberon walk and Squeaky Beach.

Day 11 takes you 224 km into Melbourne. Two nights let you return a hired car or visit the city by train from a holiday park on the edge of town, and restock before the coast road. Melbourne's CityLink and EastLink are tolled, so check how your hire company charges tolls before you drive across the city.
tips: Longest leg: Lakes Entrance to the Prom

sections.heading: Week three: the Great Ocean Road, the Grampians and the Coorong
body: Drive the Great Ocean Road westbound, 197 km from Melbourne to Apollo Bay, so the lookouts are on your side of the road, and spend two nights there for the Otways. Day 15 covers the Twelve Apostles and Loch Ard Gorge on the way to Port Fairy, 185 km in all. Day 16 turns inland, 156 km to Halls Gap in the Grampians National Park, for two nights of walking among the sandstone ranges.

From Halls Gap it is 221 km to Mount Gambier and its crater lakes, then 133 km to Robe and 187 km along the Coorong to Meningie. The last day is 149 km into Adelaide. South Australia runs on Central time, half an hour behind Victoria, and restricts carrying some fresh fruit and vegetables into the state, so run the fridge down before the border.
tips: Westbound on the Great Ocean Road
Half an hour back at the SA border

sections.heading: When to go
body: October to April is the season for this coast. Summer from mid-December to the end of January brings school holidays, full campgrounds and the minimum stays at places like Tidal River, so book the national park nights first. March and April are often the calmest months, with warm water and fewer people.

Summer is also fire season along the whole route. Check the fire danger rating for each district the evening before you drive, and keep the next day's plan flexible: the Princes Highway through East Gippsland has closed in past bushfire summers.
tips: Book national parks first in summer

sections.heading: Making three weeks work in a campervan
body: Two-night stops are the difference between a holiday and a delivery job. Use them to empty the waste tanks, do laundry at a holiday park and buy food, then leave the van parked for the day. Plan at least one powered site each week to charge everything and run the fridge without worrying about the battery.

Fill up before the quieter stretches: between Eden and Orbost, and between Mount Gambier and Meningie, towns are smaller and further apart. Finish each day before dusk, when kangaroos and wombats are on the roads of Gippsland and the Coorong.

sections.heading: Plan the three weeks in AussieCamps
body: Add each night to a trip in AussieCamps and it keeps the stops in order, shows the driving distance and time for every leg and the whole journey, and gives the forecast for each stop on the day you plan to arrive. AussieCamps lists campgrounds, national parks, rest areas and dump points along the route from the park agencies and road authorities, with their facilities and fees.
Place details stay readable with no signal, which helps at Croajingolong and the Prom. The map, directions and weather need a connection. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

cyclone-flood-season-camping-australia.title: Cyclone and Flood Season Camping in Australia 2026-27: Warnings and Road Closures
cyclone-flood-season-camping-australia.description: Australia's cyclone season runs 1 November to 30 April. Where cyclones and floods hit, the three warning levels, which apps to follow, and how to check road closures by state.
cyclone-flood-season-camping-australia.imageAlt: A flooded road in the Herbert River catchment of north Queensland, with a Road Subject to Flooding sign and a car driving through water
cyclone-flood-season-camping-australia.intro: Australia's tropical cyclone season runs from 1 November to 30 April, and the same months bring the wet season to the north, when rivers rise and roads close for days. Cyclones form off Queensland, the Northern Territory and northern Western Australia; flooding can happen anywhere after heavy rain, including the south-east. For campers the rules are simple: follow the warnings each day, never drive into floodwater, and be ready to move to solid shelter or wait out a closed road. We read each warning agency and road authority page on 9 November 2026.

sections.heading: The 2026-27 season
body: The Bureau of Meteorology no longer issues a seasonal cyclone outlook, saying climate change has made the old statistical methods less reliable. ABC News reported on 1 November 2026 that modelling from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts points to five to eight cyclones in the Australian region this season, against a long-term average of 11, with the strongest signal for fewer cyclones off Western Australia and in the central Coral Sea.

A quiet season still only needs one cyclone to reach your coast. Since 1970, three to four systems a year have crossed the Australian coast at cyclone strength on average, and the first usually does so in late December. Near-normal activity is expected off the Northern Territory, in the Gulf of Carpentaria and near the Queensland coast.

sections.heading: Where cyclones and floods hit
body: Cyclones affect the tropical coasts: north and central Queensland, the Top End of the Northern Territory and the Gulf, and Western Australia from the Kimberley to the Pilbara and Gascoyne. The Bureau defines a tropical cyclone as a low with winds of at least 63 km/h, gusting above 90 km/h, around most of its centre. Rain from a cyclone or the monsoon can flood inland roads hundreds of kilometres from the coast.

Floods are not only a northern problem. Heavy rain can close roads in New South Wales, Victoria and south-east Queensland in any season. In the wet-season north, low-level crossings called floodways carry depth markers, and a road can be open in the morning and under water by afternoon.

sections.heading: The three warning levels
body: Australia uses one warning system for floods, cyclones, storms, bushfires and extreme heat, with three levels shown by the same coloured icons in every state. Advice, in yellow, means an incident has started and there is no immediate danger, so stay up to date. Watch and Act, in orange, means conditions are changing and you need to start taking action now. Emergency Warning, in red, means you may be in danger and need to act immediately.

For cyclones the Bureau also issues a Cyclone Watch when gales could start within 24 to 48 hours, and a Cyclone Warning when they are expected within 24 hours. A watch is the signal for a campground: decide where you will go, fill the tank and buy food while shops are open.
tips: Act early, not at the last minute

sections.heading: Where to get warnings in each state
body: Install the BOM Weather app for forecasts, radar and warnings, and add the emergency site or app for the state you are in. National warnings are collected on Hazard Watch, and the ABC broadcasts emergency information on local radio, which keeps working when mobile networks are busy or down.

Check them while you still have signal each morning: a warning issued after you lose reception on a remote road will not reach you. Save the emergency number 000, and the SES number 132 500 for help in floods and storms.

ABC local radio in an emergency

sections.heading: Floodwater: if it's flooded, forget it
body: Queensland's Get Ready campaign says it can take as little as 15 cm of water for a car to lose traction and be swept away, that modern cars are light and buoyant, and that the pressure of floodwater can stop you opening the doors and windows. The wading depth in a vehicle manual is for still water, not a current. You cannot see whether the road under the water is still there.

Wait for the water to drop below the marker on the floodway, or turn around. Driving on a road closed by flooding can bring a fine as well as the risk, and in the north, floodwater and river edges can carry saltwater crocodiles. Never camp in a dry creek bed or on a low river flat in the wet season: rain far upstream can fill it overnight.

sections.heading: If a cyclone is coming
body: A tent or campervan is no place to sit out a cyclone. When a watch is issued for your area, leave the coast early, or book a room built to cyclone standards in a larger town, or go to a public cyclone shelter if the local authority opens one. Tourism NT tells visitors to follow advice on local radio and to ask about tying down a caravan or other light structure.

Fill the tank and water containers, buy food for several days, charge every battery and keep the car pointed at your exit. After the cyclone passes, roads can stay closed for days with fallen trees, damaged bridges and floodwater, so stay put until the authorities say routes are open.
tips: Roads stay shut after it passes

sections.heading: Planning a wet-season trip
body: Travelling the north between November and April is possible with flexible plans. Build spare days into the itinerary, pick sealed roads and accommodation over remote tracks, and check the road report for every leg each morning. Many remote national park roads and campgrounds close for the whole wet season, and four-wheel-drive tracks such as the Gibb River Road are often shut.

Hire agreements usually forbid driving on closed roads and through floodwater, and insurance rarely covers it. If a closure holds you in a town, treat it as a rest day rather than looking for a way round.
tips: A closure is a rest day

sections.heading: Keep a fallback in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists campgrounds, national parks and rest areas across the north with the access notes the park agencies publish, and a 7-day forecast on each place page. When a camp floods or a road closes, it also lists holiday parks, motels and B&Bs you can book in the app, so a solid roof is a few taps away.

Save a trip with each night's stop and AussieCamps shows the forecast on the day you plan to arrive. Place details stay readable with no signal; the map, directions and weather need a connection. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: When is cyclone season in Australia?

From 1 November to 30 April. Cyclones affect the coasts of Queensland, the Northern Territory and northern Western Australia, and on average the first one to cross the coast does so in late December. The Bureau of Meteorology no longer publishes a seasonal outlook, so follow the daily forecasts and warnings instead.
Can you drive through a flooded road in Australia?

No. The official advice in every state is if it's flooded, forget it. Queensland's Get Ready campaign says as little as 15 cm of water can make a car lose traction and be swept away, and driving on a road closed by flooding can bring a fine. Wait for the water to drop or take another route.

is-camping-in-australia-dangerous.title: Is Camping in Australia Dangerous? The Real Risks and How to Stay Safe (2026)
is-camping-in-australia-dangerous.description: What actually hurts campers in Australia, from driving, heat and water to crocodiles, stingers, snakes and spiders, with where each risk is and what to do.
is-camping-in-australia-dangerous.imageAlt: A Queensland Government sign warning of a recent crocodile sighting, telling people to keep out of the water and away from its edge
is-camping-in-australia-dangerous.intro: Camping in Australia is not especially dangerous if you plan for the few risks that matter. The ones that hurt the most campers are ordinary: driving long days when tired, heat, swimming in the wrong place and fire or flood weather. The animals that worry visitors are real but predictable: crocodiles live in the tropical north, box jellyfish in northern seas in the warmer months, and snakes avoid people unless provoked. This guide sets out where each risk is and what to do about it, from official health, parks and safety pages we read on 9 November 2026.

sections.heading: The real risks, ranked by where they bite
body: Most trips go without a scare, and the order of what goes wrong surprises people. The road comes first, because Australian trips mean long distances, animals at dusk and tired drivers. Heat, the sun and water come next. Fire and flood depend on the season and the region. Wildlife comes last for most campers, and nearly all of it is avoided by reading the signs.
The table sums up where each risk applies and the one habit that deals with it. The sections below explain each in more detail.
tips: The road is the biggest risk

table.caption: The main risks for campers in Australia, where they apply and what to do. Read 9 November 2026.
head: Risk
Where and when
What to do
rows: Everywhere, worst on long outback days
Short days, breaks every two hours, no driving at dawn or dusk
Inland and the north in summer

sections.heading: On the road: the risk that matters most
body: Distances between towns in Australia are long, and the hours behind the wheel catch out visitors who plan days like a European road trip. Fatigue, kangaroos and other animals on the road at dawn and dusk, and long trucks on two-lane highways are the everyday dangers. Plan driving days you can finish in daylight, stop every two hours, and pull into a rest area when you feel tired, not when you reach the next town.

Remote roads add their own risks: unsealed surfaces, single-lane bridges, cattle on unfenced highways and long gaps between fuel. Hire companies also ban some roads. Our guides on fatigue and wildlife, road trains and fuel range cover each of these properly.
tips: Rest areas are there to be used

sections.heading: Heat, sun and drinking water
body: Australian summers bring heatwaves, and the Bureau of Meteorology runs a heatwave service that maps where one is coming and how severe it will be. Inland, in the north and in a tent or van without shade, a hot day becomes dangerous faster than visitors expect. Plan the hottest days around shade, a pool, a cooler coast or an air-conditioned town.

Healthdirect lists heatstroke as a medical emergency: confusion, a very high temperature, and hot, red or dry skin mean calling Triple Zero (000). Drink before you are thirsty, carry more drinking water than you think you need in the outback, and use a hat and sunscreen from mid-morning, because the UV is strong even when the air is cool.

sections.heading: Beaches, rivers and crocodile country
body: On surf beaches, swim between the red and yellow flags, where lifesavers are watching, and stay out of the water where there are none. Rip currents are hard to spot from the shore, and Surf Life Saving Australia's Beachsafe app and website list which beaches are patrolled and when. Rivers, dams and waterholes have cold water, hidden snags and sudden drop-offs, so never swim alone or after drinking.

In the tropical north, crocodiles change the rules. Queensland says estuarine crocodiles live between Gladstone and Cape York Peninsula and throughout the Gulf of Carpentaria, and they are also found across the Top End of the Northern Territory and the Kimberley. Treat any river, creek, estuary, billabong or beach there as crocodile habitat unless a sign says it is a safe swimming area. Camp well back from the water, stand back from the edge when fishing, and never clean fish or leave food scraps near it.

Box jellyfish are the other northern danger. Healthdirect says the major box jellyfish lives in the far north and that its sting can kill. Swim inside stinger nets where they are provided, wear a full stinger suit, and if someone is stung in tropical waters, call 000, pour vinegar on the sting and get them to hospital.
tips: Vinegar and 000 for a tropical sting

sections.heading: Snakes, spiders and other bites
body: Australia has some of the world's most venomous snakes, but they avoid people, and bites usually happen when someone tries to catch, kill or step over one. Leave any snake alone and walk away. Wear closed shoes and use a torch around camp at night, and keep the tent zipped. Healthdirect's first aid is to call 000, keep the person still and calm, and apply a pressure immobilisation bandage over the bite and up the whole limb. Do not wash the bite, cut it, suck it or use a tourniquet.

Most spiders are harmless. Healthdirect says a funnel-web or any big black spider bite is a medical emergency, that redback bites are very painful but not life-threatening, and that white-tails are not dangerous. Shake out boots and clothing left outside overnight.

Mosquitoes carry Ross River virus, Barmah Forest virus and, in some areas, Japanese encephalitis, so use repellent and cover up at dawn and dusk, especially near rivers and wetlands. Ticks live in coastal bush on the east coast; check yourself after walks.

sections.heading: Fire, flood and storms
body: Fire and flood are seasonal and regional, and both are handled by checking the warnings each morning. In the southern summer, check the fire danger rating, any total fire ban and the warnings for your campsite, and leave bush country on a Catastrophic day. In the north, the wet season from about November to April brings cyclones, storms and roads cut by water.

Never drive into floodwater, because you cannot see the depth, the current or the road under it. Do not camp in a dry creek bed, and move to higher ground when heavy rain is forecast upstream. Our guides to bushfire safety and severe weather explain the warning levels and the apps for each state.
tips: Do not camp in creek beds

sections.heading: Remote areas, phone signal and getting help
body: In an emergency, call Triple Zero (000) for police, fire or an ambulance. Healthdirect notes that if 000 does not work on a mobile, you can try 112. Mobile coverage disappears quickly outside towns and along most outback roads, so before you leave coverage, tell someone your route and when you will check in.

For remote trips, carry a personal locator beacon or a satellite messenger, plus extra water, food and fuel, and stay with your vehicle if it breaks down: it is easier to find than a person on foot. Download what you need while you still have signal.

sections.heading: Plan safer stops with AussieCamps
body: Most of the risks above shrink when you know where the next stop is. AussieCamps puts campgrounds, rest areas, dump points and drinking water points from park agencies and road authorities on one map, so you can plan shorter driving days with a real place to stop and see the weather forecast for each stop on your dates.

Place details are saved on the phone, so you can still read a campsite's facilities without signal; the map, directions and weather need a connection, so check them before you drive out of coverage. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.
