Check forecasts before you lose coverage

faq: Is camping in Australia dangerous?

Not for a prepared camper. The things that hurt people most are ordinary: long drives when tired, heat, water and fire weather. Snakes, spiders and crocodiles are real, but they are predictable, and following the signs and local warnings avoids almost all of the risk.
What is the most dangerous animal for campers in Australia?

On the road it is the kangaroo, because collisions at dawn and dusk cause far more harm than bites. Around water in the tropical north, the estuarine crocodile is the one to take seriously: do not swim where there are warning signs, and camp well back from the water.
Is it safe to camp in crocodile country?

Yes, if you follow the Crocwise advice. Queensland says estuarine crocodiles live between Gladstone and Cape York Peninsula and throughout the Gulf of Carpentaria, and they also live across the Top End and northern Western Australia. Swim only where it is signed as safe, keep away from the water's edge and never leave fish scraps or food near it.
What should I do if a snake bites me?

Call Triple Zero (000), keep still and stay calm, and apply a pressure immobilisation bandage over the bite and along the whole limb. Healthdirect says not to wash the bite, cut it, suck it, use a tourniquet or try to catch the snake. If 000 does not connect on a mobile, try 112.
Is it safe to free camp alone in Australia?

Many people do. Tell someone your plan and when you will check in, choose sites where other campers stay if you are unsure, and carry a personal locator beacon or satellite messenger where there is no mobile coverage.

free-camping-new-south-wales.title: Free Camping in NSW 2026: State Forests, Free Park Sites and Rest Areas
free-camping-new-south-wales.description: Where you can camp for free in New South Wales: state forests for up to four weeks, no-fee national park sites, council camps and rest areas, with the rules for each.
free-camping-new-south-wales.imageAlt: Tall pine trees against a blue sky at The Pines in the Watagans, a state forest camping and picnic area west of Lake Macquarie, New South Wales
free-camping-new-south-wales.intro: Yes, you can camp for free in New South Wales, and state forests are the easiest place to do it: every state forest except Cumberland and Strickland allows free camping with no booking for up to four weeks. Some national park campgrounds charge no camping fee but still take a $6 booking, a few remote park sites need no booking at all, and many country towns run free or cheap camps to bring travellers in. Rest areas are for a break from driving, and councils can fine you for camping where a sign says no.

sections.heading: State forests: the main free option
body: Forestry Corporation of NSW manages the state forests, and camping in them costs nothing. Sites are first come, first served, you can stay up to four weeks, and nothing can be booked, so on long weekends and in the school holidays the well-known forest camps can fill early. Keep a second forest or a cheap town camp in mind.

Facilities range from a toilet, tables and fire rings to a flat clearing with nothing at all, and many forests have no bins. Bring your own water and a shovel or portable toilet, and carry every bag of rubbish out. Dogs are welcome in state forests if kept under control, which is why forests are the usual choice for anyone travelling with one.
tips: Free, no booking, up to four weeks

sections.heading: Where the forest camps are
body: The widest choice is inland and along the Great Dividing Range. The Pilliga, the huge cypress and ironbark forest between Coonabarabran and Narrabri, has quiet forest camps off the Newell Highway. Barrington Tops State Forest has cool, high campgrounds above the Hunter Valley, and the Watagans, west of Lake Macquarie, have camping areas under tall trees within easy reach of Newcastle and the Central Coast.

Closer to Sydney, Belanglo State Forest in the Southern Highlands has a free camping area, and the forests around Tumut and Batlow in the Snowy Valleys hold camps beside dams and creeks. Forestry Corporation's website lists each forest's camping areas and any closure, and harvesting or wet roads can shut part of a forest at short notice.

sections.heading: National parks: free sites that still need a booking
body: NSW national parks have more than 365 campgrounds, and a number of them charge no camping fee. Most of those must still be booked on the NSW National Parks website, with a $6 booking fee, as at Brou Lake on the south coast. A few basic sites need no booking, such as Tuross River campground in Wadbilliga National Park, and neither does remote bush camping away from listed campgrounds, where NPWS suggests filling in a trip intention form.

Camping fees and park entry are separate. About 45 parks charge a vehicle entry fee, such as $8 a day at Myall Lakes and Murramarang, so a free campground inside one of those parks still costs the entry. Pets are not allowed in national parks.
tips: $6 to book a free park site

sections.heading: Council camps, showgrounds and country towns
body: Many country councils let travellers stay free, or for a small fee, at a riverside reserve or a camping area on the edge of town, because campers spend money in the main street. Each council sets its own rules: some take only self-contained vehicles with a toilet on board, some ask for a donation, and the stay limit is on the sign.

Showgrounds are the other cheap standby. Many take campers for a modest fee, with toilets, hot showers and sometimes power, except when a show or event is on. The visitor centre usually knows the current arrangement better than any listing.

Away from those places, camping on council land needs council approval unless an exemption applies, and ignoring a council's no camping sign brings a $110 on-the-spot fine. Crown reserves follow the rules of whoever manages them.

sections.heading: Rest areas and the roadside
body: Rest areas are built for driver fatigue, and the official word on sleeping in them is mixed. Service NSW says they are not for camping, while a July 2026 planning practice note says camping in one may be allowed unless a no camping or no overnight stays sign is up.

Treat a rest area as a place to sleep in the vehicle and move on in the morning, not as a campsite: no awning, no chairs spread across the grass, no second night. Park in the car and caravan bays, keep the truck bays clear for heavy vehicles, and if a sign says no overnight stays, drive on to the next town or forest.
tips: A sign against it means go

sections.heading: Fire, water and the best season
body: The NSW Bush Fire Danger Period runs from 1 October to 31 March, and on a Total Fire Ban day no fire may be lit in the open. State forests also declare solid fuel fire bans, which allow gas cooking only, with a maximum penalty of $2,200 for lighting a wood fire, so check the RFS rating and Forestry Corporation's ban list each morning.

Water decides how long you can stay. Most free forest camps have no drinking water, so carry enough for every night and refill in town. The inland forests, such as the Pilliga, are at their best in autumn, winter and spring, while the high camps at Barrington Tops suit the warmer months and can be cold and wet even in summer.

sections.heading: Find free sites in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps maps 372 NSW national park campgrounds, 869 roadside rest areas and 347 public dump points, each with the facilities, fees and rules the agency publishes. You can filter by cost, including free sites, save the ones you like to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.

State forest camping areas are not in the app yet, so use Forestry Corporation's pages for those. Place details are saved on the phone for use without signal, while the map, routing and weather need a connection. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Where can I camp for free in NSW?

In most state forests, which allow free camping with no booking for up to four weeks. Some national park campgrounds charge no camping fee but still take a $6 booking, a few remote park sites need no booking at all, and some country councils run free or low-cost camps. A rest area with no sign against it can do for one night in the vehicle.
Is free camping legal in NSW?

Yes, where the land manager allows it. State forests, no-fee park campgrounds and council camps that say so are all legal places to stay. Camping elsewhere on council land needs approval, and ignoring a council's no camping sign brings a $110 on-the-spot fine.
Can you camp anywhere in a NSW state forest?

In almost all of them, yes: camping is free and first come, first served for up to four weeks, except in Cumberland and Strickland state forests. Check Forestry Corporation's website before you go, because harvesting, fire or wet weather can close a forest or a road into it.
Can I take my dog free camping in NSW?

Yes, in state forests, where dogs are welcome if kept under control and Forestry Corporation asks that they stay on a lead. Dogs are not allowed in NSW national parks, so a forest camp or a council camp that allows pets is the usual choice.

free-camping-victoria.title: Free Camping in Victoria 2026: State Forests, Free Park Camps and the Coast
free-camping-victoria.description: Where to camp for free in Victoria: 28 nights in state forests, 300 free forest campgrounds, free Parks Victoria sites, river frontages and the coastal towns that fine.
free-camping-victoria.imageAlt: Stone chimneys and a fenced clearing at Balt Camp, an old forest settlement site in Wombat State Forest, Victoria
free-camping-victoria.intro: Victoria is one of the easiest states for free camping. In state forests you can camp almost anywhere at least 20 metres from a waterway for up to 28 consecutive nights, and every one of the more than 300 forest campgrounds is free except Murrindindi Scenic Reserve. A handful of Parks Victoria campgrounds are free with no booking, and Crown land along rivers opens up more spots. The catch is the coast: some coastal councils fine people for sleeping in a vehicle, so the free camps are mostly inland.

sections.heading: State forests: camp almost anywhere
body: The state forests are managed by DEECA, the Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action, and they follow a simple rule: find a spot at least 20 metres from a river, creek or lake and stay no more than 28 consecutive nights. Nobody takes bookings, and nobody charges. The one exception is a forest reserve, where you must use the campground provided.

More than 300 forest campgrounds come with something extra, usually a pit toilet, a table and a fireplace, and all of them are free except Murrindindi Scenic Reserve. Dispersed spots have nothing at all, so carry water, a shovel and your rubbish. Dogs are allowed in state forests on a lead or under control, unlike most national parks.

table.caption: Where you can camp for free in Victoria, and the main limit at each.

sections.heading: The forests worth driving to
body: Within two hours of Melbourne, Wombat State Forest near Daylesford, Mount Disappointment north of Whittlesea and Big River State Forest beyond Marysville all have free camps among tall eucalypts, and Big River's spots along the water are popular in summer. Further north-east, the Howqua River camps near Mansfield, such as Sheepyard Flat, are a classic first taste of the High Country.

West of Melbourne, the Pyrenees and the forests around the goldfields towns hold quiet camps in box-ironbark country. The Otways, Gippsland and the north-east all have more, and the High Country guide covers the alpine tracks and huts in detail.

sections.heading: Free campgrounds in parks
body: Most Parks Victoria campgrounds that you book carry a fee, which is half price until July 2027, but some charge nothing and take no bookings. Warby-Ovens National Park near Wangaratta and King Hut in the Alpine National Park are free, first come campgrounds, and at Cape Conran Coastal Park the beach camps at Binn Beach, Gunnai Beach and Pearl Point take no bookings either.

In the Alpine National Park you can also camp away from campgrounds in many areas, but not within 200 metres of the Bogong High Plains or Pretty Valley roads. Pets are not allowed in most national parks, so check the park page before you bring a dog.
tips: Check pets on the park page

sections.heading: River frontages and the Murray
body: Crown land along rivers is another free option. On an unlicensed Crown river frontage you can camp more than 20 metres from the water and 200 metres from a house for up to 28 consecutive nights. Where the frontage is licensed, often grazed by the farm next door, you may camp only in designated areas, for up to 14 nights and without dogs.

Along the Murray, much of the Victorian bank is reserve, forest or park, and sandy river beaches make some of the state's best free camps. Each stretch has its own manager, so read the signs at the track entry, and leave the river as clean as you found it.
tips: Read the sign at the track

sections.heading: The coast, rest areas and towns
body: Free camping on the coast is limited. Surf Coast Shire, covering Torquay, Anglesea and Lorne, makes sleeping in a vehicle anywhere in the shire an offence with a $300 on-the-spot fine, and other coastal councils patrol their car parks. Along the Great Ocean Road, budget for a campground or a caravan park.

Rest areas on major roads are run by Transport Victoria and those on local roads by councils, and each follows its own sign, so stay overnight only where a sign allows it. Some inland towns run free or low-cost camping areas, and a few showgrounds take campers, so check with the council or the visitor centre.

sections.heading: Seasons, closures and fire
body: Many forest and park roads close from June to November to protect tracks that are easily damaged when wet. In 2026 most Parks Victoria closures lifted on 29 October, and the Forest Fire Management Victoria closures map shows state forest roads, with a fine for driving a closed one.

The Fire Danger Period is set council by council, usually from spring until April or May. In a state forest, keep a campfire under one metre across with three metres cleared all round, and never leave it. On a Total Fire Ban day no campfire may be lit, so bring a gas stove. Dig toilet holes 30 cm deep and 100 metres from water.

sections.heading: Find free camps in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps maps 438 Victorian campgrounds, 350 of them state forest and Crown land sites managed by DEECA and 88 run by Parks Victoria, plus 651 roadside rest areas and 181 public dump points. You can filter by cost, including free sites, and save the camps you like to a trip with dates and notes.
Place details are saved on the phone for use without signal, which helps once you are down a forest track. The map, routing and weather need a connection, and AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Where can I camp for free in Victoria?

In state forests, where you can camp almost anywhere at least 20 metres from a waterway for up to 28 nights, and at more than 300 forest campgrounds, all free except Murrindindi Scenic Reserve. A few Parks Victoria campgrounds are also free with no booking, such as those in Warby-Ovens National Park and King Hut in the Alpine National Park.
Is free camping allowed in Victoria?

Yes, on land where the manager allows it: state forests, some park campgrounds and some council sites. Rest areas follow the sign at each stop, and some coastal councils ban sleeping in a vehicle altogether, such as Surf Coast Shire with a $300 on-the-spot fine.
How long can you free camp in a Victorian state forest?
Up to 28 consecutive nights. Pick a spot at least 20 metres from any river, creek or lake, and in forest reserves use only the campgrounds the land manager provides.
Can I free camp near Melbourne?

Yes, in the state forests within about two hours of the city, such as Wombat State Forest near Daylesford, Mount Disappointment north of Whittlesea and Big River State Forest near Marysville. They fill quickly on warm weekends, so arrive early or have a second forest in mind.

free-camping-queensland.title: Free Camping in Queensland 2026: Council Camps, Rest Areas and Cheap Park Sites
free-camping-queensland.description: Where you can camp for free in Queensland: council camps, the outback, 20-hour rest areas and the roadside rule, plus park permits at $7.75 a night when free runs out.
free-camping-queensland.imageAlt: A picnic shelter and toilet block on red gravel at the Peak Creek rest area north of Boulia, outback Queensland, where overnight stops are allowed
free-camping-queensland.intro: Queensland has plenty of free camping, but none of it is in parks or forests: every camp there needs a permit, at $7.75 per person a night in 2026. Free camps are run by councils, mostly inland and in the outback, where many towns keep a riverside camping area to bring travellers in. Roadside rest areas let you stop for up to 20 hours unless a sign says otherwise, which covers a night's sleep on a long drive. The coast is different: big tourist towns such as Cairns ban camping on council land.

sections.heading: Why parks are not free in Queensland
body: In most states the cheapest night is in a state forest. In Queensland it is not: Queensland Parks and Wildlife runs about 525 camping areas in its parks, forests and recreation areas, and every one of them needs a permit booked and paid before you arrive. That includes bush camps with nothing more than a clearing.

The fee is low, $7.75 per person or $31 for a family a night from 1 July 2026, with under-fives free, so a park camp is still a cheap night when no free site is close. Book online through the Queensland National Parks Booking Service, up to 12 months ahead.
tips: Every park camp needs a permit

rows: The limit on the sign, often a few nights
Not camping sites; truck bays are for trucks

sections.heading: Outback council camps
body: The further west you drive, the more free camping you find. Councils along the Matilda Way, the Warrego Highway and the roads into the Channel Country keep camping areas beside rivers, creeks and waterholes, some free and some asking a few dollars or a donation, because a camp full of travellers keeps the bakery, pub and fuel station busy.

Each council sets its own stay limit, often a few nights, and some ask for a self-contained vehicle. Facilities range from toilets, water and a dump point to nothing at all. The visitor information centre in each town knows the current rules, and many towns post them at the camp entrance.

sections.heading: Rest areas and the 20-hour rule
body: Transport and Main Roads lets general and recreational vehicles stop at a rest area for up to 20 hours unless a sign says otherwise. That makes Queensland one of the clearest states for a night's sleep on a long drive, but the department is just as clear that rest areas are not camping sites: no tents spread across the grass, no week-long stays.

Heavy-vehicle rest areas are for truck drivers only, so leave them free. Many outback rest areas have a shelter and a toilet, and some, like Peak Creek north of Boulia, say on their sign that overnight stops are allowed. Arrive before dark to get a spot away from the road.
tips: Keep out of truck rest areas

sections.heading: The roadside and the coast
body: Pulling over on the verge is legal only in narrow cases. Camping on a state-controlled road is allowed only to manage fatigue between 4pm and 8am, outside a built-up area, at least 200 metres from any kerb and 9 metres from the traffic lane, where no sign bans it and never on a motorway or toll road, with no fire or generator.

The coast is much stricter than the outback. Cairns bans camping on council land, including roadsides, the Esplanade, parks, car parks and beaches, and other tourist towns patrol their foreshores. Along the coast, plan on park camps, showgrounds and holiday parks, and save the free nights for inland.

sections.heading: Heat, crocodiles and the wet season
body: Estuarine crocodiles live from Gladstone north and around the Gulf, in rivers, lagoons and swamps far inland as well as the sea. At a riverside free camp in croc country, pitch well back from the water, never swim or wade, and read every warning sign.

Queensland's cyclone season runs from 1 November to 30 April, and wet-season rain can cut outback roads for days. The free camps of the west are at their best from April to September, when nights are cool and the roads are dry. Queensland declares local fire bans rather than Total Fire Bans, and they apply to camps too.

sections.heading: Find free camps in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps maps 517 Queensland park and forest campgrounds, 1,688 roadside rest areas and 324 public dump points, with each place's facilities and fees as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, including free sites, and build a trip that adds up the distance between stops, which helps on long outback legs.
Place details are saved on the phone for use without signal. The map, routing and weather need a connection, and AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Is there free camping in Queensland?

Yes, but not in national parks or state forests, where every camp needs a paid permit. Free camping in Queensland means council camping areas that allow it, which are most common inland and in the outback, and roadside rest areas, where you can stop for up to 20 hours unless a sign says otherwise.
Can you sleep at rest areas in Queensland?

Yes. General and recreational vehicles can stop at a rest area for up to 20 hours unless a sign says otherwise. The state says rest areas are not camping sites, so sleep in the vehicle and move on, and keep out of heavy-vehicle rest areas, which are for truck drivers.
How much does it cost to camp in a Queensland national park?

From 1 July 2026 a camping permit costs $7.75 per person per night, or $31 for a family, and children under five camp free. It is not free, but it is a low fee, and permits are booked before you arrive.
Can I free camp on the beach in Queensland?

Generally not. Beach camping on K'gari, Bribie Island, Mulgumpin, Minjerribah and at Cooloola is in parks and recreation areas that need a camping permit and a vehicle access permit, and towns such as Cairns ban camping on their beaches, parks and roadsides.

free-camping-western-australia.title: Free Camping in Western Australia 2026: 24-Hour Rest Stops, Shire Camps and the Law
free-camping-western-australia.description: Where you can camp for free in WA: signed 24-hour rest stops, shire camps and private land, why camping elsewhere needs approval, and the cheap park sites in between.
free-camping-western-australia.imageAlt: A picnic shelter, toilet block and red gravel parking area at the Lyndon rest area on the North West Coastal Highway, Western Australia
free-camping-western-australia.intro: Free camping in Western Australia is tighter than in the eastern states. The law says you may camp outside a licensed caravan park or camping ground only with approval, so the main free option is a rest area signed for overnight stops, where you can stay up to 24 consecutive hours. Some shires run free or low-cost camps of their own, and a landowner can let you stay up to 5 nights. National park campgrounds are never free, but at $10 to $20 a night they keep a long trip cheap.

sections.heading: Why WA is stricter
body: Western Australia's caravan park and camping ground rules treat camping as something that happens in a licensed park or camping ground. Camping anywhere else without approval risks an offence, whether the land belongs to the state, a shire or a farmer. That rules out the easy forest camping of New South Wales and Victoria.

What is left is still plenty for a road trip: signed overnight rest stops, approved shire camps, private land with permission, and national park campgrounds at a low fee. The trick is knowing which kind of stop you are at before you set up.

sections.heading: Rest areas: the 24-hour rule
body: Main Roads WA allows no overnight stop at a rest area unless a sign says you can, and where one does, the stay must not exceed 24 consecutive hours. Main Roads also says its rest areas are not intended for camping, so keep to the vehicle, skip the awning and move on the next day.

On the long highways north, the North West Coastal and the Great Northern, overnight rest areas are the backbone of a budget trip, often with a shelter, a toilet and space for vans. Road trains use them too, so keep the heavy-vehicle bays clear and park well away from the trucks that start before dawn.
tips: Only where a sign allows it

sections.heading: Shire camps and station stays
body: Some shires run their own free or low-cost camping areas for travellers, beside a river, a beach or the edge of town, each with its own stay limit and conditions. They change often, so ask the shire or the visitor centre, and pay attention to the sign at the gate.

Station stays are a distinctly WA option. Pastoral properties open camping areas to travellers for a fee, and on remote stretches they can be the only stop between towns. Confirm the price, payment and road access with the station before you arrive.

sections.heading: Private land and farm stays
body: On private land, the owner's permission covers a stay of up to 5 nights, and a longer stay also needs local government approval. Ask before you pull in, even on a quiet back road, and leave gates as you found them.

Farm stays and paddock camps often charge a small fee and come with a hot shower or a fire pit, which can be a better night than a highway rest stop. Agree the price and what is included before you set up.
tips: Leave gates as you find them

sections.heading: When free runs out: cheap park camps
body: National park campgrounds cost $10 an adult at sites without facilities, $15 with basic facilities and $20 with more, and children aged 5 and under camp free. Many are booked through Park Stay WA up to 180 days ahead, while first come campgrounds take cash or a self-registration envelope.
Some parks charge vehicle entry on top, such as $17 a standard vehicle at Karijini and Cape Range, so an All Parks Pass at $130 a year pays for itself quickly on a run up the coast.

sections.heading: Distance, water and the seasons
body: The gaps are what make WA different. Plan each night within your fuel range, carry water for several extra days, and keep a second stop in mind in case a rest area is full or a campground is closed.

The north is best in the dry season, roughly May to October, and the cyclone season runs from November to April. In the south-west, many parks stop campfires from about 1 December to 31 March, and firewood collection is banned in national parks, so bring a gas stove.

sections.heading: Find overnight stops in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps maps 260 Western Australian park campgrounds and 238 public dump points, with each place's facilities and fees as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost and build a trip with ordered stops and the driving distance for each leg, which shows the long gaps before you leave.
Place details are saved on the phone for use without signal, which matters on WA's empty stretches. The map, routing and weather need a connection, and AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Can you free camp in Western Australia?

Only in limited places. WA lets you camp outside a licensed caravan park or camping ground only with approval, so the main free option is a rest area signed for overnight stops, where you can stay up to 24 consecutive hours. Some shires run free or low-cost camps, and a landowner can let you stay on private land for up to 5 nights.
How long can you stay at a rest area in WA?

Up to 24 consecutive hours, and only at rest areas with a sign that allows overnight stops. Main Roads WA says its rest areas are not intended for camping, so sleep in the vehicle, keep the road train bays clear and move on the next day.
Is free camping illegal in WA?

Camping outside a licensed caravan park or camping ground without approval can be an offence, on public or private land. Signed 24-hour rest stops, approved shire camps and private land with the owner's permission are the legal exceptions.
What is the cheapest way to camp in WA if not free?

National park campgrounds cost $10 to $20 per adult a night, and children aged 5 and under camp free. Shire camps and station stays are often cheap too, and an All Parks Pass at $130 a year covers park entry on a long trip.

free-camping-tasmania.title: Free Camping in Tasmania 2026: Bay of Fires, Free Park Camps and Council Sites
free-camping-tasmania.description: Where to camp for free in Tasmania: the Bay of Fires, free park campgrounds, council sites for self-contained vans and forestry land, and when a parks pass still applies.
free-camping-tasmania.imageAlt: Granite boulders covered in orange lichen beside clear blue water at the Bay of Fires on Tasmania's north-east coast
free-camping-tasmania.intro: Yes, you can camp for free in Tasmania, and some of the island's best coast is free. The Bay of Fires campgrounds on the north-east coast charge nothing and take no bookings, Huon and Teds Beach in Southwest National Park are free park camps, and many councils let self-contained vehicles stay a night or two. Most Sustainable Timber Tasmania land is open to campers unless a sign says no. Inside national parks you still need a parks pass, and roadside camping on reserved land is not allowed.

sections.heading: The free camps on the coast
body: The Bay of Fires, north of St Helens, is the best known free camping in Tasmania: a string of campgrounds behind white beaches and orange granite, managed by Parks and Wildlife, free and first come. Camp only in the designated campgrounds, and arrive early in summer, when the beachfront sites go first.

The northern end of the bay lies inside Mount William National Park, where a parks pass is needed. Further along the east coast, several coastal reserves and conservation areas have basic free or low-cost camps, with pit toilets at most and no drinking water, so fill up in town.
tips: Bay of Fires: free, no booking

head: Where
Booking

rows: Only in Mount William National Park
None at Huon and Teds Beach

sections.heading: Free park campgrounds
body: Some Parks and Wildlife Service campgrounds charge no camping fee. Huon and Teds Beach in Southwest National Park take no bookings and cost nothing, and the walker camps at Wineglass Bay, the Hazards and Cooks Beach in Freycinet, and Encampment Cove on Maria Island are free to camp as well.

A free campground inside a national park still needs a parks pass, which every visitor needs to enter any Tasmanian national park. If you plan to visit several parks, the holiday pass covers them all for up to two months.

sections.heading: Council sites for campervans
body: Many Tasmanian councils welcome travellers but set their own conditions, and most free council sites are for self-contained vehicles with a toilet and grey water tank on board. Northern Midlands Council issues a free permit for self-contained vehicles to stay up to 48 hours, and Central Coast Council allows up to three nights but is moving its sites to a paid permit of $15 a night.

Because the rules change from one council to the next, read the sign at each site and check the council's page rather than an old review. Without a self-contained vehicle, a low-cost showground or a caravan park is often the better night.

sections.heading: Forestry land and the roadside
body: Sustainable Timber Tasmania welcomes camping on the land it manages, except where signs prohibit it, which opens up quiet bush camps on forest roads across the island. Harvesting can close roads, so obey closure signs and keep out of active coupes.

Pulling over on the roadside is another matter. On reserved land you must not camp in a camping-prohibited area or within 500 metres of a road outside a designated camping area, with a fine of up to 20 penalty units. Find a signed camp instead.
tips: No camping near roads on reserves

sections.heading: Fires, weather and getting there
body: Much of the wilderness, including Cradle Mountain-Lake St Clair, Freycinet and Mount Field, is a Fuel Stove Only Area where campfires are banned all year, and on a Total Fire Ban day all outdoor fires are banned in parks. Bring a gas stove and expect to use it.

Tasmanian weather turns cold, wet and windy in any month, even at sea level in summer, so pack for rain. Most travellers bring a vehicle on the Spirit of Tasmania, and fresh fruit and vegetables cannot come with you, so eat or bin them before you sail.
tips: Fuel stove only in many parks
No fresh produce on the ferry

sections.heading: Find free camps in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps maps 27 Tasmanian park campgrounds and 80 public dump points, with the facilities, fees and rules each agency publishes. You can filter by cost, including free sites, and save camps to a trip that adds up the driving between them.
Place details are saved on the phone for use without signal, useful on the west coast and in the south-west. The map, routing and weather need a connection, and AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Where can I camp for free in Tasmania?

At the Bay of Fires campgrounds on the north-east coast, which are free and take no bookings; at free Parks and Wildlife Service campgrounds such as Huon and Teds Beach in Southwest National Park; at council sites that allow it, often for self-contained vehicles only; and on most Sustainable Timber Tasmania land unless a sign says no.
Do I need a parks pass to free camp in Tasmania?

Only inside a national park. Free campgrounds in a national park, such as Huon and Teds Beach, still need a valid parks pass. The Bay of Fires campgrounds south of Mount William National Park are in a conservation area, but the northern end of the bay lies inside the park, where the pass applies.
Can you free camp in a campervan in Tasmania?

Yes, at council sites that take self-contained vehicles, at free park and conservation area campgrounds, and on forestry land where no sign prohibits it. Northern Midlands Council, for example, issues a free permit for self-contained vehicles to stay up to 48 hours.
Is free camping allowed anywhere on the roadside in Tasmania?

No. On reserved land you must not camp in a camping-prohibited area or within 500 metres of a road outside a designated camping area, and councils set their own rules on their land. Use a signed camp instead.

free-camping-south-australia.title: Free Camping in South Australia 2026: Crown Land, the Murray and Council Camps
free-camping-south-australia.description: Where to camp for free in South Australia: 21 days on Crown land, River Murray camps, cheap council sites on the peninsulas, rest areas, and the councils that ban it.
free-camping-south-australia.imageAlt: A campfire burning beside reeds and kayaks at a riverside campsite on the River Murray, South Australia
free-camping-south-australia.intro: Yes, South Australia is one of the better states for free camping. Unallocated Crown land is open to campers for up to 21 days without approval, and long stretches of the River Murray are Crown land or council reserve with free riverside camps. Councils on the Eyre and Yorke peninsulas and in country towns run free or cheap sites, often on an honesty box. National park campsites are never free, though, and some councils, such as the Barossa, ban camping on public land altogether.

sections.heading: Crown land: up to 21 days
body: South Australia has a rule most states do not: you can camp on unallocated Crown land for up to 21 days without asking anyone. The Department for Environment and Water asks campers to keep vehicles on established tracks, collect no firewood and leave the land as they found it.

The hard part is knowing the land is Crown land. A fence, a gate or a sign usually means it is private or reserved for another use, and pastoral leases are not open camping. The Department for Environment and Water or the local council can tell you, and misusing Crown land can bring a $315 expiation.

table.caption: Where you can camp for free in South Australia, and the main limit at each.

Cost

sections.heading: The River Murray
body: The river from the Victorian border to Lake Alexandrina is South Australia's favourite free camping country. Much of the bank is Crown land or council reserve, and the river councils run camping areas among the red gums, some free and some for a small fee, with sandy landings for a boat or kayak.

Each stretch has its own manager, so a free bend can sit beside a private shack block or a no camping reserve. Read the sign at every track entry and check the council's page. The Riverland has fruit fly controls, so buy produce from accredited shops rather than roadside stalls.
tips: Red gum bends, free or cheap
Read the sign at each track

sections.heading: Eyre and Yorke peninsulas
body: The councils of the Eyre Peninsula and Yorke Peninsula manage a long chain of coastal camps, from beach clearings to sheltered bays. Many charge a few dollars a night through an honesty box or a permit bought online, and a few are free. Facilities are basic: a drop toilet if any, no water and no power.

These camps suit self-sufficient travellers who carry water and take their rubbish out. Stay limits are set by each council, and some sites close in fire season or over winter, so check before you drive a long dirt road to reach one.

sections.heading: Rest areas and the councils that say no
body: South Australia has 391 roadside rest areas in AussieCamps, and the rules on sleeping in them follow the sign and the local council. Where no sign or council rule prohibits it, keep it to a night in the vehicle, not a camp set up for days.

Some councils ban it outright. The Barossa Council says camping or overnight stays are prohibited in any public reserve, car park, road or rest area in its region, and people found camping can face an on-the-spot fine. Around Adelaide and the wine regions, plan on a caravan park or a booked campground.

sections.heading: Parks are booked, not free
body: Almost every national park campsite must be booked and paid before you arrive, up to 12 months ahead, and a booking usually covers vehicle entry to that park. Ikara-Flinders Ranges sites start at $12.30 a night, so a park night stays cheap when no free site is close.

In the far north, the Desert Parks Pass covers 12 months of entry and camping in the desert parks, and the Simpson Desert parks close every year from 1 December to 15 March. Most parks do not allow dogs, which makes Crown land and council camps the choice with a pet.

sections.heading: Fire season and the border
body: The Fire Danger Season is set by district and in 2026-27 starts on 15 October in the Flinders, Eastern Eyre, West Coast and pastoral districts and on 1 November in the South East, Murraylands and Riverland, running into April. During it, a campfire must sit in a trench 30 cm deep with 4 metres cleared around it, and on a Total Fire Ban day no campfire may be lit at all.
Crossing into the state, fruit fly host fruit and vegetables must be eaten or binned before the border, and from 1 July 2026 the fine for carrying them is up to $423. Restock once you are across.

sections.heading: Find free camps in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps maps 115 South Australian park campgrounds, 391 roadside rest areas and 199 public dump points, each with the facilities and fees the agency publishes. You can filter by cost, including free sites, and save camps to a trip with dates and notes.
Place details are saved on the phone for use without signal, which helps on the peninsulas and along the river. The map, routing and weather need a connection, and AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Can you camp for free in South Australia?

Yes. South Australia lets you camp on Crown land without approval for up to 21 days, and some councils run free or low-cost camps along the River Murray, on the Eyre and Yorke peninsulas and in country towns. National park campsites are not free and must be booked before you arrive.
What is Crown land camping in SA?

Unallocated Crown land is state land not set aside for a park or another use. You can camp on it for up to 21 days without approval, keeping vehicles on established tracks and without collecting firewood. Misusing it can bring a $315 expiation.
Can I free camp along the Murray in South Australia?

In many places, yes. Long stretches of the riverbank are Crown land or council reserve, and several river councils run free or cheap camping areas. Others are private or banned, so read the sign at each track and check the council's page first.
Where is free camping banned in South Australia?

Wherever a council or land manager says so. The Barossa Council, for example, prohibits camping or overnight stays in any public reserve, car park, road or rest area in its region, and people found camping can be fined on the spot.

big-lap-of-australia-guide.title: The Big Lap of Australia 2026: Route, Direction, Timing, Budget and Camping
big-lap-of-australia-guide.description: The Big Lap is a drive around Australia on Highway 1, about 14,500 km in 3 to 12 months. Direction, season by region, fuel and budget, camping and where to start.
big-lap-of-australia-guide.imageAlt: A campervan parked beside a quiet outback road at sunset on a long Australian road trip
big-lap-of-australia-guide.intro: The Big Lap is the classic Australian road trip: a full circuit of the country on Highway 1, about 14,500 km if you stay on the main road. People do it in three months or in two years, in a campervan, a caravan or a 4WD with a rooftop tent, and the main decisions are which direction to drive, when to be in the north and how much to carry.

sections.heading: What the Big Lap is
body: The Big Lap follows Highway 1 around the coast: from Sydney or Melbourne north through Queensland to Cairns, across the Top End to Darwin, down the Western Australian coast through Broome, Exmouth and Perth, then across the Nullarbor to South Australia and back east. Many people add Tasmania, the Red Centre and the Kimberley, which push the total well beyond 14,500 km.
There is no single rule for how long it takes. A fast lap is three or four months, a comfortable one is nine to twelve, and some take longer so they can work along the way.

sections.heading: Which direction and when to start
body: The Top End and the Kimberley are best from about May to September, in the dry season, and the south is best in summer. That means most people start in the east in autumn or winter, head north, cross the top in the dry season and be in the west and south by spring and summer. If you start at the wrong time you can still do the lap, but you will drive some roads in the wet season, when roads and camps close.

Clockwise from Sydney or Melbourne means the Queensland coast first and the Nullarbor last; anticlockwise reverses that. Pick the direction that puts you in the north in the dry season, and the wet season camping guide covers what changes if you cannot.

sections.heading: Fuel, budget and camping
body: Fuel is the biggest running cost, and the gaps between fuel stops on the Nullarbor, in the Pilbara and across the Top End are long, so fill up at every roadhouse. The road trip fuel planning guide covers range, and the fuel cost and budget guides cover the numbers.

Most nights are in caravan parks, roadhouse camps or free rest areas and bush camps where allowed, and the camping rules guides explain where overnight stays are legal in each state. Book popular camps in the dry season.

sections.heading: Planning and tools
body: A lap of the country is a trip of dozens of stops, and a planning app helps more than a paper list. The best apps for a lap of Australia guide compares what is on offer, and the AussieCamps planning guide covers building a long trip as ordered stops with dates and notes.
Rules and conditions vary a lot by state, so it is worth reading the camping rules and biosecurity guides before you cross each border.
tips: Read the rules for each state

body: Build the lap as a trip in AussieCamps: add each overnight stop in order and it shows the distance and drive time of each leg, with a forecast for the day you expect to arrive. AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities those sources publish.
Open each leg while you still have a connection, because map tiles, routing and weather need one. The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.
tips: Open the trip before the long legs

faq: How long does the Big Lap of Australia take?
Most people allow 9 to 12 months to go around the country at a relaxed pace, and about 3 to 4 months for a fast lap. The Highway 1 route is around 14,500 km, and detours add thousands more.
Which direction should I drive the Big Lap?
It depends on the season you start. Clockwise or anticlockwise, the aim is to be in the north during the dry season, from about May to September, and in the south during summer.
How much does the Big Lap cost?
Plan on a campervan or caravan, fuel and camping each night, plus food and insurance. Fuel is the largest cost for most people, and the road trip fuel cost and budget guides cover the numbers.
Do I need a 4WD for the Big Lap?
No. The Highway 1 route is sealed the whole way, and a campervan or caravan is fine. A 4WD is only needed for side trips such as the Gibb River Road or Cape York.

hipcamp-in-australia.title: Hipcamp in Australia 2026: How It Works, What It Covers and When to Use It
hipcamp-in-australia.description: Hipcamp lists private land and campgrounds you book in Australia. How it works, where it fits beside a camping directory, and what to use for free camps, rest areas and dump points.
hipcamp-in-australia.imageAlt: A tent pitched on a quiet farm paddock in the Australian countryside at dawn
hipcamp-in-australia.intro: Hipcamp started in the United States as a way to book private land, farm stays and campgrounds, and it now lists sites in Australia too. It is a booking marketplace rather than a directory, so it answers a different question from WikiCamps or AussieCamps: it helps you book a specific private site, not find every place you can legally stay.

sections.heading: What Hipcamp is and how it works
body: Hipcamp is a marketplace: landowners and campground operators list sites, you pick a date and book and pay through the app or website. In Australia that means farms, vineyards, private bush blocks and some campgrounds and holiday parks, in addition to the much larger set of listings in the United States.

It is like a booking site for accommodation, with photos, reviews and prices, and the listings are only the places whose owners have joined. That is a small share of all the places you can stay in Australia.

sections.heading: What Hipcamp does not cover
body: Hipcamp does not list rest areas, free camps, national park campgrounds run by state agencies, or dump points. Those are the places most campervan trips use most nights, and the camping rules guides and the dump points guide cover how to find them.
If you are planning a long trip, you will probably use a directory for most nights and Hipcamp for a few special ones. The Hipcamp alternatives guide compares the options in more detail.
tips: No rest areas or free camps
Use a directory for most nights

sections.heading: When Hipcamp makes sense
body: It is a good fit when you want a private, quiet site on a farm or in the bush, you do not mind booking ahead, and you are happy to pay for it. It is less useful for last-minute stops, free camping or a trip that depends on facilities such as dump points, toilets or powered sites on every leg.
Before you book private land, read the camping on private land guide, and check what the listing says about vehicle access, water, toilets and fire rules.

sections.heading: Plan the whole trip in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps is a directory and trip planner rather than a booking marketplace: it lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities those sources publish. You build a trip as ordered stops with dates and notes and see the distance, drive time and forecast for each leg.
You can use it alongside a booking site: plan the route in AussieCamps and book a special night wherever you like. The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: Does Hipcamp work in Australia?
Yes. Hipcamp lists private land, farms and some campgrounds in Australia that you book through the app or website, in addition to its much larger US listings.
Is Hipcamp the same as WikiCamps?
No. Hipcamp is a booking marketplace for private landowners and campgrounds, while WikiCamps and similar apps are directories of public and private camping places you find and plan yourself.
Can I find free camps on Hipcamp?

Hipcamp is mainly for bookable sites and private land, so it is not the place to find free camps. Rest areas, national park campgrounds and free camps are covered by directory apps such as AussieCamps.
Should I use Hipcamp for a campervan trip in Australia?
It is useful for a few special nights on a farm or a private bush site, but most campervan trips rely on a directory of rest areas, campgrounds and dump points, which Hipcamp does not provide.

campervan-relocations-australia.title: Campervan Relocations in Australia 2026: How They Work, What They Cost and Where to Find Them
campervan-relocations-australia.description: Campervan relocations in Australia often cost about $1 a day for a fixed number of days. How they work, typical routes, what to check, and how to plan the camping on the way.
campervan-relocations-australia.imageAlt: A white campervan parked at a quiet roadside rest area in the Australian bush
campervan-relocations-australia.intro: A campervan relocation is a cheap way to cross Australia: hire companies need their vans moved between cities, so they offer them for about $1 a day for a fixed number of days. You drive the route they pick, often with some fuel help, and pay for fuel, insurance and camping on the way. The catch is that the dates and routes are set by the company.

sections.heading: How relocations work
body: Hire companies run into the same problem: vans end up in the wrong city, for example after one-way hires from Melbourne to Sydney. To move them back they offer relocations, usually at about $1 a day, for a fixed number of days. The listing shows the pick-up and drop-off, the dates and what is included.
Offers appear and disappear quickly, and the popular routes, such as Sydney to Melbourne, fill fast. If you have flexible dates you will have more choice.

sections.heading: What you pay and what to check
body: Even at $1 a day you still pay for fuel, insurance and camping, and some companies charge a bond, an insurance excess or a cleaning fee. Fuel allowance or ferry cover is included on some routes, which helps on a long drive. The campervan hire cost guide covers the usual extras and the budget guide covers the full cost of a trip.
Read the days allowed, the kilometre limit, the bond, the insurance and the pick-up and drop-off times before you book. A tight deadline on a long route leaves little time to stop.

sections.heading: Typical routes and timing
body: Common relocation routes run between the east coast cities, such as Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane, and from Perth and Darwin across the north and west. A route like Melbourne to Perth or Brisbane to Darwin is a long drive with few days, so plan the stops before you commit.
The drive guides for each route show where to stop, and the road trip fuel guide covers the fuel gaps. If the dates are tight, book the camps ahead on popular legs.
tips: East coast routes are most common

sections.heading: Camping on a relocation
body: Relocations are usually in a campervan, so you can sleep in it and stay in caravan parks, roadhouse camps and free rest areas where allowed. The camping rules guides explain where overnight stays are legal in each state, and the overnight rest area guide covers the signs.
Because the days are fixed, it helps to plan which night is where before you start, and book popular camps early.

AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities those sources publish.
Open the trip while you still have a connection, because map tiles, routing and weather need one. The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: What is a campervan relocation in Australia?

Hire companies need vehicles moved between cities, so they offer them at a very low price, often $1 a day, for a fixed number of days. You get the campervan and often some fuel or ferry help, and they get the vehicle where they need it.
How much does a campervan relocation cost?
Many relocations cost about $1 a day, plus fuel, insurance and sometimes a bond. Terms vary by company and route, so read the offer carefully.
How long do I get for a relocation?
Usually between 3 and 14 days, depending on the distance. Some companies add extra days or a fuel allowance on long routes such as Melbourne to Perth or Brisbane to Darwin.
Who can do a relocation?

Drivers need a full licence and must meet the age and licence rules of the hire company, which are usually the same as for a normal hire. International visitors need a licence in English or an accompanying translation, or an international driving permit.

australia-or-new-zealand-campervan-first.title: Australia or New Zealand First by Campervan? How to Choose in 2026
australia-or-new-zealand-campervan-first.description: Choosing between a campervan trip in Australia or New Zealand: distances, driving, camping rules, cost, seasons and which suits a first trip. Plus how to do both.
australia-or-new-zealand-campervan-first.imageAlt: A campervan parked beside a lake with snow-capped mountains behind, on a road trip in New Zealand
australia-or-new-zealand-campervan-first.intro: Australia and New Zealand are both great campervan countries, but they are very different trips. New Zealand is compact, scenic and easy to plan, with a camp or a town within an hour almost everywhere. Australia is vast and varied, with long empty stretches and a much bigger choice of free camps. The right one to do first depends on how long you have and how adventurous you are.

sections.heading: Size and driving
body: New Zealand's two islands together are smaller than most Australian states, so drives between sights are short, often one to three hours, and a two-week trip covers a lot. Roads are winding and often narrow, so average speeds are lower than the distance suggests.
Australia is huge: the drives between cities are many hours or days, and some stretches have no fuel for hundreds of kilometres. It suits a longer trip, or a trip focused on one region.

sections.heading: Camping and rules
body: Australia has a large network of free and low-cost camps, rest areas and national park campgrounds, with rules that vary by state. New Zealand has a smaller network and tighter freedom camping rules, with many sites requiring a self-contained vehicle and a certificate, and fines for breaking local rules.
The Australian camping rules guides cover each state, and the New Zealand site covers its own rules. Rules matter more in New Zealand, so a campervan trip there needs more planning of where to stay.

sections.heading: Cost and seasons
body: Both countries have high season in summer, and campervans, parks and ferries book out then. New Zealand is cooler and wetter, with a good season from about November to April. Australia has regional seasons: the north is best in the dry season, from about May to September, and the south is best in summer.
Costs vary with the hire company, the fuel price and the number of nights in paid camps. The campervan hire cost and budget guides give the Australian numbers, and the New Zealand site has its own.
tips: Summer is high season in both

sections.heading: Which first
body: If you have two or three weeks and want an easy, scenic trip with little planning, New Zealand is the safer first choice. If you have more time, want to camp free and see wide open country, start in Australia, ideally with a single region such as the east coast or the south-west.
If you can do both, many people do a few weeks in each, and they can use the same planning approach in each country.
tips: Long trip or free camping: Australia

sections.heading: Plan the Australian side in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps covers Australia: it lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities those sources publish. Build a trip as ordered stops and it shows the distance, drive time and forecast for each leg.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: Should I do Australia or New Zealand first by campervan?
New Zealand is the easier first trip: it is smaller, the distances are short and the roads and camps are easy to plan. Australia is bigger and wilder, and suits a longer trip or a second visit.
Which is cheaper to campervan, Australia or New Zealand?

It depends on the trip. Australia has more free camping and cheaper fuel in many places, while New Zealand has shorter distances so you drive less. Compare the hire cost, fuel and camping fees for your dates.
How many days do I need for each country?
Two to three weeks covers a good New Zealand trip on one or both islands. Australia needs three weeks for a single region, or months for a long route like the east coast or the west.
Can I do both on one trip?
Yes. Many people do a few weeks in each, starting with New Zealand and flying to Australia, or the other way round. Check each country's visa rules and the campervan hire terms for each.

regional-work-working-holiday-visa-campi.title: Regional Work for a Second or Third Working Holiday Visa: Camping and Living on the Road in 2026
regional-work-working-holiday-visa-campi.description: How backpackers camp and live in a van while doing regional work for a second or third working holiday visa in Australia: where to stay, what to check, harvest seasons and planning the route.
regional-work-working-holiday-visa-campi.imageAlt: A backpacker's campervan parked beside an orchard in rural Australia
regional-work-working-holiday-visa-campi.intro: A second or third working holiday visa in Australia depends on doing specified work in a regional area, and many backpackers do it from a van or a tent. Camping cuts costs and gives you freedom to follow the work, but the farms, regions and rules matter more than the campsite. Here the focus is the camping and travel side. The visa rules themselves come from the Department of Home Affairs and change, so check them before you commit.

sections.heading: What counts as regional work
body: The Department of Home Affairs lists the industries, such as plant and animal cultivation, fishing, forestry, mining and construction, and the regional postcodes where the work counts. For a second or third year you need to complete a set number of days of specified work, and the rules differ by visa type and year, so read the official page before you start.
Because the rules change, check the current list of eligible postcodes and industries and keep payslips and employer details. This guide does not repeat them in detail.

sections.heading: Where to sleep while you work
body: Many farms offer camping, cheap caravan sites or accommodation to workers, and some regional towns have caravan parks with long-stay or weekly rates. Others expect you to find your own place, so ask before you accept the job.

Free camping near a work site is often restricted by local councils and signs, so read the rules rather than assume. The overnight rest area guide and the camping rules guides explain what is allowed, and a caravan park is often the safer choice for a long stay.
tips: Check council rules for free camps

sections.heading: Harvest seasons and routes
body: Work follows the seasons: fruit and vegetable picking is busiest in different regions at different times of year, and a route that follows the harvest can keep you in work. Popular regions include Queensland's Bundaberg and Bowen, the Riverland and Sunraysia on the Murray, the Goulburn Valley, Tasmania and the south-west of Western Australia.
A van gives you flexibility to move from one harvest to the next. Plan fuel and camps for each leg, and the road trip fuel and budget guides cover the costs.
tips: Plan fuel and camps for each leg

sections.heading: Budget and vehicle
body: Your costs are the vehicle, fuel, camping and food, and the working holiday budget guide covers them. If you are buying a campervan for the year, the buying and selling guides cover registration, inspection and resale.
Keep a small buffer for repairs, and sell the van before you fly home so you are not left with it.

sections.heading: Plan the route in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities those sources publish. Build a trip as ordered stops with dates and notes and it shows the distance, drive time and forecast for each leg, which helps when you move between work sites.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: What is regional work for a second working holiday visa?

Backpackers on a Working Holiday visa (subclass 417) or Work and Holiday visa (subclass 462) can qualify for a second or third year by doing a set number of days of specified work in a regional area. The Department of Home Affairs lists the industries, regions and days.
Where can I camp while doing regional work?
Many farms, caravan parks and rural towns offer camping or cheap sites for workers, and some employers provide accommodation. Check the rules for the property and the local council.
Do I need a campervan for regional work?
Not always, but it gives you freedom to move between work sites and cut accommodation costs. A van also helps if work is spread across a wide area.
Which areas count as regional?
The Department of Home Affairs publishes a list of postcodes. Check the postcode of the work place against the current list before you start, because the rules change.

wikicamps-vs-camps-australia-wide-vs-cam.title: WikiCamps vs CAMPS Australia Wide vs CamperMate 2026: Which Camping App to Use
wikicamps-vs-camps-australia-wide-vs-cam.description: WikiCamps, CAMPS Australia Wide and CamperMate compared on price, how listings are built and who each suits, with AussieCamps alongside as a trip planner built on park and road data.
wikicamps-vs-camps-australia-wide-vs-cam.imageAlt: A phone showing a camping app map on the dashboard of a campervan on an Australian road trip
wikicamps-vs-camps-australia-wide-vs-cam.intro: WikiCamps, CAMPS Australia Wide and CamperMate are the three camping apps most Australian travellers know, and they work in different ways: one is a community database, one is a team-checked guide and one is a free app that also covers New Zealand. We make AussieCamps, so we say where it fits after the three. Prices and ratings below were checked on the Australian App Store on 20 and 21 October 2026.

sections.heading: The three apps side by side
body: WikiCamps is built on listings and reviews added by its community, and it is the largest of the three. CAMPS Australia Wide lists sites its own team says it has visited, with no paid listings. CamperMate is free and lists points of interest across Australia and New Zealand, from free camps and holiday parks to dump stations and toilets.
The table is the quick version. It describes what each app says about itself and what the store listing shows, and it is not a verdict on which is best.
tips: All three are good at different things

sections.heading: WikiCamps
body: WikiCamps is the app many Australian travellers install first, because it has the largest set of sites and reviews, and the one-off price suits people who do not want a subscription. The weakness of any community database is quality: some entries are old, and you need to read recent reviews before you drive to a free camp.
If you want the widest choice and you are happy to read reviews, it is the default. The WikiCamps alternatives guide covers when another app is better.

sections.heading: CAMPS Australia Wide
body: CAMPS lists sites that its team says it has visited and checked, with filters for price, pets and whether a site suits a campervan, camper trailer or big rig. The yearly fee is the main reason people look elsewhere, but if you want a smaller set of sites checked by the same team, it suits a long caravan trip.
The CAMPS alternatives guide covers when a different app does the job better.

sections.heading: CamperMate
body: CamperMate is free and covers Australia and New Zealand, which makes it a good first install if you are doing both countries. It lists free camps, holiday parks, dump stations, toilets and wifi, and it is a general travel app as much as a camping one.
The CamperMate alternatives guide covers when you want something with more detail on camping.

sections.heading: Where AussieCamps fits
body: AussieCamps is a camping directory and trip planner: it lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities those sources publish. You build a trip as ordered stops with dates and notes, and it shows the distance, drive time and forecast for each leg.
Most travellers settle on one main camping app and add a trip planner, and AussieCamps is built to be that planner. The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: Which is better, WikiCamps, CAMPS Australia Wide or CamperMate?

They suit different people. WikiCamps has the biggest community database for a one-off price, CAMPS Australia Wide lists sites its team has visited for a yearly fee, and CamperMate is free and covers Australia and New Zealand.
What does WikiCamps cost?
WikiCamps Australia is a one-off purchase of A$9.99 on the Australian App Store as of 20 October 2026, with no subscription.
What does CAMPS Australia Wide cost?
The app is free to download and free for 7 days, then A$14.99 a year, as of 21 October 2026.
Is CamperMate free?
Yes. CamperMate is free with no in-app purchases on the Australian App Store as of 20 October 2026, and it covers both Australia and New Zealand.

easter-long-weekend-camping-australia-20.title: Easter and Long Weekend Camping in Australia 2027: When to Book and Where to Go
easter-long-weekend-camping-australia-20.description: Easter 2027 falls on 26 to 29 March, with Anzac Day and the King's Birthday after. When to book, where camps fill first, what to do if you miss out, and quieter alternatives.
easter-long-weekend-camping-australia-20.imageAlt: Tents and caravans filling a coastal campground on an Easter long weekend in Australia
easter-long-weekend-camping-australia-20.intro: Easter is the busiest camping weekend of the year in Australia: a four day weekend, school holidays in most states and autumn weather that is mild nearly everywhere. Good Friday 2027 is 26 March, and Easter Monday is 29 March. Anzac Day on Sunday 25 April and the King's Birthday on Monday 14 June add two more chances to camp, and the best sites go early.

sections.heading: The 2027 dates
body: Easter 2027 runs from Good Friday on 26 March to Easter Monday on 29 March, with Easter Sunday on 28 March. School holidays in most states cluster around it, and they differ by state, so the school holidays guide has the dates. Anzac Day is Sunday 25 April, and some states give a substitute public holiday on the Monday. The King's Birthday is on Monday 14 June in most states.
Public holiday dates differ by state and some are not national, so confirm yours with the state government before you book.

sections.heading: When to book
body: Popular national park campgrounds and coastal caravan parks open bookings months ahead and fill within days of release, so decide where you want to go and set a reminder. Some parks release Easter dates earlier than other times of year. If bookings are not open, check the park page for the opening date.
Free camps and rest areas cannot be booked, and the best ones fill by Thursday afternoon. Arrive early, and read the rules for overnight stays in your state.
tips: Book as soon as dates open

sections.heading: Where to go and what to do if you miss out
body: If the coastal parks are full, look inland and a little further out: inland rivers, lakes and bush camps are often quieter, and mid-week or Sunday nights are easier than the Friday and Saturday peak. A non-bookable campground is a backup, but plan another option in case it is full.
The camping fees guide covers what camps cost, the choosing a campsite guide covers what to look for, and the national park guide covers when you can camp without booking.

sections.heading: Weather and fire
body: Autumn is mild in most of the country, but storms, cold nights and fire bans still happen, and the north can still be in the wet season. Check the forecast and fire danger rating before you go, and the camping weather safety guide covers what to carry.
If a total fire ban is declared, campfires are not allowed, and some campgrounds close, so check the park alerts.

sections.heading: Plan the weekend in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities those sources publish. Save a shortlist of places, build the drive as ordered stops and it shows the distance, drive time and forecast for each leg.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: When is Easter 2027 in Australia?
Good Friday is 26 March 2027, Easter Saturday 27 March, Easter Sunday 28 March and Easter Monday 29 March. Most states add school holidays around it, so check your state's dates.
Do I need to book camping for Easter?
Yes, for popular national parks, coastal campgrounds and caravan parks. They often open bookings months ahead and fill within days, so book as soon as the dates are open.
When is Anzac Day 2027?
Anzac Day falls on Sunday 25 April 2027. Some states give a substitute public holiday on the Monday, which can make a long weekend, so check your state.
What are the other long weekends in 2027?
Australia Day is on Tuesday 26 January, and the King's Birthday long weekend is on Monday 14 June in most states. Labour Day dates vary by state, so check the state government's list.

australian-winter-camping-whales-snow-wa.title: Australian Winter Camping 2026: Whales, Snow and Warm Camps by Region
australian-winter-camping-whales-snow-wa.description: Where to camp in Australia in winter: warm dry-season camps in the north, whale watching on the east, south and west coasts, snow camping in the Alps, and how to stay warm in a campervan.
australian-winter-camping-whales-snow-wa.imageAlt: A humpback whale breaching off the Australian coast in winter
australian-winter-camping-whales-snow-wa.intro: Winter is a great time to camp in Australia if you pick the right region. The north is in the dry season, with sunny days and cool nights. The east and west coasts have whales passing from about May to November, the south coast gets southern right whales, and the Alps have snow. The south can be cold and wet, so the trick is to match the region to what you want.

sections.heading: Warm camps in the north
body: The Top End, the Kimberley, the Pilbara and the north Queensland coast are in the dry season from about May to September, with sunny days, mild nights and few storms. It is peak season for the Darwin, Kakadu and Litchfield loop, the Perth to Broome drive and the Red Centre, so book popular camps ahead.
The wet season guide covers what changes after September, when roads and camps close. In winter the north is the place to be.

sections.heading: Whales on the coast
body: Humpback whales migrate along the east and west coasts from about May to November, and Hervey Bay, the Gold Coast, Byron Bay, Port Stephens, Eden and Albany are popular places to see them. Southern right whales visit the south coast from about June to October, including the Head of Bight on the Nullarbor, and Ningaloo near Exmouth has whale sharks and humpbacks in season.
Many coastal caravan parks and national park campgrounds are close to the viewing spots, and they fill in school holidays. The Perth to Exmouth guide covers the Ningaloo coast.
tips: Southern right whales June to October

sections.heading: Snow and cold camps in the south
body: The Snowy Mountains and the Victorian Alps get snow from about June to September, and some campgrounds stay open in winter, but roads can need chains and may close, so check conditions before you drive. Tasmania has snow on the high country and cold nights near the coast.
The Australian Alps camping route guide covers the high country in summer, and in winter the same places need warm gear and an alternate plan for closures.

sections.heading: Staying warm in a campervan
body: Nights in the south can drop below freezing, so carry extra bedding, warm clothes and a heater that is safe to use in a van, and ventilate when you use it. Condensation builds quickly in a cold van, so open a vent and wipe the windows.
Powered sites let you run an electric heater, so book powered sites in the cold regions. The packing list guide covers what to bring.

sections.heading: Plan your winter trip in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities and a forecast. Build the trip as ordered stops and it shows the distance, drive time and forecast for each leg, which helps you choose between warm and cold regions.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: Where is the best camping in Australia in winter?

The north is best: the Top End, the Kimberley, Exmouth and the Queensland coast are in the dry season from about May to September, with sunny days and mild nights. The south has cold nights but some of the best whale watching and the snow.
When can I see whales in Australia?

Humpback whales migrate along the east and west coasts from about May to November, and Hervey Bay and Albany are popular. Southern right whales visit the south coast and the Head of Bight from about June to October.
Is there snow camping in Australia?
Yes. The Snowy Mountains and the Victorian Alps get snow from about June to September, and some campgrounds are open in winter. Check road conditions and carry chains where required.
Do I need a heater in a campervan in winter?
In the south, yes. Nights can drop below freezing, so carry extra bedding, a heater that is safe to use in a van, and warm clothes, and ventilate when you use it.

free-camping-near-sydney.title: Free Camping Near Sydney: Where to Stay for Free Within a Few Hours
free-camping-near-sydney.description: Where to camp for free near Sydney: state forests, council camps and rest areas within two or three hours, why the city itself is off limits, and what to do instead.
free-camping-near-sydney.intro: You cannot camp for free in Sydney itself, but you do not have to go far. Within two or three hours the state forests of the Southern Highlands, the Watagans and the ranges allow free camping with no booking, and country councils on every side run free or cheap camps for travellers. In the city, parks, beaches and streets are signed against overnight stays, so the plan is to base yourself at a holiday park, then head out for the free nights.

sections.heading: Why Sydney itself is off limits
body: Greater Sydney is covered by dozens of councils, and almost all of them sign against camping and overnight stays in parks, on beaches, in car parks and on streets. Rangers patrol the popular spots, particularly in summer, and an on-the-spot fine is the usual result of a night in the van beside the beach.

Sydney Harbour National Park and the other national parks inside the city have no vehicle camping either. The workable options are a holiday park or a caravan park at the edge of town, then a drive out to the free camps.
tips: No camping in parks or on beaches
