sections.heading: State forests an easy drive away
body: Forestry Corporation of NSW lets you camp in its state forests for free, with no booking, for up to four weeks. Belanglo, in the Southern Highlands, has a free camping area that suits a weekend out of the city, and the Watagans, west of Lake Macquarie, have camping and picnic areas under tall trees.

Both are first come, first served, so on a long weekend arrive early or have a second forest in mind. Facilities are basic: a toilet and tables if you are lucky. Bring your own water and take every bag of rubbish out. Dogs are welcome in state forests if kept under control.
tips: Free for up to four weeks

sections.heading: The Blue Mountains and the national parks
body: The Blue Mountains and Wollemi have campgrounds a couple of hours from Sydney, but they are booked and paid, not free, and dogs are not allowed in NSW national parks. They are worth it for the scenery, and they give a legal, safe night at the price of a booking fee.
If you have a weekend, our Blue Mountains guide covers where to stay and how to plan it. For the south, the Sydney south coast guide covers beach and forest camps from Wollongong to Eden.

sections.heading: Country council camps
body: Many towns within a few hours of Sydney, in the Hunter, the Central West and the Southern Tablelands, run free or low-cost camps on a riverside reserve or the edge of town. Some take only self-contained vehicles with a toilet on board, some ask for a donation, and the stay limit is on the sign.
Showgrounds are the other cheap standby: a modest fee for toilets, hot showers and sometimes power, except when an event is on.
tips: Some need a toilet on board

sections.heading: Rest areas and the roadside
body: Rest areas along the Hume, Pacific, Newell and Great Western highways are built for driver fatigue. Treat one as a place to sleep in the vehicle for a night, not a campsite: no awning, no chairs out across the grass, no second night.
Where a sign says no overnight stays, drive on to the next town or forest. Our guide to sleeping at a rest area explains the rules state by state.
tips: A sign against it means go

sections.heading: Fire, weather and long weekends
body: The NSW bush fire danger period runs from 1 October to 31 March, and on a Total Fire Ban day no fire may be lit in the open. State forests also declare their own fire bans, which allow gas cooking only. Check the RFS rating each morning in summer.
Long weekends and school holidays are when free camps near Sydney fill. Go midweek, arrive before lunch, and keep a booked national park or holiday park night as the fallback.
tips: Gas cooking only on ban days

sections.heading: Find free camps near Sydney in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps maps 372 NSW national park campgrounds, 869 roadside rest areas and 347 public dump points, each with the facilities, fees and rules the agency publishes. You can filter by cost, including free sites, save the ones you like to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.

State forest camping areas are not in the app yet, so use Forestry Corporation's pages for those. Place details are saved on the phone for use without signal, while the map, routing and weather need a connection. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Can you camp for free near Sydney?

Not in Sydney itself, but within two or three hours there are free options: state forests such as Belanglo and the Watagans, a few council camps in country towns, and rest areas for a night in the vehicle. Camping in city parks, beaches and streets is banned and councils fine for it.
Is it legal to sleep in a campervan in Sydney?

Usually not on the street or in a park. Councils across Sydney sign against overnight camping, and rangers and parking officers do patrol popular beaches and car parks. A holiday park is the safe base for the city itself.
Where is the nearest free camping to Sydney?

Belanglo State Forest in the Southern Highlands and the forests of the Watagans near Lake Macquarie are the usual picks, both roughly two hours away. Check Forestry Corporation's page for closures first.
What should I do with a campervan for a few days in Sydney?
Park it at a caravan park on the edge of the city and use trains and ferries to get in. Driving a van into the CBD and finding overnight parking is slow, tolled and expensive.

free-camping-near-melbourne.title: Free Camping Near Melbourne: State Forests and Cheap Camps Within Two Hours
free-camping-near-melbourne.description: Where to camp for free near Melbourne: Victorian state forests within a couple of hours, the rules on water and fire, and why the city and its beaches are off limits.
free-camping-near-melbourne.imageAlt: Candlebark campsite beside Lake Eildon, Victoria
free-camping-near-melbourne.intro: Camping for free in Melbourne itself is not on, but the state forests an hour or two out are some of the easiest free camping in the country. Victoria lets you camp in many state forests without a booking, usually for up to 28 nights and at least 20 metres from water, and the ranges north and east of the city are full of options. Beaches, city parks and streets are signed against it, so use a holiday park for the city nights.

sections.heading: Why not in the city
body: Melbourne and its suburbs are covered by councils that ban camping and overnight stays in parks, beaches and streets, and rangers do patrol the bayside car parks and the Great Ocean Road trailhead towns in summer. A night in the van in the wrong place is an easy fine.
For the city days, a caravan park or holiday park on the edge of town is the sensible base, with trams and trains to get you in. The free nights come once you are out in the ranges.
tips: No camping in parks or on beaches

sections.heading: State forest camping
body: Victoria allows free camping in many state forests and reserves with no booking, usually for up to 28 nights and at least 20 metres from a waterway. Within a couple of hours of Melbourne the options include the forests around Toolangi and the Yarra Ranges, the Wombat State Forest near Daylesford and the Gippsland forests to the east.

Facilities are basic or none: bring water, a toilet if you are not at a signed site, and carry out all rubbish. Dogs can come to state forests but not to most national parks. Forests can close for logging, burns or fire danger, so check before you drive.

sections.heading: Parks Victoria campgrounds
body: The popular parks near Melbourne, Wilsons Promontory, the Grampians, Brisbane Ranges and Bunyip State Park, have campgrounds that you book and pay for, and they fill fast over summer and long weekends. A park night is not free, but it is cheap and safe, and a good fallback when a forest is closed or crowded.
Book through Parks Victoria well ahead for school holidays, and keep a second option in case of closures.

sections.heading: Country towns, showgrounds and rest areas
body: Many Victorian country towns welcome travellers at a showground, a riverside reserve or a free council camp, often with a stay limit and sometimes a requirement that you are self-contained. The visitor centre or council page has the current rule.
Rest areas on the Hume, Western and Calder highways are for a break or, where not signed against it, one night in the vehicle. No awning, no chairs out, and keep truck bays clear.
tips: Rest area: one night in the van

sections.heading: Fire season and the weather
body: The Victorian fire danger period runs through summer, and on Total Fire Ban days no open fires are allowed, with some forests banning wood fires earlier. Check the CFA's fire danger rating each morning.
Nights in the ranges are cold outside summer and the forests can be wet and muddy, so a rooftop or hard-floored van handles it better than a tent on soft ground.

sections.heading: Find free camps near Melbourne in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps maps 438 Victorian park campgrounds, 651 roadside rest areas and 181 public dump points, each with the facilities and fees the agency publishes. You can filter by cost, including free sites, save camps to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.

State forest dispersed camping is not mapped in the app, so use Parks Victoria's pages for that. Place details are saved on the phone for use without signal, while the map, routing and weather need a connection. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Can you camp for free near Melbourne?

Yes, in state forests an hour or two from the city. Victoria allows free dispersed camping in many state forests with no booking, as long as you camp away from water and follow the fire rules. Camping inside Melbourne, on beaches or in city parks is banned.
Is free camping legal in Victoria's state forests?

Yes, in most. Free camping is allowed in many state forests and reserves, typically up to 28 nights and at least 20 metres from water, but each area has its own closures and fire rules, so check before you go.
Where is the closest free camping to Melbourne?

State forests in the ranges north and east of the city, such as around Toolangi, Wombat and the Yarra Ranges, are about an hour or two away. Parks Victoria and the state forest pages list what is open.
Can I sleep in my campervan in Melbourne?
Not on the street or in a park, in most council areas. Use a holiday park on the city's edge as your base, then head out for free nights.

free-camping-near-brisbane.title: Free Camping Near Brisbane: What Is Free, What Is Cheap and Where to Go
free-camping-near-brisbane.description: Where to camp near Brisbane: why free camping is rare in south-east Queensland, the low-cost permit camps and council sites within a couple of hours, and the rules.
free-camping-near-brisbane.intro: Free camping near Brisbane is harder to find than near Sydney or Melbourne. Queensland's national parks and state forests need a booked permit, so the free options are council-run camps and showgrounds in country towns, plus rest areas for a night in the vehicle. The upside is that park permits are cheap, so a night in the ranges costs only a few dollars a person, and the hinterlands north, west and south of the city have plenty of choice.

sections.heading: Why free is rare here
body: Queensland charges for camping in its national parks, conservation parks and state forests, and the permit must be booked before you arrive, often for a specific named campground. There is no equivalent of the free state forest camping you find in New South Wales and Victoria.

In Brisbane and the surrounding councils, camping in parks, on beaches and on streets is banned, and signs and patrols make that clear. The realistic plan is a holiday park for the city, then permit camps and council camps for the rest.
tips: Parks and forests need a permit

sections.heading: Permit camps in the ranges
body: The best nearby camping is in the hinterland: the Scenic Rim and the Lamington side, the Main Range, the D'Aguilar Range and the Glass House Mountains area on the way to the Sunshine Coast. All need a booked camping permit through Queensland Parks.

The sandy islands and the Great Sandy region have their own permits, and some need a vehicle access permit as well. Book early for school holidays and long weekends, when the popular campgrounds sell out.

sections.heading: Council camps and showgrounds
body: Councils in the Somerset and Lockyer valleys and the Scenic Rim run low-cost camps at lakes and reserves, and many country showgrounds take campers for a modest fee. They are the closest thing to cheap, no-frills camping near the city.
Each place sets its own stay limit and rules about generators, dogs and toilets, so check the council page before you set off.

sections.heading: Rest areas and the highways
body: Queensland's rest areas on the Bruce, Warrego, New England and Cunningham highways are for fatigue stops. Many allow up to 20 hours or a night in the vehicle, but the limit is on the sign, and some councils ban overnight stays near towns.
Keep the stop short, keep truck bays clear and move on in the morning.

sections.heading: Heat, storms and the season
body: South-east Queensland is hot and humid in summer, with afternoon storms and flash flooding on creek crossings. Winter, from May to September, is the best camping season, with dry, mild days and cool nights.
Fire bans apply in the dry months, so check the local rating before you light anything.

sections.heading: Find camps near Brisbane in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps maps 517 Queensland park campgrounds, 1,688 roadside rest areas and 324 public dump points, each with the facilities and fees the agency publishes. You can filter by cost, save camps to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.
Place details are saved on the phone for use without signal, while the map, routing and weather need a connection. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Can you camp for free near Brisbane?

Free camping is thin near Brisbane. Queensland national parks and state forests need a camping permit and a fee, so the free options are mainly council camps in country towns further out and rest areas for a night in the vehicle. Camping inside Brisbane, on its beaches or in its parks is banned.
Is camping free in Queensland national parks?
No. Camping in Queensland's national parks and forests needs a booked permit, which costs a few dollars per person per night. The cost is low, but it is not free.
Where can I stay cheaply near Brisbane?
Permit camps in the ranges and on the islands, council-run camps in the Somerset and Scenic Rim regions, showgrounds in country towns, and holiday parks on the city's edge.
Can I sleep in a campervan in Brisbane?
Not on streets or in parks in most areas. Councils sign against overnight stays, so use a holiday park or caravan park as your base.

free-camping-near-perth.title: Free Camping Near Perth: Rest Stops, Shire Camps and Cheap Park Sites
free-camping-near-perth.description: Where to camp near Perth: the few free options within a day's drive, how cheap park camps work, and why camping in Perth itself is banned.
free-camping-near-perth.imageAlt: A rocky coast with a grassy headland and low heath under a pale evening sky, north of Sugarloaf Rock in Leeuwin-Naturaliste National Park
free-camping-near-perth.intro: Free camping near Perth is limited. Western Australia expects camping to happen in licensed camping grounds or with approval, so the free options are signed rest stops that allow up to 24 hours, a few shire camps in the Wheatbelt and along the coast, and private land with the owner's permission. The good news is that park campgrounds in the hills and on the coast cost only $10 to $20 per adult a night, which keeps a trip from Perth cheap.

sections.heading: Why WA is strict
body: Western Australia's rules treat camping outside a licensed caravan park or camping ground as needing approval, whether the land is state, shire or private. That rules out the easy forest camping of the eastern states, and the Perth metro councils all sign against camping in parks, on beaches and in car parks.
What is left is still enough for a weekend: signed rest stops, approved shire camps, private land with permission and park campgrounds at a low fee.

sections.heading: Park camps in the hills and on the coast
body: The Perth Hills and the Darling Range have campgrounds under the jarrah and marri, Lane Poole Reserve near Dwellingup is a favourite for a weekend, and the coast north of the city has camps at Yanchep and further up. Most take bookings through the state parks system and cost $10 to $20 per adult a night.
Spring is wildflower season and the busiest time, so book early. Summer is hot and fire-prone, with total fire bans common.

sections.heading: Rest stops and shire camps
body: Rest stops signed for overnight stops on the Brand, Great Northern and South Western highways allow up to 24 hours. Without the sign, treat the stop as a break, not a bed.
Some Wheatbelt and coastal shires run free or low-cost camps to bring travellers into town, often for self-contained vehicles. The shire's website or the visitor centre has the current rule.

sections.heading: Private land and the landowner rule
body: A landowner can let you stay on their property, and WA's rules let a visitor stay up to five nights with permission. Ask first, leave gates as you found them and pay in goods or a fee if offered.

sections.heading: Weather and fire
body: Perth summers are hot and dry, with fire bans on bad days and heat that makes a tent miserable. Spring and autumn are the best camping seasons, with wildflowers from August to November.
Check the DFES fire danger rating each morning in summer.

sections.heading: Find camps near Perth in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps maps 260 Western Australian park campgrounds, 1,661 roadside rest areas and 238 public dump points, each with the facilities and fees the agency publishes. You can filter by cost, save camps to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.
Place details are saved on the phone for use without signal, which matters on WA's empty stretches, while the map, routing and weather need a connection. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Can you camp for free near Perth?

Only in a few places. Western Australia treats camping outside a licensed camping ground as something that needs approval, so free options are signed rest areas for up to 24 hours and some shire camps further out. Camping in Perth, on its beaches or in its parks is banned.
Is free camping legal in Western Australia?

Only where it is approved. Signed rest stops allow overnight stops for up to 24 hours, some shires run free or low-cost camps, and a landowner can let you stay on private land. Anywhere else risks a fine.
Where can I camp cheaply near Perth?
Park campgrounds in the Perth Hills, the Darling Range and along the coast cost $10 to $20 per adult a night, and caravan parks in the coastal towns are the easy alternative.
Can I sleep in my campervan in Perth?
Not on the street, in car parks or on beaches in most councils. Use a caravan park or holiday park as your base.

free-camping-near-adelaide.title: Free Camping Near Adelaide: Crown Land, the Murray and Peninsula Camps
free-camping-near-adelaide.description: Where to camp for free near Adelaide: 21 days on Crown land, River Murray camps, cheap peninsula council sites and the councils that ban it.
free-camping-near-adelaide.intro: Adelaide is a good city to camp near. South Australia lets you camp on unallocated Crown land for up to 21 days without approval, long stretches of the River Murray have free riverside camps, and councils on the Yorke and Fleurieu peninsulas run free or low-cost sites. In Adelaide, the Adelaide Hills and the Barossa the rules are stricter, so use a holiday park for the city and keep the free nights for the country.

sections.heading: Crown land and the 21-day rule
body: South Australia's unallocated Crown land is open to campers for up to 21 days without approval. Keep vehicles on established tracks, collect no firewood and leave the land as you found it. A fence, a gate or a sign usually means it is not Crown land.
In Adelaide and its hills, camping in parks, on beaches and on streets is banned, and misuse of the Crown land rule can bring an expiation of $315.
tips: Up to 21 days on Crown land

sections.heading: The River Murray
body: The river from the Victorian border to Lake Alexandrina is South Australia's favourite free camping country. Much of the bank is Crown land or council reserve, and the river councils run camping areas among the red gums, some free and some for a small fee.
Each stretch has its own manager, so a free bend can sit beside a banned one. Read the sign at every track.

sections.heading: Yorke and Fleurieu peninsulas
body: The Yorke Peninsula, an easy drive from Adelaide, has a long chain of council coastal camps, many on an honesty box. The Fleurieu has beach and bush camps and the booked park sites at Deep Creek.
Facilities are basic: a drop toilet if any, no water, no power. They suit self-sufficient travellers.

sections.heading: The councils that say no
body: Some councils ban free camping outright. The Barossa Council, for example, prohibits camping or overnight stays in public reserves, car parks, roads and rest areas across its region, and on-the-spot fines follow.
When there is no sign, check the council page before you stay.

sections.heading: Fire season
body: The Fire Danger Season starts in October or November depending on district and runs into April. On a Total Fire Ban day no campfire may be lit, and during the season fires must be in a trench with a cleared area around them.
Check the CFS before you light anything.

faq: Can you camp for free near Adelaide?

Yes, within a few hours. South Australia lets you camp on unallocated Crown land for up to 21 days without approval, and councils along the River Murray and on the Yorke and Fleurieu peninsulas run free or cheap camps. Camping in Adelaide itself is not allowed.
Can I camp in the Adelaide Hills?
In booked park campgrounds, yes. The Barossa Council bans camping or overnight stays in public reserves, car parks, roads and rest areas, so do not assume a quiet spot is fine.
Where is the closest free camping to Adelaide?
River Murray camps at the Riverland end of the Murraylands, and council camps on the Yorke Peninsula, are the nearest, about two to three hours away.
Can I sleep in a campervan in Adelaide?
Not on the street or in parks in most council areas. Use a caravan park or holiday park on the city's edge as your base.

free-camping-near-cairns.title: Free Camping Near Cairns: What to Expect in Tropical North Queensland
free-camping-near-cairns.description: Where to camp near Cairns: why free camping is scarce in Far North Queensland, the cheap permit camps and council sites, and wet-season and crocodile cautions.
free-camping-near-cairns.imageAlt: Cape Tribulation and the Daintree coast
free-camping-near-cairns.intro: Free camping near Cairns is rare. Queensland charges for camping in its national parks and forests, councils ban it in and around the city, and the tropical climate adds wet-season floods and crocodiles to the mix. What you can do is stay cheaply at permit camps on the Tablelands and the Daintree coast, use a holiday park for the city, and keep the odd free night for a rest area or council camp further out.

sections.heading: Why free is rare in the tropics
body: Queensland's parks and forests need a booked camping permit, so there are no free park camps. Cairns and the coast between Palm Cove and Port Douglas are tourist country, and councils sign against camping in streets, car parks and on beaches. Rangers patrol in the dry season when the town is full.
The practical plan is a holiday park for the city nights and a few permit camps or council camps for the rest.

sections.heading: The Tablelands and the coast
body: The Atherton Tableland is cooler than the coast and has lakes, waterfalls and cheap camps, including council-run sites in the small towns. It is the best place near Cairns for a low-cost night.
North to the Daintree and Cape Tribulation the camps are privately run or in national park, with fees and bookings. South to Mission Beach and Innisfail has holiday parks and a few forest camps.

sections.heading: Wet season and cyclones
body: The wet season, roughly December to April, brings heavy rain, flooding and the risk of cyclones. Roads, causeways and fords close, and some parks shut their campgrounds. Check Queensland Parks and Traffic and Travel Information before you drive.
Winter, from May to October, is the best time: dry, warm days and cool nights.

sections.heading: Crocodiles and stingers
body: Saltwater crocodiles live in estuaries, rivers and some creeks and waterholes. Do not swim or camp close to the water's edge where signs warn of them, and never clean fish or leave food at the water.
From about November to May, marine stingers make the sea unsafe without a stinger suit; swim only in netted areas.

faq: Can you camp for free near Cairns?

Very little. Queensland charges for national park and forest camping, and Cairns-area councils ban camping in the city, on beaches and in parks. Free options are limited to some rest areas and a few council camps further out on the Atherton Tableland and along the highways.
Is it safe to camp near Cairns in the wet season?
The wet season, roughly December to April, brings heavy rain, flooding and cyclones, and some roads and camps close. Winter, May to October, is the best camping season.
Are there crocodiles near Cairns campsites?
Yes, in estuaries, rivers and some waterholes. Obey crocodile warning signs, do not swim in the north's creeks and keep camp well back from the water.
Where should I stay in a campervan in Cairns?
A holiday park or caravan park in or near the city. Councils sign against overnight stays in streets, car parks and beaches.

free-camping-near-darwin.title: Free Camping Near Darwin: Rest Stops, Park Camps and the Dry Season
free-camping-near-darwin.description: Where to camp near Darwin: the few free rest stops, how Litchfield, Kakadu and Mary River camps work, crocodile cautions, and why the dry season matters.
free-camping-near-darwin.intro: Free camping near Darwin is rare. The Northern Territory allows free overnight stops only at signed rest stops for up to 24 hours, park campgrounds at Litchfield, Kakadu and Mary River are booked and paid, and camping in Darwin itself is banned. The camps are cheap and well worth it, and the dry season from May to October is when the Top End is at its best.

sections.heading: Why free is rare here
body: Northern Territory rules limit free camping to signed rest stops with a 24-hour limit. Park camps are booked online at roughly $10 to $20 per adult a night, and visitors need an NT Parks Visitor Pass. Darwin's council area bans camping in parks, on beaches and on streets.
The Top End is a long way from anywhere, so the free rest stops matter on the long drives, but the camps near Darwin are cheap enough that most people book them.

sections.heading: Litchfield, Kakadu and Mary River
body: Litchfield is the easy one: waterfalls, swimming holes and campgrounds within two hours of Darwin. Kakadu is bigger and further out, with its own park entry fee and camps at Mardugal, Merl and others. Mary River National Park is closer and quieter.
Book your camp online ahead of time in the dry season, when the popular ones fill.

sections.heading: The wet season
body: From about November to April storms, flooding and heat arrive. Roads and tracks close, many park camps shut and the Top End slows down. Our wet season guide explains what stays open.
The dry season, May to October, brings sunny days and cool nights, and it is when most travellers come.

sections.heading: Crocodiles and water safety
body: Saltwater crocodiles live in rivers, billabongs, estuaries and some waterholes. Obey every sign, do not swim where a sign warns of them, camp back from the water and never clean fish or leave food at the edge.
Swimming holes at Litchfield are checked and signed, but follow the sign rather than assuming.

faq: Can you camp for free near Darwin?

Almost not. The Northern Territory allows free camping only at signed rest stops for up to 24 hours. Park campgrounds at Litchfield, Kakadu and Mary River are booked and paid, and camping in Darwin itself is banned.
How much does camping near Darwin cost?
Territory park campgrounds are booked online and cost roughly $10 to $20 per adult a night, and visitors need an NT Parks Visitor Pass. Private camps and caravan parks charge their own rates.
Is it safe to camp near Darwin in the wet season?
The wet season, roughly November to April, brings storms, floods and closed roads, and many camps and tracks shut. The dry season, May to October, is the camping season.
Are there crocodiles at Top End campsites?
Yes, in rivers, billabongs, estuaries and some creeks. Obey the warning signs, camp back from the water and never swim where signed.

free-camping-near-canberra.title: Free Camping Near Canberra: Booked ACT Camps and Free NSW Forests Nearby
free-camping-near-canberra.description: Where to camp near Canberra: why the ACT has no free camping, the booked camps at Cotter and Namadgi, and the free NSW forests and council camps a short drive away.
free-camping-near-canberra.intro: There is no free camping in Canberra. The ACT only allows vehicle camping at booked campgrounds, and camping on other public land without a permit is an offence. The free nights are just over the border: New South Wales state forests allow free camping with no booking, and country councils on the Southern Tablelands and in the Snowy Valleys run free or cheap camps within an hour or two of the city.

sections.heading: The ACT: booked campgrounds only
body: Parks ACT lists every place you can camp: Cotter, Honeysuckle, Orroral, Mount Clear, Kowen and others. All need a booking and fee, and camping on public land elsewhere without a permit can bring a fine of up to 20 penalty units.
Commercial holiday parks around the city are the easy base for a visit, with powered sites the park campgrounds do not offer.

table.caption: Where you can stay near Canberra, how far it is, and the main limit.

sections.heading: Free camping just over the border
body: Forestry Corporation of NSW allows free camping in its state forests, with no booking, for up to four weeks. The forests east, south and west of Canberra, around Tallaganda, the Brindabella ranges and the Tumut and Batlow country, are the closest.
They are first come, first served, basic, and can close for harvesting, burns or fire. Bring your own water and take your rubbish out.

sections.heading: Namadgi and the high country
body: Namadgi National Park, south-west of the city, has booked campgrounds at Honeysuckle, Orroral and Mount Clear, and walk-in camping for bushwalkers. Nights are cold, and the Orroral fire of 2020 burnt much of the park, so check each track.
Further south, the Snowy Mountains and Jindabyne have lakeside camps and a different set of rules; the alps camping route guide covers them.

sections.heading: Fire and winter
body: The ACT bushfire season runs from 1 October to 31 March, and on Total Fire Ban days no fires are allowed. Canberra winters are frosty, and the high country has snow, so check the forecast and road status before you head up.
The best camping months are autumn and spring.

faq: Can you camp for free in Canberra?

No. The ACT has no free camping: vehicle camping is only allowed at booked campgrounds such as Cotter, Honeysuckle and Kowen, and camping on other public land without a permit is an offence. The free options start across the border in New South Wales.
Where is the closest free camping to Canberra?

In New South Wales state forests, which allow free camping with no booking, and at some council camps in country towns around the Southern Tablelands and the Snowy Valleys, about an hour to two hours away.
Can I camp at Namadgi National Park?
Yes, at booked campgrounds such as Honeysuckle, Orroral and Mount Clear, and bushwalkers can camp in remote parts. Park entry is free but the campgrounds need a booking and a fee.
Can I sleep in a campervan in Canberra?
Not on the street or in parks. Use a holiday park or a campground, such as the showground camping at Exhibition Park, as your base.

powered-campsites-australia-by-state.title: Powered Campsites in Australia by State: Where to Find Power on a Road Trip
powered-campsites-australia-by-state.description: Where to find powered campsites in each Australian state: holiday parks, showgrounds and the few park campgrounds with power, and how to plan power nights on a long trip.
powered-campsites-australia-by-state.imageAlt: Caravans and motorhomes parked on red ground at the Eighty Mile Beach caravan park on the north-west coast of Western Australia
powered-campsites-australia-by-state.intro: Powered campsites in Australia are mostly in holiday parks, caravan parks and showgrounds, not in national parks. Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria have the densest networks, South Australia and Tasmania have good coverage along the main routes, and Western Australia and the Northern Territory have fewer, spread out along the highways. Plan a powered night every few days to charge batteries and run the fridge, and book ahead in the school holidays.

sections.heading: Where power is, and where it is not
body: Powered sites are a commercial feature. Holiday parks and caravan parks offer them in every state, many showgrounds have a powered section, and a handful of park campgrounds do too. National park and state forest camps are almost always unpowered, with a toilet and sometimes water.
That shapes a trip: free and park camps for the bush nights, a powered holiday park or showground every few days to recharge, wash and fill up.

sections.heading: The east coast
body: Between Melbourne, Sydney and Cairns the coast is lined with holiday parks, most with powered sites, and showgrounds fill the gaps inland. This is the easiest stretch in the country for power, and prices rise in school holidays and on long weekends.
Book the coastal powered sites early for summer and Easter.

sections.heading: The west, the north and the Nullarbor
body: In Western Australia and the Top End, powered sites sit in caravan parks and roadhouses a long way apart, so work out the gaps before you leave. On the Nullarbor, roadhouses are the usual option and power is limited.
Carry enough battery or solar to cover the stretches in between.

sections.heading: Showgrounds
body: Many country showgrounds take campers for a modest fee, with a powered section, toilets and hot showers. They are a good cheap alternative to a holiday park, but close when a show or event is on.
The council or showground website has the current price and rules.

sections.heading: Booking and price
body: Powered sites cost more than unpowered ones, and the gap varies by park. In school holidays and over summer, popular parks sell out weeks ahead. Our powered versus unpowered guide has examples of the price difference.
Ask about the amp rating if you run an air conditioner, and about the lead length.

body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save camps to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.
Place details are saved on the phone for use without signal, while the map, routing and weather need a connection. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Do national park campgrounds in Australia have power?

Rarely. Most national park campgrounds are unpowered, with a toilet, sometimes water and not much else. Powered sites are a holiday park, caravan park and showground feature, and a few parks have a powered section.
Where can I find powered campsites in Australia?
In holiday parks and caravan parks in every state, at many showgrounds, and in a small number of park campgrounds. The park or showground's own page says which sites have power.
Which state has the most powered sites?

Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria have the densest networks of holiday parks and showgrounds, so powered sites are easiest to find there. The Northern Territory and the Western Australian outback have fewer, spread far apart.
How do I find powered sites on a long road trip?
Plan a powered night every few days to charge the batteries and run the fridge, and book it in school holidays. Holiday parks and showgrounds near the main highways are the reliable choice.

esperance-camping-guide.title: Esperance Camping Guide: Cape Le Grand, Lucky Bay and the South Coast
esperance-camping-guide.description: Camping at Esperance: the Cape Le Grand and Cape Arid campgrounds, Lucky Bay's kangaroos, how far it is from Perth, the best season and how to book.
esperance-camping-guide.imageAlt: Greens Pool near Denmark, Western Australia
esperance-camping-guide.intro: Esperance is the end of a long road and worth it. The white beaches of Cape Le Grand and Cape Arid have some of the best coastal camping in Western Australia, and Lucky Bay's campground lets you wake to kangaroos on the sand. Park camps are booked and paid, there is no free camping on the beaches, and the town has caravan parks for the rest. Plan two days from Perth and book before school holidays.

sections.heading: Getting there
body: Esperance is about 720 kilometres from Perth, 8 to 9 hours of driving. Most people take the inland route by Coolgardie or go via Albany and the south coast, and split it over two days. The road is sealed, with long gaps between fuel and rest stops.
Fill up in Ravensthorpe or Norseman and watch for kangaroos at dawn and dusk.
tips: Watch for kangaroos at dawn and dusk

sections.heading: Cape Le Grand National Park
body: Cape Le Grand, 50 kilometres east of Esperance, is the main draw. The Lucky Bay campground sits behind the beach, where kangaroos graze on the sand, and Le Grand Beach has a smaller campground. The park has granite peaks to climb, including Frenchman Peak, and clear blue bays.
Camping is booked and paid through the state parks system, and park entry applies. The campgrounds fill in school holidays and at Easter, so book early.

sections.heading: Cape Arid and the east
body: Cape Arid National Park, further east, is quieter and wilder, with campgrounds at Thomas River and Seal Creek. Some tracks need a 4WD and the park is remote, so carry water, fuel and a recovery kit.
Check road conditions with the park before you go, particularly after rain.

sections.heading: In and around town
body: Esperance has caravan parks close to the beaches, and the Great Ocean Drive loop passes the pink lake, the wind farm and the coast. Pink Lake is no longer reliably pink, so do not make it the reason you come.
The town has a good supermarket and the usual services, so stock up before the national parks.
tips: Pink Lake is not always pink

sections.heading: Season and weather
body: Spring, September to November, brings wildflowers and mild days. Autumn is calm and warm. Summer is warm and busy, with fire risk, and winter is cool, wet and quiet.
The south coast is windy and the sea is cold and rough, so swim at the sheltered bays.

faq: Where can you camp near Esperance?

At Cape Le Grand National Park, which has campgrounds at Lucky Bay and Le Grand Beach, at Cape Arid and Stokes National Parks, and at caravan parks in town. Park campgrounds are booked and paid, and there is no free camping on the beaches.
How far is Esperance from Perth?
About 720 kilometres, or 8 to 9 hours of driving, by Albany Highway and the south coast or by the Coolgardie-Esperance Highway. Most people split it over two days.
Is Lucky Bay worth camping at?
Yes. It is famous for white sand and kangaroos on the beach. The campground fills early in school holidays and the long weekends, so book ahead.
When is the best time to camp at Esperance?
Spring and autumn are the best, with mild days and wildflowers in spring. Summer is warm and busy, and winter is cool and wet.

karijini-national-park-camping.title: Karijini National Park Camping: Dales Campground, Gorges and When to Go
karijini-national-park-camping.description: Camping at Karijini National Park: Dales Campground and the eco retreat, booking, the best season, gorge safety and how to get there from Perth, Tom Price or Newman.
karijini-national-park-camping.intro: Karijini is the Pilbara's great gorge country, and the way to see it is to camp. Dales Campground sits near Dales Gorge and Fortescue Falls, the Karijini Eco Retreat has powered and unpowered sites, and both take bookings ahead of the cooler months. It is a long way from Perth, so plan the trip as part of a bigger loop, go between April and October and treat the gorges with respect.

sections.heading: Getting there
body: Karijini is about 1,400 kilometres from Perth, roughly 15 hours of driving. Most people come from Tom Price, Newman or on the road between Perth and Broome, and fly into Paraburdoo or Newman if they are short of time.
The main roads in are sealed or good gravel. Fill up at Tom Price or Newman, carry water and check Main Roads for closures after rain.
tips: Fill up at Tom Price or Newman

sections.heading: Where to camp
body: Dales Campground is the park's own camp, close to Dales Gorge and Fortescue Falls, with toilets and basic facilities, and you book it through the state parks system. The Karijini Eco Retreat, outside the main gorge area, has powered and unpowered sites and glamping tents.
Both fill in the cooler months, so book early. Dispersed camping inside the park is not allowed.

sections.heading: The gorges and safety
body: Dales Gorge, Hancock, Weano, Knox and Joffre are the main gorges, and some involve scrambles and wading through cold water. Wear grippy shoes, carry water and never enter a gorge if rain is forecast or has fallen upstream.
Flash floods are a real danger in summer storms. Heed park signs and closures.

sections.heading: Season and heat
body: The best time is April to October, with warm days and cool nights. Summer is very hot, with storms and flooding, and some gorges close.
Carry plenty of water and plan walks for the cooler part of the day.

faq: Where can you camp at Karijini National Park?

At Dales Campground, run by the park, and at the Karijini Eco Retreat, which has powered and unpowered sites and glamping tents. Dales is booked and paid, and there is no free camping inside the park.
Do I need to book Karijini camping?
Yes. Dales Campground takes bookings through the state parks system and fills in the cooler months, so book before you drive up.
When is the best time to camp at Karijini?
April to October, in the dry season. Summer brings extreme heat, storms and flash flooding in the gorges, and some tracks and gorges close.
Can I take a 2WD campervan to Karijini?
Usually yes. The main roads in are sealed or good gravel, but check road conditions before you go, particularly after rain.

kalbarri-coral-coast-camping.title: Kalbarri and the Coral Coast: Camping Along WA's North-West Coast
kalbarri-coral-coast-camping.description: Camping at Kalbarri and along the Coral Coast: the Pinnacles, Geraldton, Kalbarri National Park, Shark Bay and Ningaloo, with free rest stops, park camps and the best season.
kalbarri-coral-coast-camping.imageAlt: A sandy Ningaloo coast beach at sunset, with a low reef offshore and dunes with low scrub behind
kalbarri-coral-coast-camping.intro: The Coral Coast is the road north from Perth to Exmouth, and Kalbarri is its best stop for gorges, river and coast. You can camp in caravan parks in the towns, at park campgrounds with a booking, and at signed rest stops for a free night, but there is no free camping on the beaches. Go between April and October, fuel up at every town and keep an eye out for the long gaps.

sections.heading: The route
body: The Coral Coast follows the Brand and North West Coastal highways from Perth to Cervantes, Geraldton, Kalbarri, Shark Bay, Carnarvon, Coral Bay and Exmouth, roughly 1,250 kilometres in all. Kalbarri sits about 570 kilometres north of Perth, a day's drive.
The big gaps are north of Geraldton and between Carnarvon and Coral Bay, so fuel and water up at each town. Our Perth to Exmouth drive guide covers the route stage by stage.
tips: Kalbarri is a day north of Perth

sections.heading: Kalbarri
body: Kalbarri National Park has the gorges of the Murchison River, Nature's Window and the Skywalk. Camps in town are caravan parks, and park campgrounds are basic, booked and paid. Walks are best in the cool morning, and gorge walks close in extreme heat.
The coast at Kalbarri has surf, cliffs and pelican feeding at the river mouth.

sections.heading: Shark Bay, Ningaloo and the north
body: Shark Bay has Monkey Mia's dolphins and the shell beaches, and Francois Peron National Park has 4WD camps. At the end of the road, Coral Bay and Exmouth sit by Ningaloo Reef, where you can snorkel off the beach and swim with whale sharks on tours.
Camping inside the Ningaloo and Cape Range area is booked and paid, and the camps fill in school holidays.

sections.heading: Free stops and the season
body: Signed rest stops along the highways allow a night in the vehicle, up to 24 hours. Some shires also run low-cost camps. The best season is April to October, when the weather is dry and mild, and whale shark and humpback season come mid year. Summer is very hot and cyclone-prone in the north.

faq: What is the Coral Coast in Western Australia?

The stretch of coast north of Perth, from Cervantes and the Pinnacles through Geraldton, Kalbarri and Denham to Coral Bay and Exmouth, with Ningaloo Reef at the far end. It is the classic Perth to Exmouth road trip.
Where can I camp at Kalbarri?
In caravan parks in town, and at park campgrounds in Kalbarri National Park, where the camps are basic and booked. There is no free camping in the park or on the beaches.
Is there free camping on the Coral Coast?
Only at signed rest stops, where you can stay up to 24 hours, and at some shire camps. Park camps and station stays are paid.
When is the best time to drive the Coral Coast?
April to October. Summer is very hot and the gorges close in the heat.

byron-noosa-gold-coast-campervan-rules.title: Campervan Rules in Byron Bay, Noosa and the Gold Coast: Where You Can Stay
byron-noosa-gold-coast-campervan-rules.description: Where you can and cannot sleep in a campervan in Byron Bay, Noosa and the Gold Coast: the council bans, the fines, and the holiday parks and hinterland camps that work instead.
byron-noosa-gold-coast-campervan-rules.imageAlt: Aerial view of Cape Byron and its lighthouse, with surf along the coast and the green headland rising from the sea
byron-noosa-gold-coast-campervan-rules.intro: Byron Bay, Noosa and the Gold Coast are the most popular stretch of the east coast and the strictest for campervans. All three councils ban sleeping in vehicles in streets, car parks, reserves and on beaches, and rangers patrol, particularly in summer and school holidays. The reliable answer is a holiday park or caravan park, with booked camps in the hinterland for a quieter night.

sections.heading: Why these three are strict
body: The three places are some of the most visited in the country, with limited parking, residents who complain about vans on their streets and councils that have chosen to act. Each has its own local law banning overnight camping in vehicles in public places.
Fines are issued, and in peak season the patrols start early and finish late. Treat the rule as enforced, not theoretical.

sections.heading: Byron Bay
body: Byron Shire Council bans camping in vehicles in public places, and the town's holiday parks are close to the beach and the centre. They fill early, so book well ahead for school holidays, Easter and summer.
Out in the Byron hinterland and across the Tweed, booked national park camps and small private camps offer a quieter option.

sections.heading: Noosa
body: Noosa Council signs against overnight stays in streets and car parks, and enforces it. Caravan parks in Noosa, Tewantin and Noosaville are the straightforward choice, and the Noosa hinterland and the Great Sandy region have permit camps.
Our first campervan trip guide covers a Brisbane to Noosa run.
tips: Caravan parks in Noosa and Tewantin

sections.heading: The Gold Coast
body: The City of Gold Coast bans camping and sleeping in vehicles in parks, on beaches and on streets. Holiday parks line the coast from Coolangatta to the Spit, and the Gold Coast hinterland, including Lamington and Springbrook, has booked camps.
If a sign or a ranger says move on, do so; arguing leads to a fine.

sections.heading: Tips for a campervan trip on this coast
body: Book holiday parks weeks ahead in summer and school holidays, check each council's page for the current rule, and use the hinterland camps for the nights you want to be quiet.
If you are travelling Brisbane to Byron Bay, our drive guide covers the route and where to stop.

faq: Can you sleep in a campervan in Byron Bay?

Not in public places. Byron Shire Council bans camping in vehicles on streets, in car parks and in reserves, and rangers patrol, particularly in summer. Stay at a holiday park or caravan park instead.
Can you sleep in a campervan in Noosa?
No, not on public land. Noosa Council signs against overnight stays in streets, car parks and at the beaches, and enforces it. Use a caravan park or holiday park in the area.
Is it legal to sleep in a campervan on the Gold Coast?
Not on public land. The City of Gold Coast bans camping and sleeping in vehicles in parks, on beaches and on streets, with fines for breaking the rule. Use a caravan park or holiday park.
Where can I park a campervan overnight near the Gold Coast?
In a caravan park or holiday park, or at a booked campground in a hinterland national park. Check each council's page for current rules before you stay anywhere else.

campervan-holiday-with-kids-australia.title: Campervan Holiday With Kids in Australia: Planning, Safety and Where to Stay
campervan-holiday-with-kids-australia.description: Planning a campervan trip in Australia with kids: choosing a van and child seats, short driving days, holiday parks with playgrounds, heat and safety, and what to pack.
campervan-holiday-with-kids-australia.intro: A campervan holiday with kids is one of the easiest ways to see Australia, as long as the plan matches the family. Keep driving days to 2 or 3 hours, book holiday parks with playgrounds and pools, check the van has proper child seat anchor points, and pick a season that is not too hot. A mix of powered holiday park nights and the odd bush camp keeps everyone happy.

sections.heading: Choosing the van
body: Pick a van by the number of seatbelts and the sleeping layout, not just the number of beds. Child seats must be fitted to the correct anchor points, so ask the hire company which seats are suitable and whether it supplies seats.
A van with a toilet and shower makes a big difference with young kids, and an awning gives a shaded play area at camp.

sections.heading: Short driving days
body: Distances in Australia are long, and kids get tired of the back seat. Aim for 2 to 3 hours of driving a day, with a stop at a playground, beach or park in the middle, and fewer one-night stops.
Our road trip guides give distances and stage times for the main routes.

sections.heading: Where to stay
body: Holiday parks are the easy choice: playgrounds, pools, camp kitchens and powered sites. Book early for school holidays. Park camps give a bush night, and free camps suit older kids, with basic facilities and no showers.
Our school holidays guide lists the dates by state so you can avoid the peaks.

sections.heading: Heat, sun and water safety
body: Summer is hot, so travel in spring or autumn where you can, or head south or to the mountains. Use sunscreen, hats and shade, carry plenty of water and never leave kids or pets in a parked van.
Swim between the flags where there are patrolled beaches, and obey crocodile and stinger signs in the north.
tips: Never leave kids in the van

sections.heading: Packing and routines
body: Pack games, books and a tablet for the longer drives, a night light, sleeping bags and a few of the comforts of home. Keep bedtimes close to normal, and build in a rest day every few days.
Our packing list guide covers the basics.

faq: Is a campervan holiday good with kids in Australia?
Yes, if you plan short driving days, book holiday parks with playgrounds and pools, and choose a van with proper child seat anchor points. Most families do best with 2 to 3 hours of driving a day.
Do child car seats work in a campervan?

Child seats must be fitted to approved anchor points and seatbelts, and not every seat in a campervan is suitable. Check with the hire company before you book and ask what seats and anchors are fitted.
How many kids fit in a campervan?
It depends on the van. Two-berth vans suit one child or a baby, four-berth vans suit two kids, and larger motorhomes sleep five or six. Check the number of seatbelts as well as beds.
Where should families stay on a campervan trip?
Holiday parks with playgrounds, pools and powered sites are the easy choice, with a few park camps on the way for a bush night. Free camps suit older kids.

rest-areas-western-australia-south-austr.title: Rest Areas in Western Australia and South Australia: Where You Can Stay the Night
rest-areas-western-australia-south-austr.description: How rest areas work in WA and SA: signed 24-hour stops in Western Australia, the sign-and-council rule in South Australia, facilities, the Nullarbor and how to use them well.
rest-areas-western-australia-south-austr.imageAlt: Eyre Highway across the Nullarbor Plain
rest-areas-western-australia-south-austr.intro: Rest areas are the backbone of a long drive across Western Australia and South Australia, and the rules differ. In WA you can stay up to 24 hours at stops signed for overnight camping. In SA the rule follows the sign and the local council, and some councils ban overnight stays entirely. Either way, treat a rest area as a place to sleep in the vehicle for a night, not a campsite.

sections.heading: Western Australia: the 24-hour rule
body: WA rest areas signed for overnight stops allow you to stay up to 24 consecutive hours. They are the main free option in the state, and they run along the North West Coastal, Great Northern, Great Eastern and South Western highways.
Where there is no sign, the stop is for a break, not a bed. Camping elsewhere without approval risks a fine.

sections.heading: South Australia: sign and council
body: South Australia has no blanket rule. Where no sign or council rule prohibits it, you can stop for a night in the vehicle, and where a sign says no overnight stays, you must move on.
Some councils ban it entirely. The Barossa Council, for example, prohibits camping or overnight stays in public reserves, car parks, roads and rest areas across its region.

sections.heading: The Nullarbor and the long roads
body: On the Eyre Highway across the Nullarbor, the gaps between fuel and rest stops are long. Roadhouses sell fuel, water and meals and often have paid camping, and signed rest stops fill the gaps. Our Nullarbor guide covers it.
Fatigue is the point of rest areas: pull in when you are tired and do not push on.

sections.heading: Using a rest area well
body: Park in the car and caravan bays, keep truck bays clear and leave no rubbish. Do not set up awnings and chairs across the grass, do not run a generator and do not stay a second night.
Carry your own water, because tanks at rest areas may not be drinkable, and a torch for night.

sections.heading: Find rest areas in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps maps 1,661 Western Australian roadside rest areas and 391 in South Australia, with each place's facilities as the road authority publishes them. You can filter by facilities, save stops to a trip and see the driving distance between them, which shows the long gaps before you leave.
Place details are saved on the phone for use without signal, which matters on the Nullarbor. The map, routing and weather need a connection, and AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Can you sleep at rest areas in Western Australia?
Only at rest areas signed for overnight stops, where you can stay up to 24 hours. At others, treat the stop as a break and not a camp.
Can you sleep at rest areas in South Australia?
Where no sign or council rule prohibits it, you can stop for a night in the vehicle. Some councils ban overnight stays outright, such as the Barossa Council, so follow the sign.
How long can I stay at a rest area on the Nullarbor?
The stops signed for camping allow up to 24 hours in Western Australia and follow local rules in South Australia. Roadhouses sell fuel, water and meals and often have paid camping.
Do WA and SA rest areas have toilets and water?
Many have toilets and tables, and some have shelters, but water is often not drinkable or not provided. Carry your own.

buying-camping-gear-australia.title: Buying Camping Gear in Australia: Kmart, Anaconda and BCF Compared
buying-camping-gear-australia.description: Where to buy camping gear in Australia: what Kmart, Anaconda and BCF each do well, what to buy first, when to spend more and how to avoid buying things you will not use.
buying-camping-gear-australia.imageAlt: Tent, sleeping bag and backpack at an Australian campground
buying-camping-gear-australia.intro: Camping gear in Australia is easy to buy and easy to overspend on. Kmart covers cheap basics, Anaconda and BCF have the wider ranges of tents, stoves, coolers and 4WD gear, and Bunnings and the supermarket fill in the small items. Buy cheap for a short trip, spend more on the sleeping bag, mat and tent, and skip anything you cannot name a use for.

sections.heading: What each store is good for
body: Kmart is the cheap starting point: basic tents, chairs, mats, lanterns and cookware at low prices. It is fine for a first trip or a short holiday. Anaconda and BCF are the camping specialists, with a wider range of tents, sleeping bags, stoves, fridges, awnings and recovery gear, and staff who can help.
Bunnings has gas bottles, tarps, rope, buckets and tools, and the supermarket has the small things, from matches to wet wipes.

sections.heading: What to buy first
body: Start with sleep and safety: a sleeping bag suited to the season, a mat or stretcher, a headlamp, water containers, a stove and fuel, and a first aid kit. Then add the tent or shelter, a cooler or fridge and cookware.
If you are hiring or buying a campervan, much of this is in the van already, so buy less.

sections.heading: When to spend more
body: Spend on what you use every day: the sleeping bag, the mat and the tent. Cheap versions leak, tear or leave you cold, and the saving is not worth a bad night. Cheap is fine for chairs, tables and cookware.
Sales at Anaconda and BCF around long weekends and the end of the financial year make the bigger items cheaper.

sections.heading: Buy, hire or borrow
body: For a short holiday you can hire a tent or buy at Kmart and sell it at the end. For a long trip, buy, and sell or donate when you leave. Our campervan buying and selling guides cover the larger decisions.
Check the weather: Australian nights in the high country and desert are cold, and a cheap summer sleeping bag will not cut it.

faq: Where can I buy camping gear in Australia?
At Kmart for cheap basics, Anaconda and BCF for a wider range of tents, sleeping bags, stoves and coolers, and outdoor specialists for hiking gear. Supermarkets and Bunnings cover the small items.
Is Kmart camping gear any good?

For a short trip or a first time out, yes. It is cheap and does the job, but it is not built for years of heavy use or harsh weather, so upgrade the pieces that matter, like the tent and the sleeping bag, as you go.
Is it cheaper to buy or hire camping gear?
For a trip of a few weeks, buying cheap basics is usually cheaper than hiring, and you can resell or donate afterwards. A campervan with a kitchen and bedding hire avoids most of it.
What should I buy first for camping in Australia?
A good sleeping bag or bedding, a mat, a torch or headlamp, a stove and fuel, water containers and a first aid kit. Then add the tent or shelter that suits the season.

glamping-australia-by-state.title: Glamping in Australia by State: Where to Find Comfortable Camping
glamping-australia-by-state.description: Where to go glamping in each Australian state: bell tents, safari tents and eco retreats by region, what to expect for price and season, and when to book.
glamping-australia-by-state.imageAlt: Sunset campsite in Hattah-Kulkyne National Park, Victoria
glamping-australia-by-state.intro: Glamping is camping with the discomfort taken out: a bed, often power, sometimes a private bathroom, in a tent, dome or cabin in a good spot. Australia has plenty, from vineyards in the Hunter and Yarra valleys to eco retreats at Karijini and the Top End. Book early, choose the season for the region and keep the budget in mind, because the best sites cost several times a normal campsite.

sections.heading: What glamping is
body: Glamping, or glamorous camping, covers bell tents, safari tents, domes, yurts and cabins with a real bed and often power, in campgrounds, on farms, at vineyards and beside beaches. Some have private bathrooms, some share a block, and the extras vary.
Check what is included before you book: bedding, power, heating, cooking, linen and whether pets are allowed.

sections.heading: The south-east: NSW, Victoria and Tasmania
body: Glamping near Sydney and Melbourne runs from Hunter Valley vineyards and Blue Mountains domes to Yarra Valley and Great Ocean Road tents. Tasmania has retreats on the east coast and at Cradle Mountain.
These are weekend trips, so they book out on Fridays and Saturdays; a midweek stay is cheaper and quieter.

sections.heading: Queensland, the Top End and the west
body: In Queensland, glamping is mostly rainforest and coast: Noosa's hinterland, the Daintree and the islands. In the Top End, Kakadu and Litchfield have tents and cabins that suit the dry season, May to October. In the west, Margaret River, Karijini and Ningaloo have eco tents and retreats.
Remote sites charge more and book out early in the cooler months.

sections.heading: South Australia
body: The Barossa has vineyard stays, Kangaroo Island has tents among the wildlife, and the Flinders Ranges has retreats in the outback. Autumn and spring are the best times, with summer hot and the Flinders cold in winter.

sections.heading: Price and booking
body: Glamping costs more than a standard campsite, from the price of a good holiday park cabin up to several hundred dollars a night at remote or luxury sites. Prices rise in school holidays and in the high season, and many places set a two-night minimum on weekends.
Read the cancellation terms and ask about weather policies, particularly in cyclone or fire season.

Place details are saved on the phone for use without signal, while the map, routing and weather need a connection. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.
tips: Fit a cheap night between stays

faq: What is glamping in Australia?
Camping with the comfort left in: a bell tent, safari tent, cabin or dome with a real bed, power and sometimes a private bathroom, set in a campground or on a farm, vineyard or beach.
How much does glamping cost in Australia?
It ranges from around the price of a good cabin at a holiday park to several hundred dollars a night at remote or luxury sites. Prices rise in school holidays and in peak season.
Where is the best glamping in Australia?

Popular regions include the Hunter Valley, the Blue Mountains, the Yarra Valley and Great Ocean Road, the Tasmanian east coast, the Margaret River region, Kangaroo Island, the Daintree and the Top End. The best choice depends on the state and the season.
Do I need to book glamping in advance?
Yes. The popular sites book out for weekends, school holidays and the cooler months, so book weeks or months ahead.

free-camping-broken-hill.title: Free Camping in Broken Hill: Outback NSW Stays That Cost Little
free-camping-broken-hill.description: Where to camp near Broken Hill: why the town itself is off limits, the national park and river camps, rest areas on the Barrier Highway, Silverton and how to plan the long drive.
free-camping-broken-hill.imageAlt: Rawnsley Bluff in the Flinders Ranges
free-camping-broken-hill.intro: Broken Hill is the gateway to outback New South Wales, and it is not a free camping town. The council signs against sleeping in parks and on streets, so a van parked beside a lookout is likely to be moved on. The good news is that the country around it has plenty of cheap options: rest areas on the Barrier Highway, river camps at Kinchega and Menindee, Mutawintji in the ranges, and a few small free spots with a sign. Plan the water and the fuel first, because the nearest town is always a long way off.

sections.heading: Why Broken Hill itself is off limits
body: Broken Hill City Council does not allow camping in parks, reserves or on the street, and rangers do patrol the lookouts and the edge of town. The council would rather you used a caravan park, and there are several, with powered and unpowered sites and showers.
That is a sensible base for a night or two while you see the Sculptures at Living Desert, the mining history and the galleries, then head out into the bush.

sections.heading: Kinchega and the Menindee Lakes
body: Kinchega National Park runs along the Darling River about two hours south east of Broken Hill. It has riverside camping, a historic woolshed and big birdlife when the lakes are full. Camping is booked and paid through the park system, and it is much cheaper than a holiday park.
The lakes and the river rise and fall with the seasons, so how green the camp looks changes a lot from year to year. Wet weather closes the dirt roads quickly, so ask before you go.
tips: Closed when the roads are wet

sections.heading: Mutawintji and the ranges
body: Mutawintji National Park is about 130 kilometres north east of Broken Hill and is run jointly with its Aboriginal owners. It has gorges, rock pools and Aboriginal rock art, and a campground at Homestead Creek. Some sites can only be seen on a guided tour, so check what is open before you plan the day.
The last stretch of road is unsealed and can close after rain. Take plenty of water, because there is none to buy in the park.

sections.heading: Rest areas and the highways
body: The Barrier Highway between Broken Hill and Cobar, and the road towards South Australia, have rest areas built for driver fatigue. Treat them as a place to sleep in the vehicle for a night, not a campsite: no awning, no chairs, no second night.
Silverton, the old mining town, has a pub and a few places that take campers for a small fee. Ask at the pub or the gate before you set up, because the rule can change from one visit to the next.
tips: Ask at Silverton before you camp

sections.heading: Heat, water and the long drive
body: Summer days at Broken Hill regularly pass 40 degrees, nights in winter are cold, and the closest shop can be a hundred kilometres away. Carry more water than you think you need, keep the fuel above half, and let someone know your route.
Phone signal fades fast outside the town. Download your maps and camp details before you leave, and do not leave the road to find a better camp.

sections.heading: Plan the outback in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops, which helps in country where fuel is far apart.
Council, pub and station camps are not all in the app, so check the council page or ask at the pub for those. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Can you camp for free in Broken Hill?

Not in the town itself. The council signs against camping in parks and on streets, so the free nights are on the highways out of town and at a few outback camps with a council or station sign. Check the sign and the stay limit before you unpack.
Where can you camp near Broken Hill?

Kinchega National Park on the Darling River near Menindee and Mutawintji National Park are the main bush options, both with a booked, paid camping fee. Town caravan parks suit a night with power, and rest areas on the Barrier Highway suit a night in the vehicle.
Is Broken Hill in a different time zone?
Yes. Broken Hill is in New South Wales but keeps South Australian time, so its clocks are half an hour behind Sydney all year. Check the time before you book a tour or a check-in.
What should I carry on the road to Broken Hill?
Plenty of water, spare fuel range, a spare tyre and a plan for no phone signal. Distances are long, towns are small and the sealed road is fine, but a breakdown can mean a long wait in summer heat.

free-camping-coober-pedy.title: Free Camping in Coober Pedy: Where to Stay in the Opal Town
free-camping-coober-pedy.description: Where to camp around Coober Pedy: why free camping in town is limited, the caravan parks and underground stays, rest areas on the Stuart Highway and how to stay safe on the opal fields.
free-camping-coober-pedy.intro: Coober Pedy sits halfway between Adelaide and Uluru, and almost everyone stops for a night. Free camping in town is limited, because the council keeps camping to caravan parks and signed spots and the opal fields are riddled with old mine shafts. The best value is a powered site at a caravan park, or a rest area on the Stuart Highway if you only need to sleep. Plan around the heat, the long fuel gaps and the underground stays that most visitors come for.

sections.heading: What the town allows
body: Coober Pedy is a mining town, and the council does not allow camping across town and the opal fields. You can camp at the caravan parks, which have powered and unpowered sites, and at a few signed places. Rangers and locals notice a van parked where it should not be.
The old opal mine shafts are the real reason to follow the rules. Many are open or lightly covered, and they are very dangerous in the dark.
tips: Old shafts are a real danger

table.caption: Where to stay in and around Coober Pedy.
head: Where
Cost

rows: Overnight on the road to Uluru

sections.heading: Underground and powered stays
body: Coober Pedy is the one place where sleeping underground is normal. Several hotels and a caravan park have rooms and sites dug into the hillside, which stay around the same temperature all year. In a summer that regularly passes 40 degrees, that alone is worth the booking.
Book ahead in the cooler months, when the town is full of travellers heading to or from Uluru.

sections.heading: Rest areas on the Stuart Highway
body: The Stuart Highway north and south of town has rest areas designed for drivers to sleep in the vehicle. Treat them as a night's stop, not a camp: no awning, no chairs, no second night, and take your rubbish with you.
Some roadhouses along the road, such as Marla and Cadney Park, let you camp for a small fee and sell fuel, water and a meal. Check opening hours, because they can be a long way apart.

sections.heading: The Breakaways and the Painted Desert
body: The Breakaways, about 30 kilometres from town, is a reserve of colourful hills that is best at sunrise and sunset. A pass is needed to enter and camping is not allowed inside, so go for the light and return to town.
The Painted Desert is further out, on a station that offers camping and tours. Check the conditions and the road before you go, because the dirt turns to bull dust or mud quickly.
tips: Go for the light, not a camp

sections.heading: Heat, water and fuel
body: Summer in Coober Pedy is extreme and the desert between the towns is dry. Carry more water than you expect to use, keep fuel above half, and avoid driving at dawn and dusk when kangaroos and emus are on the road.
Mobile signal is patchy outside the town. Tell someone your route and your arrival time, and never leave the road to find a camp.

sections.heading: Plan the Stuart Highway in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops, which is the number that matters on the way to Uluru.
Caravan parks and roadhouse camps are not all in the app, so check their own pages for those. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Can you camp for free in Coober Pedy?

Not freely around town. The council keeps camping to caravan parks and signed places, and the opal fields are dotted with old mine shafts that are dangerous in the dark. The free nights are at rest areas on the Stuart Highway, where the sign allows it.
Is it safe to walk around the opal fields?
Take care. There are old and unmarked shafts, and a fall can be fatal. Stay on the marked tracks and paths, keep children and pets close, and do not walk the fields at night.
Can you stay underground in Coober Pedy?
Yes. Several hotels and a caravan park have underground rooms and sites that stay cool in summer and warm in winter, which is the usual reason to stay in town.
How far is Coober Pedy from Uluru?
It is roughly 700 kilometres from Coober Pedy to Uluru by road, with long stretches between fuel. Most people split it with a night at Marla or Erldunda.

free-camping-longreach.title: Free Camping in Longreach: Cheap Stays in the Heart of Outback Queensland
free-camping-longreach.description: Where to camp in and around Longreach: council and river camps, showgrounds and caravan parks, free rest areas, what to see and how to plan the outback loop.
free-camping-longreach.intro: Longreach is the capital of outback Queensland and the best base for the Stockman's Hall of Fame, the Qantas Founders Museum and the Thomson River. It is not a classic free camping town, but cheap and free stays are close: council camps, showgrounds, pub camps and rest areas along the highways. Plan one or two nights in town for the museums and the sunset cruise, then drive on to Winton or Barcaldine with water and fuel in hand.

sections.heading: What Longreach allows
body: Longreach Regional Council keeps camping to its own camps and the caravan parks, and signs against sleeping on streets and in parks. Outback councils generally welcome travellers who pay for a night in town, and the money keeps the museums and pubs open.
A powered or unpowered site in a caravan park or at the showground is cheap by coastal standards, and you get a shower and a tap.

sections.heading: Two days in town
body: Plan the Australian Stockman's Hall of Fame for one half day and the Qantas Founders Museum, with its old aircraft, for another. A sunset cruise on the Thomson River is a classic way to end a day, and the outback shows are popular in the dry season.
Longreach is also the best base for Winton and its dinosaur trail, about two hours north west.

sections.heading: Rest areas on the highways
body: The Landsborough, Capricorn and Matilda highways have rest areas where one night in the vehicle is fine and a second is not. Look for the sign, keep the awning in and leave no rubbish behind.
Between Longreach, Winton and Barcaldine the distances are long, so plan the day's driving and finish before dark, when kangaroos and cattle are on the road.

sections.heading: Winter days, summer storms
body: The best months are May to September, with warm days and cool nights. In summer the heat is severe and storms can close the dirt roads for days.
If you plan to leave the sealed road, check the council's road report each morning and carry extra water. A stranded vehicle in the outback is a serious problem.

sections.heading: Water and fuel
body: Water is the main constraint. Fill your tank in town, keep spare drinking water, and use the free water points only where they are signed as drinkable. Fuel stations are far apart and may close early, so top up when you pass one.
Mobile signal is patchy outside the towns. Share your route, and do not leave the road for a closer look at anything.
tips: Top up fuel at every town

sections.heading: Plan the outback loop in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops, which helps a lot when towns are 200 kilometres apart.
Council, showground and pub camps are not all in the app, so check the council page for those. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Can you camp for free in Longreach?
Council rules apply, and the town prefers you use its camps and parks. There are cheap and free options in the area and along the highways, but check the sign and the stay limit before you unpack.
What is there to do in Longreach?
The Australian Stockman's Hall of Fame, the Qantas Founders Museum, which tells the story of the airline's beginnings, Thomson River cruises and the outback shows. Most people spend two nights.
What route is Longreach on?
The Capricorn and Landsborough highways, the main inland route from Rockhampton through Longreach and Winton to Mount Isa. It suits a campervan, with about a day's drive between the main towns.
When is the best time to camp in Longreach?
May to September, when days are warm and nights are cool. Summer is very hot and storms can close dirt roads for days.

free-camping-echuca.title: Free Camping Near Echuca: River Camps on the Murray
free-camping-echuca.description: Where to camp near Echuca and Moama: river camps on public land on both banks, caravan parks, the rules on fires and flooding, and what to see on the Murray.
free-camping-echuca.imageAlt: The Calder Highway curving past scrub and a vineyard at Merbein near Mildura under a clear blue sky
free-camping-echuca.intro: Echuca is a classic Murray River stop, with paddle steamers, a historic port and a lot of river. You cannot camp in the town, but the forests and reserves on both banks have riverside camps for free or a low fee, and it is easy to base yourself in a caravan park and head out for the nights you want to be in the bush. Check the fire rules, the river level and the stay limit, and bring your own water.

sections.heading: What Echuca allows
body: Councils on both banks sign against camping on streets and in town parks, and Echuca is no exception. The easy options in town are the caravan parks and holiday parks on both sides of the river, with powered sites and a short walk to the port.
For a bush night, head out to the forests and reserves. They are managed by public land agencies, and the rules are on the sign.
