sections.heading: Riverside camping on the Victorian bank
body: The Victorian side of the Murray has a string of river reserves and forest camps where you can camp close to the water, often with no booking and a small fee or none. The Barmah and Gunbower forests are the best known, with red gums, birdlife and sandy beaches in a dry year.
Bring your own water and a portable toilet if you are not in a self-contained vehicle, and take every piece of rubbish with you.

sections.heading: The New South Wales bank
body: Across the river at Moama, the state forests and regional parks have camping areas and the Forestry Corporation lists them on its camping page. Some are free and some charge a small fee.
Rules differ between the two states, including fires, dogs and how long you can stay, so check which side of the river you are camping on.

sections.heading: Fire, floods and mosquitoes
body: The river and the forests flood in wet years, and camps can close for months. Check the closures with the agency that manages the site before you drive out, and never camp on a bank that could slump.
Fire bans apply across the region in summer, and gas cooking is the safe default. In warm weather the mosquitoes are bad at dusk, so bring repellent and cover up.

sections.heading: What to see in Echuca
body: The Port of Echuca was once the busiest inland river port in Australia, and it still has restored wharves and paddle steamers that run cruises on the river. The town also has wineries and a growing food scene.
Allow a day for the port and the river, and another to explore the forests.

sections.heading: Plan the Murray in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.
State forest and river reserve camps are not all in the app yet, so check the managing agency's page for those. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Can you camp for free in Echuca?

Not in the town or on its streets, but the Murray River has free and low-cost camping on public land close by, mostly in the forests and reserves on both banks. The rules cover where you can camp, how close to the water, and for how long.
Where can you camp near Echuca?

On the Victorian side, the Gunbower and Barmah forests and Murray River reserves have riverside camping. On the New South Wales side, state forests and regional parks near Moama offer more. Caravan parks in Echuca and Moama suit a night with power.
Can I light a campfire on the Murray?
Only where the sign allows it and not on a fire ban day. Rules vary between Victoria and New South Wales, so check the day's fire danger rating and use a gas stove when in doubt.
When does the Murray flood?

River levels rise in winter and spring and some years flood the riverside camps. Check the managing agency's closures before you go, and never camp in a spot that is under water or at the edge of a bank.

free-camping-jervis-bay.title: Free Camping at Jervis Bay: What to Do When There Is None
free-camping-jervis-bay.description: Where to camp at Jervis Bay: why free camping is rare, the Booderee and Jervis Bay national park campgrounds, holiday parks at Huskisson and Hyams Beach and cheaper options inland.
free-camping-jervis-bay.imageAlt: Eden Beach on the Sapphire Coast
free-camping-jervis-bay.intro: Jervis Bay has some of the whitest sand in Australia and almost no free camping. Shoalhaven council signs against sleeping in vehicles and parking overnight in the villages, and the best bush camps are booked and paid. The sensible plan is to book a Booderee or holiday park night, spend the days on the beach, and find your free night elsewhere on the south coast, inland or on the way.

sections.heading: Why there is no free camping
body: The villages around Jervis Bay are small, popular and busy all summer, and the council does not allow camping or overnight parking on streets, beaches or reserves. Rangers patrol, and the fines are real.
The bush around the bay is national park or Commonwealth land, so camping there is booked and paid. That is the trade: the beaches are protected and the camps are well kept.

sections.heading: Booderee National Park
body: Booderee is on the southern side of the bay and is owned by the Wreck Bay Aboriginal Community and managed jointly with Parks Australia. It has the clearest water, the whitest beaches and the best campgrounds in the area, including Green Patch, Bristol Point and Cave Beach.
Camping is booked and paid, there is a vehicle entry fee as well, and the summer and Easter dates sell out months ahead. Dogs are not allowed in the park.

sections.heading: Jervis Bay National Park and the villages
body: Jervis Bay National Park has smaller camps on the northern shore and a beach that is easy to reach. Huskisson, Vincentia and Hyams Beach have holiday parks with powered sites and cabins, and are the easy way to stay when the park camps are full.
Hyams Beach is a tiny village. Park outside the village in summer, because the street parking fills by mid morning.

sections.heading: Where to find a free night
body: You will not find one on the bay, so use the drive. The Princes Highway and the roads inland from Nowra have rest areas for one night in the vehicle, and the state forests to the west run free camping under Forestry Corporation rules.
If you are heading south to the coast around Batemans Bay or Eden, or north to Sydney, our south coast guide has more camps and our free camping guide covers how the rules work.
tips: Use rest areas on the highway

sections.heading: Busy dates and the weather
body: Summer holidays, Easter and long weekends are the busiest times. Midweek and the shoulder months of March to May and September to November are quieter, with warm water and fewer cars.
Fire danger rises through the summer, and the national park can close at short notice. Check the park alerts before you drive.

sections.heading: Plan the south coast in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.
Holiday parks and council camps are not all in the app, so check their own pages for those. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Can you camp for free at Jervis Bay?

Realistically no. Jervis Bay has beautiful beaches but almost no free camping: the council and the national parks keep camping to booked and paid sites. Plan a campground in Booderee or a holiday park, and use the free time for the beaches.
Where can you camp at Jervis Bay?

Booderee National Park has the main bush campgrounds, including Green Patch, Bristol Point and Cave Beach, and Jervis Bay National Park has smaller ones. Holiday parks at Huskisson, Vincentia and Hyams Beach suit powered sites and cabins.
Do I need a pass for Booderee National Park?
Yes. Booderee is Commonwealth land owned by the Wreck Bay Aboriginal Community and charges a vehicle entry fee as well as a camping fee, so pay for both and keep the receipt in the windscreen.
Are dogs allowed at Jervis Bay?
Not in Booderee National Park and not in most of Jervis Bay National Park. Some council beaches allow dogs on a lead, and signs say where, so check before you walk.

free-camping-batemans-bay.title: Free Camping Around Batemans Bay: Forests, Beaches and Cheap Stays
free-camping-batemans-bay.description: Where to camp near Batemans Bay: why the town is off limits, Murramarang campgrounds, inland state forests, holiday parks and rest areas on the Princes and Kings highways.
free-camping-batemans-bay.imageAlt: The Federal Highway curving above the green Lake George basin in New South Wales, with a few cars on the road and low cloud over the hills
free-camping-batemans-bay.intro: Batemans Bay is where Canberra meets the coast, and it fills on every long weekend. The town and its beaches do not allow free camping, but the country around it does better: beachside national park campgrounds to the north, state forests inland and rest areas along the highways. Book the coast in advance, use the forests for a cheaper night, and keep the highway stops for a night in the vehicle.

sections.heading: What Batemans Bay allows
body: Eurobodalla Shire Council signs against camping and overnight parking in the town, on the beaches and in the reserves, and rangers do patrol in summer. Holiday parks in Batemans Bay and the nearby villages are the legal, easy choice.
The good news is that the coast around the town has more bush camping than most places on the NSW south coast, so a free or cheap night is not far.

table.caption: Where to stay around Batemans Bay.

sections.heading: Murramarang National Park
body: Murramarang is about 30 minutes north of Batemans Bay and has campgrounds right on the beach at Pretty Beach, Depot Beach and Pebbly Beach. Pebbly Beach is known for wild kangaroos that graze near the sand.
Camping is booked and paid, and the dates around Christmas and Easter sell out. Dogs are not allowed in NSW national parks.

sections.heading: State forests and the hinterland
body: The forests behind the coast, around Mogo and along the Clyde River, are run by Forestry Corporation of NSW and some allow free or low-cost camping. Facilities are basic, so bring water and take your rubbish out.
Check the forest's page for closures and fire bans before you drive, because logging and fire can close roads.

sections.heading: Rest areas on the highways
body: The Princes Highway along the coast and the Kings Highway to Canberra have rest areas for driver fatigue. Use one for a night in the vehicle, not a campsite, and leave no rubbish.
If the sign says no overnight stays, move on. The next forest or holiday park is rarely far.

sections.heading: Busy dates and bushfire
body: Long weekends and school holidays fill the coast, and Canberra visitors arrive on Friday night. Midweek and the shoulder months are much easier.
Bushfires and smoke have closed this part of the coast in recent summers, so check the fire danger rating and park alerts each morning and keep a second plan.

sections.heading: Plan the south coast in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.
State forest and council camps are not all in the app, so check the Forestry Corporation and council pages for those. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Can you camp for free in Batemans Bay?

Not in the town or on the beaches, where Eurobodalla council signs against overnight camping. Free and cheap camps are in the forests inland and along the highways, and the coast has booked national park campgrounds and holiday parks.
Where can you camp near Batemans Bay?

Murramarang National Park to the north has beachside campgrounds such as Pretty Beach, Depot Beach and Pebbly Beach, all booked and paid. Holiday parks in Batemans Bay and Surf Beach suit powered sites, and state forests inland suit a low-cost bush night.
Can I see kangaroos on the beach?
At Pebbly Beach in Murramarang, yes, wild eastern grey kangaroos graze near the sand. Keep your distance, do not feed them and keep food out of reach.
How far is Batemans Bay from Canberra?
About a 2.5 hour drive down the Kings Highway, which makes it a popular weekend trip, so the coastal parks fill on long weekends and school holidays.

free-camping-margaret-river.title: Free Camping Near Margaret River: Cheap Camps in Wine and Surf Country
free-camping-margaret-river.description: Where to camp near Margaret River: why free camping is not allowed in town, national park campgrounds at Conto and Boranup, holiday parks, forest camps and how to book for summer.
free-camping-margaret-river.imageAlt: A rocky coast with a grassy headland and low heath under a pale evening sky, north of Sugarloaf Rock in Leeuwin-Naturaliste National Park
free-camping-margaret-river.intro: Margaret River is one of the most popular holiday spots in Western Australia, and one of the hardest places to camp for free. The Shire and park rangers sign against it, and the camps that are open are booked weeks ahead in summer. The honest advice is to book a Leeuwin-Naturaliste campground or a holiday park, spend days on the beaches and in the wineries, and find a cheap or free night further inland on your way through the South West.

sections.heading: Why it is hard to camp free here
body: The Shire of Augusta Margaret River has strict rules, and rangers patrol the beaches, car parks and roadsides, especially in summer. The region has a lot of visitors and not many places to put them, so freedom camping is not allowed and fines are common.
The rest areas are for drivers to rest, not to sleep overnight in the popular parts of the region. Look for the sign, and if in doubt, go to a paid camp.

sections.heading: Leeuwin-Naturaliste National Park
body: The national park runs along the coast from Cape Naturaliste to Cape Leeuwin and has several camps, including Conto and Boranup. They are booked and paid through Parks and Wildlife Service, and they are the best value in the region.
Facilities are basic, with a toilet and a tap in some. Bring your own water and cooking gear, and check the park alerts for closures and fire bans before you go.

sections.heading: Holiday parks and the towns
body: Margaret River, Prevelly, Augusta, Dunsborough and Busselton all have holiday parks with powered sites and cabins. They are the easy way to stay close to the wineries and the beaches, and they cost far less than a motel in the same season.
Book as early as you can for December to February and for Easter.

sections.heading: Free and cheap nights inland
body: The forests and towns of the South West have cheaper stays than the coast. Nannup, Pemberton and the Blackwood River have bush and council camps with low fees, and the rest areas on the main roads suit a night in the vehicle.
Our South West camping loop guide links the camps and the drives, and our free camping guide explains how the rules work in Western Australia.

sections.heading: When to go
body: The region is at its best from September to November and from March to May, when it is warm, wildflowers or whales may be out, and the crowds are smaller. December to February is the peak, with warm water and a full coast.
Winter is wet and windy, and good for the wineries and waves.

sections.heading: Plan the South West in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.
Holiday parks and some council camps are not all in the app, so check their own pages for those. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Can you camp for free in Margaret River?

Not in the town or along the coast, where the Shire and Parks and Wildlife rangers sign against it. The region is a paid-camping area, and the cheapest nights are national park campgrounds and low-cost bush camps inland.
Where can you camp near Margaret River?

Leeuwin-Naturaliste National Park has campgrounds such as Conto and Boranup, booked and paid through Parks and Wildlife. Holiday parks in Margaret River, Prevelly and Augusta suit powered sites, and the forests further inland have cheaper bush camps.
Is Margaret River busy in summer?
Very. From December to February and at Easter the region fills with Perth families, so book camps and holiday parks well ahead and look at the shoulder months.
How far is Margaret River from Perth?
About three hours by road, which is why the region is full on Friday evenings. Our Perth to Margaret River drive guide has the route and the stops.

free-camping-exmouth.title: Free Camping Near Exmouth: What to Do When There Is None
free-camping-exmouth.description: Where to camp near Exmouth and Ningaloo: why free camping is banned, Cape Range National Park campgrounds, station stays near Coral Bay, caravan parks and the best time to go.
free-camping-exmouth.imageAlt: A sandy Ningaloo coast beach at sunset, with a low reef offshore and dunes with low scrub behind
free-camping-exmouth.intro: Exmouth and the Ningaloo coast are some of the best camping in Western Australia, and there is no free camping to be had. Rangers patrol the town and the coast, and the Cape Range campgrounds and the stations to the south are booked and paid. The trade is a reef you can snorkel from the beach. Book early, go outside school holidays, and find your free nights on the long drive from Perth.

sections.heading: Why you cannot camp free
body: Ningaloo Reef is a World Heritage area, and the coast gets many more visitors than it has room for. Freedom camping is banned in Exmouth and on the coast, and rangers patrol the car parks and the roadsides, including at night.
Spending the night in a legal camp also protects the reef and the dunes, and the money pays for the rangers and the toilets.

sections.heading: Cape Range National Park
body: The national park on the west side of the peninsula has campgrounds close to the reef, plus Turquoise Bay, Yardie Creek and the snorkelling that Ningaloo is known for. Camping is booked and paid through Parks and Wildlife, and the sites sell out in the dry season.
Facilities are basic, so bring your own water and shade. Fires are not allowed in the park.

sections.heading: Stations and Coral Bay
body: South of Coral Bay, working stations such as Warroora offer paid beach camping on the Ningaloo coast. The roads are long gravel tracks, and a 4WD is a good idea. Coral Bay has caravan parks and a small shop.
Stay on the tracks and pay the fee, because the station and the reef depend on it.

sections.heading: Free nights on the way
body: The long drive from Perth has rest areas and roadhouses where a night in the vehicle is fine and a small fee gets you a camp. Our Perth to Exmouth guide lists the stops, and our free camping guide explains the rules.
Plan fuel and water for each leg, because the towns are far apart.

sections.heading: Seasons and cyclones
body: The best time is April to October. Whale sharks swim from about March to July and humpbacks pass from August to October. Summer is hot, and cyclone season runs from November to April, when roads and parks can close at short notice.
Check the weather warnings before you go and book flexible dates in the shoulder months.

sections.heading: Plan Ningaloo in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.
Station camps and caravan parks are not all in the app, so check their own pages for those. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Can you camp for free in Exmouth?
No. Freedom camping is not allowed in the town or on the Ningaloo coast, and rangers patrol. The cheapest stays are national park and station camps, which are booked and paid.
Where can you camp near Exmouth?

Cape Range National Park has campgrounds along the Ningaloo coast, booked through Parks and Wildlife, and coastal stations such as Warroora offer paid camping south of Coral Bay. Exmouth's caravan parks suit powered sites.
When is the best time to visit Exmouth?

April to October, when it is dry and the water is clear. Whale sharks arrive from about March to July, and humpback whales pass from August to October. Summer is hot and cyclone season runs from November to April.
How far is Exmouth from Perth?
About 1,250 kilometres by road, so most people take two or three days. Our Perth to Exmouth drive guide has the stops.

free-camping-savannah-way.title: Free Camping on the Savannah Way: Cairns to Broome Across the Top End
free-camping-savannah-way.description: How to camp along the Savannah Way from Cairns to Broome: free rest areas and low-cost camps in Queensland, the Northern Territory and the Kimberley, the dry season window and where to carry fuel and water.
free-camping-savannah-way.imageAlt: A giant boab tree inside a low fence at a rest area on the Great Northern Highway in the Kimberley, with red dirt in front of it
free-camping-savannah-way.intro: The Savannah Way is the long road across the top of Australia, from Cairns to Broome through the Gulf Country, Katherine and the Kimberley. It is a good route for free and cheap camping, because there are roadside rest areas, riverside camps and roadhouses all the way, but the rules change across three states and territories and the distances are huge. Go in the dry season, carry water and fuel, and read each sign.

sections.heading: How the route works
body: The Savannah Way is a series of highways: from Cairns inland to the Gulf, across to Katherine, then through the Victoria Highway to Kununurra and along the Great Northern Highway to Broome. It crosses Queensland, the Northern Territory and Western Australia, and the camping rules change with each border.
Most of the main road is sealed, but fuel and water are far apart, so plan each leg.

sections.heading: Queensland: the Gulf Country
body: Between Cairns and the Gulf, towns such as Normanton, Karumba and Georgetown have council camps and caravan parks, and the highways have rest areas where a night in the vehicle is fine. Normanton and Karumba are popular for fishing and sunsets.
The Burke and Wills Camp 119 near Normanton is a free camp with a sign and a history. Check the sign for the stay limit.

sections.heading: The Northern Territory
body: Across the NT, free camping is limited to signed rest areas and some stations and roadhouses. Camping in the open outside those places is not allowed, and fines apply.
Katherine and Timber Creek are the big stops, with caravan parks and the Nitmiluk and Judbarra national parks near by.

sections.heading: The Kimberley and Broome
body: From Kununurra to Broome the camps are mostly paid, at stations, roadhouses and caravan parks. The Great Northern Highway has rest areas, and some are free, but the heat and the distances make a powered site attractive.
Allow time for Kununurra, the Gibb River Road turn off, Fitzroy Crossing and Broome's beaches.

sections.heading: The dry season window
body: Go between May and October. In the wet season floods close roads, camps and roadhouses shut, and temperatures and humidity are extreme. Our wet season camping guide explains the closures and the risks.
Check each state's road conditions before you drive, and keep a few days' spare in your schedule.

sections.heading: Plan the Savannah Way in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.
Roadhouse, station and council camps are not all in the app, so check their own pages for those. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Can you camp for free on the Savannah Way?

In places. The route across Queensland, the Northern Territory and the Kimberley has roadside rest areas and a few free or low-cost camps, but each state sets its own rules and some stretches have none. Look for the sign at each stop.
How long is the Savannah Way?
About 3,700 kilometres from Cairns to Broome, which most people drive over two to three weeks. It crosses the Gulf Country, Katherine and the Kimberley.
When is the Savannah Way open?
The dry season, roughly May to October. In the wet, floods close roads and some sections turn impassable, and many camps and roadhouses shut.
Do I need a 4WD on the Savannah Way?

Much of the route is sealed, so a 2WD campervan can drive the main road. Some side trips, including Lawn Hill and parts of the Gulf Developmental Road, are gravel or 4WD only, and rental conditions often forbid them.

free-camping-queensland-outback.title: Free Camping in the Queensland Outback: How the Rules Work
free-camping-queensland-outback.description: How free and cheap camping works in outback Queensland: council camps, showgrounds, highway rest areas and station stays, what the signs mean and how to plan fuel and water.
free-camping-queensland-outback.imageAlt: A cattle road train driving past a blue and yellow monument on a street in Hughenden, Queensland, on the Flinders Highway
free-camping-queensland-outback.intro: Outback Queensland is one of the friendliest regions in Australia for free and cheap camping. Towns that would like you to stop run council camps, showgrounds and riverside reserves, and the highways have rest areas for one night. The skill is in reading the sign, because each council sets its own limit and some camps ask for a donation or a small fee. Carry water and fuel, travel in the dry season, and spend a night in town to support the pub and the museum.

sections.heading: What types of camp you will find
body: Outback Queensland has four main kinds of stay: council camps on the edge of a town, showgrounds with toilets and showers, highway rest areas, and station stays on working properties. Each has its own rules.
Free is common. Expect basic facilities, a stay limit of one to a few days and a donation box or a small fee at some camps.

sections.heading: Reading the sign
body: A camp sign usually tells you the stay limit, whether you must be self-contained and where the nearest toilets are. Some camps ask for a small donation, which goes to the town. Follow the sign, even if the camp looks empty.
If you are not self-contained, use the town's caravan park or showground, where there are toilets, and keep your waste out of the bush.

sections.heading: Towns worth a night
body: Charleville has the Cosmos Centre for stargazing, Longreach has the Stockman's Hall of Fame and Qantas Founders Museum, Winton has the dinosaur trail and Cloncurry has the Flying Doctor story. All have a camp or a caravan park.
Our Longreach guide and our Queensland Outback Way guide cover the central towns in more detail.

sections.heading: Rest areas and road trains
body: Highway rest areas are for one night in the vehicle. Keep out of truck bays, and do not camp beside the road. Road trains can be 50 metres long and need a lot of room to stop.
Our road trains guide explains how to overtake and how to share the road safely.

sections.heading: Fuel, water and the weather
body: Fill the tank at every town and carry spare water. Between towns the distance can be 200 kilometres or more, and the next station may be closed.
The dry season runs from May to September. Summer storms flood roads and close dirt tracks, so check the council's road report each day.

body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.
Council and showground camps are not all in the app, so check the council page for those. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Can you camp for free in outback Queensland?

Often, yes. Many outback towns run free or low-cost camps for travellers, and roadside rest areas allow a night in the vehicle. The rules are set by each council and the sign at the camp, so check the stay limit.
What are the best free camps in the Queensland outback?
Council camps beside rivers and on the edge of towns, such as those around Charleville, Longreach, Winton and Cloncurry, and the highway rest areas. Our Longreach guide covers the central towns.
Do I need a 4WD in outback Queensland?
Not for the main highways, which are sealed. Dirt side roads become impassable after rain, so a 2WD can reach most towns in the dry season but should not leave the highway.
How much fuel and water do I need?
Fill the tank at every town and carry spare water, at least 10 litres per person per day. Distances between fuel are often 200 kilometres or more.

camping-near-uluru.title: Camping Near Uluru: Where to Stay in and Around the Park
camping-near-uluru.description: Where to camp near Uluru: Ayers Rock Campground at Yulara, roadhouse camps on the Lasseter Highway, why there is no camping in the park and how to plan sunrise and sunset.
camping-near-uluru.imageAlt: A straight sealed stretch of the Lasseter Highway running through red-soil scrub in central Australia, with two 100 km/h signs
camping-near-uluru.intro: Uluru is the one place where you cannot camp for free and rarely want to. Camping inside Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park is not allowed, the only camp in the area is at Yulara, and everything else is a roadhouse an hour or more down the highway. Book your night at Ayers Rock Campground well ahead in the dry season, buy a park pass, and plan the days around sunrise and sunset, the base walk and Kata Tjuta.

sections.heading: Why you cannot camp in the park
body: Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park is owned by the Anangu traditional owners and jointly managed with Parks Australia. Camping, fires and driving off the road are not allowed inside it. Rangers patrol, and the fines are heavy.
The accommodation is at Yulara, a small resort village about 20 kilometres from the rock, so the camp, the shops and the fuel are all in one place.

table.caption: Where to stay for Uluru and what it costs.
head: Where
Cost
Best for
Watch for
rows: Roadhouse camp, about an hour away
A long drive from the rock

sections.heading: Ayers Rock Campground
body: The campground at Yulara has powered and unpowered sites, a pool, a shop and showers, and is the closest place to sleep. It is much cheaper than the resort hotels and fills in the dry season from May to September, so book as early as you can.
Yulara has a supermarket, fuel and a few restaurants, so you do not need to bring everything with you.

sections.heading: Roadhouses on the Lasseter Highway
body: Curtin Springs, Mount Ebenezer and Erldunda are the usual roadhouse stops between Alice Springs and Uluru. Each has camping for a fee, a bar and fuel, and some have a small shop.
They are the easy way to split the drive from Alice Springs, which is about five hours, and to avoid the busy times at Yulara.
tips: Split the drive from Alice Springs

sections.heading: Pass, sunrise and the base walk
body: You need a park pass to enter, valid for several days, which you can buy online or at the gate. Sunrise and sunset viewing areas fill early, so arrive well before the light.
The climb is closed, and the base walk of about 10 kilometres is a great way to see the rock. Start early, carry water, and respect the signs asking you not to photograph some sacred places.
tips: Buy a pass before you go

sections.heading: Heat, flies and the dry season
body: From May to September the days are warm and the nights are cold. In summer temperatures often pass 40 degrees and the walks close in the middle of the day. Carry water, wear a hat and fly net, and start walks at dawn.
The Red Centre is remote. Fuel up at every opportunity and carry spare water.
tips: Carry water and a fly net

sections.heading: Plan the Red Centre in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.
Yulara and roadhouse camps are not all in the app, so check their own pages for those. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Can you camp for free at Uluru?

No. Camping inside Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park is not allowed, and Ayers Rock Resort's campground at Yulara is paid. Free or cheaper options are rest areas and roadhouses on the Lasseter Highway, an hour or more away.
Where can I camp near Uluru?

Ayers Rock Campground at Yulara is the main place, with powered and unpowered sites. Roadhouses along the Lasseter Highway, such as Curtin Springs and Mount Ebenezer, offer camping for a fee and are an easy stop on the way.
Do I need a park pass for Uluru?
Yes. Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park charges an entry pass for visitors, which is valid for several days. Buy it online or at the gate and keep it with you.
Can I climb Uluru?
No. The climb was permanently closed in October 2019 at the request of the Anangu traditional owners. The base walk, which takes a few hours, is the best way to see the rock.

sources.label: Parks Australia: Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park

kgari-fraser-island-camping-permits.title: K'gari (Fraser Island) Camping Permits: What You Need and How to Book
kgari-fraser-island-camping-permits.description: How to camp on K'gari (Fraser Island): vehicle access and camping permits, fenced camps and beach zones, the barge crossings from Hervey Bay and Inskip Point, dingo safety and tide planning.
kgari-fraser-island-camping-permits.imageAlt: Four-wheel drives parked on the sand and tyre tracks on the beach at K'gari (Fraser Island), Queensland
kgari-fraser-island-camping-permits.intro: K'gari, the island formerly known as Fraser Island, is the largest sand island in the world, and one of the best places in Australia for a 4WD camping trip. It is also one of the most regulated. You need a camping permit for every night and a vehicle access permit for your 4WD, both booked before you go, and you can only camp in named zones and campgrounds. Book early, plan the tides, and take the dingo rules seriously.

sections.heading: What permits you need
body: You need two permits to camp on K'gari with a vehicle: a camping permit for each night, and a vehicle access permit for the 4WD. Both are booked through the Queensland parks booking service and paid in advance, and they cost less if you book online before you arrive.
Camping outside a zone or campground is not allowed, and rangers check permits on the beach and at the camps.

table.caption: Permits and camps on K'gari.
head: What
Where
Cost
Watch for

sections.heading: Fenced camps and beach zones
body: Fenced campgrounds such as the one at Central Station are the safest choice if you have children, because they keep dingoes out. They have toilets and water.
Beach camping zones on the east coast are the classic K'gari experience, with the surf at your door, but there are no fences, so food must be locked away and children kept close.

sections.heading: Getting there by barge
body: Vehicle barges cross from River Heads, near Hervey Bay, and from Inskip Point at Rainbow Beach. Book the barge in advance in the school holidays, and check the times against the tide, because the beach is the road.
Rental vehicles are rarely allowed on the island, so check your hire company's rules before you book anything.
tips: Barges from Hervey Bay and Rainbow Beach

sections.heading: Tides, tracks and sand
body: The east coast beach is a highway, but only at low tide. Check the tide table every day, lower your tyre pressure and drive slowly. Sand tracks inland are soft and rutted.
Carry recovery boards, a compressor and a shovel, and tell someone your plan, because phone coverage is patchy.

sections.heading: Dingoes and the rules
body: The dingoes on K'gari are wild and the island's dingo rules are strict. Never feed or approach them, lock food and rubbish in a locked vehicle or container, and keep children within arm's reach.
Fines apply for feeding dingoes, and the island's rangers will move you on if your camp is not safe.

sections.heading: Plan the Fraser Coast in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.
Island camping zones are booked through the Queensland parks service, so use that for permits. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Do I need a permit to camp on K'gari (Fraser Island)?

Yes. You need a camping permit for each night, and a vehicle access permit if you take a vehicle. Book both before you go through the Queensland parks booking service, because camps and permits sell out in the school holidays.
Can you camp for free on K'gari?
No. All camping on the island is permitted and paid, in a named camping zone or campground. Camping outside a zone is not allowed.
Do I need a 4WD on K'gari?
Yes. The island is sand, and only high clearance 4WD vehicles are allowed on the tracks and beach. Rental campervans are not allowed, and many hire companies forbid the barge crossing.
Are the dingoes dangerous?

They are wild and can be dangerous. Never feed them, keep food and rubbish locked away, camp in a fenced area if you have children, and keep children within arm's reach. Fines apply for feeding or approaching them.

dampier-peninsula-cape-leveque-camping.title: Camping on the Dampier Peninsula and at Cape Leveque
dampier-peninsula-cape-leveque-camping.description: How to camp on the Dampier Peninsula north of Broome: community camps at Cape Leveque, Middle Lagoon and Gumbanan, permits, road conditions, the dry season and respectful visiting.
dampier-peninsula-cape-leveque-camping.imageAlt: A giant boab tree inside a low fence at a rest area on the Great Northern Highway in the Kimberley, with red dirt in front of it
dampier-peninsula-cape-leveque-camping.intro: The Dampier Peninsula, north of Broome, has some of the most beautiful camping in the Kimberley, with red cliffs, white sand and turquoise water. It is also Aboriginal land, and the camps are run by the communities that own it. There is no free camping, but the camps are cheap by resort standards and the money goes back to the community. Go in the dry season, book ahead, and travel with respect.

sections.heading: What the peninsula is like
body: The Dampier Peninsula is a long finger of land north of Broome, about a two hour drive to Cape Leveque. The communities of Beagle Bay, Lombadina and Ardyaloon (One Arm Point) have homes, shops and camps, and welcome visitors who follow the rules.
The scenery is the point: pindan red earth, white beaches and clear water, with some of the biggest tides in Australia.

table.caption: Camps on the Dampier Peninsula.
head: Where
Cost
Best for
Watch for

sections.heading: Permits, fees and respect
body: Most camps charge a nightly fee, and some communities ask visitors to buy a permit to enter or to take a tour. Check each camp's own page before you go, and carry cash in case the card machine is down.
Alcohol restrictions apply in some communities. Do not take photos of people without asking, and stay on the roads and the camp.

sections.heading: Roads and vehicles
body: The main road to Cape Leveque is sealed for much of the way, and the dirt sections are graded. The side tracks to Middle Lagoon and Pender Bay are sand, and a high clearance 4WD is the safe choice.
Rental conditions often forbid unsealed roads, so check yours before you book.

sections.heading: Fuel, water and supplies
body: Fuel is available at Broome and at some communities, but not at every camp. Fill up in Broome, carry spare water and buy supplies before you leave.
Mobile signal is patchy outside the communities, so tell someone your plan.

sections.heading: When to go
body: May to October is the dry season, with warm days and cool nights, and it is also when the camps are busiest. In the wet season roads flood, camps shut and the heat is extreme. Our wet season camping guide explains the closures.
Whales pass offshore from July to October, and Cape Leveque is a good lookout.

sections.heading: Plan the Kimberley in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.
Community camps are not all in the app, so check each camp's own page. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Can you camp for free on the Dampier Peninsula?
No. The land is Aboriginal-owned and the camps are run by the communities, so camping is booked and paid. Camping outside a camp or on a beach is not allowed.
Do I need a permit to drive the Dampier Peninsula?
Not for the main road, but some communities and sites ask for a visitor permit or a fee. Check each camp's page and buy any permit before you arrive.
Do I need a 4WD?

The main road to Cape Leveque is much better than it was, but the side tracks to many camps are deep sand, and a high clearance 4WD is the safest choice. A 2WD campervan can reach some camps in the dry season.
When is the best time to go?
May to October, when it is dry. In the wet season, roads flood and camps close, and in the build-up it is extremely hot and humid.

purnululu-bungle-bungles-camping.title: Camping at Purnululu and the Bungle Bungles
purnululu-bungle-bungles-camping.description: How to camp at Purnululu National Park: Walardi and Kurrajong campgrounds, the 53 kilometre 4WD track, bookings, the season, the main walks and how to plan the Kimberley drive.
purnululu-bungle-bungles-camping.intro: Purnululu National Park, home of the Bungle Bungles, is one of the most remarkable places in Western Australia. The striped beehive domes only became widely known in the 1980s, and the park is World Heritage listed. It is also a serious trip: a 53 kilometre 4WD track, a short season and campgrounds that sell out. Book early, bring everything you need and give yourself at least two nights.

sections.heading: Getting there
body: The park is off the Great Northern Highway, about halfway between Kununurra and Halls Creek, roughly 250 kilometres south of Kununurra. The turn off leads to a 53 kilometre track that takes two to three hours, with creek crossings and corrugations.
A high clearance 4WD is needed, and rental campervans are not allowed. Check your tyres and carry spares.
tips: Two to three hours each way

table.caption: Camping and access at Purnululu.
head: What
Where
Cost
Watch for

sections.heading: Camping in the park
body: Walardi and Kurrajong are the two campgrounds, each with basic toilets and no showers. You book through the Parks and Wildlife Service, and sites sell out in the dry season from June to September.
There is no fuel, no shop and no water to buy in the park, so bring everything with you. Pets are not allowed.

sections.heading: The walks
body: Piccaninny Gorge, Echidna Chasm, Cathedral Gorge and the Domes walk are the highlights. Cathedral Gorge is a huge amphitheatre, and Echidna Chasm is a narrow slot with orange walls that glow at midday.
The walks are hot and the sun is strong. Start early, carry plenty of water and take a hat. Scenic flights from the park give a view of the full dome range.

sections.heading: The season
body: The park is open from about April to December, depending on the wet season, and the best months are May to September. In the wet season the track floods and the park closes. Our wet season camping guide explains the closures.
Check the park alerts and the road conditions before you drive in, and allow extra days in case the track is wet.

sections.heading: Supplies and safety
body: Fuel up in Kununurra or Halls Creek and carry spare fuel and water. There is no mobile signal in the park, so tell someone your plan and carry a satellite messenger or a UHF radio if you can.
Travel in a group if you can, and do not leave the marked tracks.

sections.heading: Plan the Kimberley in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.
Remote park camps are best checked on the Parks and Wildlife Service page. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Can you camp at Purnululu National Park?
Yes, at Walardi and Kurrajong campgrounds inside the park. Both are booked and paid through Parks and Wildlife Service, and they sell out in the dry season, so book early.
Do I need a 4WD to get to the Bungle Bungles?
Yes. The 53 kilometre track from the Great Northern Highway is rough and takes two to three hours, with creek crossings. A high clearance 4WD is required, and rental campervans are not allowed.
When is Purnululu open?
Roughly from April to December, depending on the wet season. The track and the park are closed when the roads flood, so check the park alerts before you go.
Can I take my dog to Purnululu?
No. Pets are not allowed in the park, which is a World Heritage area and a key wildlife refuge.

how-to-change-a-tyre-campervan-australia.title: How to Change a Tyre on a Campervan in Australia
how-to-change-a-tyre-campervan-australia.description: A flat tyre in a hire campervan is common on long outback roads. Check the spare before you leave, know when to call the hire company, and follow the steps to change a wheel safely.
how-to-change-a-tyre-campervan-australia.imageAlt: A campervan parked beside a rural road in Australia
how-to-change-a-tyre-campervan-australia.intro: Flat tyres are one of the most common problems on a long Australian road trip, and the next town can be a long way off. Most hire companies run a roadside assistance line, and that is the first call, but it helps to know where the spare is, how to use it and when to stop and wait for help. Below are the checks to make at pick-up and the steps for changing a wheel safely.

sections.heading: Check the spare before you leave
body: Do this at pick-up, not on the side of the road. Find the spare, the jack, the wheel brace and the locking wheel nut key if the van has one, and make sure the spare has air in it. Ask the hire company where each item is stored, because it varies from van to van, and ask who to call and what the policy is for tyres.

Check the tyre pressures on the placard in the door jamb and keep an eye on them on long hot days. Under-inflated tyres wear faster and are more likely to fail. If the vehicle is a 4WD that will go on gravel, ask whether it carries one spare or two.
tips: Find the spare, jack and wheel brace

sections.heading: When to call for help instead
body: If you are on a busy highway, on a bend or hill with no safe place to stop, on soft ground, or the van is heavy and loaded, call roadside assistance rather than changing the wheel yourself. If a nut is stuck, the jack will not lift the van or you do not feel confident, the same applies.

Out of mobile range, stay with the van, because it is easier to find than a person on foot, and flag down a passing vehicle if you need help. The no phone signal guide covers how to prepare for the long stretches without coverage.
tips: Call if the roadside is unsafe
Stay with the van if there is no signal
Never crawl under a van held up by a jack

sections.heading: Steps to change a wheel
body: Pull well off the road onto firm, flat ground, turn on the hazard lights, put the handbrake on, select park or first gear and have everyone wait well away from traffic. Put something under the wheel on the opposite corner so the van cannot roll. Loosen the wheel nuts about a half turn while the wheel is on the ground, then raise the van with the jack at the jacking point marked in the manual until the tyre is clear of the ground.

Remove the nuts, take off the wheel, fit the spare, hand-tighten the nuts in a star pattern, lower the van and then tighten them fully with the brace. Check the nuts again after the first 50 to 100 km. Keep the flat tyre, and tell the hire company as soon as you can.
tips: Check the nuts after 50 to 100 km

sections.heading: After the change
body: Drive carefully on a space-saver spare, keep to the speed printed on the wheel, which is usually about 80 km/h, and get the tyre repaired or replaced at the next town. Many hire agreements treat tyres as an exclusion, so call the company before you pay a bill and keep the receipt.
The campervan driving safety guide covers the rest of the daily checks, and the hire cost guide explains what the excess and the extras cover.
tips: Keep to the spare's speed limit
Call the hire company before paying

sections.heading: Plan the route in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities those sources publish. Build the trip as ordered stops and it shows the distance and drive time for each leg, which helps you see how far apart towns are before a long stretch.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: Do I have to change a flat tyre myself in a hire campervan?

Not always. Most hire companies run a roadside assistance line, and some will send help or tell you to use a local tyre shop. Read your rental agreement before you leave, because tyre damage is often not covered by the basic insurance and you may have to pay for the repair or replacement yourself.
Where is the spare tyre in a campervan?

It depends on the vehicle. It can be under the rear of the van, on a rack on the back door, inside a cargo area or under the floor. Ask at pick-up, and check that the jack, the wheel brace and the locking wheel nut key, if there is one, are on board.
How fast can I drive on a space-saver spare?

A temporary space-saver spare usually has a speed limit of about 80 km/h printed on the wheel or in the manual. Keep to it, avoid long distances and get the proper tyre repaired or replaced at the next town.
How do I loosen wheel nuts that are too tight?

Loosen them while the wheel is still on the ground, using the wheel brace and your body weight on the handle. If a nut will not move, call roadside assistance rather than risk rounding it off or hurting yourself.

hit-a-kangaroo-what-to-do-australia.title: What to Do If You Hit a Kangaroo in Australia
hit-a-kangaroo-what-to-do-australia.description: Kangaroo strikes are common on country roads at dawn and dusk. What to do straight after a collision, who to call, how it affects hire insurance, and how to reduce the risk.
hit-a-kangaroo-what-to-do-australia.imageAlt: Camel, wombat and kangaroo warning signs at Border Village on the Eyre Highway
hit-a-kangaroo-what-to-do-australia.intro: Kangaroos are most active around dawn and dusk, and a collision on a country road is one of the most common ways for a hire campervan to be damaged. If it happens, the first jobs are safety, then the hire company, then the animal. Below are the steps to follow straight after a strike, and the ways to reduce the chance of one in the first place.

sections.heading: Right after the collision
body: Slow down, pull off the road if you can and put the hazard lights on. Check that everyone is unhurt, and call 000 if anyone is injured or if the van is blocking the road. If the van is on a bend or over a crest, get people out and well away from traffic before you do anything else.

Look at the van for leaks, a bent bumper over a tyre, broken lights or a radiator that is steaming. If the van is not safe to drive, do not drive it, and call roadside assistance. Take photos of the damage and the scene, and note the time, the road and the nearest town.
tips: Call 000 for injuries or a blocked road
Photograph the damage and the scene

sections.heading: Call the hire company
body: The rental agreement sets out what you must do after an incident, and the hire company will tell you whether the van is safe to continue, who will repair it and what is covered. Many policies treat animal strikes differently from other collisions, and some exclude them or charge a higher excess, so call early and keep the photos and any paperwork.
The hire insurance and excess guide explains the usual exclusions, and the campervan hire cost guide explains what the extras cover.

sections.heading: The animal
body: Do not approach an injured kangaroo, because they kick and scratch and can hurt you badly. Call the wildlife rescue group for the state you are in, or the RSPCA, and tell them where the animal is and what you can see. If a female has been killed, tell the rescuer, because a joey may be in the pouch and a trained carer can check it.
If an animal is dead on the road and is a hazard, report it to the local council or the road authority, or to the police on the non-emergency line, so it can be moved.
tips: Do not touch an injured animal
Call wildlife rescue or the RSPCA

sections.heading: How to reduce the risk
body: Avoid driving at dawn, dusk and at night, and stop for the day while it is still light. The risk is highest on country roads after rain, when green grass pulls kangaroos towards the verge, and when you see one, expect more nearby. Slow down in areas with warning signs.

If an animal runs out, brake firmly and stay in your lane. Swerving at speed is more dangerous than hitting the animal. The fatigue and wildlife guide covers the rest of the daily habits that keep a long drive safe.
tips: Be off the road before dusk

sections.heading: Plan the day in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities those sources publish. Build the trip as ordered stops and it shows the distance and drive time for each leg, so you can plan to be at the next camp before dusk.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: What should I do if I hit a kangaroo in a hire campervan?

Slow down and stop in a safe place, turn on the hazard lights and check that everyone is unhurt. Call 000 if anyone is injured or the vehicle is blocking the road. Photograph the damage and the scene, then call the hire company as soon as you can, because the rental agreement sets out how to report an incident.
Should I swerve to miss a kangaroo?

No. Brake firmly and stay in your lane. Swerving at speed is how many serious crashes happen, because the van can roll or cross into oncoming traffic. A collision with an animal at a lower speed is usually less dangerous than a rollover.
When are kangaroos most active on the road?

At dawn and dusk and through the night, especially on country roads after rain when roadside grass is green. Many hire companies advise against driving at these times, and it is the simplest way to avoid a collision.
Who do I call about an injured kangaroo?

Call the wildlife rescue group for the state you are in, or the RSPCA. Do not approach an injured animal, because kangaroos can kick and scratch. Tell the rescuer where the animal is and, if you can see it, whether a pouch is visible, and let a trained carer handle the animal.

long-distance-driving-tips-australia.title: Long-Distance Driving Tips for Australia: Distances, Rests and Fuel
long-distance-driving-tips-australia.description: Australia is big, and a campervan trip often means long days behind the wheel. How far to drive in a day, when to stop, how to plan fuel and water, and how to stay alert.
long-distance-driving-tips-australia.imageAlt: The Eyre Highway running straight across the Nullarbor Plain
long-distance-driving-tips-australia.intro: Australia is big, and a campervan trip often involves days where the road runs straight for hours. The trick is to plan shorter days than the map suggests, stop often, fill up whenever you can and arrive before dark. Below are the habits that make long-distance driving safer and more enjoyable, from daily distances to fuel gaps and sleep.

sections.heading: Plan shorter days than the map suggests
body: A distance that looks easy on a map often takes longer once you add stops, speed limits, road works, towns and traffic. Four to five hours of driving, or about 250 to 400 km, is a comfortable day in a campervan, and it leaves time to set up camp, cook and enjoy the stop.

Check each leg for the next fuel stop, the next town and the next place to camp, and plan to arrive in daylight. The east coast, the Nullarbor and the Red Centre all have long distances between places, so allow extra time on those routes.
tips: 250 to 400 km is a comfortable day
Leave time to enjoy the stops

sections.heading: Stop often and stay alert
body: Fatigue is a major cause of crashes on long straight roads. Stop at least every two hours at a rest area, roadhouse or town, walk around, drink water and swap drivers if you can. If you feel drowsy, stop and rest, rather than pushing on to the next sign.
Rest areas along the highways are set up for this, and many have toilets, tables and shade. The fatigue and wildlife guide covers the signs of tiredness and how to deal with them.
tips: Stop at least every two hours
Pull over if you feel drowsy

sections.heading: Fuel, water and food
body: In remote country the next fuel can be 200 km or more away, so fill up whenever you can and do not wait for the gauge to drop. Carry more water than you think you need, enough food for a day or two, and a first aid kit. Roadhouses sell fuel, food and often a bed or a camp spot, but they have limited hours.
The fuel planning guide covers range, jerry cans and fuel gaps, and the water planning guide covers how much to carry.

sections.heading: Other road users and conditions
body: On long routes you will share the road with road trains, caravans and trucks. Give them room, do not overtake on a hill or a bend and be ready for dust, glare and crosswinds. Overtaking a road train takes a long distance, so be patient and wait for a clear stretch.
Wildlife is most active at dawn and dusk, so keep your driving to daylight, and be ready for sudden weather changes, floods and fire in the right season.
tips: Stay off the road at dusk

sections.heading: Plan the route in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities those sources publish.
