Add a stop to break a long day

faq: How far should I drive in a day in Australia?

Most campervan travellers plan between 250 and 400 km a day, or about four to five hours behind the wheel, and leave time to stop. Distances look short on a map but roads, speed limits, road works and fuel stops add time, and the best trips leave room for a swim, a lookout or a late start.
How often should I stop on a long drive?
At least every two hours, and sooner if you feel tired. Rest areas and roadhouses are spaced along the major highways for this, and a short walk, a drink and a stretch does more than coffee.
How far apart are fuel stops in the outback?

On the Nullarbor, Eyre Highway roadhouses can be up to about 190 km apart, and some northern and central routes have gaps of 200 km or more. Fill up whenever you can in remote country and carry water.
What is the speed limit on Australian highways?

It varies by state and road. Most national highways are 100 or 110 km/h, and a few sections in the Northern Territory allow 130 km/h. Hire campervans are often slower than that, and some hire companies set their own limits, so read your agreement and keep to the posted limit.

4wd-basics-hire-vehicles-australia.title: 4WD Basics for Hire Vehicles in Australia: Sand, Dirt and Water
4wd-basics-hire-vehicles-australia.description: The basics of driving a hire 4WD in Australia: what your rental agreement allows, how to drive on sand and corrugations, river crossings, recovery gear and when to turn back.
4wd-basics-hire-vehicles-australia.imageAlt: A four-wheel-drive camper with a pop-top roof parked at a bush campsite in the northern Flinders Ranges
4wd-basics-hire-vehicles-australia.intro: A hire 4WD opens up beaches, gorges and outback tracks that a two-wheel-drive van cannot reach, but it also carries rules and risks of its own. The first thing is the rental agreement, which sets where you can drive, and the second is the technique for the surface. Below are the basics for sand, dirt, corrugations and water, plus the gear and the habits that keep a remote trip safe.

sections.heading: Read the rental agreement first
body: Hire companies set limits on where a vehicle can go, and the limits are usually listed in the agreement. Many ban unsealed roads, beaches, river crossings and some named tracks, and some 4WD hire companies allow all of them with the right insurance. Driving where the agreement forbids can void the insurance and leave you liable for the full cost of damage and recovery.

Ask at pick-up whether the vehicle has low range, how many spare tyres it carries, whether it has recovery gear and whether tyre and underbody damage is covered. The 2WD campervan guide covers the same question for vans without 4WD.
tips: Ask what gear is on board

sections.heading: Driving on dirt and corrugations
body: On a gravel or dirt road, slow down, keep the steering light and give other vehicles plenty of room, because stones and dust reduce grip and visibility. Corrugations are ridges across the road that can shake a vehicle apart, and a steady moderate speed usually handles them better than going very slowly or very fast.
After rain, clay roads can turn slippery or close. Check road conditions with the local council, park or shire before you go, and be ready to turn back if the road is closed or flooded.
tips: Hold a steady speed on corrugations
Check road conditions before you go

sections.heading: Sand and beach driving
body: Soft sand needs momentum and light, smooth inputs, so avoid sudden braking and steering, and drive in the tracks of other vehicles. Lowering the tyre pressure improves traction, but only do it if the hire company allows it and you can pump the tyres up again afterwards.

Beaches have tides, and some need a permit, so plan around the tide and keep clear of the water's edge. The beach driving guide covers the rules, and K'gari and other sand islands have their own permits.

sections.heading: Water crossings and recovery
body: Never cross water you cannot see the bottom of. Walk it first if it is safe to do so, check the depth and the current, and look out for crocodiles in the north. A deep or fast crossing can wreck the engine and is rarely covered by insurance. If in doubt, turn back or wait for the water to drop.

Carry recovery tracks, a shovel and a way to call for help, and tell someone your route. Out of mobile range, a satellite messenger or satellite phone is the safest backup, and the no phone signal guide covers the options.
tips: Never cross water you cannot see

sections.heading: Plan the route in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities those sources publish. Build a trip as ordered stops and it shows the distance, drive time and forecast for each leg, so you can plan fuel and camps along a remote route.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.
tips: Plan fuel and camps along the route

faq: Can I take a hire 4WD off the sealed road in Australia?

Only if the rental agreement allows it. Many hire companies restrict where their vehicles can go, and some ban unsealed roads, beaches and river crossings entirely. Driving where the agreement says you must not can void the insurance and leave you liable for the full cost of damage and recovery.
What is low range in a 4WD?

Low range is a lower gear set that gives more engine braking and control at slow speed, and it is used for steep tracks, deep sand and difficult climbs and descents. For most dirt roads and beach driving, high range 4WD is enough.
Should I let the tyres down on sand?

Lowering tyre pressure improves traction on soft sand and corrugations, but check the hire company's rules first, and re-inflate before you return to the sealed road. A compressor or a pump is needed to put the air back.
What should I carry on a remote 4WD track?

Extra water, food, a first aid kit, a spare tyre or two, a shovel, recovery tracks and a way to call for help such as a satellite messenger or a hired satellite phone. Tell someone your route and when you expect to arrive.

solar-power-for-campers-australia.title: Solar Power for Campers in Australia: Panels, Batteries and Free Camps
solar-power-for-campers-australia.description: How solar works on a campervan: the panel, the battery, the controller and the loads, how much power a fridge needs, and how to camp for days away from a powered site.
solar-power-for-campers-australia.imageAlt: Caravans and tents under trees and palms at the Eighty Mile Beach caravan park on the north-west coast of Western Australia
solar-power-for-campers-australia.intro: Solar power is what lets a campervan stay away from powered sites for days, and Australia has plenty of sun for it. A panel on the roof charges a battery, the battery runs the fridge, the lights and the phone chargers, and a controller keeps it all safe. Below is how the pieces fit together, how much power you really use and what to check if you hire or buy a van with solar.

sections.heading: How a campervan solar set-up works
body: A solar panel makes electricity from sunlight. A charge controller sits between the panel and the battery and stops it overcharging, and the battery stores the power for the fridge, the lights, the pump and the phone chargers. Most vans also charge the house battery from the engine while you drive, using a DC to DC charger or a simpler link, and from mains power at a powered site.

An inverter turns the battery's 12 volt power into 240 volt for a laptop or a small appliance, but it uses power too, so run it only when needed. Large heaters, kettles and air conditioners are not realistic loads for a small solar system.
tips: Engine and mains also charge the battery

sections.heading: How much power do you use
body: The fridge is the biggest daily load in most vans, followed by lights, a water pump, phones and a laptop. A 12 volt compressor fridge cycles on and off, and it uses more in hot weather and when it is full or opened often. A roof panel of about 100 to 200 watts with a modest battery is a common set-up for a fridge and the small loads.

Add up what you use in a day, and then see how many days the battery lasts without sun. If it falls short, drive for an hour, move to a powered site or add battery capacity. If you are not sure, ask the hire company or the seller for the battery size and the panel rating.
tips: The fridge is the main load
Check battery size and panel rating

sections.heading: Camping with solar
body: Solar makes free camps, rest areas and national park campgrounds practical, because you do not need a power post. Park in the sun to charge, angle the van if you can and keep the panel clear of dust and leaves. Shade from trees cuts the output, and a few cloudy days can run the battery low.

Many campgrounds ban generators, which makes solar the quieter and more widely allowed option. The generator guide covers the rules by state, and the powered and unpowered sites guide covers when it is worth paying for a powered site.
tips: Solar is quiet and widely allowed

sections.heading: If you hire or buy a van
body: Ask whether the van has solar, what the battery size is and how long the fridge runs without hook-up. If you are buying, ask for the details of the install and the age of the battery, because batteries wear out and are one of the costlier items to replace.
The buying a campervan guide covers the checks for a used van, and the campervan hire cost guide explains what the extras cover.
tips: Ask about battery size and age
Know how long the fridge lasts

sections.heading: Plan the route in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities those sources publish. Build a trip as ordered stops and it shows the distance, drive time and forecast for each leg, which helps when you want sunny days for solar and a powered site when the forecast turns cloudy.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.
tips: Check the forecast for each stop

faq: Do hire campervans in Australia have solar panels?

Some do and many do not. Most hire vans run their fridge and lights from a house battery that charges from the engine while you drive and from a mains lead at a powered site. Ask the hire company how the van charges and how long the battery lasts.
How much solar do I need for a campervan fridge?

A 12 volt compressor fridge is the biggest daily load in most vans. A panel of roughly 100 to 200 watts on the roof, with a good battery and a controller, is a common set-up for a fridge, lights and phone charging, and Australian sun makes it work well. Your own needs depend on the fridge, the battery and the weather.
Will solar work on a cloudy day?
Yes, but at a much lower output. A few cloudy days in a row can flatten a small battery, so park in the sun when you can, drive for an hour to charge from the engine or move to a powered site.
Can I use a generator instead of solar?
Only where the campground allows it. Many national parks and quiet camps ban generators, so solar is the more flexible option. The generator guide covers the rules by state.

easy-campervan-meals-australia.title: Easy Campervan Meals in Australia: Simple Cooking on the Road
easy-campervan-meals-australia.description: Easy meals to cook in a campervan with one burner, how to shop and store food on a road trip, free barbecues, and what to check about fire bans and border rules.
easy-campervan-meals-australia.imageAlt: A tent, sleeping bag and backpack at an Australian campground
easy-campervan-meals-australia.intro: Cooking in a campervan is simpler than it sounds. A gas burner, a couple of pans and a small fridge are enough for most meals, and the best ones use one pot and few ingredients. Below are easy meals for breakfast, lunch and dinner, how to shop and store food on the road, and what to check about fire bans and fresh produce at state borders.

sections.heading: Simple meals for one burner
body: Breakfast can be eggs and toast, porridge or yoghurt with fruit. Lunch is often wraps, sandwiches or a salad made at a rest area, with tuna, cheese or cold meat. Dinner is where one-pot meals shine: pasta with a jar sauce, rice with a stir fry, a curry from a pack, tacos or sausages in bread with salad.

Pick food that keeps without much fridge space, such as eggs, hard cheese, cabbage, carrots, tinned fish, rice, pasta and wraps, and add fresh food when you pass a town. Cooking once and eating twice saves gas and time.

sections.heading: Shopping and storing food
body: Coles, Woolworths and ALDI are in most large towns, and IGA and smaller stores in country towns. Prices rise and the range shrinks in remote country, so stock up before long stretches. The grocery prices guide gives an idea of what a basket costs.

Keep the fridge organised, with raw meat at the bottom in a sealed container, and use the freshest food first. In hot weather, buy ice or frozen items in the last town. Keep a bag for rubbish and take it to a bin at the next town or campground.

sections.heading: Barbecues, fire bans and borders
body: Many parks, rest areas and holiday parks have free or coin-operated barbecues, and cooking on them is a cheap and social way to eat. Campfires are only allowed in some places and never on total fire ban days, and the campfire guide covers the rules by state.
Some states restrict fresh fruit, vegetables and honey at the border, with Western Australia and South Australia the strictest. The biosecurity guide covers what to eat or leave before you cross.
tips: No fires on total fire ban days
Check border rules for fresh produce

sections.heading: Water, washing up and waste
body: Plan how much drinking and washing water you carry, and keep wash water away from creeks and lakes. At free camps and rest areas, take all rubbish and food scraps out and do not feed wildlife. Dump points are where you empty a grey water tank or cassette.
The water planning guide covers how much to carry, and the dump points guide covers where to empty.
tips: Do not wash up in a creek

sections.heading: Plan the route in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities those sources publish, including toilets and barbecues where the source lists them. Build a trip as ordered stops and it shows the distance, drive time and forecast for each leg.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: What are easy meals to cook in a campervan?

One-pot dishes work best: pasta with a jar sauce, rice with a stir fry, curry from a pack with rice, eggs and toast, tacos, wraps and sausages with salad. Choose food that keeps without much fridge space and cooks on a single burner.
Where can I buy groceries on a road trip in Australia?
Coles, Woolworths and ALDI are in most large towns, and IGA and smaller stores in country towns. Prices rise and the range shrinks in remote country, so stock up before long stretches.
Can I take fresh food across state borders?

Some states restrict fresh fruit, vegetables and honey, and Western Australia and South Australia are the strictest. Check the rules for your route and eat the produce before you cross, or leave it in the bins provided.
Can I cook on an open fire?
Only where it is allowed, and not on total fire ban days. A gas burner or a camp stove is the simplest option, and free electric or gas barbecues are provided at many parks and rest areas.

best-campervan-for-backpackers-australia.title: Best Campervan for Backpackers in Australia: Types, Costs and What to Check
best-campervan-for-backpackers-australia.description: How backpackers choose a campervan in Australia: small vans and wagons, what to check on the rental, whether to hire or buy, and the extras that matter on a budget trip.
best-campervan-for-backpackers-australia.imageAlt: A campervan parked near Noosa Heads on the Queensland coast
best-campervan-for-backpackers-australia.intro: For a backpacker on a budget, the best campervan is usually the smallest one that lets you sleep and cook comfortably. Small two-berth vans, converted wagons and minivans are cheap to hire, easy to drive and cheap to fuel, and they work for most east coast routes. Below are the types to consider, the checks to make and the choice between hiring and buying.

sections.heading: Small vans and wagons
body: A two-berth van, a converted wagon or a minivan is the usual backpacker choice. These vehicles have a bed, often a small kitchen, and are cheaper to hire and run than a full motorhome. They fit in ordinary car parks, handle city streets and need less fuel on long drives.

If you are three or four people, or travelling for months, a bigger van or a motorhome gives more room, but costs more to hire and to fuel. Hire companies publish vehicle types, daily rates and what each one sleeps.

sections.heading: What to check before you book
body: Check what the daily rate includes, because insurance, kilometres, bedding, a kitchen kit and extras vary. Look at the excess, the one-way fee and the bond, and read the rules for unsealed roads and for drivers under 25. Make sure the van has what you need to camp for a few days, such as a fridge, a stove, a water container and a way to charge your phone.
The hire cost guide covers typical prices and the extras, and the first campervan trip guide covers the first days. If you are on a working holiday, see the working holiday budget guide.
tips: Read the age and road rules
Check the cooking and fridge kit

sections.heading: Hire or buy
body: For a few weeks, hire is simple, because the vehicle is checked, insured and supported by a roadside service. For several months, buying can cost less overall, but you take on repairs, registration, insurance and the work of selling it at the end. The buying a campervan guide covers the checks and the paperwork.
A good plan for a short trip is to hire a small van on the east coast and spend your nights at holiday parks and free camps with toilets and showers.
tips: Budget for repairs if you buy

sections.heading: Camps that suit backpackers
body: Holiday parks and caravan parks have showers, kitchens and laundries, and often a powered site, which is useful on a small van. Free camps and rest areas are cheaper, but check the local rules and whether toilets are on site. Mixing the two, with a free camp most nights and a holiday park every few, keeps costs down and gives you showers and laundry.
The caravan park and holiday park guide compares them, and the free camping legality guide covers where you can stay for free.
tips: Mix free camps and holiday parks
Use parks for laundry and showers

sections.heading: Plan the trip in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities those sources publish. Build a trip as ordered stops and it shows the distance, drive time and forecast for each leg, which helps a backpacker plan fuel and nights on a budget.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.
tips: Plan each leg's distance and time

faq: What is the best campervan for backpackers in Australia?

For one or two people on a budget, a small two-berth van or a converted station wagon or minivan is the usual choice: it is cheap to hire, easy to drive and cheap to fuel. Larger vans suit groups or longer trips, and the best pick depends on how many people, how long and how much you want to do on unsealed roads.
Do I need a self-contained campervan?

Not in Australia, where most camps and holiday parks have toilets and showers, but a van with a fridge, a stove and a sink makes free camping and long trips far easier. Check whether the van has a toilet if you plan to camp away from facilities.
Should I hire or buy as a backpacker?

Hire is simpler for a few weeks, because the vehicle is checked and insured. Buying can cost less over several months, but you take on repairs, registration and the work of selling it. The hire and buying guides compare the costs.
Can backpackers under 25 hire a campervan?
Many companies hire to drivers aged 21 or older, and some add a young driver fee or a higher excess for under 25s. Check the age rules and the extra costs before you book.

campervan-hire-insurance-excess-australi.title: Campervan Hire Insurance and Excess in Australia: What Is Covered
campervan-hire-insurance-excess-australi.description: Campervan hire insurance in Australia explained: what the standard cover includes, how the excess and bond work, what is usually excluded, and how to reduce the risk of a big bill.
campervan-hire-insurance-excess-australi.imageAlt: A remote stretch of the Anne Beadell Highway in the Australian outback
campervan-hire-insurance-excess-australi.intro: The hire price of a campervan is only part of the cost. The excess, the amount you pay towards any damage claim, is often several thousand dollars, and a list of exclusions can leave you paying the full bill for things like tyres, glass or a mistake on a dirt road. Below is how hire insurance usually works, what to look for in the agreement and how to reduce the risk of a big bill.

sections.heading: What standard cover includes
body: Hire companies include basic insurance in the price, covering the vehicle and third-party damage up to a limit, subject to an excess. Compulsory third party insurance for injury is part of the vehicle registration in each state, and it is separate from the hire company's cover.
The agreement lists the terms: the excess, who can drive, where you can drive, what is excluded and what you must do after an accident. Read it before you pay, not at the counter.
tips: Read the agreement before you pay

sections.heading: The excess and the bond
body: The excess is what you pay if the van is damaged, and the company usually holds an amount on your credit card as a bond, released when you return the van undamaged. Standard excess is often several thousand dollars, so a small mistake such as a scraped panel can be a large bill.

Most companies sell an excess reduction option, charged per day, that cuts the excess to a few hundred dollars or to zero. Compare the total over your trip with the saving, and check that the reduction covers the things you worry about, because many exclusions apply even with it.
tips: Excess is often thousands of dollars
The bond is held on your card

sections.heading: Common exclusions
body: Typical exclusions include tyres and wheels, windscreens and glass, the underbody, the roof and overhead damage, driving on unsealed roads, beaches or river crossings that the agreement does not allow, water damage, putting in the wrong fuel, driving after drinking and breaking the agreement. Some animal strikes are excluded or carry a higher excess.
The kangaroo guide covers what to do after an animal strike, the 4WD guide covers where you may drive, and the tyre guide covers flat tyres, which are often an exclusion.

sections.heading: Ways to reduce the risk
body: Walk around the van at pick-up and photograph every scratch and dent, and again at drop-off. Know the van's height and watch for low clearances at car parks, drive-throughs and service stations. Check whether it takes petrol or diesel before you fill up, and keep to the roads the agreement allows.

Travel insurance can cover your own medical costs, cancellations and belongings, and some policies cover rental excess, but read the product disclosure statement. Third-party excess cover may cost less than the hire company's reduction.
tips: Photograph the van at pick-up and drop-off

sections.heading: Plan the route in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities those sources publish. Build a trip as ordered stops and it shows the distance, drive time and forecast for each leg, so you can plan daylight driving and avoid the long, tired days where mistakes happen.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: What is the excess on a campervan hire in Australia?

The excess is the amount you pay towards a damage claim before the hire company covers the rest. On standard cover it is often several thousand dollars, and the company usually holds it on your card as a bond. Check the exact amount in the agreement before you book.
Can I reduce the excess?

Most hire companies offer a daily fee that cuts the excess to a few hundred dollars or to zero, and some offer a separate package. Compare the total cost over your hire period with the saving it buys.
What does hire insurance usually not cover?

Common exclusions include tyres, windscreens, the underbody and roof, damage on unsealed roads or beaches, water damage, a wrong fuel type, driving under the influence and breaches of the agreement. Always read the list for your hire company.
Do I need extra travel insurance for a campervan trip?

Hire insurance covers the vehicle and third parties, not you, your luggage or your trip. Travel insurance covers medical costs, cancellations and belongings, and some policies cover rental excess, so check the product disclosure statement.

solo-campervan-travel-australia.title: Solo Campervan Travel in Australia: Safety, Camps and Staying in Touch
solo-campervan-travel-australia.description: Travelling alone in a campervan in Australia: where to camp, how to stay safe and in touch, what to do about fatigue and remote roads, and how to meet people on the way.
solo-campervan-travel-australia.imageAlt: Glass House Mountains on the Sunshine Coast, Queensland
solo-campervan-travel-australia.intro: Plenty of people travel Australia alone in a campervan, and it can be a great way to see the country at your own pace. The risks are mostly the ordinary ones of a long road trip, tiredness, wildlife and remote roads, and a few habits help with the rest. Below are where to camp, how to stay in touch and how to look after yourself on your own.

sections.heading: Where to camp on your own
body: For the first nights, holiday parks and busy campgrounds are the easiest choice, with other people, lights, showers and a manager on site. Free camps and rest areas are fine too, but pick ones where other vehicles are parked, arrive before dark and leave if the place does not feel right.

Trust your instincts. If a spot feels wrong, drive on, and have a second option in mind. The choosing a campsite guide covers what to look for, and the city sleeping guide covers where you cannot stay.
tips: Drive on if it feels wrong

sections.heading: Staying in touch
body: Tell someone your route and when you will next check in, share your phone location with them and message at set times. Much of the outback and many national parks have no mobile signal, so tell them when you will next be in range, and what to do if you are late.
On remote routes, a satellite messenger or satellite phone is worth carrying. The no phone signal guide covers the options. In an emergency, call 000, or 112 from a mobile phone.
tips: Share your route and check-in times
Expect no signal in remote areas

sections.heading: Safety on the road and at camp
body: The biggest risk on a solo trip is fatigue, because there is nobody to swap with. Drive shorter days, stop every two hours and avoid dawn and dusk when wildlife is active. Keep the van locked when you are away from it, keep valuables out of sight and keep fuel, water and a charged phone on hand.
At camp, keep the doors locked at night and park with your exit clear, and carry a torch. The fatigue and wildlife guide covers the daily habits for long drives.
tips: Lock the van and hide valuables
Keep fuel, water and a charged phone

sections.heading: Meeting people and looking after yourself
body: Camping alone does not mean being lonely. Holiday parks have shared kitchens and barbecues, many campgrounds are friendly and tours and walks are a good way to meet people. Plan some rest days and some company, and keep a few nights in a town between the remote stretches.
Look after the basics: eat properly, drink water, rest when you are tired and carry a first aid kit. A small trip plan helps you see the long days coming.

sections.heading: Plan the trip in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities those sources publish. Build a trip as ordered stops and it shows the distance, drive time and forecast for each leg, so you can plan daylight arrivals and see how far apart the stops are.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: Is it safe to travel solo in a campervan in Australia?

Many people do, and most trips go without trouble. The main risks are the same as for any road trip: fatigue, wildlife, remote roads and heat. Sensible habits such as telling someone your plans, choosing camps in daylight and keeping the van locked help with the rest.
Where should a solo traveller camp?

Holiday parks and busy campgrounds are the easiest places to start, because there are other people, lights and facilities. Rest areas and free camps are fine too, but pick ones with other vehicles and arrive before dark.
How do I stay in touch on a solo trip?

Share your route and a check-in time with someone, share your phone location and message at set times. In areas without signal, tell them when you will next be in range, and carry a satellite messenger on remote routes.
What number do I call in an emergency?

Call 000 from any phone in Australia. If you have no signal on your own network, 112 from a mobile phone can connect through any available network. Out of range, you need a satellite device or help from a passing vehicle.

waterfalls-with-campsites-australia.title: Waterfalls With Campsites in Australia: Where to Camp Near a Waterfall
waterfalls-with-campsites-australia.description: Camping near waterfalls in Australia, from Litchfield and Kakadu to the Kimberley, Queensland and Tasmania: when the falls run, what to book and how to stay safe at a waterhole.
waterfalls-with-campsites-australia.imageAlt: Florence Falls in Litchfield National Park, Northern Territory
waterfalls-with-campsites-australia.intro: A campsite within walking distance of a waterfall is one of the best things about a road trip, and Australia has a handful of them, from the Top End to Tasmania. The falls run strongest at different times in different regions, and some camps are only open in the dry season. Below are the places to start, when to go and what to check before you swim.

sections.heading: Top End: Litchfield and Kakadu
body: Litchfield National Park has campgrounds near Florence Falls and Wangi Falls, plus Walker Creek, and Kakadu has Gunlom Falls and the Maguk camping area. The dry season, from about May to September, is the main time to visit, with the falls running but swimming open and roads passable, and some places need booking or a fee.
Swimming rules change with the season, and crocodile checks may close waterholes, so read the park signs. The Darwin, Kakadu and Litchfield loop guide covers the route.
tips: Dry season is the main window

sections.heading: The Kimberley and the north-west
body: Bell Gorge has a campground at Silent Grove, and Manning Gorge has a camp at Mount Barnett Roadhouse, both on the Gibb River Road. The road is unsealed and closes in the wet season, so go in the dry season, and check your hire agreement before taking a vehicle there.
The Gibb River Road guide covers the route, the gorges and the camps.
tips: Gibb River Road closes in the wet

sections.heading: Queensland and New South Wales
body: In Queensland, Wallaman Falls near Ingham drops about 268 metres and has a small campground near the lookout, and Lamington National Park in the Gold Coast hinterland has camping at Binna Burra with rainforest walks to waterfalls. In New South Wales, Oxley Wild Rivers National Park has campgrounds near Apsley Falls and Wollomombi Falls.
Check each park's website for closures after rain and fire, and whether you need to book ahead.

sections.heading: Tasmania and staying safe
body: Mt Field National Park, about an hour from Hobart, has Russell Falls and a campground close to the start of the walk. The south is best in winter and spring, when the falls run, but nights are cold.

At any waterfall, keep to the signs. Do not swim after heavy rain or where signs forbid it, because currents and submerged rocks are the main hazards, and diving into unknown water is a common cause of serious injury. The weather safety guide covers floods and storms.
tips: Do not swim after heavy rain

sections.heading: Plan the route in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities those sources publish. Build a trip as ordered stops and it shows the distance, drive time and forecast for each leg, so you can line up the camps near the waterfalls you want to see.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: Where can I camp near a waterfall in Australia?

Examples include Florence Falls and Wangi Falls in Litchfield National Park, Gunlom Falls in Kakadu, Bell Gorge's Silent Grove campground in the Kimberley, Binna Burra near the Lamington National Park falls, Wallaman Falls in Queensland, and Russell Falls at Mt Field National Park in Tasmania.
When is the best time to see waterfalls in Australia?

In the tropical north, falls run strongest at the end of the wet season, from about March to May, but roads and some camps close earlier. In the south, falls are strongest in winter and spring. Check closures before you travel.
Is it safe to swim at a waterfall?

Not always. Follow park signs about currents, depth, crocodiles and closures, and do not swim after heavy rain or where signs say not to. Cliff jumping and diving into unknown water are a common cause of serious injuries.
Do I need to book waterfall campsites?
Many national park campgrounds, such as those in Litchfield and Kakadu, are popular in the dry season and some need booking or a permit. Check the park's website before you go.

wa-wildflower-season-camping-australia.title: WA Wildflower Season: Where and When to Camp for the Bloom
wa-wildflower-season-camping-australia.description: Western Australia's wildflower season runs from about July to November. Where the bloom starts and moves, the best regions to drive, and where to camp and book.
wa-wildflower-season-camping-australia.imageAlt: Greens Pool near Denmark on the south coast of Western Australia
wa-wildflower-season-camping-australia.intro: Every spring, Western Australia's south-west and Mid West put on one of the world's great wildflower shows, with thousands of species that grow nowhere else. The bloom starts in the north around July and moves south through September and into November, so the best trip follows it. Below are the regions to see, when to go and where to camp.

sections.heading: When the bloom happens
body: The main season runs from about August to October, with the peak usually in September. It starts in the north, around Kalbarri and the Mid West, in July and August, and moves south through the Wheatbelt and Perth in September, reaching the south coast and the Stirling Range into October and November.
The bloom varies with the rain each year, so check recent reports from local visitor centres before you set the route. Spring weather can be cool and wet, and nights are cold in the south.
tips: August to October is the main season

sections.heading: Where to go
body: The Mid West, around Mullewa, Geraldton and Kalbarri, is known for everlastings and wreath flowers. The Wheatbelt has roadside displays and the south coast has the Stirling Range and Fitzgerald River National Park, which is famous for its wide range of plant species. Kings Park in Perth has a wildflower festival in spring.
The south-west camping loop and Perth to Albany drive guides cover the southern part of the route, and the Perth to Exmouth guide covers the Coral Coast north of Geraldton.

sections.heading: Where to camp
body: Holiday parks and national park campgrounds are common in the Mid West, the Stirling Range and the south coast, and many country towns have a caravan park or a showground. Free camps and rest areas are listed along the main highways, and the Western Australia camping rules guide covers the rules.
It is peak season, with school holidays in the middle of it, so book popular campgrounds ahead, especially on weekends.
tips: Holiday parks and national park camps

sections.heading: Looking after the flowers
body: Wildflowers in Western Australia are protected, and picking them without a licence is illegal. Stay on tracks and paths, do not trample the bush and clean your shoes and tyres if you can, because plant disease can spread on mud.
Weather and wildlife matter in spring too. Roads in the Wheatbelt are used by trucks, and kangaroos are active at dawn and dusk.
tips: Watch for wildlife at dawn and dusk

sections.heading: Plan the route in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities those sources publish. Build a trip as ordered stops and it shows the distance, drive time and forecast for each leg, so you can follow the bloom north to south and see where the cold nights are.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.
tips: Follow the bloom north to south

faq: When is wildflower season in Western Australia?

The main season runs from about August to October, with the peak usually in September. It starts in the north, around Kalbarri and the Mid West, in July and August, and moves south through Perth and the south coast into October and November.
Where are the best places to see wildflowers in Western Australia?

Popular areas include the Mid West around Mullewa, Geraldton and Kalbarri, the Wheatbelt, Kings Park in Perth, the Stirling Range, and Fitzgerald River National Park on the south coast. The bloom varies each year, so check recent reports.
Can I pick wildflowers?
No. Wildflowers in Western Australia are protected, and picking them without a licence is illegal, so look and photograph, and stay on tracks and paths.
Is it busy during wildflower season?
Yes. It is spring, school holidays fall in the season and popular towns and campgrounds fill, so book holiday parks and national park camps ahead, especially in September and on weekends.

sources.label: Parks and Wildlife Service Western Australia

silo-art-trail-camping-australia.title: The Silo Art Trail: A Campervan Route Through Victoria's Wimmera and Mallee
silo-art-trail-camping-australia.description: A road trip route past giant painted silos in Victoria's Wimmera and Mallee, with the towns to stop at, where to camp, and how the trail fits a drive from Melbourne to Adelaide or Mildura.
silo-art-trail-camping-australia.imageAlt: The Calder Highway curving past scrub and a vineyard at Merbein near Mildura
silo-art-trail-camping-australia.intro: Giant painted silos have turned small wheat towns in Victoria's Wimmera and Mallee into a road trip destination. The artworks stand beside the grain silos at Brim, Sheep Hills, Rupanyup, Lascelles, Patchewollock and other towns, and they make a good loop for a few days in a campervan, with free and cheap camps along the way. Below are the route, the towns to stop at and where to stay.

sections.heading: The route and the silos
body: The Silo Art Trail runs through the Wimmera and Mallee in north-west Victoria, a few hours north-west of Melbourne. Large murals of local people and landscapes cover the silos at Brim, Sheep Hills, Rupanyup, Lascelles, Patchewollock, Rosebery and other towns, and the route passes wheat fields, salt lakes and small country pubs.
Distances between towns are long and services are limited, so fill up when you can and carry water. The Melbourne to Mildura drive guide covers the main road through the region.
tips: Fuel and water are far apart

sections.heading: How long to allow
body: You can see the main silos in two or three days, and a long weekend is enough for a loop. The trail fits well into a longer drive between Melbourne, Adelaide and Mildura, or into a trip to the Grampians. Allow time to stop in each town, because the pubs, bakeries and small museums are part of the point.
Silos outside Victoria, such as Kimba and Coonalpyn in South Australia, Weethalle in New South Wales and Thallon in Queensland, can be added to a longer lap.
tips: Two or three days is enough
Add silos on the Adelaide or Mildura route
Stop for the towns, not just the art

sections.heading: Where to camp
body: Many Wimmera and Mallee towns have a caravan park, a showground or a free camp, and the national parks nearby, Wyperfeld and Hattah-Kulkyne, have campgrounds with a bush setting. Some towns allow a short free stay with a donation or a small fee, so check the local rules and the signs.
The free camping legality guide covers the rules, and the Victoria camping rules guide covers national parks and state forests.

sections.heading: Seasons and road tips
body: Spring and autumn are the most comfortable seasons, with mild days and cool nights. Summer can be very hot, and winter nights are cold, with fog on some mornings. Check fire danger in summer and avoid unsealed roads after heavy rain.
Watch for kangaroos at dawn and dusk and for farm vehicles on country roads. The dump points guide covers where to empty tanks between towns.

sections.heading: Plan the route in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities those sources publish. Build the silo route as ordered stops and it shows the distance, drive time and forecast for each leg, so you can plan fuel and a camp in each town.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.
tips: Plan fuel and a camp in each town
Add each silo as a stop

faq: Where is the Silo Art Trail in Victoria?

It runs through the Wimmera and Mallee in north-west Victoria, with painted silos in towns such as Brim, Sheep Hills, Rupanyup, Lascelles, Patchewollock and Rosebery. The towns are small and far apart, so plan fuel and food along the way.
How long does the Silo Art Trail take?
You can see the main silos in two or three days, or a long weekend, depending on how many you add. It pairs well with a drive between Melbourne, Adelaide and Mildura.
Is there camping along the Silo Art Trail?

Yes. Many Wimmera and Mallee towns have a caravan park, a showground or a free camp, and national parks such as Wyperfeld and Hattah-Kulkyne have campgrounds close to the route. Check each town's rules and any limits on stays.
Are there silo art trails outside Victoria?
Yes. South Australia, New South Wales, Queensland and Western Australia have painted silos, including Kimba and Coonalpyn in South Australia, Weethalle in New South Wales and Thallon in Queensland.

oodnadatta-track-camping-guide.title: Oodnadatta Track Camping Guide: Marree to Marla, Camps, Fuel and Conditions
oodnadatta-track-camping-guide.description: How to camp and drive the Oodnadatta Track in South Australia: Marree to Marla, Farina, Coward Springs, William Creek, Oodnadatta, fuel, road conditions and the best time to go.
oodnadatta-track-camping-guide.imageAlt: A motorhome and a 4WD camped among palm trees at Coward Springs camping area, South Australia
oodnadatta-track-camping-guide.intro: The Oodnadatta Track is one of Australia's great outback drives. It runs about 620 kilometres from Marree to Marla through gibber plains, dry lakes and spring-fed oases, following the old telegraph and railway line. It is a gravel road a long way from help, so it rewards a plan: fuel at every chance, water for the whole trip, a vehicle in good shape and a camp chosen each night before dark. Go between April and October, and give it three or four days.

sections.heading: The route in short
body: Most people drive from Marree to Oodnadatta and on to Marla or Coober Pedy, though it also works in reverse. Marree is about 700 kilometres north of Adelaide, and Marla sits on the Stuart Highway.

The track passes Lake Eyre South, Coward Springs, the mound springs, William Creek, Algebuckina Bridge and the Painted Desert. Fuel and a meal are at Marree, William Creek, Oodnadatta and Marla, so plan each tank around them.
tips: Three or four days is comfortable

table.caption: The main stops on the Oodnadatta Track.
head: Stop
What is there
Camping
Watch for
rows: Last supplies for the Flinders side
Date palms and a warm spa
Fuel and a pub on the Dalhousie side

sections.heading: Where to camp
body: There is a good spread of camps along the way. Coward Springs has date palms and a warm spring bath, William Creek and Oodnadatta have hotel and roadhouse camps with showers, and Farina is a simple bush camp near the old town ruins. Bush camps beside waterholes and dry creeks are common, but only where camping is allowed and never in a creek bed when rain is forecast.

Most camps charge a small fee, paid at the hotel or into an honesty box, so carry some cash. Dalhousie Springs, a hot pool oasis in Witjira National Park, sits off the track and needs a Desert Parks Pass.
tips: Dalhousie needs a Desert Parks Pass

sections.heading: Road conditions and vehicle
body: The track is well graded in places and rough in others, with corrugations, loose stones and the occasional creek crossing. After rain it can become impassable within hours and may be closed. Check the South Australian road report before you set out and again along the way.

Many rental agreements prohibit the track, so confirm yours in writing. Carry two spare tyres, a compressor, extra fuel if your tank range is under 500 kilometres and a satellite messenger or a UHF radio. For the basics, read our guide to 4WD driving for hire vehicles.

sections.heading: Season and heat
body: April to October is the season, with warm days and cool nights. Summer is very hot, regularly above 40 degrees, and flash rain can close the road for days.
Carry at least 10 litres of water per person per day plus a reserve, and if you break down, stay with your vehicle. Tell someone your route and when you expect to arrive.
tips: 10 litres of water per person a day

sections.heading: Lake Eyre, springs and extras
body: The mound springs near Coward Springs, including Blanche Cup and The Bubbler, are small oases that feed a unique wetland and should be viewed from the paths. From William Creek, scenic flights give the best view of Lake Eyre, Kati Thanda, and in a wet year the lake fills with water and birds.
If you have time, add the Painted Desert, Algebuckina Bridge and the opal town of Coober Pedy, where our free camping guide shows where to stay.
tips: Mound springs: stay on the paths

sections.heading: Plan the Oodnadatta Track in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops, which shows the long gaps between fuel on a route like this.
Check conditions on the road report before you drive. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Where can you camp on the Oodnadatta Track?

At Farina, Coward Springs, William Creek, Oodnadatta and Mount Dare, where there are campgrounds with different levels of facilities, and at bush camps beside waterholes and creeks along the way. Always camp at a marked site or on land where camping is allowed.
Do I need a 4WD for the Oodnadatta Track?

In dry weather the track is often passable in a high clearance 2WD, but it is a long gravel road with corrugations and sharp stones, and most rental agreements prohibit it. A 4WD with good tyres is the safer choice.
How long does the Oodnadatta Track take?
About 620 kilometres from Marree to Marla. Allow two to four days with stops, and more if you add Dalhousie Springs or Lake Eyre.
Is the Oodnadatta Track open all year?
Technically yes, but it closes after rain and summer is dangerously hot. April to October is the season. Check the road report before you set out.

tanami-track-camping-guide.title: Tanami Track Camping Guide: Alice Springs to Halls Creek, Fuel, Camps and Rules
tanami-track-camping-guide.description: How to drive and camp the Tanami Track between Alice Springs and Halls Creek: distance, road conditions, fuel, camps, Aboriginal land rules, the season and Wolfe Creek Crater.
tanami-track-camping-guide.imageAlt: 4WD on the red-dirt Great Central Road near Tjukayirla, Western Australia
tanami-track-camping-guide.intro: The Tanami Track is the outback shortcut between Alice Springs and the Kimberley. It runs about 1,000 kilometres through desert country to Halls Creek, saving a long loop through Darwin or Western Australia's coast, and it is quieter than most outback roads. It is also remote, with few services, rules for Aboriginal land and weather that changes quickly. Plan fuel carefully, camp only where you are allowed and travel in the dry season.

sections.heading: The route in short
body: The track leaves the Stuart Highway north of Alice Springs and heads north-west across the Tanami Desert, past Yuendumu and Rabbit Flat, then crosses into Western Australia and runs through Billiluna and Balgo country before reaching the Great Northern Highway near Halls Creek.

It is a shortcut compared with the long loop through Darwin, and it links up well with Wolfe Creek Crater, Purnululu and the Gibb River Road. Fill up in Alice Springs and treat every other fuel stop as a top up.
tips: Fuel and supplies in Alice Springs

table.caption: The main stops on the Tanami Track.
head: Stop
What is there

Watch for
rows: Near the start of the track

Check fuel before you rely on it

sections.heading: Where to camp
body: Camp at the roadhouses and caravan parks, at Tilmouth Well, Rabbit Flat in season and Halls Creek, and at marked rest areas. Do not pull off into the bush, because the track crosses Aboriginal land where camping outside designated sites needs permission.
Wolfe Creek Crater, a short drive south of Halls Creek, has a campground and is an easy side trip. Our guide to camping on Aboriginal land explains the rules.
tips: Camp at roadhouses and marked sites
No bush camping on Aboriginal land

sections.heading: Road conditions and vehicle
body: The surface is a mix of sealed sections and gravel, and the gravel can be rough, with corrugations and loose stones. Rain closes sections, so check the Northern Territory road report and Main Roads Western Australia before you set out and again along the way.

Many rental agreements prohibit the Tanami, so confirm in writing. Carry two spare tyres, a compressor, spare water and a satellite messenger or a UHF radio, and pull well off the road when a road train comes through.

sections.heading: Season, heat and weather
body: May to September is the season, with warm days and cool nights. Summer is hot, and the wet season from about December to March can close the track for days.
Plan fuel for the full gap between stops, carry at least 10 litres of water per person per day and tell someone your plan. Phone coverage is limited to the communities, so do not rely on it.
tips: 10 litres of water per person a day

sections.heading: Permits and respect
body: You can drive the main road without a permit, but you cannot go off it onto Aboriginal land without one, and alcohol restrictions apply in many communities. Our outback alcohol guide explains how to carry it legally.
Keep to the road, ask before taking photos of people or places and do not collect souvenirs. Slow down through communities, where children, dogs and people may be on the road.

sections.heading: Plan the Tanami Track in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops, which shows the long gaps between fuel.
Check conditions on the road reports before you drive. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: How long is the Tanami Track?
About 1,000 kilometres from the Stuart Highway near Alice Springs to Halls Creek. Allow two to three days, and more if you stop at Wolfe Creek Crater or add Purnululu.
Is the Tanami Track sealed?

Parts of it are. The Northern Territory end has been sealed in stages, but long stretches are still gravel with corrugations and loose stones, and conditions change quickly. Check the road report before you go.
Can I camp along the Tanami Track?
Camp at roadhouses, campgrounds and marked rest areas. Much of the road crosses Aboriginal land, where camping outside designated sites needs permission, so do not pull off and set up anywhere.
Do I need a permit for the Tanami Track?
You do not need a permit to drive the main road, but you cannot leave it onto Aboriginal land without one. Alcohol restrictions apply in many communities along the way.

mitchell-falls-mitchell-plateau-camping.title: Mitchell Falls and Mitchell Plateau Camping: Roads, Camps and the Dry Season
mitchell-falls-mitchell-plateau-camping.description: How to camp at Mitchell Falls and on the Mitchell Plateau in the Kimberley: the Kalumburu Road, the 4WD track, the campground, the walk to the falls, fuel and the season.
mitchell-falls-mitchell-plateau-camping.intro: Mitchell Falls is one of the Kimberley's most remote and spectacular places. The four-tier waterfall falls over the Mitchell Plateau at the end of a long, rough road, and the walk in crosses rock, streams and pools. It is a serious trip with a short season, a 4WD requirement, and few services between the Gibb River Road and the falls. Plan fuel and water carefully, book camping ahead where you can and give yourself at least two nights on the plateau.

sections.heading: Getting there
body: Mitchell Falls is reached from the Gibb River Road by the Kalumburu Road and then the Mitchell Plateau road. The whole route from the Gibb is roughly 250 to 300 kilometres of rough gravel, with corrugations, creek crossings and long stretches where you will not see another vehicle.
A high clearance 4WD is needed, and standard rental campervans are not allowed. Many people hire a 4WD in Broome or Kununurra, or join a tour.

table.caption: The main stops on the way to Mitchell Falls.
head: Stop
What is there
Camping
Watch for
rows: Last easy fuel is on the Gibb
Slow going, allow half a day

sections.heading: Where to camp
body: The campground in Mitchell River National Park is the base for the falls, with basic facilities and a short walk to the start of the trail. Drysdale River Station, on the Kalumburu Road, is the usual overnight stop on the way in and out, with fuel, meals and a camp.
Camping elsewhere along the road is limited, and much of the country is Aboriginal land. Stay at marked camps, pay the fees and carry cash where card machines are not available.
tips: Drysdale River Station on the way

sections.heading: The walk to Mitchell Falls
body: The trail is about 4 to 5 kilometres each way from the car park and crosses rock, streams and pools, passing Little Merten Falls and Big Merten Falls before reaching the main falls. Swimming is possible at some pools, but follow the signs, because estuarine crocodiles are present in some Kimberley waterways.
Start early, because the walk is hot and exposed. Carry water, wear sturdy shoes and allow half a day for the round trip.

sections.heading: Season and conditions
body: The roads are usually open from about May to October. They close in the wet season and can be rough early in the dry, before grading is finished. Our wet season guide explains what the closures mean across the Top End and the north of Western Australia.
Check the road report and call ahead to confirm conditions at Drysdale River Station. Flights from the plateau give a view of the falls from above if you do not want to walk.

sections.heading: Fuel, water and safety
body: There is fuel at Drysdale River Station and none beyond it, so fill every tank and carry spare fuel for the return. Take at least 10 litres of water per person per day, spare tyres and a satellite messenger or a UHF radio, because there is no mobile coverage.
Tell someone your route and your return date. Slow down on the corrugations, which are the main cause of tyre damage and vehicle failures.

sections.heading: Plan the Kimberley in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.
Remote park camps are best confirmed on the Parks and Wildlife Service page and the road report. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Can you camp at Mitchell Falls?
Yes, at the campground in Mitchell River National Park near the walk to the falls. It is run by the park managers, has basic facilities and needs a camping fee, so check the park page before you go.
Do I need a 4WD to reach Mitchell Falls?

Yes. The route runs from the Gibb River Road along the Kalumburu Road and then the Mitchell Plateau road, which is rough, with corrugations and creek crossings. A high clearance 4WD is needed, and rental campervans are not allowed.
When can you visit Mitchell Falls?
Roughly May to October, in the dry season. The roads close in the wet, and conditions are better after the roads are graded in the early dry.
How far is the walk to Mitchell Falls?
About 4 to 5 kilometres each way from the car park, over rock and creek crossings. It is hot and rough, so start early and carry water.

Main Roads Western Australia: road conditions

pilbara-camping-beyond-karijini.title: Camping in the Pilbara Beyond Karijini: Millstream, Cape Keraudren and Roadhouse Stops
pilbara-camping-beyond-karijini.description: Where to camp in the Pilbara beyond Karijini: Millstream Chichester National Park, Cape Keraudren, Port Hedland, Karratha, Marble Bar, roadhouses, the season and cyclone risk.
pilbara-camping-beyond-karijini.imageAlt: Caravans and tents under trees and palms at the Eighty Mile Beach caravan park on the north-west coast of Western Australia
pilbara-camping-beyond-karijini.intro: The Pilbara is more than Karijini. Millstream Chichester National Park has spring-fed pools in red country, Cape Keraudren is a wild coastal camp, and towns such as Karratha, Port Hedland and Marble Bar make useful bases between long, empty stretches of highway. It is hot, remote and busy with mining traffic, so go between May and September, book where you can and plan fuel and water at every stop.

sections.heading: Where to camp
body: The Pilbara has a good mix of camps, from national park campgrounds to caravan parks. Millstream Chichester National Park, near Karratha, has campgrounds close to the pools and in the ranges, and Cape Keraudren Nature Reserve, south of Port Hedland, has coastal camps on the edge of the Indian Ocean.

Roadhouses such as Pardoo and Auski, and caravan parks in Karratha, Port Hedland, Newman and Tom Price, give you showers, power and a meal. Rest areas along the highways are free for a night or two where signed.

table.caption: Camping options in the Pilbara beyond Karijini.
head: Where
Cost
Booking

rows: Karratha and Port Hedland caravan parks

sections.heading: Millstream and the coast
body: Millstream Chichester National Park has Python Pool, a cool swimming hole under red cliffs, and the Millstream pools fed by springs on the Fortescue River. The roads in are mostly gravel and passable in a standard vehicle in dry weather, but check conditions after rain.

On the coast, Cape Keraudren is a remote fishing and beach camp with no services, so bring water and everything you need. Port Hedland and Karratha are the service hubs, and Cossack, a ghost town near Karratha, makes an easy half day.

sections.heading: Marble Bar and the inland towns
body: Marble Bar is known as one of the hottest towns in Australia, with Chinaman Pool and Doolena Gorge close by. Newman and Tom Price are the main inland bases, with caravan parks, fuel and supplies on the way to Karijini.
Distances are long and traffic includes road trains and mining vehicles. Read our guide to driving with road trains before you set off.
tips: Newman and Tom Price as bases
Share the road with road trains

sections.heading: Season, heat and cyclones
body: May to September is the season, with warm days and cool nights. Summer is extremely hot, and from about November to April the Pilbara can see cyclones and flooding that close roads for days. Our cyclone and flood season guide explains what to watch.
Carry at least 10 litres of water per person per day, fill the tank at every town and tell someone your route. Mobile coverage is good in the towns and patchy elsewhere.
tips: 10 litres of water per person a day

sections.heading: Fuel, supplies and planning
body: Fuel is available at Karratha, Port Hedland, Newman, Tom Price, Marble Bar and the roadhouses on the highways, but distances between towns are long. Stock food in the bigger towns, where prices are lower than at the roadhouses.
Combine the Pilbara with the road to Broome or Exmouth, and see our Perth to Broome and Karijini guides for the bigger picture.
tips: Stock up in the bigger towns

sections.heading: Plan the Pilbara in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops, which shows the long gaps between fuel in the Pilbara.
Check park pages and road conditions before you drive. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Where can you camp in the Pilbara apart from Karijini?

At Millstream Chichester National Park, Cape Keraudren on the coast south of Port Hedland, roadhouses such as Pardoo, caravan parks in Karratha, Port Hedland and Newman, and rest areas on the highways.
Is Millstream Chichester National Park worth visiting?
Yes. Python Pool and Chinderwarriner Pool are cool, spring-fed swimming spots in red country, and the park has campgrounds with basic facilities. Check the park page for bookings and road conditions.
When is the best time to camp in the Pilbara?
May to September. Summer is extremely hot, and the cyclone season from about November to April can bring flooding and road closures.
Can I free camp in the Pilbara?
Only at signed rest areas where it is allowed, usually for a night or two. Mining and pastoral land is private, so do not pull off onto it.

queensland-outback-national-parks-campin.title: Queensland Outback National Parks Camping: Boodjamulla, Currawinya and More
queensland-outback-national-parks-campin.description: Camping in Queensland's outback national parks: Boodjamulla (Lawn Hill), Currawinya, Carnarvon Gorge, Diamantina and Munga-Thirri, with permits, roads, the season and what to carry.
queensland-outback-national-parks-campin.intro: Outback Queensland has some of Australia's most rewarding national park camping. Boodjamulla has a turquoise gorge in the dry country of the north-west, Currawinya holds wetlands and wildlife on the border with New South Wales, and Carnarvon Gorge has sandstone walls and rock art. Each park has a campground that you book through the state parks system, long approach roads and a short season, so plan permits, fuel and water before you set out.

sections.heading: The parks at a glance
body: Boodjamulla, also called Lawn Hill, is in the north-west and has a gorge you can paddle. Currawinya sits in the south-west near Hungerford, Carnarvon Gorge is in the central highlands, and Diamantina and Munga-Thirri lie in the far west and south-west, in desert country around Birdsville and Bedourie.
Each has its own character and road conditions. Many visitors link two or three of them on a longer outback loop, using the highways between.

table.caption: Queensland outback national parks and what to know.
head: Park
Main draw
Roads
Watch for
rows: Partly sealed, gravel at the end
Closes in the wet, books out

sections.heading: Permits and booking
body: A camping permit is required in every Queensland national park campground. You book online through the state parks system and the permit comes with a modest per-person fee, which is paid in advance. Remote parks often have no phone coverage, so book before you leave a town with a signal.
Popular parks such as Boodjamulla and Carnarvon Gorge fill at school holidays and in the cooler months, so book early. Our guide to camping rules in Queensland covers the state's wider rules.

sections.heading: Roads, vehicle and fuel
body: The main highways are sealed, but the roads into the parks are often gravel and turn to bog after rain. Check the QLDTraffic road report and the park alerts before you set off, and be ready to stay put if rain arrives.
Fill every tank at every town, carry spare fuel for remote parks and bring at least two spare tyres on gravel. Many rental agreements prohibit unsealed roads, so confirm yours in writing.

sections.heading: Season, heat and water
body: April to October is the season, with warm days and cool nights. Summer is very hot, regularly above 40 degrees, and the wet season from about December to March can close roads and parks.
Carry at least 10 litres of water per person per day and treat or boil any water you collect. Tell someone your route and your return date.
tips: 10 litres of water per person a day

sections.heading: Linking the parks and the outback towns
body: Link the parks with the towns in between. Longreach, Winton and Mount Isa have caravan parks and council camps, and our guide to free camping in the Queensland outback shows where to stay between the parks.
For a longer loop, the Savannah Way and the Queensland Outback Way connect the north-west and central parks and join the highways to the coast.

sections.heading: Plan the outback in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops, which shows the long gaps between fuel.
Book the permit and check road conditions on the state parks site before you drive. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.

faq: Do I need to book camping in Queensland national parks?

Yes. A camping permit is required in every Queensland national park campground and is booked online through the state parks system. Remote parks have patchy phone coverage, so book before you leave town.
Which outback Queensland national parks are best for camping?
Boodjamulla (Lawn Hill) for its gorge and canoeing, Carnarvon Gorge for walks and rock art, Currawinya for birds and wetlands, and Diamantina and Munga-Thirri for remote desert country.
Do I need a 4WD for outback Queensland national parks?
For Carnarvon Gorge and Boodjamulla in dry weather a 2WD can often manage, but roads turn to bog after rain. Diamantina, Munga-Thirri and the back tracks of Currawinya need a high clearance 4WD.
When is the best time to camp in outback Queensland parks?
April to October. Summer is very hot, and the wet season from about December to March can cut roads and close parks, including Munga-Thirri, which closes in summer.

free-camping-near-shepparton-goulburn-va.title: Free Camping Near Shepparton and the Goulburn Valley
free-camping-near-shepparton-goulburn-va.description: Where to camp for free or cheaply around Shepparton and the Goulburn Valley: river camps, state forests, small-town reserves, the rules to check and a fallback when they are full.
free-camping-near-shepparton-goulburn-va.imageAlt: Tents on a sandy river beach at sunrise, Hattah-Kulkyne National Park, Victoria
free-camping-near-shepparton-goulburn-va.intro: Shepparton sits in the middle of Victoria's Goulburn Valley, the fruit and dairy country between Melbourne and the Murray. The city has a council caravan park, but the cheaper and more scenic camps are out on the rivers and in the forests: the Goulburn at Nagambie, Murchison and Seymour, and the Murray and its forests to the north. Below are where to look, the rules to check and a paid fallback when the free camps are full.

sections.heading: Free camping around Shepparton
body: Shepparton is a regional city about two hours north of Melbourne, and free camping inside it is not allowed. Victoria Park Lake is the council's caravan park, with powered and unpowered sites, and it is the sensible base if you want showers and shops close by. The free and low-cost camps are within an hour or so, in the forests and river towns that surround the city.
Camping rules depend on who manages the land, so check each place before you set up.
tips: No free camping in the city
Victoria Park Lake is the paid base
Free camps are an hour out

sections.heading: River camps on the Goulburn
body: The Goulburn River runs from the high country through Seymour, Nagambie and Murchison before it reaches Shepparton. Its banks have a mix of state forest, council reserves and small camps, many with a boat ramp, fishing and shade from river red gums. Nagambie's lakes are popular for boating and rowing, and the river towns usually have a pub and a bakery in walking distance.

Some of these camps are free and some charge a small fee or ask for a donation. Stay limits, fire rules and closures after floods vary by site and season, so read the sign or the land manager's page on the day.
tips: Fishing, boats and river red gums

sections.heading: The Murray and its forests
body: North of Shepparton the Murray forms the border with New South Wales, and the forests along it are among the best bush camping in northern Victoria. Barmah is the best known, a large river red gum forest with riverside camping and a lot of wildlife, and Cobram and Yarrawonga have river beaches and caravan parks close to the water.

Rivers rise and the forests flood, so check closures before a long drive, and take a camp stove rather than counting on a fire. The Victoria camping rules guide covers state forests and the fire season.

sections.heading: Small-town camps and showgrounds
body: Many towns in the Goulburn Valley run a showground, a recreation reserve or a community camp that takes campers for a low fee, often with toilets and sometimes power. Tatura, Kyabram, Rushworth and Euroa are examples of the kind of town to look at, and many are on the way to somewhere else.
These camps are managed by councils or committees, so the price, the stay limit and whether you can book can change. Ring or check the council page if you are travelling at a busy time.

sections.heading: Rules, seasons and safety
body: Autumn and spring are the best seasons, with mild days and cool nights. Summer is hot and fire danger can be high, and a total fire ban means no campfires or solid-fuel stoves. Winter nights are cold, with fog in the valley, and floods can close river camps for weeks.
Take your own water and take your rubbish out. The responsible camping guide covers the basics and the free camping legality guide explains why the rules differ from site to site.

sections.heading: Plan the trip in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities and fees those sources publish. Filter by cost to see the free and cheaper places along the Goulburn and the Murray, then build the loop as ordered stops with the distance and drive time for each leg.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: Can you camp for free near Shepparton?

Yes, in places. Victoria allows camping in many state forests and some parks, and a number of towns along the Goulburn and Murray rivers have free or low-cost community camps. Shepparton itself has a council caravan park rather than a free camp, so the free options are in the forests and small towns around it.
Where do people free camp in the Goulburn Valley?

Along the Goulburn River at towns such as Nagambie, Murchison and Seymour, in the state forests and parks beside the Murray, including the Barmah forest, and at small-town reserves and showgrounds. Check each place's current rules, because stay limits and closures change.
Is free camping allowed in Victoria?

It depends on the land. State forests and some parks allow camping at set sites or in set areas, towns set their own rules for council land, and camping on the roadside or in most rest areas is not allowed. Read the signs and the land manager's page.
When is the best time to camp in the Goulburn Valley?
Autumn and spring are the most comfortable, with mild days and cool nights. Summer is hot, with high fire danger and busy river camps, and winter nights are cold, with fog on some mornings.

glow-worm-caves-camping-australia.title: Glow-Worm Caves You Can Camp Near in Australia
glow-worm-caves-camping-australia.description: Where to see glow-worms in Australia and camp close by: Natural Bridge in Queensland, the Glow Worm Tunnel in New South Wales, Mole Creek in Tasmania and Melba Gully in Victoria, with the rules and the best time to go.
glow-worm-caves-camping-australia.imageAlt: Griffiths Creek Campground in Kroombit Tops National Park, Queensland
glow-worm-caves-camping-australia.intro: Australia has its own glow-worms, and you can see them without a long trip: in limestone caves, in an abandoned railway tunnel and in wet rainforest gullies after dark. Some of the best places have a campground within a short drive, so you can camp, walk in at night and sleep close by. Below are four places to try, how to see them without harming them, and when to go.

sections.heading: What you are looking at
body: Australian glow-worms are the larvae of fungus gnats, and each one hangs from the ceiling of a cave or the bank of a gully on a silk thread and glows blue-green to attract insects. They need damp, still, dark places, which is why they live in caves, tunnels and rainforest gullies. At full dark the roof looks like a small night sky.
New Zealand's Waitomo caves are the famous ones, but Australia has the same kind of animal in several states.

sections.heading: Natural Bridge in Queensland
body: Natural Bridge is in the Springbrook National Park in the Gold Coast hinterland, where a waterfall drops through a cave in the rock and glow-worms light the walls after dark. It is a short walk from the car park and one of the easiest glow-worm sightings in the country. The National Park has no campground at the bridge itself, so most people camp elsewhere in the hinterland.
Lamington National Park, close by, has campgrounds at Green Mountains and Binna Burra, and the Sunshine Coast hinterland guide covers more bush camps in the same region.
tips: Short walk from the car park

sections.heading: The Glow Worm Tunnel in New South Wales
body: The Glow Worm Tunnel is an old railway tunnel in Wollemi National Park, north-west of the Blue Mountains, with a walk through the bush to the entrance. Glow-worms grow on the damp walls, and you can see them if you turn your torch off inside. The road in is long and partly unsealed, and the weather can change the track, so check conditions first.
There is camping in the Newnes area, and the New South Wales camping rules guide covers national park and state forest rules.

sections.heading: Mole Creek in Tasmania and Melba Gully in Victoria
body: The Mole Creek Karst National Park in northern Tasmania has caves where you can see glow-worms on a guided tour, and the Marakoopa Cave is known for them. The nearest camps are in and around the town of Mole Creek, and the Tasmania camping rules guide has the rules for parks and reserves.

Melba Gully in the Otway Ranges is a damp fern gully where glow-worms appear on the banks after dark, on a short walk from the car park. The Great Ocean Road camping guide covers the campgrounds nearby.

sections.heading: How to see them without harming them
body: Go after dark, let your eyes adjust for ten minutes and keep your torch off or use a dim red light. Do not use a camera flash, do not touch the threads and stay on the track. Talk quietly, because noise and vibration can make the glow-worms dim.
Take a torch for the walk in and out, wear shoes with grip and tell someone where you are going. Rainforest tracks at night are slippery, and caves and tunnels can flood.
tips: Tell someone where you are going

sections.heading: Plan the trip in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, and each place page shows the facilities and fees those sources publish. Search near each glow-worm site, save the campgrounds you like and build the trip as ordered stops with the distance and drive time for each leg.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: Where can you see glow-worms in Australia?

In caves, old railway tunnels and damp rainforest gullies, mostly along the east coast and in Tasmania. Well-known places include Natural Bridge in Springbrook National Park in Queensland, the Glow Worm Tunnel in Wollemi National Park in New South Wales, the Marakoopa Cave at Mole Creek in Tasmania and Melba Gully in Victoria's Otways.
Are Australian glow-worms the same as the ones in New Zealand?

They are close relatives. Both are the larvae of fungus gnats in the genus Arachnocampa, which glow blue-green to attract insects into sticky threads. New Zealand has one species, and Australia has several.
When is the best time to see glow-worms?

After dark, once your eyes have adjusted, and on a night without a bright moon. They can be seen all year in caves and tunnels, and are usually easier to see in the wetter months in rainforest gullies.
Can you use a torch or take photos?
Keep your torch off or covered with red light, and do not use flash. Bright light makes the glow-worms dim their lights, and touching the threads or the walls harms them.
