stargazing-camps-northern-territory.title: Best Stargazing Camps in the Northern Territory
stargazing-camps-northern-territory.description: Where to camp under the darkest skies in the Northern Territory: Karlu Karlu, the West MacDonnell Ranges, Kings Canyon, Henbury Meteorites, Uluru and the Top End, with the best season and how to prepare.
stargazing-camps-northern-territory.imageAlt: A split granite boulder at Karlu Karlu (Devils Marbles) Conservation Reserve in the Northern Territory, with other orange boulders behind it
stargazing-camps-northern-territory.intro: The Northern Territory has some of the darkest skies you can reach in a campervan. Towns are far apart, the air in the dry season is clear and the Milky Way can cast a faint shadow on a moonless night. Below are the camps that work best for stargazing, from the Red Centre to the Top End, when to go and how to keep warm while you look.

sections.heading: Why the Northern Territory
body: Most of the Territory has no light pollution to speak of. The towns are small, the roads are long and a campground an hour from Alice Springs or Katherine can have a sky that most Australians never see from home. In the dry season the air is clear and dry, and the stars reach the horizon.
The Red Centre is the best bet, with its flat horizon and low humidity, and the Top End has good skies too once the wet season has gone.
tips: Dry, clear air from April to October
Flat horizon in the Red Centre

sections.heading: Karlu Karlu, Henbury and the Stuart Highway
body: Karlu Karlu (Devils Marbles) is a conservation reserve of round granite boulders beside the Stuart Highway, with a basic campground and a wide sky. It is a natural stop on the Darwin to Alice Springs drive, and the boulders make good foreground shapes for photos. Henbury Meteorites Conservation Reserve, south of Alice Springs, has a camping area beside a group of small craters made by an ancient meteorite.
Both are small, basic camps, so carry your own water and check the fees and facilities before you go. The Darwin to Alice Springs drive guide covers the road.

sections.heading: The West MacDonnell Ranges and Kings Canyon
body: The West MacDonnell Ranges, west of Alice Springs, have campgrounds at waterholes and gorges such as Ellery Creek Big Hole, Ormiston Gorge and Redbank Gorge. The rock walls block the light of other camps, so the sky is dark overhead, and you can walk out from camp after dinner.
Kings Canyon, in Watarrka National Park, has camping close by, and the Red Centre Way guide covers the loop between Alice Springs, Kings Canyon and Uluru.
tips: Kings Canyon on the Red Centre Way

sections.heading: Uluru and the Top End
body: The camps around Uluru are the most convenient place to see the stars at the Rock, and campers can book a campsite at the resort area, which has other services. Free camping is not allowed in the national park, so check the rules.

In the Top End, Litchfield and Kakadu have good dark skies from May to September once the wet season has passed. Camps there are closer to the water and the trees, so the sky is narrower than in the Red Centre.
tips: No free camping in the park

sections.heading: When to go and what to pack
body: The best season is the dry season, from April to October, and the best nights are in the week around the new moon. A full moon washes out the Milky Way, so check the moon phase before you book.

Winter nights in the Red Centre are close to freezing, so bring a warm sleeping bag, a beanie, gloves and a folding chair. Use a red torch so your eyes stay adjusted, and a star map app to name what you see.

sections.heading: Plan the trip in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus rest areas, with each place's facilities and fees as the agency publishes them. Look at the camps along the Stuart Highway and in the West MacDonnell Ranges, save the ones you like and build the trip as ordered stops with the distance and drive time for each leg.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: Where is the best stargazing in the Northern Territory?

Anywhere away from town lights in the dry season. Popular camps include Karlu Karlu (Devils Marbles), the West MacDonnell Ranges, Kings Canyon, Henbury Meteorites and the campgrounds around Uluru, and the Top End's Litchfield and Kakadu on clear nights.
When is the best time to see the Milky Way in the Northern Territory?

The dry season, from about April to October, has the clearest skies, with the Milky Way high overhead in the middle of the night from roughly May to August. Pick a few nights around the new moon, when the sky is darkest.
How cold does it get at night in the Red Centre?
Winter nights are often close to freezing, and sometimes below, even after a warm day. Pack a warm sleeping bag, a beanie and layers, and a hot drink for the long wait outside.
Do I need a telescope or special gear?

No. A dark site, a few minutes for your eyes to adjust and a red light will show the Milky Way, planets and a lot of stars. A star map app helps name what you see, and a tripod helps if you want photos.

sources.label: Parks and Wildlife Commission of the Northern Territory: parks and reserves

safe-swimming-queensland-crocodiles-stin.title: Safe Swimming in Queensland: Crocodiles, Stingers and Where to Swim
safe-swimming-queensland-crocodiles-stin.description: How to swim safely in Queensland: where crocodiles live, when stingers are in the water, patrolled beaches, lagoons, stinger nets and freshwater swimming holes to choose, with tips for campers.
safe-swimming-queensland-crocodiles-stin.intro: Queensland has some of the best swimming in Australia and some of the biggest hazards: saltwater crocodiles in the north, stingers in the warm months and rips and surf along the whole coast. You can still swim, but you need to pick the place. Below is where the risks are, when they apply and where campers can swim with confidence.

sections.heading: Crocodiles in the north
body: Saltwater crocodiles live in the rivers, creeks, estuaries and mangroves of tropical Queensland, from roughly the central coast up to Cape York, and they move between the sea and the rivers. A waterway with no sign can still hold a crocodile, and a calm creek is not a safe one.

Do not swim in rivers, creeks or the sea in crocodile country unless a sign says swimming is allowed, camp well back from the water's edge and never clean fish or leave food near the water. Never feed or approach a crocodile.
tips: Treat all tropical waterways as crocodile habitat
No signs does not mean no crocodiles

sections.heading: Stingers: box jellyfish and Irukandji
body: Marine stingers are in the warm tropical waters of the north coast and islands, most often from about November to May, and they can be present at other times. Beaches in the area put up stinger nets and signs, and a lifesaver or a council sign will tell you whether it is stinger season.
Swim inside the net, wear a full-body stinger suit, and get out of the water if you feel a sting. Pour vinegar on the sting and call 000 for a serious reaction.
tips: November to May is the main season
Swim in a net, wear a suit

sections.heading: Where campers can swim safely in the north
body: Patrolled beaches with a stinger net, such as Palm Cove, Mission Beach and Port Douglas, are the safest places to swim in the sea in summer. Lagoons are even safer, including the Cairns Esplanade Lagoon and the Airlie Beach Lagoon, which are free and have no crocodiles or stingers.

Freshwater swimming holes in the rainforest, in places such as the Atherton Tablelands, are popular, and crater lakes such as Lake Eacham are well known. Swim only where a sign allows it, because some creeks and gorges have strong currents or crocodiles.
tips: Free lagoons at Cairns and Airlie Beach

sections.heading: Southern Queensland and K'gari
body: South of the crocodile range, the risks are rips, surf and bluebottles. Swim between the red and yellow flags at a patrolled beach, ask the lifeguards where it is safe and avoid swimming alone. On the Sunshine Coast, the Gold Coast and in the hinterland, many creeks and rock pools are safe for a swim in the warmer months.
On K'gari (Fraser Island) the ocean has strong currents and sharks and swimming in it is not recommended, so swim in the freshwater lakes such as Lake McKenzie instead.
tips: Rips and surf are the risk

sections.heading: Camping tips for water safety
body: Choose a campground with a pool, a lagoon or a patrolled beach in north Queensland, and read the signs at the beach and the boat ramp. Do not leave children unsupervised near the water, and do not swim at dusk, at night or after rain, when rivers and creeks run higher and murkier.

Carry a first aid kit with vinegar, and know where the nearest help is. The Queensland camping rules guide covers national parks and the wet season, and the weather safety guide covers floods and storms.
tips: Pick a camp with a pool or lagoon
Not at dusk or after rain

sections.heading: Plan the trip in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, and each place page shows the facilities and fees those sources publish. Look for camps with a beach or a pool, save the places you want to stay and build the trip as ordered stops with the distance and drive time for each leg.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: Where are there crocodiles in Queensland?

Saltwater crocodiles live in rivers, creeks, estuaries and some beaches from roughly the central coast north to Cape York, and they can turn up in any waterway in that range, including places with no warning sign. Treat all tropical north Queensland waterways as crocodile habitat unless a sign says otherwise.
When is stinger season in Queensland?

Box jellyfish and Irukandji are most common in the tropical north from about November to May, and they can be there at other times. Swim inside a stinger net where there is one, wear a full-body stinger suit, and get out of the water if you feel a sting.
Is it safe to swim at Queensland beaches?

It is safest at patrolled beaches, between the red and yellow flags, and in the south, where there are no saltwater crocodiles. Rips, surf and bluebottles are the main risks there, so read the signs and ask the lifeguards.
Where can you swim safely in north Queensland?

In stinger nets at beaches such as Palm Cove, Mission Beach and Port Douglas, in lagoons such as the Cairns Esplanade and Airlie Beach lagoons, in pools at campgrounds and in freshwater swimming holes with signs that say swimming is allowed. Always read the local signs first.

best-family-holiday-parks-australia.title: Best Family Holiday Parks in Australia: What to Look For and Where to Go
best-family-holiday-parks-australia.description: How to choose a family holiday park in Australia: the facilities that matter, the regions where family parks cluster, cabin or powered site, when to book and what to pack, plus where to find them.
best-family-holiday-parks-australia.imageAlt: Grassed camping area under eucalypts at the Flaxmill Caravan Park in Boyup Brook, Western Australia
best-family-holiday-parks-australia.intro: A holiday park is the easiest way to camp with children in Australia. You get a pool, a playground, a camp kitchen and clean bathrooms, often beside a beach or a river, and you can choose a powered site for a campervan or a cabin with beds. Below is what makes a park good for a family, the regions where the best ones cluster and how to book one without overpaying.

sections.heading: What makes a park good for a family
body: The basics are a pool, a playground, a camp kitchen and clean bathrooms. The best family parks add a jumping pillow or a water play area, a games room for wet days, a kiosk and a quiet corner for adults. A park near a beach, a river or a lake lets children burn energy in the day and sleep early.
Look at the park's own photos and facilities list, and check the reviews for noise and cleanliness. A big park is lively, and a small one is quieter.
tips: Camp kitchen and a games room

sections.heading: Where family parks cluster
body: Family parks are thickest where the weather and the water are good: the Gold Coast, the Sunshine Coast, the northern New South Wales coast around Byron Bay, Coffs Harbour and the mid north coast, the south coast around Jervis Bay and the Great Ocean Road in Victoria. In the west, the Margaret River region and Busselton are popular, and Tasmania's east coast has quiet ones by the sea.
These regions fill in school holidays, so book early or aim for a shoulder-season week.
tips: Northern New South Wales and the south coast
Margaret River and Tasmania's east coast

sections.heading: Cabin or powered site
body: A cabin has beds, a bathroom and a kitchen, so it suits young children and wet weather, and some have a bunk room for a family of four or five. A powered site is cheaper and works well in a campervan or caravan with beds and a fridge, and you can use the park's pool and camp kitchen.
Prices vary by season and by park. The holiday park prices guide shows what published tariffs charge for a powered site and a cabin, and the powered or unpowered guide covers when each makes sense.

sections.heading: When to book and how to save
body: Book as early as you can for school holidays, long weekends and summer. The 2027 school holidays guide has the dates by state, and the best parks fill months ahead. A midweek stay or a term-time week is cheaper and quieter.

The big chains offer membership discounts, and councils and local operators often charge less for a similar site. Compare the same dates in a chain park and a council or independent park in the same town.
tips: Midweek and term time are cheaper

sections.heading: What to pack and check
body: Pack a few board games, a deck of cards, beach towels and a torch for each child. Many parks have a camp kitchen with a stove and a fridge, but few supply pots and plates, so bring your own.
Check the check-in time, the quiet hours, whether pets are allowed and the cancellation terms before you book. A park with a pool should have a fence and a gate, and a lifeguard is not guaranteed.
tips: Bring your own pots and plates
Check pets, quiet hours and cancellation

sections.heading: Plan the trip in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps carries 1,838 campgrounds from park agencies, and you can filter by cost and facilities. Holiday parks, cabins and farm stays listed by BookEasy can be booked in the app, with the price shown when you check dates, and a trip adds up the nights and the driving distance between stops.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: What makes a good family holiday park in Australia?
A pool, a playground, a camp kitchen and clean amenities, plus something to do on wet days. The best ones also sit by a beach, river or lake, and run holiday activities in school breaks.
Which chains run family holiday parks in Australia?

BIG4, Discovery Parks, G'day Parks and NRMA Parks and Resorts run parks across the country, and many councils and local operators run independent ones. The chains publish their parks and facilities on their sites, but they show nightly prices only once you enter dates.
When should I book a family holiday park?
As early as you can for school holidays, long weekends and summer, because the best parks fill months ahead. A midweek or term-time stay is cheaper and quieter.
Is a cabin or a powered site better for a family?
A cabin has beds, a bathroom and cooking, so it suits younger children or bad weather. A powered site is cheaper and works well if you have a campervan or caravan with beds and a fridge.

campfire-cooking-damper-australia.title: Campfire Cooking in Australia: Damper, Camp Oven and Billy Tea
campfire-cooking-damper-australia.description: How to cook on a legal campfire in Australia: damper, camp oven meals, foil parcels, jaffles and billy tea, plus what to do when fires are banned.
campfire-cooking-damper-australia.imageAlt: A campfire burning beside a lake in Queensland
campfire-cooking-damper-australia.intro: Cooking on a campfire is one of the best parts of camping in Australia, and the classic dish is damper, a simple bread baked in the coals. Before anything else, check that a fire is allowed where you are, because many campgrounds ban fires or have a total fire ban in force. Where a fire is legal, a camp oven, foil parcels, a jaffle iron and a billy of tea cover most of what you will want to cook, and a gas stove is the backup for the days it is not.

sections.heading: Check that a fire is allowed first
body: A campfire is legal only when there is no fire ban for the district, the land manager allows fires at that site and you use the fire ring or follow the clearance rules. The campfire rules guide covers the rules state by state, and the campground page or the park alert is where you confirm the place itself.

Many campgrounds, especially in national parks, ban wood fires for part or all of the year, and others provide free gas or electric barbecues instead. A barbecue plate cooks most of what is in this guide, so a place without a fire ring is not a reason to skip a hot meal.
tips: Check the fire ban and the park rules
Free barbecues are a good backup

sections.heading: Damper, the classic
body: Damper needs only self-raising flour, a good pinch of salt and enough water to make a soft dough, with a little butter rubbed in if you have it. About three cups of flour and a cup of water make a loaf for four. Mix it, knead it briefly, shape it into a round and cut a cross in the top.

Cook it in a camp oven or a heavy pot with a lid, set on a bed of coals with more coals on the lid, for about 25 to 40 minutes. It is done when the base sounds hollow when you tap it. Without a camp oven, wrap the dough around a clean stick and turn it over the coals until it is golden, or flatten small rounds and cook them in a greased pan.
Eat it warm with butter, jam or golden syrup, or use it to mop up a stew. Make a double batch the first time, because it disappears.
tips: Camp oven with coals under and on top
Done when the base sounds hollow

sections.heading: Camp oven and foil meals
body: A cast-iron camp oven turns a fire into an oven. Stews, roasts, curries and baked potatoes all work, and heat from coals on the lid cooks the top as well as the base. Use a lid lifter, heat-proof gloves and a shovel for the coals, and learn the rough rule of thumb: more coals on top for baking, more underneath for stewing.

Foil parcels are the easiest option for a first fire. Wrap fish, chicken or sausages with vegetables, a little oil and some seasoning in a double layer of foil and leave them in the coals for around 20 to 30 minutes, turning once. Potatoes and sweet potato in foil need longer, and corn cobs can go in their husks.
Let the flames die down first. Cooking is best over glowing coals, not over a fire that is still burning high.
tips: Use a lid lifter and gloves

sections.heading: Jaffles, billy tea and sweet things
body: A jaffle iron is a hinged iron that toasts a sealed sandwich over the coals, and it is a good use of spare bread with cheese and ham, baked beans or banana and chocolate for dessert. Grease the plates and keep it moving so it does not burn.

Billy tea is boiled water in a billy, a lidded can, with a handful of loose tea leaves added. Many people swing the billy to settle the leaves, which is optional, and the smoky taste of the tea is the point. A mug of it beside the fire is as Australian as camping gets.
Marshmallows on a stick and bananas split and filled with chocolate in foil make an easy dessert.

sections.heading: Safety and putting the fire out
body: Never leave a fire unattended and keep water beside it. Keep the fire small, clear flammable material from around it and never light one in strong wind. Hot coals stay hot for hours, so keep children and dogs well back.

Put the fire out cold: douse it with water, stir the ashes and douse again until the remains are cold to the touch. Collecting firewood is banned in many parks, so bring clean untreated wood from outside the park where fires are allowed. Never cook inside a tent, an awning or a closed vehicle.

sections.heading: When fires are banned
body: On a fire ban day, solid-fuel fires and barbecues are illegal in the district, and the campground's own rules may add to that. A gas stove is often still allowed, but not everywhere, so check the park's rule for cookers too.
Plan a no-flame meal for the days a ban is forecast. A pan on a gas burner can do eggs, pasta and one-pot stews,. Save the damper for a day you can have a legal fire.
tips: Keep a gas stove in the vehicle
Plan meals that need no fire

sections.heading: Plan the camp in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities those sources publish, including barbecues and fire pits where the source lists them. Build a trip as ordered stops and it shows the distance, drive time and forecast for each leg.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: What is damper?

Damper is the classic Australian bush bread: self-raising flour, salt and water, sometimes with a little butter or milk, kneaded briefly and baked in hot coals or a camp oven. It is eaten warm with butter, jam, golden syrup or with a stew.
Can I cook on a campfire at any campground in Australia?

No. Campfires are allowed only where the land manager permits them, in the fire ring provided, and never on a fire ban day. Many campgrounds have free gas or electric barbecues or ban fires altogether, so check the place first and carry a gas stove as the backup.
What do I need to cook on a campfire?

A fire ring or a legal fire spot, clean untreated wood from outside the park, a camp oven or a pan with a long handle, heat-proof gloves, a shovel or tongs for coals and water to put the fire out cold. Foil and a billy are cheap extras.
How long does damper take to cook?
A damper in a camp oven usually takes about 25 to 40 minutes in a bed of coals with coals on the lid, depending on size and heat. It is done when the base sounds hollow when you tap it.

sources.label: NSW RFS total fire ban rules

easy-camping-breakfasts-australia.title: Easy Camping Breakfasts in Australia: Quick Ideas for Every Gear Setup
easy-camping-breakfasts-australia.description: Easy camping breakfast ideas for Australia: eggs, porridge, pancakes, bacon rolls and no-cook options, with coffee, storage tips and what to do on fire ban days.
easy-camping-breakfasts-australia.imageAlt: A tent, sleeping bag and backpack at an Australian campground
easy-camping-breakfasts-australia.intro: A good camp breakfast is quick, uses one pan or none, and keeps for a few days without much fridge space. Eggs, porridge, pancakes and bacon and egg rolls are the staples, and overnight oats or muesli cover the mornings when you want to be on the road early. Below are easy ideas by gear setup, how to make a decent coffee, how to keep breakfast food fresh, and what to do on a fire ban day.

sections.heading: One-pan breakfasts
body: With a gas burner and a frying pan, breakfast is easy. Scrambled eggs on toast, bacon and eggs, and eggs in a bread hole all cook in minutes. A tin of baked beans warmed in the pan and spooned on toast is a classic Australian camp breakfast, and Vegemite toast needs no cooking beyond the toasting.

Pancakes from a shake-and-pour mix are the easy win with kids. Shake the bottle at camp, pour a pancake into a greased pan and top with fruit, maple syrup or honey. Porridge from rolled oats or instant sachets cooks in a few minutes, with water or milk, and is cheap and filling.

sections.heading: Barbecue and fire breakfasts
body: Many campgrounds, parks and rest areas have a free or coin-operated barbecue plate, and it cooks a good breakfast: bacon, eggs, sausages, halloumi, mushrooms and tomatoes, with bread rolls toasted on the edge. Bacon and egg rolls are a camping tradition for a reason.

Where a campfire is legal, the damper and foil parcel ideas in the campfire cooking guide also work for breakfast. Bananas in their skins with chocolate in foil is a sweet morning treat. Always check the fire rules first, and never light a fire on a fire ban day.
tips: Bacon and egg rolls on the barbecue

sections.heading: No-cook breakfasts
body: Overnight oats are made the night before by stirring rolled oats, milk or yoghurt and fruit in a jar and leaving it in the cooler. Muesli with long-life milk or yoghurt, wraps with peanut butter or cheese, fruit and pastries from the last bakery work when you are packing up early or the weather is wet.
These are the breakfasts for fire ban mornings, early starts and tired days, and a few of them in the cooler mean you are never stuck for something to eat.

sections.heading: Coffee and tea
body: A stovetop espresso pot, a plunger, a pour-over cone or good instant sachets all work on a camp stove. Pre-ground coffee keeps best in an airtight container, and a small kettle or a billy saves time. A hot drink in a thermos keeps for a morning on the road.
If you are cooking on a legal campfire, a billy of tea is the traditional choice, and the campfire cooking guide has the method.

sections.heading: Shopping and keeping it fresh
body: Supermarket eggs in Australia are sold unrefrigerated, but at camp, keep the carton in the cooler and use the eggs in the first few days. Bacon and fresh milk should stay cold and be used first. Long-life milk, powdered milk, rolled oats, pancake mix and tinned beans keep for weeks.

In remote country the range shrinks and prices rise, so stock up before long stretches. The grocery prices guide gives an idea of what a basket costs, and the packing list guide covers the cooking gear to carry.

sections.heading: Fire bans and mornings in the rain
body: On a fire ban day, wood and charcoal fires are illegal in the district, and some parks ban gas cookers as well. Keep a gas stove in the vehicle and plan a no-flame breakfast in case the park's rules are stricter.

In wet weather, cook under an awning or vehicle tailgate only if it is open, and never run a gas stove inside a tent or a closed vehicle. Wash up away from creeks and lakes, and take all rubbish and food scraps with you.
tips: Never cook in a closed tent

sections.heading: Plan the camp in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 1,393 dump points from park agencies, road authorities and public datasets, and each place page shows the facilities those sources publish, including barbecues where the source lists them. Build a trip as ordered stops and it shows the distance, drive time and forecast for each leg.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: What is an easy breakfast to make when camping?

Eggs and toast, porridge, pancakes from a shake-and-pour mix, bacon and egg rolls on a barbecue, and muesli with yoghurt or long-life milk all need one burner or no cooking at all. Pick the one that fits your gear and the morning's weather.
How do I keep eggs and milk fresh when camping in Australia?

Keep eggs in their carton in the coolest part of the cooler or fridge, and use them in the first few days. Long-life milk and powdered milk keep without a fridge, and fresh milk should stay cold in the cooler and be used first.
Can I cook breakfast on a fire ban day?

Not on a wood or charcoal fire. A gas stove is often still allowed, but some parks ban gas cookers on the worst days, so check the park's rules. Cold options such as muesli, overnight oats and wraps need no flame at all.
What is the easiest camping breakfast with no cooking?
Overnight oats made in a jar the night before, muesli with long-life milk or yoghurt, fruit, wraps with peanut butter or cheese and bakery items from the last town. None of them needs a stove.

sources.label: NSW RFS total fire ban rules

camper-trailer-guide-australia.title: Camper Trailer Guide for Australia: Towing, Setup and Where to Camp
camper-trailer-guide-australia.description: A guide to camper trailers in Australia: how they differ from caravans, towing basics, brakes and weight, setting up camp and where you can take one.
camper-trailer-guide-australia.imageAlt: Tents, a camper trailer and solar panels laid out at a bush campsite among casuarinas on the Queensland coast
camper-trailer-guide-australia.intro: A camper trailer folds out into a bed and a tent-style living space, tows low behind a car or 4WD, and sets up in minutes. It sits between a tent and a caravan in price, weight and comfort, and it goes more places than a caravan because it is smaller and, on an off-road model, built for rough tracks. Below are the types, the towing basics, how to set up at camp and where a camper trailer is welcome in Australia.

sections.heading: Types of camper trailer
body: Soft-floor camper trailers have a canvas tent on a fold-out frame and are the cheapest and lightest. Hard-floor models fold out from a rigid base, usually with a kitchen at the back or the side, and are more comfortable and quicker to set up. Hybrid and hard-top models are the most weatherproof and the most expensive.

Off-road camper trailers have a stronger chassis, longer travel suspension and a narrower body, so they follow a 4WD along a rough track. A standard on-road camper trailer is cheaper and does well on sealed roads and graded tracks. Pick the type that matches where you plan to go, not the most capable one.
tips: Soft floor, hard floor or hybrid
Match the trailer to the trip

sections.heading: Towing basics
body: Check your vehicle's rated towing capacity and the trailer's gross trailer mass, the mass of the trailer fully loaded, and stay under both. A common guide for the load on the tow ball is around 10% of the trailer's loaded mass, and a trailer that sits level behind the car tows more steadily.

Brakes depend on the trailer's gross mass. New South Wales requires none up to 750 kg, brakes on at least one axle from 751 to 2,000 kg, and brakes on all wheels above that, with a breakaway system over 2,000 kg. Other states have their own limits, so check your road authority.

Check the safety chains, the lights, the plug, the tyres and the coupling before every drive. The towing laws guide covers licence, weight and speed rules, and the first trip is a good time for a practice in an empty car park, because reversing a trailer takes a few tries to learn.

sections.heading: Setting up camp
body: Pick a level spot with room to open the trailer, chock the wheels and put the handbrake on before you unhitch. Level the trailer with the jacks or the legs, unlatch it and open it out in the order the manual says, and check that guy ropes and pegs are secure if the wind is up.

Most models set up in 10 to 30 minutes, and it gets quicker with practice. Do a dry run at home first, so the first time you open the trailer is not in the dark at a campground. Pack down dry where you can, or air the canvas as soon as you can, because damp canvas grows mould.

sections.heading: Where you can take a camper trailer
body: Caravan parks and holiday parks take camper trailers on powered and unpowered sites, and many have a drive-through or a slab for the trailer. Powered sites are handy for a fridge and lights, and the powered versus unpowered guide explains the difference.

Many national park campgrounds suit a camper trailer, and some are designed for them. Others limit trailers because of narrow tracks, steep access, soft sand or tight sites, and some beach and 4WD tracks do not allow trailers at all. Free camps and rest areas depend on the land manager and the council, with stay limits and size rules that vary.
Check the place before you go, because arriving with a trailer at a camp that cannot take it is a long reverse.
tips: Some tracks and beaches say no

sections.heading: Camper trailer or something else
body: A camper trailer is cheaper than most caravans and campervans, stores in a garage and keeps the tow vehicle free to unhitch and explore. The trade-off is setup time, which a campervan avoids, and less weather protection than a hard-sided caravan.

If you are visiting on a working holiday, a campervan is simpler because it is one vehicle to buy, register and sell. The campervan versus caravan guide compares the options on licence, registration and where each suits.
tips: Visitors often find a campervan simpler

sections.heading: Check each place's vehicle details in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities. A place page shows facilities and a Vehicles and RVs section, such as a car park or caravan sites, as the agency publishes it, so you can see what a place says about your setup before you drive there.
You can save places and build a trip with ordered stops, dates, notes and route distance. The app does not tell you a trailer's size limits for a given road, so read the agency's page.
tips: Read the Vehicles and RVs section
Check size limits on the agency page

faq: What is a camper trailer?

A camper trailer is a trailer that folds out into a bed and a tent-style living space. It tows low behind a car or 4WD, goes up in minutes and is lighter and cheaper than most caravans, so it suits couples and families who want more comfort than a tent.
Can I tow a camper trailer on a car licence in Australia?

Generally yes, within the limits of your licence and your vehicle. Check your tow vehicle's rated towing capacity and the trailer's gross mass, and read the road authority's rules for your state, especially if you hold a learner or provisional licence.
Does a camper trailer need brakes?

It depends on its weight. New South Wales requires no brakes up to 750 kg gross trailer mass, brakes on at least one axle from 751 to 2,000 kg, and brakes on all wheels above that, with a breakaway system over 2,000 kg. Other states have their own limits, so check yours.
Can I take a camper trailer to a national park campground?

Often yes, but not everywhere. Many national park campgrounds take camper trailers, while small bush camps, steep tracks and some beaches are unsuitable or restricted. Check the park agency's page for the specific campground before you go.

buying-selling-a-car-australia-rego-road.title: Buying and Selling a Car in Australia: Rego, Roadworthy and Pink Slip FAQs by State
buying-selling-a-car-australia-rego-road.description: Plain answers on rego, roadworthy certificates and the NSW pink slip when you buy or sell a car in Australia, with what each state asks for and the checks to do first.
buying-selling-a-car-australia-rego-road.imageAlt: A sealed stretch of the Eyre Highway west of Nullarbor Roadhouse, South Australia, with a warning sign for camels, wombats and kangaroos
buying-selling-a-car-australia-rego-road.intro: Rego, roadworthy and pink slip all mean something different depending on the state you buy or sell in. Rego is the yearly registration, a roadworthy or safety certificate is a mechanic's check that a car is safe to drive, and a pink slip is the New South Wales name for a safety inspection. This guide answers the common questions by state, lists the checks to run before you pay, and points to the road authority that has the final word.

sections.heading: The words, in plain English
body: Rego is registration: the yearly fee that lets a vehicle use public roads, with the plates and a sticker or an online record that shows it is current. In most states the fee already includes compulsory third party insurance, which covers injury to other people in a crash, and in a few states you pick a CTP insurer yourself.

A roadworthy certificate, called a safety certificate in Queensland, is a licensed inspector's statement that the car met the minimum safety standard on the day. It is not a mechanical warranty and it says nothing about the engine's future. A pink slip is the New South Wales word for its safety inspection, and a blue slip is a New South Wales inspection that checks a vehicle's identity, used for cars coming from interstate or overseas.
Comprehensive insurance is separate from all of this. Rego and CTP cover other people, not your own car, so arrange comprehensive or third party property cover before you drive away.
tips: A certificate is not a warranty

sections.heading: Which state wants what
body: The table is a guide to the usual rule for a private sale, not a promise. Rules change and have exemptions, so read your state's page before you advertise or hand over cash.
Where a state has no certificate requirement for a private sale, the buyer can still book an independent inspection, and for a car that is more than a few years old it is money well spent.
tips: Victoria and Queensland usually need a certificate
NSW calls it a pink slip

table.caption: The usual private-sale rules by state. Each road authority has the final word.

sections.heading: Checks before you buy
body: Start with a PPSR search, the national register that shows whether money is owed on a car and whether it has been written off or reported stolen. It costs a couple of dollars online, and it is the single best protection a private buyer has. Match the vehicle identification number on the car to the one on the paperwork and on the search.

Look at the rego record, which in most states you can check online with the plate, to see that it is current and to see the expiry. Ask for the service history, check the odometer against it, and take the car for a test drive that includes a motorway stretch and a cold start. If you can, pay for an independent inspection by a mechanic who is not connected to the seller.

Remember what the law gives you. The ACCC says a licensed dealer must meet consumer guarantees and often a state warranty, and that a private seller gives no warranty or cooling-off period but must still hold clear title. Buying privately is cheaper because the buyer carries more of the risk.
tips: Dealers carry more of the risk than private sellers

sections.heading: Selling: what you hand over
body: Give the buyer a signed receipt or sale agreement with the names, the price, the date, the odometer reading and the vehicle identification number, and keep a copy. Hand over the registration papers, the service history, the keys and the certificate your state needs.

Tell the road authority about the sale straight away or within the time your state gives, through the authority's online account or form. Keep the confirmation, and cancel or move your insurance and toll account the same day. The selling guide for campervans has the steps state by state, and the same steps apply to a car.
tips: Notify the road authority on the day

sections.heading: Visitors and working holiday travellers
body: A visitor can buy and register a car in most states, but the authority wants proof of identity and an address, and some states want an address inside the state. A friend's or a hostel's address does not always satisfy that, so ask first.

If you are staying a year or less, a car or a campervan with several months of rego left sells more easily, because the next buyer inherits the registration. The campervan buying guide covers the visitor rules in more detail, and the licence guide explains which licence you can drive on.
tips: Proof of identity and an address
Leave months of rego on the car

sections.heading: Plan the trip once you have the car in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps does not list or sell cars and cannot check a car's registration or history. What it can do is help you plan a trip with the car you have bought: campgrounds, national parks and rest areas, each with the facilities and fees the agency publishes.
You can save places to a trip with ordered stops, dates, notes and route distance, which is handy for a loop that ends in the city where you plan to sell. AussieCamps runs on iPhone.
tips: No car listings or history checks

faq: What is rego in Australia?

Rego is short for registration, the yearly permission to drive a vehicle on public roads. It is paid to the state or territory road authority, and in most states it includes compulsory third party (CTP) injury insurance, which in a few states you buy separately from an insurer.
What is a pink slip?

A pink slip is the New South Wales name for a safety inspection of a vehicle, done at an authorised inspection station. The rules for when one is needed have changed over the years, so check Service NSW for your vehicle before you buy or sell.
What is a roadworthy certificate?

A roadworthy certificate, or safety certificate in Queensland, is a mechanic's statement that a vehicle met the minimum safety standard on the day it was inspected. Victoria and Queensland generally need one when a private seller sells a registered vehicle, and other states have their own rules.
Do I need a roadworthy to sell my car?

In Victoria and Queensland, usually yes for a private sale, unless an exemption applies. In other states the seller often needs no certificate, but the buyer may need an inspection to register the car. Ask your state's road authority before you advertise.
How long do I have to transfer a car into my name?

Most states give the buyer about 14 days to transfer the registration, and the seller must tell the authority about the sale straight away or within a short window. Do both on the day of the sale, because until the transfer is done the old owner can be chased for tolls and fines.
Can a visitor buy and register a car in Australia?

Yes in most states, but each authority wants proof of identity and an address in the state. Queensland, for example, wants a Queensland address, so check the rules of the state where you buy before you hand over any money.

riverland-murray-river-camping-south-aus.title: Riverland Camping: The Murray River in South Australia
riverland-murray-river-camping-south-aus.description: Where to camp on the Murray River in South Australia's Riverland: national park river camps, Lake Bonney, Overland Corner, the river towns, fruit fly rules and when to go.
riverland-murray-river-camping-south-aus.imageAlt: A campsite at sunset in Hattah-Kulkyne National Park, on the Murray floodplain upstream of the Riverland
riverland-murray-river-camping-south-aus.intro: The Riverland is the stretch of the Murray River in South Australia between the Victorian border and Morgan, a run of river red gums, sandy bends, lagoons and irrigated orchards around the towns of Renmark, Berri, Loxton, Barmera and Waikerie. It is one of the easiest places in the state to camp by water: national park river camps, lakeside reserves and caravan parks with their own river frontage. Below is where to camp, the rules that catch visitors out and the best time to go.

sections.heading: Where the Riverland is
body: The Riverland sits in the east of South Australia, where the Murray enters the state from Victoria and New South Wales and winds west towards Morgan before turning south to the sea. The Sturt Highway runs through it on the way between Adelaide and Mildura or Sydney, so many people meet it on a longer drive, but it rewards a few slow days of its own.
The main towns are close together, which makes it easy to camp on the river at night and drive a short way for supplies, a bakery or a pub meal during the day.
tips: East of Adelaide, on the Sturt Highway
Good on the way to Mildura or Sydney

sections.heading: Murray River National Park and Chowilla
body: The Murray River National Park is split into sections along the river, including Katarapko near Loxton and Berri, Lyrup Flats and Bulyong Island near Renmark. Each has bush campsites on the river or its creeks, usually with few or no facilities, so bring water, a toilet plan and everything you need. National Parks South Australia takes bookings and fees for these sites online.

Further upstream, the Chowilla area near the border has remote river and creek camping among red gums and floodplain. Tracks can be sandy, and they close when the river floods or after rain, so check access before you take a campervan or a caravan in.
tips: Bring water and a toilet plan

sections.heading: Lake Bonney and Overland Corner
body: Lake Bonney at Barmera is a large, shallow freshwater lake beside the river, with sandy foreshore, swimming in the warmer months and a caravan park and camping areas along its shore. It is a popular base for families, and the water is calmer than the river for kayaks and kids.

Overland Corner, a short drive from Barmera, is one of the Riverland's oldest stops, with a historic hotel and river country around it. Riverfront camping in the area is a mix of reserves and private land, so read the signs, camp only where it is allowed and treat the pub as a lunch stop rather than a campground.

sections.heading: River towns and caravan parks
body: Renmark, Berri, Loxton, Waikerie and Morgan all have caravan parks, many right on the water with powered sites, cabins, showers and a boat ramp nearby. They are the easy choice in summer, in school holidays and when you want a hot shower after a few nights in the bush.

Some councils also run low-cost or free short-stay areas for self-contained vehicles. Stay limits and conditions vary from town to town and change over time, so check the current rule on the day rather than trusting an old list.

sections.heading: Fruit fly rules and fresh produce
body: The Riverland protects its orchards with strict fruit fly rules. Fresh fruit and some vegetables cannot be brought into the region, and there are quarantine bins on the main roads in. The rules can tighten during an outbreak, so check the current restrictions before you travel and plan to arrive with an empty fruit box.

The upside is the produce itself: oranges, stone fruit, nuts and wine from roadside stalls, farm gates and markets across the region. Buy it inside the Riverland and eat it there. The biosecurity guide explains the wider interstate rules.

sections.heading: When to go and what to watch for
body: Autumn and spring are the best seasons, with warm days, cool nights and calm water. Summer is very hot in the Riverland, often well over 35 degrees, which is fine for swimming and houseboats but hard work in a tent. Winter days are mild and nights can be cold.

The river itself sets the rules. High water floods campsites and closes tracks, and low water can expose snags and sandbars. Swim only where it is safe, never dive into the river, keep children close to the bank and watch for submerged logs. Fire bans apply through the warmer months, so carry a gas stove.

sections.heading: Seasonal work and longer stays
body: The Riverland is one of South Australia's main fruit and wine regions, and harvest work draws working holiday makers through much of the year. If you are staying for work, a caravan park with weekly rates is usually more practical than moving between free camps, and it gives you a reliable address and power.
The regional work guide covers the visa side and how to find a cheap place to stay while you work.

sections.heading: Plan the trip in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.
tips: Save river camps to a trip

faq: Can you camp on the Murray River in South Australia?

Yes. The Murray River National Park, Chowilla and several council and riverfront reserves in the Riverland have camping, and the river towns all have caravan parks on or near the water. Many national park sites are booked and paid online before you arrive, so check the park page first.
Is there free camping in the Riverland?

Some, but less than many people expect. A few riverfront reserves and towns allow short stays for free or for a small fee, and the rules change with floods, river levels and council decisions. Read the sign at each site and check the council page, and keep a paid campground as the fallback.
How far is the Riverland from Adelaide?

Renmark, at the far end of the Riverland, is roughly three hours from Adelaide along the Sturt Highway. Waikerie and Morgan are closer, at around two hours, which makes the lower river a good weekend trip.
Can I take fruit into the Riverland?

Usually not. The Riverland has strict fruit fly rules, and fresh fruit and some vegetables cannot be carried in from outside the region. Eat it or drop it in the quarantine bins on the way in, then buy fresh produce from the Riverland's own growers.

fleurieu-peninsula-camping.title: Fleurieu Peninsula Camping: Deep Creek, Beaches and the South Coast
fleurieu-peninsula-camping.description: Where to camp on South Australia's Fleurieu Peninsula: Deep Creek and Newland Head, beach camps on the gulf, the south coast towns, Cape Jervis for Kangaroo Island, and when to go.
fleurieu-peninsula-camping.imageAlt: The Coorong coast in South Australia, east of the Fleurieu Peninsula
fleurieu-peninsula-camping.intro: The Fleurieu Peninsula is the green, hilly country south of Adelaide, with the calm water of Gulf St Vincent on one side and the surf of the Southern Ocean on the other. In an hour or two from the city you reach bush campgrounds above wild coast at Deep Creek, beach camps on the gulf, whale-watching towns on Encounter Bay and the ferry to Kangaroo Island. It is small, busy and mostly paid camping, so the trick is knowing where to book and when to go.

sections.heading: Getting your bearings
body: The peninsula runs south-west from Adelaide to Cape Jervis. The west coast faces Gulf St Vincent, with sheltered beaches and small towns such as Normanville, Second Valley and Rapid Bay. The south coast faces the open ocean, with high cliffs, surf beaches and the larger towns of Victor Harbor, Port Elliot and Goolwa on Encounter Bay.
In between are farmland, forest and the McLaren Vale and Langhorne Creek wine areas. Distances are short, so one or two bases can cover most of it.
tips: Gulf coast in the west, ocean in the south
One or two bases are enough

sections.heading: Deep Creek and the wild south coast
body: Deep Creek is the largest area of natural bush on the peninsula, with steep valleys running down to a rugged coast, kangaroos at dusk and long views across Backstairs Passage to Kangaroo Island. It has several campgrounds, from car-based sites with toilets to walk-in camps, and all of them are booked and paid online through National Parks South Australia.

Some of the access roads are steep, unsealed and narrow, so check which campgrounds suit a two-wheel-drive campervan before you set off, and leave the big caravan at a sealed site. The Heysen Trail starts nearby at Cape Jervis and runs through the park, so day walks on it are easy to fit in.
tips: Walk part of the Heysen Trail

sections.heading: Newland Head and Waitpinga
body: Further east, Newland Head sits between Deep Creek and Victor Harbor, with campgrounds behind the dunes near Waitpinga Beach. The beach is beautiful and powerful, with strong rips, so it is a place for walking and watching the surf rather than swimming.
Like Deep Creek, it is a national parks campground with online bookings and limited facilities, so arrive with water and everything you need.

sections.heading: Beach camps on the gulf
body: The gulf side is calmer and better for swimming, snorkelling and fishing. Rapid Bay has a beachfront campground run by the council, close to the old jetty that divers and snorkellers visit, and Second Valley and Normanville have caravan parks a short walk from the water.
These are popular with Adelaide families, so book well ahead for summer weekends, long weekends and school holidays. Midweek outside those times you can often find a site at short notice.

sections.heading: Victor Harbor, Port Elliot and Goolwa
body: Encounter Bay's towns have the most caravan parks and the most facilities, with powered sites, cabins and easy shopping. Victor Harbor is the base for Granite Island and, from about June to October, for watching southern right whales close to shore.

Goolwa sits near the Murray mouth, where the river meets the sea and the Coorong begins. From here it is a short step to the coastal route east towards Melbourne, or north to the Riverland for more river camping.
tips: Whales from about June to October

sections.heading: Cape Jervis and the Kangaroo Island ferry
body: Cape Jervis is the tip of the peninsula and the departure point for the vehicle ferry to Kangaroo Island. Many people camp a night on the Fleurieu before an early sailing, which makes the crossing far less rushed.

Book the ferry well ahead in summer, check whether your hire company allows the vehicle on it, and plan your Kangaroo Island campsites before you go. The Kangaroo Island guide covers the island itself.
tips: Camp nearby before an early ferry

sections.heading: When to go and what to watch for
body: Spring and autumn are the best times, with mild weather and fewer crowds. Summer brings warm beach days, busy campgrounds and high fire danger, and total fire bans are common. Winter is cool, wet and windy on the south coast, but quiet, green and good for whales.
Swim at patrolled or sheltered beaches, stay off the cliff edges in wind and keep a gas stove for fire ban days. Most campgrounds sell out on long weekends, so book those early.

sections.heading: Plan the trip in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: Where can you camp on the Fleurieu Peninsula?

In Deep Creek and Newland Head, the two main parks on the south coast, at council-run beach camps such as Rapid Bay, and at caravan parks in towns like Normanville, Second Valley, Victor Harbor, Port Elliot and Goolwa. Park campsites are booked and paid online before you arrive.
Is there free camping on the Fleurieu Peninsula?

Very little. It is close to Adelaide and busy, so most camping is in parks, council campgrounds and caravan parks that charge a fee. Short low-cost stays exist in a few places, but plan on paying and booking, especially on weekends and in summer.
How far is the Fleurieu Peninsula from Adelaide?
The north of the peninsula is under an hour south of Adelaide, and Victor Harbor and Cape Jervis are about an hour and a half. That makes it one of the easiest weekend camping trips from the city.
Can I take a campervan from the Fleurieu to Kangaroo Island?

Yes. The vehicle ferry to Kangaroo Island leaves from Cape Jervis at the tip of the peninsula. Book the ferry well ahead in summer and in school holidays, and check your hire company allows the crossing.

australian-road-trip-food-to-try.title: Australian Road Trip Food: 15 Things to Eat on the Way
australian-road-trip-food-to-try.description: The food to try on an Australian road trip: bakery pies, sausage sizzles, fish and chips, pub classics, roadhouse burgers, sweet treats and regional produce, plus fruit rules at the borders.
australian-road-trip-food-to-try.imageAlt: Apples stacked on a stall at Queen Victoria Market in Melbourne
australian-road-trip-food-to-try.intro: Part of the fun of a road trip in Australia is what you eat between the camps: a hot pie from a country bakery, a sausage sizzle outside the hardware store, fish and chips on a jetty, a pub parmi after a long drive. Below are fifteen things worth trying on the way, where to find them, and the one rule that catches travellers out, which is carrying fruit across a border.

sections.heading: Bakery stops
body: 1. A meat pie. The country bakery is the classic road-trip stop, and a hot meat pie with tomato sauce is the classic order. Many bakeries make their own, with steak, pepper steak, chicken or curry fillings, and some towns are known for theirs.
2. A sausage roll or a pasty. The other bakery staples, good hot or cold and easy to eat in the car.

3. A vanilla slice or a lamington. A lamington is a square of sponge cake dipped in chocolate and rolled in coconut, and a vanilla slice is thick custard between pastry. Either goes well with a coffee before the next stretch of road.

sections.heading: Barbecues, chips and the pub
body: 4. A sausage sizzle. A sausage in white bread with onions and sauce, cooked by a local club or charity outside a hardware store or at a market. Buying one supports the club.
5. Fish and chips. Best eaten on the beach or a jetty in a coastal town, often with local fish such as flathead, whiting or barramundi depending on where you are.

6. A chicken parmi. A crumbed chicken schnitzel topped with tomato sauce, ham in some places, and melted cheese, served with chips and salad. Every country pub has one, and the name changes from parmi to parma depending on the state.
7. A burger with the lot. The Australian takeaway burger adds beetroot, a fried egg, bacon, cheese and often pineapple. Roadhouses and corner takeaways do the best ones.
tips: Fish and chips by the water
Parmi or parma at the pub

sections.heading: Pantry classics for the campervan
body: 8. Vegemite on toast. A salty yeast spread to scrape thinly on hot buttered toast, never spread thick. It is a good camp breakfast once you get the amount right.
9. Tim Tams. Chocolate biscuits that are a staple of every road-trip snack bag. Try a Tim Tam slam with a hot drink at camp.
10. Anzac biscuits. Oat, golden syrup and coconut biscuits that keep well for days in a tin, which makes them a good long-drive snack.
11. Damper. The bush bread of flour, water and salt baked in the coals. If you can have a legal campfire, the campfire cooking guide has the method.

sections.heading: Regional produce worth stopping for
body: 12. Tropical fruit in the north. Mangoes in the Top End and north Queensland in the warmer months, plus bananas, pineapples and other fruit from roadside stalls around the tropics.
13. Seafood on the coast. Oysters in Tasmania, on the New South Wales south coast and on South Australia's Eyre Peninsula, prawns in many coastal towns, and fresh fish from the co-op or the wharf.

14. Farm-gate fruit, nuts and cheese. Orchards, dairies and growers in regions such as the Riverland, the Adelaide Hills, the Goulburn Valley and the Atherton Tablelands sell straight from the farm gate or at weekend markets.
Many of these are seasonal, so ask locally what is good that week rather than hunting for something out of season.
tips: Oysters and fresh fish on the coast

sections.heading: Something for the hot afternoons
body: 15. An iced coffee or an ice cream from the servo. A flavoured milk or an iced coffee from the fridge at a country service station is a road-trip habit, and South Australians are loyal to their own brand. A paddle-pop or a Golden Gaytime on a hot afternoon is the other option.
On long hot days, though, water matters more than snacks. Carry plenty in the vehicle and refill at every town.
tips: A cold drink from the servo

sections.heading: Carrying food across borders
body: Australia's states protect their crops from pests such as fruit fly, and several of them, plus regions such as the Riverland and parts of Victoria and Tasmania, restrict what fresh fruit and vegetables you can bring in. There are quarantine bins and checkpoints on the main roads, and fines for carrying the wrong things.

Plan your shopping around the borders: run the fruit bowl down before you cross, eat what is left or drop it in the bin, and buy fresh again on the other side. The biosecurity guide covers the rules state by state.
tips: Run the fruit down before a border
Buy fresh on the other side

sections.heading: Eating well without spending a fortune
body: Bakery stops and pub meals add up over a long trip, so most people mix them with simple cooking at camp. Stock up in the bigger towns, where the supermarkets are cheaper than in remote general stores, and save the treats for the places they are famous.
The easy campervan meals guide has simple dinners for a small kitchen, and the eating out guide covers what to expect at pubs and cafes.
tips: Save treats for the famous places

sections.heading: Plan the stops in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: What food should I try on an Australian road trip?

A meat pie from a country bakery, a sausage sizzle, fish and chips by the water, a pub chicken parmi, a burger with the lot, Vegemite on toast, a lamington and a Tim Tam, plus local produce such as mangoes in the north, oysters on the south coast and stone fruit from the farm gates.
Where do you find the best food on a road trip in Australia?

In country bakeries, pubs, fish and chip shops near the water, farm gates and roadside stalls, and weekend markets. Roadhouses keep you fed on long empty stretches, but the small-town bakery is usually the better stop.
Can I carry fruit between states on a road trip?

Often not. Several states and regions restrict fresh fruit and some vegetables to keep out fruit fly and other pests, and there are quarantine bins and checkpoints on the main roads. Eat it or bin it before the border, and buy fresh again on the other side.
What is a sausage sizzle?

A sausage in a slice of white bread with fried onions and tomato sauce, cooked on a barbecue, usually by a local club or charity outside a hardware store, at a market or on election day. It is cheap, quick and very Australian.

australia-road-trip-mistakes-to-avoid.title: Australia Road Trip Mistakes to Avoid: 12 Common Ones
australia-road-trip-mistakes-to-avoid.description: The mistakes that catch people out on an Australian road trip: distances, driving at dusk, fuel and water, unsealed roads in a hire vehicle, camping rules, fire bans, fruit at borders and booking too late.
australia-road-trip-mistakes-to-avoid.imageAlt: A campervan parked near Noosa Heads, Queensland
australia-road-trip-mistakes-to-avoid.intro: Most road trips in Australia go well, and the ones that go wrong tend to go wrong in the same few ways: too many kilometres a day, a drive at dusk, a fuel stop missed, a dirt road a hire vehicle was not allowed on, or a night spent somewhere camping was not allowed. Here are twelve common mistakes and the simple habit that avoids each one.

sections.heading: Planning mistakes
body: 1. Underestimating the distances. Australia is about as big as mainland Europe or the lower forty-eight states of the US, and the gaps between towns get longer the further you go from the coast. Plan your days in hours, not kilometres, and leave a spare day for every week.
2. Trying to see everything. A two-week trip that covers the whole east coast and the Red Centre is mostly a view through a windscreen. Pick one region or one route and go slower.

3. Booking too late for peak times. Christmas, Easter, long weekends and school holidays fill popular campgrounds, caravan parks and ferries months ahead. If your trip falls in one of them, book the busy stops first.

sections.heading: Driving mistakes
body: 4. Driving at dawn, dusk or night. This is when kangaroos, wombats, cattle and other animals are on the road. Aim to be at camp before sunset and start after it is properly light. If something jumps out, brake in a straight line rather than swerving.
5. Pushing on when tired. Long straight roads are hypnotic. Stop every two hours, use the driver reviver stops and rest areas, swap drivers and never try to make up time at the end of the day.

6. Taking a hire vehicle where it is not allowed. Most two-wheel-drive campervans and many hire cars cannot legally go on unsealed roads under their hire terms, and the insurance stops at the bitumen. Read the terms before you plan a dirt road.
tips: Check your hire terms for dirt roads

sections.heading: Fuel, water and signal
body: 7. Passing the last fuel stop. In remote areas the next service station can be hundreds of kilometres away, and some close early or run out. Fill up whenever you can in the outback, and check opening hours before a long stretch.
8. Carrying too little water. Heat and dry air use it up fast. Carry several litres a person a day and more in summer or in the outback, plus spare in the vehicle in case of a breakdown.

9. Counting on phone signal. Mobile coverage disappears quickly outside towns and along most outback roads. Download what you need while you have signal, tell someone your plans and consider a satellite messenger or a personal locator beacon for remote trips.
tips: Fill up at every chance in remote areas
Carry more water than you think

sections.heading: Camping mistakes
body: 10. Assuming you can camp anywhere. Rules differ by state, council and park, and many towns, beaches and rest areas ban overnight stays. Camp where it is clearly allowed, check stay limits and book national park sites before you arrive.

11. Ignoring fire bans and the weather. A total fire ban means no campfires and sometimes no solid-fuel stoves, and the fines are large. Check the fire danger rating and the forecast every day, especially in summer, and leave early if a fire or flood warning affects your area.
tips: Camp only where it is allowed

sections.heading: Border and wildlife mistakes
body: 12. Carrying fruit across a border. Several states and regions ban fresh fruit and some vegetables to keep out fruit fly and other pests, with quarantine bins and checkpoints on the main roads. Run the fruit bowl down before a border and buy fresh on the other side.

A bonus one: swimming without reading the signs. Crocodiles live in rivers, estuaries and the sea across the tropical north, box jellyfish and other stingers are in northern waters in the warmer months, and surf beaches have rips. Swim only where it is clearly safe and between the flags at patrolled beaches.
tips: Empty the fruit bowl before a border

sections.heading: The habits that avoid most of them
body: Most of these mistakes come from the same thing: trying to do too much in too little time. Shorter driving days leave room to stop before dark, fill up when you can, check tomorrow's camp and enjoy the places you came to see.
The first campervan trip guide covers the first few days in a hire vehicle, and the long-distance driving guide goes deeper on rest breaks, fuel and other road users.

sections.heading: Plan the trip in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks from the state park agencies, plus 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. You can filter by cost, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.
The iPhone app is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: What is the biggest mistake on an Australian road trip?

Underestimating the distances. Places that look close on a map are often a full day's drive apart, and people who plan too many kilometres a day end up tired, driving at dusk and seeing little of where they stop.
Is it safe to drive at night in rural Australia?

It is best avoided. Kangaroos and other animals are most active around dawn and dusk and at night, and a collision can wreck a vehicle and hurt the people in it. Many hire companies also restrict driving in remote areas after dark. Plan to arrive at camp before sunset.
Can I camp anywhere in Australia?

No. Camping is allowed only where the land manager permits it, and the rules change from state to state, council to council and park to park. Many places ban overnight stays in a vehicle. Check the sign and the rules before you set up.
How far can I drive in a day in Australia?

Most people are comfortable with around 300 to 400 km a day with breaks, and less on unsealed or winding roads. Longer days are possible on empty highways, but stop every two hours and share the driving where you can.

best-campsite-booking-apps-australia.title: Best Campsite Booking Apps and Sites in Australia 2026: Where to Book in Every State
best-campsite-booking-apps-australia.description: Where to book a campsite in each state: NSW National Parks, Parks Victoria, Queensland Parks, WA Explore Parks, SA, Tasmania and the NT, plus holiday parks and AussieCamps.
best-campsite-booking-apps-australia.imageAlt: A grassy campground beside Mount Chingee National Park, Queensland
best-campsite-booking-apps-australia.intro: Australia has no single booking app for campsites. Each state's park agency runs its own system, holiday parks book through their own sites and chains, and private land uses separate marketplaces. Knowing which one to open for each state saves a lot of searching. We make AussieCamps, a directory app for finding campgrounds, so we have said where it fits and where you book on the agency's own site. The agency pages below were read in October and November 2026.

sections.heading: Quick comparison
body: Camping is booked state by state. The table shows where to book in each state and the one thing most likely to surprise you.

sections.heading: 1. NSW National Parks: website and app
body: New South Wales national park campgrounds are booked on the NSW National Parks website, and the free NSW National Parks app covers more than 225 parks and lets you locate campgrounds and book from the app. Camping fees are set campground by campground. A few have no camping fee at all, but an online booking carries a booking fee, so even a free night costs a few dollars to secure.

Most state forests are managed by the Forestry Corporation, where camping is free in most forests, first come, first served and limited to four weeks. They are not booked. The camping rules guide for NSW covers which is which.
tips: Book national park camps on the NPWS site or app
Booking fee applies even to free camps
State forests are first come, first served

sections.heading: 2. Parks Victoria: bookable and free sites
body: Parks Victoria runs the booking system for its bookable campgrounds, and fees are half price at bookable campgrounds until July 2027. Some sites are free and still bookable. Victoria's state forest campgrounds are separate: they are free and not bookable, and dispersed camping is allowed away from waterways in many forests. Parks Victoria has no app, so you book on its website.
Popular coastal and Grampians campgrounds fill around Christmas and Easter, so book those first and leave the forest nights flexible.
tips: State forest camps are free and not bookable

sections.heading: 3. Queensland Parks and Forests
body: Queensland is the strictest: a permit is needed for every camp in a national park, forest or recreation area, and it must be booked before you arrive. From 1 July 2026 camping costs $7.75 a person or $31 a family a night. Driving on K'gari and other sand islands needs a separate vehicle access permit, covered in our K'gari permits guide.
Rest areas are a different matter: Queensland's transport department says they are not camping sites or an accommodation option, with a 20-hour limit unless signed otherwise.
tips: $7.75 a person or $31 a family a night
Sand island vehicle permit is separate

sections.heading: 4. Explore Parks WA
body: The Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions books Western Australian national park camping on its Explore Parks site. Camping fees are $10, $15 or $20 an adult a night depending on the facilities, and park entry is charged separately, so add both when you cost a night.
Check the page for each park before you go, because the booking rules and fees are listed per campground.

sections.heading: 5. South Australia, Tasmania and the Northern Territory
body: South Australia books campsites and vehicle entry online before arrival through the Parks SA system. Tasmania's Parks and Wildlife Service requires a parks pass, even at free camps such as Cockle Creek and the Bay of Fires. Bookings for the Overland Track's 2026-27 season opened on 7 July 2026 through a virtual waiting room, and the peak December to March period was fully booked by 2pm that day.

In the Northern Territory you book and pay online before you arrive, and the same system covers Larapinta Trail and Jatbula Trail campsites. Fires are not allowed on the Larapinta Trail, which has a fuel stove only policy.
tips: SA: book online before you arrive
Tasmania: parks pass even for free camps
NT: book and pay online first

sections.heading: 6. Holiday parks and private land
body: Holiday and caravan parks book direct or through their chain, and prices change with the season. G'day Parks books its own network of more than 350 parks, and its G'day Rewards membership costs $50 for two years with 10% off bookings, up to $50 each. Our holiday park price guide has published rates for powered, unpowered and cabin sites.
Farm, station and vineyard stays are sold through separate private-land marketplaces, which you pay per booking and which do not replace a national park permit.

sections.heading: 7. AussieCamps: find the camp, then book it
body: AussieCamps is a directory, not a booking system for national park camps. It lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the state agency publishes them, and you can filter by cost, water, toilets, power and dogs, and save places to a trip. You then book on the agency's own system above.
Bookable holiday parks, motels and B&Bs from BookEasy can be booked in the app. It runs on iPhone and is free to download, with in-app purchases.
tips: Book national parks on the agency site
Holiday parks bookable in the app

sections.heading: How to book without losing a night
body: Look up the booking rules for the state before you plan the route, because the same trip can mix permits, passes and first-come camps. Book the peak dates first, such as school holidays, Christmas and Easter, and leave nights between them flexible for weather and road closures.

Check the cancellation terms on each system, and keep a screenshot of your confirmation in case you lose signal. If a campground is full, a nearby holiday park or a free state forest camp is usually the fallback, and our free camping apps guide covers where to find them.

faq: Is there one app that books every campsite in Australia?

No. National park and state forest camping is booked on each state agency's own system, holiday parks book direct or through their chain, and private-land stays use separate marketplaces. A directory app helps you find places, but you usually book on the agency's site.
Do I have to book a national park campsite in advance?

In Queensland, South Australia and the Northern Territory you book and pay online before you arrive, and Tasmania needs a parks pass. New South Wales and Victoria have both bookable and first-come or free campgrounds, so check the page for the one you want.
Why does a free campsite still cost something to book?
Some New South Wales campgrounds have no camping fee, but booking online adds a booking fee. Tasmania's free camps still need a valid parks pass for park entry.
When should I book for summer and school holidays?

As soon as you know your dates. Popular coastal and national park sites fill well ahead of Christmas, Easter and school holidays, and Tasmania's Overland Track sells its peak season within hours of opening in July.

best-hiking-bushwalking-apps-australia.intro: A hiking app in Australia has to do more than show a track. Most walks leave phone signal behind, the weather can turn quickly, and the best multi-day walks need a booking months ahead. No one app does all of it, so most walkers carry a trail app, a weather source and a safety app. We make AussieCamps, which is a camping directory and not a trail app, so it appears for the camp at either end of the walk, and each section says what fits when. Features and prices were read on the apps' own pages in November 2026.

sections.heading: 1. AllTrails: day walks and trail maps
body: AllTrails is the most widely used trail app for finding walks near you, with trail maps, distance and elevation, and filters for difficulty and length. The free plan covers browsing and following a trail, and a paid plan adds downloadable maps for use without signal, so download the walk at home before you leave.
Trail information is partly contributed by users. For closures, track conditions and fire bans, check the park agency's page for the day you walk, because a map does not know a track has been closed.

sections.heading: 2. ExplorOz Traveller: remote tracks and topo maps
body: ExplorOz Traveller suits walkers and drivers who go beyond the popular trails. It lists more than 100,000 places across Australia and has named roads, tracks and trails on topographic maps. It costs A$59.99 upfront, and the EOTopo maps that work without signal are purchased in the app, from A$59.99 a year or A$79.99 for a four-year edition.
That is a serious outlay for a few day walks and good value for someone crossing the outback. Our ExplorOz alternatives guide compares it with cheaper apps.
