sections.heading: 3. NSW National Parks app: one state, done properly
body: The free NSW National Parks app covers more than 225 parks, helps you locate campgrounds and lets you book from the app. It is the official source for New South Wales park alerts, so check it before the Blue Mountains, Kosciuszko or the South Coast, where closures after fire or storm are common.
Other states have no equivalent app. Parks Victoria, for example, has a website only, so check the agency's page for the park before you go.
tips: Official New South Wales park information

sections.heading: 4. Emergency+: your location for 000
body: Emergency+ is a free app, built with the emergency services, that uses your phone's GPS to show your coordinates so you can read them to a call taker. It also lets you choose a street address or a what3words address, and lists the SES and Police Assistance Line numbers.

It does not replace a way to call. You still need a mobile network to make the 000 call, and on a remote track a personal locator beacon or satellite messenger is the safer backup. Install it before you go and open it once so it is ready.
tips: Still needs a network to call

sections.heading: 5. BOM Weather: forecasts and warnings
body: The Bureau of Meteorology app gives forecasts, radar and warnings for your location, and it is the official source for severe weather. Check it the evening before and the morning of a walk, and again if the sky changes. Our weather apps guide compares it with six others.
Alpine and gorge walks can change fast. If a warning is issued, turn around: the track will still be there another day.
tips: Check the evening before and the morning of
Turn back if a warning is issued

sections.heading: 6. AussieCamps: the camp at either end
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the state agency publishes them, and you can filter by cost, water, toilets and dogs. It is useful for the night before a walk or the base for day walks. It does not show trail maps, so pair it with one of the apps above.
It runs on iPhone and is free to download, with in-app purchases.
tips: Find the camp near the trailhead

sections.heading: Booking the big walks
body: The best-known multi-day walks are booked, not turned up to. The Overland Track in Tasmania has a booking system with a pass for its season, and bookings for the 2026-27 season opened on 7 July 2026, when the peak December to March period sold out by 2pm. In the Northern Territory, the Larapinta Trail and Jatbula Trail campsites are booked and paid online before you go, and fires are not allowed on the Larapinta Trail.
Book the permit and the campsites before you buy the flights, and carry the confirmation where you can read it without signal.
tips: Overland Track sells out within hours

sections.heading: A short safety checklist
body: Tell someone your route and when you expect to be back, and carry more water than the distance suggests. Download the map and the weather before you lose signal, take a paper map for remote walks and consider a personal locator beacon.
Turn back if the weather, the light or your energy says so. Most rescues start with a walker who kept going.
tips: Carry a locator beacon on remote tracks

faq: What is the best app for bushwalking in Australia?

It depends on the walk. AllTrails suits day walks, ExplorOz Traveller suits remote tracks, the park agency's own page is the source for closures and bookings, and Emergency+ is worth installing for any walk away from town.
Do I need a booking for multi-day walks in Australia?

For the best known ones, yes. The Overland Track in Tasmania has a booking and pass for its season, and the Larapinta and Jatbula trails in the Northern Territory need campsites booked and paid online before you go.
Will walking apps work without phone signal?
Only if you download the maps first. Some apps lock map downloads behind a paid plan, so download the walk at home on wi-fi and carry a paper map or a personal locator beacon on remote tracks.
How do I call for help on a walk with no signal?
Triple zero (000) needs a mobile network, but a phone will try any available network if your own has none, and 112 does the same. A personal locator beacon works with no network at all.

sources.label: Parks and Wildlife Service Tasmania: Overland Track booking information

snow-chains-winter-driving-australia.title: Snow Chains and Winter Driving in Australia: Rules for Kosciuszko and the Victorian Alps (2026)
snow-chains-winter-driving-australia.description: When snow chains are required in Kosciuszko National Park and at Victoria's alpine resorts, which vehicles must carry them, the fines, and how to drive a campervan to the snow.
snow-chains-winter-driving-australia.imageAlt: A road with snow beside it in Kosciuszko National Park
snow-chains-winter-driving-australia.intro: Most of Australia never needs a snow chain, but the alpine roads of New South Wales and Victoria do, and the rules are strict. In Victoria all vehicles entering the main alpine resorts must carry chains throughout the declared snow season, and in Kosciuszko National Park two-wheel-drive vehicles must carry them from the June long weekend to the October long weekend. Police check, and vehicles without chains are turned back. This guide sets out the rules as the official pages state them, and what they mean for a campervan or a car with camping gear.

sections.heading: The short answer
body: If your route includes the snow, carry chains in the right size and know how to fit them. The rules differ by state, and the table shows who has to carry them and when.

table.caption: Snow chain rules for the main alpine areas, from the official pages, November 2026.
head: Area
When
Who must carry chains
rows: June long weekend to October long weekend
All two-wheel-drive vehicles; four-wheel drives are exempt from carrying
Falls Creek, Mt Buller, Mt Hotham, Mt Baw Baw and Mt Stirling, Victoria
The declared snow season, 7 June to 4 October in 2026
Every vehicle entering, including all-wheel and four-wheel drives
Decided daily by weather and road conditions

sections.heading: Kosciuszko National Park in New South Wales
body: NSW National Parks says all two-wheel-drive vehicles must carry snow chains between the June long weekend and the October long weekend. The requirement applies to Kosciuszko Road from the park boundary at the Thredbo River up to Perisher Valley, to the Alpine Way between Thredbo and Tom Groggin, and to the Guthega and Island Bend road. Four-wheel drives are exempt from carrying under the park regulations.

Chains are recommended but not required on the Alpine Way between Jindabyne and Thredbo and on the Snowy Mountains Highway. The designated sections can change, so check the NSW National Parks and Live Traffic NSW pages the day you drive.
tips: Recommended on the Snowy Mountains Highway

sections.heading: The Victorian Alps
body: Victoria is stricter. Alpine Resorts Victoria says that in the declared snow season, which ran from 7 June to 4 October in 2026, all vehicles entering Falls Creek, Mt Baw Baw, Mt Buller, Mt Hotham and Mt Stirling must carry snow chains at all times. That includes all-wheel and four-wheel drives. Lake Mountain is decided daily.

You must also fit the chains when signs, resort staff or police direct you to, in the chain fitting bays. Victoria Police's 2026 release put the fine at $407 for failing to carry chains and $1018 for failing to fit them when required, and police patrol the roads to Mt Buller, Mt Hotham and Falls Creek every day of the season. Last season, 1,471 vehicles were turned back at Mt Hotham alone for not carrying chains.

sections.heading: Buy or hire the right chains
body: Chains must match your tyre size, so check the size on the sidewall and buy or hire a set that lists it. Fit them to the drive wheels, and practise in the driveway, because the first time you fit them should not be in a snowstorm on a hillside. Resort towns and tyre shops hire chains.
Carry gloves, a torch and a waterproof mat for kneeling, and check chains for broken links before each trip.

sections.heading: Driving a campervan to the snow
body: Alpine roads are steep, winding and icy in the morning, and a loaded van is heavy and slow to stop. Drive in a low gear on descents instead of riding the brakes, leave a large gap, and expect the road to be shaded and frozen long after the sun reaches the valley.

Check the hire contract first. Many hire companies restrict where the vehicle may go and what the insurance covers, and snow roads may be excluded. If a hire van is not allowed, a day tour from Jindabyne, Thredbo or Bright is simpler than breaking the contract.

sections.heading: Camping in the alps in winter
body: Many alpine campgrounds are closed or buried in winter, and nights drop well below freezing at altitude. The lower valleys are warmer and have holiday parks with powered sites and heating, which makes them the practical base for a snow day. Our winter camping guide covers where Australia stays warm and where the snow is.
Fires and cold are the main risks at camp. Keep fuel for heating dry, ventilate a van when you use a heater, and never run a gas stove or barbecue inside a closed space.
tips: Base in a valley holiday park

sections.heading: Plan the base in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists campgrounds, national parks and holiday parks across New South Wales and Victoria, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. Use it to find a base near Jindabyne, Bright or Mansfield, and save the stops to a trip to see the driving distance between them.
It runs on iPhone and is free to download, with in-app purchases.
tips: Find a base outside the snow zone

faq: Do I need snow chains in Australia?

Only if you drive into the Australian Alps in winter. In Victoria, every vehicle entering Falls Creek, Mt Baw Baw, Mt Buller, Mt Hotham and Mt Stirling must carry chains during the declared snow season, including four-wheel drives. In Kosciuszko National Park in New South Wales, two-wheel-drive vehicles must carry them from the June long weekend to the October long weekend.
Do four-wheel drives need chains in Kosciuszko?

New South Wales exempts four-wheel drives from the carrying rule in Kosciuszko National Park, but not in Victoria, where the rule covers all-wheel and four-wheel drives too. Conditions can still require chains to be fitted, and carrying them is sensible on any alpine road.
What is the fine for not carrying chains in Victoria?
Victoria Police's 2026 snow season release put the fine for failing to carry chains at $407 and for failing to fit them when required at $1018. Amounts change each year, so check the current figure.
Can I take a hire campervan to the snow?
Check your hire contract before you plan it. Many contracts restrict where the vehicle may go and what it is covered for, and the company decides whether snow roads are allowed.

wet-weather-camping-australia.title: Wet Weather Camping in Australia: Rain, Flooded Roads and Staying Dry
wet-weather-camping-australia.description: How to camp in the rain in Australia: where to pitch, keeping gear and a campervan dry, cooking in the wet, checking road closures and when to move on.
wet-weather-camping-australia.imageAlt: A rain shower over the Albert River Valley in Lamington National Park, Queensland
wet-weather-camping-australia.intro: Rain is part of camping in Australia, from a passing coastal shower to a week of monsoon in the north. A wet trip can still be a good one if the pitch is right, the gear stays dry and you know when a road or a creek means it is time to move. Here is how to choose where to pitch, keep dry, cook and stay warm, and check the roads before you drive.

sections.heading: Choose the pitch before the rain
body: Look for slightly higher, well-drained ground, and avoid dips where water will pool. Never pitch in a dry creek bed or on a low river flat, because rain falling far upstream can fill them overnight, and keep away from dead limbs and tall trees in wind.
Pitch the tent with the door away from the wind, and put a tarp or awning over the cooking area so you have a dry place to sit. In a campervan, park on level ground that is not a runoff channel.
tips: Away from creek beds and dead limbs

sections.heading: Keep gear and bedding dry
body: Pack clothes, sleeping bags and food in waterproof bags or lidded boxes, and keep one set of dry clothes that never leaves the sleeping area. Leave wet boots and coats in the vestibule or under the awning, not in the bed.
Use a groundsheet under the tent, and check seams and guy ropes before the trip. A footprint that sticks out past the tent catches rain and funnels it underneath.

sections.heading: Condensation and ventilation
body: A closed tent or van in the rain fogs up with breath, wet clothes and cooking. Open a vent or window a little even when it is wet, wipe the inside surfaces in the morning and dry towels and clothes at a holiday park laundry or in a dryer rather than hanging them inside.
Never run a gas stove, heater or barbecue inside a closed tent or van, because of carbon monoxide and fire.

sections.heading: Cooking and keeping warm
body: Plan wet-weather meals that need one pot and little preparation, and keep a hot drink flask, soup and bread or wraps in reserve. A stove with a windshield and a dry spot under an awning makes the difference between a hot dinner and cold sandwiches.
A wet camp gets cold faster than a dry one, so keep a warm layer, a hat and dry socks for the evening. Our easy campervan meals guide has simple dinners for the days you do not want to cook.
tips: Flask and a dry spot to cook

sections.heading: Roads, creeks and closures
body: Clay and gravel roads turn slippery or close after rain, and creek crossings and floodways can go under quickly. Check road conditions before you drive, and expect closures after heavy rain in any state, not only in the tropical north.

Never drive through floodwater. Queensland's Get Ready campaign says it can take as little as 15 cm of water for a car to lose traction and be swept away, and you cannot see whether the road under the water is still there. If it is flooded, wait for it to drop or turn around.

table.caption: Where to check road conditions by state, from each road authority, November 2026.
head: State
Road conditions

sections.heading: When to move on
body: If a severe weather warning is issued for your area, if the creek is rising or if the campground is flooding, leave early. Move to a holiday park, a cabin or a motel in a larger town on higher ground, and treat a closed road as a rest day rather than looking for a way around.
It helps to know your fallback before the rain arrives, because holiday parks and motels fill quickly when a storm hits a popular coast.

sections.heading: Find a fallback in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists campgrounds, national parks and rest areas with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them, and holiday parks, motels and B&Bs from BookEasy that you can book in the app. Save a trip with each night's stop and it shows the forecast for your arrival date within the forecast range.
It runs on iPhone and is free to download, with in-app purchases.
tips: Find a roof when the weather turns

faq: Can I camp in the rain in Australia?

Yes, and plenty of trips do. Pick a pitch on slightly higher ground, put the tent or van away from dead limbs and creek beds, and keep a dry spot for cooking. Check the forecast and warnings each day, and leave if a warning is issued for your area.
How do I stop condensation in a tent or campervan?
Ventilate. Open a vent or window a little even in the rain, keep wet clothes outside the sleeping area, and wipe down surfaces in the morning. A closed, wet space fogs up quickly.
Should I drive on unsealed roads after rain?

Avoid it. Clay and gravel roads turn slippery or close after rain, and hire contracts usually ban unsealed roads anyway. Check road conditions with the council, park or road authority before you set off.
What if a creek or road floods?
Never drive through floodwater. Wait for the water to drop or turn around, and do not camp in a dry creek bed, because rain falling upstream out of sight can fill it overnight.

sources.label: Queensland Get Ready: if it's flooded, forget it

campervan-vs-car-and-tent-australia.title: Campervan vs Car and Tent in Australia: Costs, Rules and Comfort (2026)
campervan-vs-car-and-tent-australia.description: Campervan or car and tent for an Australian road trip: running costs, fuel, camping rules, where you can sleep, comfort in the weather and who each suits.
campervan-vs-car-and-tent-australia.imageAlt: A campervan parked at Aldinga, South Australia
campervan-vs-car-and-tent-australia.intro: The choice is between a campervan, which is a bed, a kitchen and a vehicle in one, and a car with a tent, which is cheaper to start but more work every day. Neither is better for everyone. The right one depends on the length of the trip, the season, the roads and how much you want to set up each night. Here is how they compare on cost, rules, comfort and the kind of trip each suits.

sections.heading: At a glance
body: A tent is cheaper to carry and gives you more places to camp, while a van is faster to set up and more comfortable in bad weather.

table.caption: Campervan and car with a tent compared for an Australian road trip, November 2026.
head: Point
Campervan
Car and tent
rows: Daily hire, or buying a vehicle
Hire car or your own car, plus a tent
Heavier, so more fuel per kilometre
Longer, and harder in rain or wind
Shelter on wet and cold nights
Wind, rain and heat are felt directly
Campgrounds only, where a tent is allowed
Hire contracts often ban unsealed roads
A car is subject to its own hire terms

sections.heading: Cost: where the money goes
body: A campervan's cost is mostly the vehicle, which you pay for every day whether you drive or not, and the add-ons around it. For example, Apollo and Maui's published High Road cover is $67 a day, which comes to $938 for 14 days, before the daily rate, a one-way fee, extra drivers or a kit. A tent has none of that.

Fuel is the line that dominates over Australian distances. The Australian Institute of Petroleum put the five-largest-city average at $2.33 a litre for petrol and $2.77 for diesel in the week ending 1 November 2026. At those prices 1,000 km costs about $280 in a campervan using 12 litres per 100 km on petrol, and about $186 in a car using 8, so a heavier van costs more every day it runs.
tips: Fuel is the largest running cost
A lighter car uses less fuel

sections.heading: Where you can sleep
body: Rules are written for the place, not the vehicle. National park campsites need a booked permit in Queensland whether you sleep in a tent or a car, and councils often count sleeping in a parked car or van as camping. A holiday park or a campground is the safe choice for either.

A tent suits fewer places than a vehicle: it needs a pitch, so it is limited to campgrounds and permitted camping, while a campervan can use a signed overnight area at a rest area. In Queensland rest areas allow up to 20 hours unless signed, and in Western Australia up to 24 consecutive hours where signed, but both are stopping places and not campsites.
tips: Rules follow the place, not the vehicle
Rest areas allow a short stop

sections.heading: Comfort, weather and safety
body: A van keeps you out of the wind and rain and cooks under cover, which counts on a wet week. A tent is cooler in hot weather with the flaps open but lets in the weather, and pegging out in strong wind takes practice. Inland and alpine nights fall below freezing in winter, so a sleeping bag rated for the conditions matters in both.

Never run the engine for heating or bring a gas stove or heater into a tent or van, because of carbon monoxide. Heat is the main limit on sleeping in a vehicle, since cabins warm quickly after sunrise.

sections.heading: Licence, size and roads
body: A car licence covers a campervan up to 4.5 tonnes gross vehicle mass seating up to 12 people, including the driver, so most campervans need no special licence. A larger motorhome is a different matter, and the road rules for towing and size are in our campervan vs caravan guide.

Most hire companies ban unsealed roads for 2WD campers, apart from a short access road to a campground, and a hire car has its own terms. Read the contract before you plan a dirt road, because the insurance can stop at the bitumen.
tips: Check hire contract for unsealed roads

sections.heading: Who each suits
body: A campervan suits a longer trip, a wet or cold season, travellers who change camp often and people who want a bed made in minutes. A car and a tent suit a short trip, a tight budget, a few nights in one place, and travellers who want national park camps and the quiet of a tent.
You do not have to choose for the whole trip. Some travellers hire a car and tent for a week and rent a cabin or a holiday park site on the wettest nights.
tips: Van for long or wet trips
Mix both on a long route

sections.heading: Plan either trip in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 745 national parks, with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them. Filter by cost, water, toilets and power, save places to a trip and see the driving distance between stops.
It runs on iPhone and is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: Is a campervan or a car and tent cheaper in Australia?

A car and tent usually costs less to run, because the car uses less fuel and a tent needs no hire add-ons. A campervan's cost is mostly the daily hire or the purchase, then fuel, which is the biggest running cost over Australian distances. Work it out for your own dates and route.
Can I sleep in my car instead of a tent?

Only where camping is allowed. Many councils count sleeping in a parked car as camping, and national park permits apply whether you sleep in a tent or the car. A booked campground or a signed rest area is the safe choice.
Do I need a special licence for a campervan?
Not for a typical one. A car licence covers a vehicle up to 4.5 tonnes gross vehicle mass seating up to 12 people, including the driver. Check your overseas licence rules for each state.
Which is better for a first trip?
Choose the one you will enjoy on a wet, cold or hot night, not only a dry one. A tent is cheap to try, and a van adds comfort and speed of setting up.

sources.label: Australian Institute of Petroleum: weekly petrol prices report

two-week-australia-trip-cost.title: How Much Money Do You Need for Two Weeks in Australia? A Camping Road Trip Budget (2026)
two-week-australia-trip-cost.description: A worked budget for two weeks in Australia by campervan or car: daily costs, hire add-ons, fuel, campsites and a reserve, with totals for a frugal and a mixed trip.
two-week-australia-trip-cost.imageAlt: The long straight Stuart Highway in the Northern Territory
two-week-australia-trip-cost.intro: Two weeks is the trip most visitors plan, and the honest answer is a range. A frugal camping trip can run on about $1,120 to $1,820 a person for food, beds and local costs, and a mixed trip with caravan parks and meals out on about $2,240 to $3,640, before flights and the vehicle. The vehicle, its fuel and the add-ons then come on top. This guide builds the total in steps, using the daily budgets from our Australia travel cost guide and published hire and fuel prices from October and November 2026.

sections.heading: The short answer
body: The two daily budgets in the travel cost guide, multiplied by 14 days, give the base for food, beds and local costs. The table adds the vehicle and fuel that a road trip needs.

table.caption: Two weeks in Australia per person for food, beds and local costs, before flights and the vehicle, based on the 2026 daily budgets.
head: Style
Per day
Fourteen days
What it assumes
rows: Cooking almost every meal, free camps and cheap national park sites, moderate distances
A caravan park every third night, some meals out and a few paid activities

sections.heading: Add the vehicle
body: A hired campervan is the largest single item. Prices vary by company and season, and daily rates are quoted at booking rather than published, so get quotes for your dates. Add-ons are published: Apollo and Maui's High Road cover is $67 a day, so a 14-day hire costs $938 for cover, plus a one-way fee such as $200 for Sydney to Cairns, an extra driver at $4 a day and an RV Essentials Kit at $155. Those add-ons come to $1,349 before the daily rate, fuel and campsites.
A car and tent trip costs less to start with, because you skip the add-ons. Our campervan vs car and tent guide compares the two.
tips: Add cover, one-way and extra driver fees
The bond is held on your card

sections.heading: Add the fuel
body: Fuel is the line that grows with distance. Multiply kilometres by litres per 100 km, divide by 100, then by the price per litre. The Australian Institute of Petroleum put the five-largest-city average at $2.33 a litre for petrol and $2.77 for diesel in the week ending 1 November 2026, and remote roadhouses charge more.

A fortnight covering 2,000 km at 12 litres per 100 km uses 240 litres, or about $559 on petrol and $665 on diesel at those averages. Add 15 per cent for detours, and budget for the higher price on remote legs.

sections.heading: Campsites and park fees
body: Campsites are usually a smaller line than people expect. Queensland's national park camping costs $7.75 a person or $31 a family a night from 1 July 2026, Western Australia's costs $10, $15 or $20 an adult by facilities, and a holiday park powered site runs from about $30 to $60 a night in the published 2026 tariffs. Park entry and booking fees are often separate.
Mix cheap or free nights with a serviced night every few days for showers, laundry and water. It usually earns its price.
tips: Cabins cost more in peak season

sections.heading: The costs that only appear once you arrive
body: Excess reduction, one-way fees, a local SIM, park passes and the bond held on your card are rarely included in a daily budget, and together they add several hundred dollars to a fortnight. Interstate quarantine can also cost you produce you bought before a border.
Contactless cards are accepted almost everywhere, but carry some cash for honesty boxes and remote roadhouses, and use a card with no foreign transaction fees.

sections.heading: A worked example
body: Take two people sharing a campervan for 14 days on a mixed budget. Food, beds and local costs run $2,240 to $3,640 each; add the hire add-ons of $1,349 for the van and about $559 to $665 for 2,000 km of fuel, plus the daily hire rate on your quote. Flights are separate.

Shared costs fall per person when two travel together, which is why a van with two people is often cheaper than two solo travellers. Hold a reserve of several hundred dollars on top, separate from the daily budget.
tips: Split the van and fuel between two

sections.heading: Track the trip in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas and 745 national parks, with each place's fees and rules as the agency publishes them, so you can compare the cost of a night before you drive. Save the stops to a trip to see the driving distance between them and work out the fuel.
It runs on iPhone and is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: How much money do I need for two weeks in Australia?

For two weeks of food, beds and local costs, about $1,120 to $1,820 a person if you cook most meals and camp cheaply, and about $2,240 to $3,640 on a mixed budget with caravan parks and some meals out. Flights and the vehicle are extra.
What costs the most on an Australian road trip?
For most trips the order is the vehicle, fuel, food, campsites and activities. Fuel is the biggest running cost over Australian distances, and a slower route saves more than a cheaper campsite.
How much fuel will two weeks of driving use?

Multiply the kilometres by litres per 100 km, divide by 100 and multiply by the price per litre. A 2,000 km trip at 12 litres per 100 km uses 240 litres, about $559 at the November 2026 city petrol average.
How much should I keep as a reserve?
Hold enough for a tyre, a windscreen or a night in a cabin when the weather turns, and keep it separate from the daily budget so you never have to decide whether an unexpected cost is affordable.

sources.label: Australian Institute of Petroleum: weekly petrol prices report
Australian Institute of Petroleum: weekly diesel prices report
Tourism Australia: Australia on a budget

wine-regions-campervan-australia.title: Australian Wine Regions by Campervan: Barossa, Margaret River, Hunter Valley and More
wine-regions-campervan-australia.description: How to visit Australia's wine regions by campervan: the Barossa, McLaren Vale, Margaret River, the Hunter Valley and the Yarra Valley, where to stay, drink-driving rules and when to go.
wine-regions-campervan-australia.imageAlt: Vineyard rows in the Barossa Valley, South Australia
wine-regions-campervan-australia.intro: A campervan and a wine region suit each other: you can base yourself near the vines, cook local produce and wake up in the country. The catch is that wine regions are built around cellar doors and accommodation, not free camping, so the stay needs more planning than the tasting. Here are five regions that work from a campervan, how to stay legally, and the rule about drinking and driving that every driver needs to follow.

sections.heading: Five regions that work by van
body: Each region is within a day's drive of a capital city, which makes them easy to add to a longer route or to do as a long weekend.

table.caption: Wine regions for a campervan trip and their nearest city, November 2026.
head: Region
State
Nearest city
Good for
rows: About an hour north-east of Adelaide
Shiraz, small towns and cellar doors close together
Coast and vineyards in one day, with the Fleurieu Peninsula beyond
About three hours south of Perth
About two hours north of Sydney
The nearest big wine region to Sydney
About an hour east of Melbourne
A day or weekend trip from Melbourne

sections.heading: Where to stay
body: Wine regions have holiday parks and caravan parks in the main towns, and that is the reliable choice for a van. Book ahead for weekends, long weekends and vintage season, because rooms and sites fill with day-trippers and festival visitors. Our holiday park price guide has published rates.

Free camping is limited. Margaret River has few free options, and our free camping guide for the region explains what is allowed. Rest areas and state forest camps are a long way from many cellar doors, so a powered site in a town often costs less than the taxis it saves.
tips: A powered site in town is practical

sections.heading: Vineyard and farm stays
body: Some vineyards and farms offer stays on their land through private-land booking sites, where you pay per night and the host sets the rules. Check what the listing allows for a van, including power, toilets and access in wet weather.
Never assume a winery car park is open to overnight stays. Camping on private land needs the owner's permission, and a cellar door that welcomes visitors by day may not welcome a van at night.
tips: Private land follows the host's rules

sections.heading: The drink-driving rule
body: The drink-driving limit is 0.05 blood alcohol concentration for a full licence holder in every state, and zero for learner, provisional and some other drivers. Random breath tests operate on country roads as well as cities, and tastings add up faster than people expect.
Pick a designated driver, book a tour or taxi, or taste at a cellar door in the town where you are camping and walk back. Our drink-driving guide for visitors covers the limits by state.
tips: Taste near camp or use a driver

sections.heading: When to go
body: Vintage in most regions is roughly February to April, which is busy and warm, with harvest festivals and full camps. Spring and early summer are milder and greener, and winter is quiet in the cooler regions, with lower prices and cold nights.
Book the busy periods early and check fire danger in summer, because dry country and hot days bring bans and closures. Our best time guide covers the climate zones.

sections.heading: Cooking with local produce
body: Regions that grow grapes also grow olives, cheese, bread and fruit, and farm gates and markets make cooking from a van easy. Buy fresh produce after a state border, not before, because quarantine rules ban fruit and some vegetables at some borders.
Keep wine secured while driving and drink it at camp, not at a rest area or on the road.

sections.heading: Plan the route in AussieCamps
body: AussieCamps lists campgrounds, national parks and rest areas with each place's facilities, fees and rules as the agency publishes them, plus holiday parks you can book in the app from BookEasy. Save the stops to a trip to see the driving distance between regions.
It runs on iPhone and is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: Can I drive a campervan between wineries?

Yes, but the drink-driving limit applies to every driver. It is 0.05 for a full licence in every state, and zero for learner, provisional and some other drivers, so name a designated driver or use a tour or taxi for tastings.
Can I camp at a winery in Australia?

Only where the winery offers it. Camping on private land needs the owner's permission, and some vineyards and farms offer stays through private-land booking sites. Do not assume a cellar door car park is open to overnight stays.
When is the best time for a wine region road trip?
Autumn is vintage season in most regions, roughly February to April, and it is busy. Spring and early summer are milder, and winter is quiet with log fires and lower prices in the cooler regions.
Which wine regions are close to a capital city?
McLaren Vale and the Barossa from Adelaide, the Yarra Valley and Mornington Peninsula from Melbourne, the Hunter Valley from Sydney and Margaret River from Perth all work as weekend trips.

wildlife-encounters-campervan-australia.title: Wildlife Encounters From a Campervan in Australia: Where to See Animals and How to Behave
wildlife-encounters-campervan-australia.description: Where to see kangaroos, koalas, wombats and whales from a campsite in Australia, the best times of day, and the rules for keeping animals and yourself safe.
wildlife-encounters-campervan-australia.imageAlt: A wild wombat grazing at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria
wildlife-encounters-campervan-australia.intro: Camping is the easiest way to see Australian wildlife: kangaroos graze at the edge of the camp at dawn, wombats wander past at dusk and whales pass offshore in winter. Seeing them well depends on knowing when and where to look, and on a few rules that protect both the animals and you. Below are places that suit a campervan, the best times of day, and how to behave when an animal walks into your camp.

sections.heading: When wildlife is out
body: Most Australian animals are most active around dawn and dusk and at night, which is when kangaroos, wombats and other animals are on the move. An early start and a quiet evening at camp will show you more than a midday drive.

The same hours are the most dangerous on the road. Aim to be at camp before sunset and start after it is properly light, and read our guide to what to do if you hit a kangaroo before you drive in the bush.
tips: Drive carefully near sunrise and sunset

sections.heading: Places that work from a campervan
body: These camps and coasts suit a van and are known for the animals around them.

Cape Le Grand National Park in Western Australia has kangaroos that graze on Lucky Bay beach. Wilsons Promontory National Park in Victoria has wombats that wander around the Tidal River campground. Along the Great Ocean Road, the road through the manna gums at Cape Otway is a reliable place to see wild koalas, though numbers change with the health of the trees.

sections.heading: Whales from the coast
body: Whales pass the east and west coasts on migration in winter and spring, and a campsite with a headland view lets you watch from your camp chair. Logans Beach at Warrnambool in Victoria is a known whale nursery between May and October, and our winter guide lists more regions.
Watch from land, or book an operator that follows the rules for approaching whales. Do not chase them in a private boat.

sections.heading: How to behave around wildlife
body: Keep your distance and watch quietly, without cornering, touching or feeding any animal. Feeding wildlife is banned in national parks, and human food makes animals sick and bold, which leads to them being moved or destroyed.

Store food, rubbish and cooking gear inside the vehicle or in a secured bin, and keep pets on a lead where dogs are allowed. At night, use a red torch to look around the camp, which disturbs animals less than white light.
tips: Use a red torch at night

sections.heading: Staying safe
body: Most wildlife wants to avoid you, but kangaroos can kick and scratch if cornered, snakes are common in warm months and many animals carry ticks. Watch where you put your hands and feet, wear closed shoes at night and check yourself and your pets for ticks after bushwalks.
In the tropical north, crocodiles live in rivers, estuaries and the sea, and signs mean it. Read our guide to safe swimming in Queensland before you get in the water.

tips: Check park pages for wildlife advice

faq: Where can I see kangaroos from a campsite in Australia?
Many campgrounds have kangaroos at dawn and dusk, including Cape Le Grand National Park in Western Australia, where they visit Lucky Bay beach. Stay at a distance and keep your food secured.
Can I feed wild animals at a campground?
No. Feeding wildlife is banned in national parks and harms the animals, and it draws them to camps and roads. Keep food and rubbish in the vehicle or a secured bin.
Where can I see koalas and wombats?

Koalas are seen in the manna gums along the Cape Otway road on the Great Ocean Road, and wombats are common at campgrounds such as Tidal River in Wilsons Promontory National Park and in Tasmania. Watch from a distance and never approach.
When can I see whales from the coast?
Whales migrate along the east and west coasts in winter and spring, with sightings from May to November. Our winter camping guide lists the regions, and a campsite with a clifftop view makes it easy.

river-crossing-floodway-safety-australia.title: River, Creek and Floodway Crossings in Australia: When to Cross and When Not To
river-crossing-floodway-safety-australia.description: How to judge a creek, causeway or floodway crossing in Australia: depth markers, current, crocodiles, hire contract limits, and when to wait or turn back.
river-crossing-floodway-safety-australia.imageAlt: A rock ford across the Avon River at West Toodyay, Western Australia
river-crossing-floodway-safety-australia.intro: Many Australian roads cross creeks and rivers at low-level causeways and floodways, with no bridge, and in the wet season a crossing that was dry in the morning can be under a metre of fast water by the afternoon.. The rules are simple: if it is flooded, forget it, and wait or turn around. Below: how to read a crossing, what a hire contract allows and what to do when the water is too high.

sections.heading: If it's flooded, forget it
body: Queensland's Get Ready campaign says it can take as little as 15 cm of water for a car to lose traction and be swept away, that modern cars are light and buoyant, and that the pressure of floodwater can stop you opening the doors and windows. The wading depth in a vehicle manual is for still water, not a current.

You also cannot see whether the road under the water is still there. Flooding can scour away the surface, and debris in the water can hit the vehicle. A crossing that looks easy may have a hole in the middle.
tips: 15 cm can sweep a car away
Wading depth is for still water

sections.heading: Read the crossing
body: Look for depth markers on floodways in the north, and for the road condition signs at the junction before it. If the water is above the marker, or you cannot see the markers, do not enter. Check road reports for closures before you set off, because a road can be closed by flooding upstream of the crossing.

Look at the water itself: speed, colour, debris, and whether it is rising. Muddy, moving water that carries branches is a warning. Check the far bank for an easy exit, because a crossing is only safe if you can get out the other side.
tips: Check the exit on the far bank

head: Check

rows: Water is below the marker and the markers are visible

sections.heading: Crocodiles and the north
body: Saltwater crocodiles live in rivers, estuaries and the sea across the tropical north, and floodwater and river edges can carry them. Never walk a crossing or wade in northern water where there are crocodile warning signs.
That means that in the north the advice to walk a crossing first does not apply, and the safe choice is to wait for the water to drop or turn around.

sections.heading: Hire contracts and insurance
body: Most hire contracts ban river crossings and driving through floodwater, and insurance rarely covers water damage to the engine. A 2WD campervan is also barred from unsealed roads, so a causeway on a dirt track is out of bounds before the water is a question.

If you are in a 4WD hire vehicle, read the terms for that vehicle rather than assuming they match a 2WD van. Driving through water the contract forbids can leave you liable for the full cost of damage and recovery.
tips: A 2WD van stays on sealed roads

sections.heading: If you are caught by the water
body: If the water rises while you are camped or stopped, move to higher ground early. Never camp in a dry creek bed or on a low river flat, because rain falling far upstream can fill them overnight. Treat a closed road as a rest day.

If a vehicle is swept off a crossing, get out through a window or door as soon as it is safe, climb onto the roof if you cannot reach the bank and call triple zero. A satellite messenger or beacon helps when there is no signal.
tips: Carry a way to call for help

body: AussieCamps lists campgrounds, national parks and rest areas with the access notes the park agencies publish, plus holiday parks and motels from BookEasy that you can book in the app, so a roof on higher ground is a few taps away. It does not show live road closures, so check the road authority's report.
It runs on iPhone and is free to download, with in-app purchases.

faq: How deep a creek can I drive through?

Less than you think. Queensland's Get Ready campaign says it can take as little as 15 cm of moving water for a car to lose traction and be swept away. The wading depth in a vehicle manual is for still water, not a current.
What does a floodway depth marker mean?

Low-level crossings in the north carry depth markers, and you should not enter if the water is above the marker or you cannot see the markers. A road can be open in the morning and under water by afternoon.
Does hire insurance cover water crossings?
Rarely. Most hire contracts ban river crossings and driving through floodwater, and water damage to the engine is usually not covered. Read the terms before you cross.
Is it safe to walk a crossing first?
Only where it is safe: not in a current you cannot stand in, not where there is a crocodile risk and not in a flood. If you cannot see the bottom or the far side, do not cross.

sections.heading: Data: community listings or official sources
body: WikiCamps' website lists more than 65,000 sites, most of them added and updated by its users, alongside their reviews and photos. That breadth catches informal spots and gives you recent first-hand comments, but entries can age and quality depends on who last visited.

AussieCamps starts from what land managers and road authorities publish: 18,687 places, including 1,838 campgrounds, 745 national parks, 5,552 rest areas, 1,393 dump points and 3,004 drinking water points. You get the agency's fees, rules and facilities, but not every informal spot a community would know about, and no reviews.

Ownership differs as well. G'day Group, which runs Discovery Parks and G'day Parks, bought WikiCamps in 2022, and park bookings and G'day prices have arrived in the app with recent updates. AussieCamps is independent and lists free camps, rest areas and national parks next to paid parks.

sections.heading: Filters
body: Several recent WikiCamps reviewers say filters they used went away with the rebuild, such as one for 4WD-only access (12 October 2026) and options for dogs (11 July 2026). WikiCamps still has filters; the complaint is that familiar ones changed.

AussieCamps filters use the names you would search for. Cost has Free and Paid. Features include Toilets, Flush Toilets, Drinking Water, Showers, Caravan Sites, Camper Trailer Sites, Tent Sites, Unpowered Sites, Boat Ramp, Heavy Vehicle Area, Sealed Surface, Campfires Allowed, Accessible Toilet, Dogs Allowed and No Dogs, plus online booking, minimum rating and state. Pick several features and a place has to have all of them. There is no 4WD filter; each place shows the vehicle access its agency publishes.

sections.heading: Planning a trip
body: WikiCamps has a trip planner with stops, and it has added bookings for parks inside the app. Some long-time users find the new planner slower to edit than the old one, and its Offline Mode keeps up to three planned trips.

In AussieCamps a trip is ordered stops you drag into driving order, with the distance and drive time of each leg, an arrival date and notes on every stop, the forecast for the stops ahead, a packing list, and an optional sync to your calendar. While you travel you tick stops off and see places worth a stop nearby. It has no home or start point and no fuel costing inside the app.
tips: AussieCamps: legs, dates, weather, packing list
No start point or fuel costing yet

sections.heading: Without signal
body: WikiCamps says its Offline Mode lets you use maps and up to three of your planned trips without phone signal. Offline start-up was a common complaint through 2025 and improved with updates in late 2025 and early 2026.

AussieCamps keeps every place's details on the phone from the moment it is installed, so names, fees, facilities and conditions open in a dead zone with no download step. Its map tiles, routing, weather and photos do need a connection, so it is not an offline map; download an area in Apple Maps or Google Maps if you need one.

sections.heading: Sharing and sync
body: Since October 2026, a shared WikiCamps trip link opens in the WikiCamps app, and your data follows your account to other devices. AussieCamps sends a trip as a readable itinerary of stops, dates, distances and weather through Messages, WhatsApp or email, and sends single places as links that open in Maps. Your own iPhones stay in step through iCloud.
Neither should be oversold. AussieCamps has no shared trip that two people edit together, and WikiCamps sync depends on staying signed in.
tips: WikiCamps: trip links in the app
AussieCamps: text itinerary and Maps links

sections.heading: Who should pick which
body: Pick WikiCamps if you use Android or an iPad as your main device, if recent reviews from other campers decide where you stop, or if you want the largest catalogue for one payment.

Pick AussieCamps if you want a camping app with no login and no ads on your iPhone, if you trust what the park agency publishes over user listings, or if you plan your trip as dated stops with the distance and weather for each leg.

If you are unsure, AussieCamps is free to download, so you can try it on your next trip next to whatever you use now. And if you are still weighing whether WikiCamps is worth keeping at all, our look at its recent reviews sets out the evidence.
tips: AussieCamps: no login, no ads, official data

faq: Is AussieCamps better than WikiCamps?
For iPhone users who want no login, no ads and places from official sources, it can be. WikiCamps is the better fit if you need Android, traveller reviews or the largest catalogue.
Does AussieCamps need an account?
No. There is no login of any kind. Saved places, collections and trips sync through your private iCloud between your own iPhones.
Does AussieCamps work offline?
Partly. Every place's details, fees and facilities are already on the phone, with no download step. The map, directions, weather and photos need signal.
Is AussieCamps on Android?
No. AussieCamps runs on iPhone only. On Android, WikiCamps is still a strong choice.
Can I move my WikiCamps trips to AussieCamps?
Not automatically, as there is no import. Search each stop by name, add it to a new AussieCamps trip and drag the stops into driving order.

wikicamps-for-pc.title: WikiCamps for PC in 2026: What Happened to the Windows App
wikicamps-for-pc.description: WikiCamps no longer runs on Windows or Mac. What changed in 2025, and how to research on a laptop with our website, then build the trip in AussieCamps on iPhone.
wikicamps-for-pc.imageAlt: Stuart Highway while travelling towards Uluṟu
wikicamps-for-pc.intro: WikiCamps for PC is gone. Official Windows support ended in August 2024, and the Windows app stopped working when version 5 was discontinued in June 2025; version 6 runs only on iOS and Android, and there is no Mac version either. We make AussieCamps, and it is a phone app too, for iPhone, so we will not pretend it replaces a desktop program. What it does offer laptop planners is a website for the research and an app with no login for the trip itself.

sections.heading: What happened to WikiCamps on Windows
body: The Windows app faded out in stages. WikiCamps says official Windows support ended in August 2024, and travellers noticed WikiCamps Australia missing from the Microsoft Store by late September that year, just as the rebuilt version 6 arrived on phones.

The final step came in June 2025. Replying to a customer on Microsoft's Q&A forum, WikiCamps wrote that "WikiCamps version 6 is only available for iOS and Android devices" and that discontinuing version 5 meant the Windows app "will not be operational". People who had bought it for Windows were offered free access on Android or iOS instead.

sections.heading: Why laptop planners miss it
body: A big screen suits the slow part of trip planning: comparing campgrounds along a stretch of highway, reading rules and fees side by side, and working out how far each day's drive should be. "Since they removed the PC capability it has become very awkward to plan a trip", one App Store reviewer wrote on 28 July 2026, and ProductReview.com.au carries complaints from people who paid for a PC version that no longer works.

Only a handful of the 150 most recent App Store reviews raise it, because most reviewers are phone users by definition. Search tells a different story: questions about WikiCamps on a laptop, on Windows and on a Mac are among the most common things Australians type about the app.
tips: Laptop questions are common in search

sections.heading: Is there a camping app for PC or Mac?
body: Honestly, few Australian camping apps are built for the desktop now; most are written for the phone you carry on the road. AussieCamps is one of those. It runs on iPhone, with no Windows, Mac, iPad or Android version, and we would rather say so here than have you find out after a download.

The useful split is to do the reading on a computer and keep the plan on your phone. That is how the AussieCamps website and app are meant to work together, and the next two sections show how. For everything else that separates the two apps, our WikiCamps vs AussieCamps comparison goes row by row.
tips: Research on a laptop, travel with the phone

sections.heading: Plan on a laptop with aussiecamps.app
body: The website works in any browser on Windows or Mac and needs no account. Each state has a camping page that sums up its campgrounds, rest areas and dump points and links to the parks with their own page, and individual place pages show a site's facilities and fees. There are separate pages for rest areas and dump points, which are what a long driving day hangs on.

Under Tools you will find a driving time calculator that works out how long a day really takes from the distance, the type of road and your stops, and a fuel calculator that prices the route from its distance, your vehicle's loaded fuel use and the price per litre. Our road trip guides cover the major routes, such as the Nullarbor crossing or Perth to Broome, with suggested overnight stops.
Write down the places you like as you go, by name and nearest town, so you can search for them in the app later.
tips: State camping pages and place pages
Rest area and dump point pages
Drive time and fuel cost calculators

sections.heading: Then build the trip on your iPhone
body: Open AussieCamps and you are on the map, with no login, no email code and nothing to sign into first. Search each place from your list, tap it to check its details, and add it to a new trip. Drag the stops into the order you will drive, and the app shows the distance and drive time for every leg.

Give each stop an arrival date and a note, such as a booking reference or the gate code, and add a packing list to the trip. Filters help fill gaps the laptop missed: Free under Cost for free campgrounds and rest areas, or features such as Drinking Water, Caravan Sites and Dogs Allowed, all of which a place must have at once.

The app is free to download, with in-app purchases, and shows no ads. Place details stay readable without signal; the map, directions and weather need a connection. Your trips sync through your private iCloud to any other iPhone on the same Apple Account.
tips: Opens on the map, no login
Stops in driving order with each leg

sections.heading: Keep the plan in view on a bigger screen
body: Two features help once the trip leaves the laptop. Turn on calendar sync for a trip with start and end dates, and AussieCamps writes the route, arrival dates, distances and packing list into a calendar on your phone, where you can check the days ahead at a glance.

To read the whole plan on a computer, use Share trip and email it to yourself. The message lists every stop in order with arrival times, distances and weather, followed by the packing list, so it prints or reads easily on any screen.

faq: Is WikiCamps available for PC?
No. As of November 2026, WikiCamps runs on iOS and Android only. Its Windows app stopped working in June 2025, when version 5 was discontinued.
Can I use WikiCamps on a laptop?
Not as an app. Version 6 has no Windows or Mac version, so WikiCamps planning now happens on a phone or tablet.
Is there a WikiCamps Mac app?
No. WikiCamps has no Mac app, and the company says version 6 is only available for iOS and Android devices.
What happened to WikiCamps for Windows?

Official Windows support ended in August 2024, and the app later left the Microsoft Store. When version 5 was switched off in June 2025, the Windows app stopped working, and Windows buyers were offered free access on Android or iOS.
Is there a camping trip planner I can use on a computer?

The aussiecamps.app website works in any browser: state camping pages, place pages, rest area and dump point pages, guides, and drive time and fuel cost calculators. The trip itself is then built in the AussieCamps iPhone app.
